Bought this on impulse purchase. Saw it on front page, liked what I saw in the trailer, bought.
Good god. This is too addicting! The auto aim may sound like a dumb thing, making the game too easy and lacking challenge, but that's far from the truth. THe speed and freneticism of the platforming, acrobatics, and varied enemies makes an adrenaline pumping reactionary experience.
And if you're not into the story experience, there are challenge modes to add an extra level of endless entertainment.
UPDATE: ONE major gripe is the "permadeath". Based on some other reviews, and the dev's response, there SHOULDN'T be perma death is you've found at least one checkpoint. The thing is, I have found checkpoints, almost one per level even. Yet I just recently died (true death, not just one death and respawn at the beginning of current level), and while I still have upgrades, the story progress has been totally reset for me.
My guess is this was not intended by the developers. I imagine it may be a glitch with how the game handles your Oaths and Transmutation upgrades both in the main story mode, and Challenge modes. I had actually died the day before as well, but at no consequence. Yet today, shortly after doign some challenge runs, I died in Story Mode, and found my progress reset. It seems like going into Challenge Mode reset my Checkpoint progress from Story mode.
Hopefully this gets fixed soon.
UPDATE: The fix is in! No longer is there a glitch where entering challenges erases your main campaign story progress!
On the flipside, the reward system for the Challenges needs serious reworking. Since it gives you rewards increasing in value based on your position on the leaderboard (75th percentile, 50th percentile, etc) even after busting my butt to get to the top 10, because there are so few players participating in the challenges, I'm still only within the top 75%! So either there needs to be a separate reward tier for the top 10, or some other revamping cuz it's plenty annoying to get as high as 11th place in the survival challenge, but get relatively meager rewards.

Seraph is everything that the description here says it is.  There's nothing misleading at all, and exactly what I paid for.  Matter of fact, i'm glad that I paid for it!  I'm just an hour into the game, but have put together a
for anyone who's interested in seeing the gameplay.
That being said, I am not a huge platform gamer.  This is way outside of my comfort zone, and not something that I'd normally pay any attention to at all.  For some reason, I decided to pick this one up the day it came out of Early Access, and fell straight in!  The excitement comes and goes in bursts, and is likely to have shaved a couple years of life off of me due to the spikes in heart rate.
The storyline revolves around Seraph, our protagonist, as she escapes her prison, fights off Daemons, and attempts to ascend back to her natural form - but she's currently in her human vessel, Thalia.
One major piece of appeal to me is the dynamic difficulty setting.  If you're doing well, or poorly, expect multipliers to be added to the creatures you're fighting.  I love it conceptually, but have a feeling it can spiral out of control quickly or at higher difficulties - but, i'm only playing it on Standard for now!
Only time will tell if Seraph has much replay value, but if you're going to be Twitch streaming, be sure to check out the Options menu.  I don't stream often, but there's a feature i've never seen before.  It boasts of allowing viewers to vote on giving the player a bonus or penalty between levels!
The description to this game is spot on and you're getting exactly what you pay for.  Great work, Dreadbit Games!

As a long time fan of the Devil May Cry series, I was fully prepared to hate this reimagining of it.  What I wasn't prepared for was actually enjoying the hell out of it.  The only area I feel this game is inferior to the rest of the series is in music.  The music isn't awful, but it's nothing I'd listen to on it's own.
The rest is excellent.  The reimagining smoothing explains away many of the weird setting quirks the games have had, and actually made you feel like this was happening somewhere real, as opposed to a gothic backdrop for killing monsters.  Also, many of the reimagined changes could be applied to the rest of the series without too much effort, if you want this game to be canon with the rest of the series. The motion capture is absolutely incredible, I could read so much from the expressions of some of the characters.  The voice acting is superb - oh man, have I missed the Devil May Cry trash talk.
The combat has been streamlined - with the removal of a lock-on button, there is now room on the controller to be able to switch weapons mid-fight without going into a menu.  The lack of the lock-on button only gave me problems twice, otherwise the game correctly predicted which enemies I was interested in attacking.  The bosses are varied and imaginative, ending with a tight, responsive final fight that tests everything you have learned in a satisfying manner.

This was actually not a bad game. It was great. If you're a fan of hack and slashers, cheesy one liners (which have always been in the DMC series), and over the top action then there's no reason not to play this. I think most everyone's problem is just that they changed Dante too much. Sure, there's the costume DLC that makes Dante look more like the original design from Devil May Cry 3, but it isn't really that great. (The clothing proportions are a little off. Yes I bought it. The nostalgia was too much to pass up on. The other outfits are alright.). But that's just it, most people complain about his look, but not enough about the combat. Now I will admit, the combat is easier than the previous titles in the series, but that doesn't mean you won't die. There's always going to be a moment where you slip up, or an enemy catches you off guard with a maneuver you may have forgotten about or you didn't have time to react fast enough to. The game's core concept is still there; Dante must die, you don't want Dante to die, everything else needs to die, "slice slice slice". The story itself is a revamp of its original, but it IS different, don't expect it to be the same. The ending somewhat catches you off guard. I won't spoil it, but you might think it's going to happen, then you don't, then you do again, but then... you get the idea. I mean if you played the first you probably already have an idea. I haven't touched the Vergil's Downfall DLC yet so I don't have anything to say about it. Overall, DmC: Devil May Cry is a great game, but not a great Devil May Cry game.

OK, Note to the developes: You get a 10/10 for graphic accuracy as playing as a female and the top down view would appear as if I am actually the character, also the character has personality. Anxiously moving around and breathing as an actual human would TOP NOTCH! But there are some other notes I would like to include that might be suggestions to the future of the game its self. First, You may want to check with the quality settings, as when you put the setting on Fantastic it causes your camera to spin wildly in one direction staring straight up at the ceiling once I brought down the quality settings it recovered. Second, There is an issue when multiple screens are in use where the mouse unhooks from the game and moves to the other monitor, which allows you to click out of the game which minimizes instantly (Quite the headache starter). Third, While you have done a decent job at making the mechanics fairly easy to learn it isn't immediately obvious from the start. A short tutorial would be a great addition. Lastly, it isn't that important but perhaps you could change the music, smooth jazz just doesn't fit with the game! I see great things for this type of game but it is a little rough around the edges at the time. Overall rating 6/10

Passing Pineview Forest... Why does this even exist?
Just a little note: I haven't played Pineview Drive yet. Since this is the prequel, I figured I'd start with it.
Okay, let's get the good out of the way - the audio and music is pretty damn good. The rustling of leaves, the owl's hooting, it's all great. The music, even though it's commonly used as a form of jump scare, is quite foreboding and was probably the biggest cause of chills in the game.
Visually? As far as I could tell, it looked fine. PPF is an incredibly dark game, so seeing the little details is really a challenge.
So I've talked about all the good things in PPF, so what about the bad? The gameplay consists of the player walking down a linear path through Pineview Forest, occasionally walking pass statues and houses, some of which are even explorable. The path forks a few times throughout the game, but choosing to go either left or right really doesn't matter, as the two paths always end up meeting further ahead. I feel this prequel would have been vastly better had there been more paths, or if the current path had been anything other than a straight line.
The "horror" aspect of the game is really weak. While walking down the previously mentioned path, you'll sometimes hear footsteps or bushes being shaken. This would be 'It' following you; the more the bushes shake the closer it is. To keep 'It' from killing you, restarting your progress, you have to move quietly. This means that running is not a viable option, and neither is using your flashlight. The game forces you to walk the majority of the path. But don't you worry, you'll never actually see 'It', as invisible walls block the player so they can't walk into the woods to look for it.

So, if you're wondering "Is that all you do? Walk slowly down a path?" then answer would be "Yes". You walk down a dark path for 20 minutes, stopping to explore empty houses and to keep 'It' from finding you. Oh, and you will be encountering jump scares every few minutes. Great.
Hopefully Pineview Drive is of a higher quality. I mean, it should be; it costs $19.99 while this is at least free.

As a young studio best known for porting Batman: Arkham City to Wii U, WB Montreal must have been desperate to prove that it belongs in the same conversation as series creator Rocksteady Games. To its credit, it's hard to tell that Batman: Arkham Origins isn't one of its sister studio's earlier releases. That's some achievement, but it's also a mixed blessing.
To begin with, the set-up is as economical as Arkham Asylum or Arkham City. Batman is thrust into Gotham on Christmas Eve after Black Mask puts a $50 million bounty on his head and invites eight super-villains to town to compete for the spoils. As with previous Arkham games, that simple set-up then evolves as Batman races to keep up with events.
Arkham Origins doesn't leave the strongest first impression though. After a CG cutscene and a short playable prologue in Blackgate Prison, Batman is dumped into a sparsely occupied Gotham that looks tiny on his Batcomputer map compared to some of the open-world playgrounds we've run around in lately. You're free to travel across it all from the start, but players used to maps dripping with icons may be surprised at its cold emptiness.
This isn't a game that lacks depth, though - it's just a game with rare patience. Story missions take place away from the streets in carefully knotted set-piece levels built around single locations - like Penguin's hidden casino♥♥♥♥♥arms-bazaar or Gotham City Police headquarters - and as you make progress the open world gradually fills up with distractions.
The initial slow burn is welcome, anyway, because it's an opportunity to luxuriate in the wonderful systems and mechanics that Arkham Origins inherits from its forebears. Batman glides through levels even when he's just walking around, those famous bat ears erect with authority, and he moves fluidly in a crouched run, too, barrel-like thighs pumping him from shadow to vent. But when you start actually gliding, it's a minor revelation, opening his wings to the wind and using the grapple to grasp the edge of a distant chimney, reeling it in and launching him over the crest to continue his flight.
Watch me play through the first level of Arkham Origins and provide an overview of some of the systems.
We had all this before, of course, but you forget how good it was. The same goes for Batman's many gadgets. You start off with quite a few - batarangs, smoke pellets and explosive gel for blowing holes in walls - and of course you have detective vision, the sonar view mode that maps Batman's surroundings so he can track enemies as they move nervously through the darkness around him. You gain other toys at intervals, including the remote batclaw for setting up tightropes between particular grapple points.
Batman remains handy in a fight, too. In hand-to-hand combat, a single attack button allows him to flow between targets, ducking and diving through dense matrices of incoming blows, repelling those that threaten to land by reaching for the counter button. It's still quick to build combos, and the final blow, which the game always puts into slow motion and frames up nicely, often has a satisfying crack to it.
The one thing Batman still lacks is a gun or grenade to deal with unsuspecting groups of enemies from afar - he can either wade in with his fists and gizmos or try to isolate and pick them off using stealth - but of course that's the point of the character. There is still a slight frustration though that the game often forces you into direct confrontation rather than letting you choose your own approach, especially as tougher enemies arrive with riot shields, knives and body armour to inject complexity into each fight.
Still, that is what Arkham Asylum and Arkham City did, so at least it's canon. As is the way the city starts to fill up with intriguing diversions. The Riddler is back, of course, custodian of unlockable fast-travel points that can only be activated when you break into them. This often involves hopping around adjacent buildings examining the exterior of your prize, like a high-tech octopus feeling around the outside of a bottle to reach the fish inside. Enigma has left his mark in other areas of Gotham, too, and you'll be on his various trails all night.
He is probably the highlight of the side missions - again, as usual - although he's far from alone in the dark night. Anarky is fed up with Gotham's corrupt rulers and plans to deal with them somewhat more explosively than Batman, so that's a thing, and there are various other threads to follow once secondary characters - friends and foes - present themselves.
2
Manoeuvring around enemies to set up stealth takedowns is still fun, although you can autopilot a lot of it with two games' experience under your utility belt.
So it's fun crawling over Gotham. It can still feel slightly empty at times - you'll never see a pedestrian who isn't a cheesy thug or a trigger-happy SWAT team member - but among the dark rooftops, smokestacks, red brick facades and Ace Chemicals billboards there emerges plenty to do, and I am loath to scold a game for rebelling against the fad of instant gratification. Besides, some of it is there from the start should you be paying attention. There are a host of character-building challenges to complete, for example, by doing things like performing certain combinations in combat or gliding through rings dotted around the city. These tasks are just sitting there quietly listed in one of the pause menus.
The one area where Arkham Origins truly distinguishes itself from Rocksteady's work, of course, is the part of the game that UK studio Splash Damage developed: multiplayer.
In Arkham Origins' online mode, three of Bane's mercenaries face off against three of Joker's gang across four maps, fighting over capture points and trying to kill the opposition until they no longer have any Battlefield-style respawn tickets left and can be wiped out.
As well as limited-use knockoff versions of Batman's see-through-walls detective vision, and loadouts that can be customised with unlockable weapons and abilities such as an explosive RC blimp, each team can also call on their master when they hit a certain threshold. Bane has powerful melee attacks, while Joker has a pair of pistols good for one-shot kills and spamming explosives.
The biggest twist, though, is that two other players control a third team of heroes. Yes! Someone gets to play as Batman! (And Robin.) The heroes have a suite of predatory tools including grapple hooks and various batarangs and can stalk their prey from underground passages as well. They are rewarded for performing a variety of takedowns.
Despite the competing objectives, matches are simple to understand and often draw to a nervous conclusion, as Bane and Joker's teams run out of respawn tickets and try to pick each other off while the heroes circle. If a player takes out a hero at this stage, their downed team-mates retake the field, while heroes who die in this endgame lose much of their score.
Things can yo-yo very quickly, and while this can mean that the preceding drama feels as though it's more for show than anything, it's tense and exciting every time, and really does result in gang members waving their guns around at the shadows in terror, just as it should.
It's a fair amount of fun, then, but it's also the kind of mode you will enjoy for an evening rather than a lifetime. Taken on those terms, it's a welcome inclusion.
They also feed into Batman's tech tree, although this is one of the weaker areas of Arkham Origins. Batman is already well outfitted and his most useful additions - like the shock gloves, which allow him to power up electrical items and rain fizzly blows down in combat - are rewarded for making progress in the story, so I generally just invested my XP in tougher armour, which is a bit boring. Tech trees where you find yourself rooting around for the least uninspiring upgrade are always disappointing,

TLDR:
This game is a return to form for the franchise. The form, being the type of game Blood Money was. Large,
detailed open levels, several approaches to taking down your targets, good stealth mechanics, decent enemy AI and a well-balanced disguise system, that is neither OP like in Blood Money, nor annoying and nearly useless like in Absolution, all contribute to a very satisfying experience once you complete a mission. One major criticism is the practically non-existent story, the weakest of any Hitman games to date, and not even comparable to Absolution, which had more story focus than all prior Hitman games. Annoying limited time "elusive targets", with their own story, voice acting, etc. also detract from the overall value. Absence of quicksave hotkey is a minor, but frustrating omission.
By the way: you are absolutely not gonna need 100 hours to beat the game. I think that amount of time is what's required to master all the levels to a point when you know every corner and all the AI partrol timings. You need to really love to sit around different spots on the same map to do that.
Hitman 6 is a game I am in two minds about. While it is a great game, no doubt, I will say right away: I do prefer Absolution. For several key reasons (and I know I am in the minority here). But let's talk about positives first:
- Excellent stealth mechanics. Fair detection, body disposal, fair and well-balanced lethal/non-lethal takedowns that also make sense.
- Fantastic, big, detailed, beautiful and well-optimized levels. Lots of things to explore, conversations to listen, disguises to obtain and kill opportunities to discover and perform.
- Classy black humour with a light sinister touch.
- Manual saving at any point, albiet without a quicksave button.
- Adequate AI, although huge penalties (both in score and in time you have to spend waiting for them to calm down) for being detected or even making someone suspicious prevent from ever engaging or provoking it to do something unscripted.

Now here are some things I did not quite like:
The levels in Hitman 6 are huge and sprawling with interactive details. But after spending a few hours going through different assassination opportunities, you will notice that most of the stuff is actually useless from gameplay perspective. For example there are a ton of objects you can find and pick up, though they have no meaning in the context of their placement.
Another example: you can rig cord extenders to kill those who step on them, but only 1 or 2 of those are actually placed where your target will walk. There are conditions on which the target follows you, but why would make them walk over an exposed wire, if there's a very entertaining murder possibility specifically attached to those conditions?
All of the above made me realize, that while there are indeed several ways to accomplish the objective, the game lead me on to believe that there were more possibilities than there actually were.
Emergent gameplay in Hitman 6 is not absent, but rather limited: this is no Watch Dogs 2. And there lies another issue: your objective is
to eliminate targets and get out. There are only 2 missions where you need to do something else, and only one of those has you do something interesting for it. This means that most of your actions are a intermediate steps to achieving a single goal in  certain way, instead of having clearly defined preliminary objectives, with a level for each, leading up to the ultimate goal, that being elimination of a high value target, which is the path that Absolution took.
As a result playing Hitman 6 was quite... tiring. First confusion sets in at the seemingly insane amount of possibilities when you get dropped into a level. Then disappointment occurs when you realise that most of those objects you can interact with are irrelevant to your objectives. After that frustration sets in when you can't find the item that is relevant (such as rat poison, or something like that), in an area where it actually is needed. In the end I ended up turning on the "opportunities" options and completing those scenarios.
Then another problem with this game is how badly delivered the storyline is. You get a few voice overs and a handful of pre-rendered short films that deliver a vaigue plot, which ends in a cliffhanger (ofc, we gotta break those up into episodes for maximum revenue. Melitele's♥♥♥♥♥♥ episodic release model is just cancer!). The story was such an afterthought that you can even watch those films without completing the levels that are supposed to lead up to them. There is no mention of fairly significant events that happened in Absolution, which must have had a rather significant impact on the main 2 characters, since it's the only Hitman game that wasn't just about killing all the bad guys and learning some secrets.
There's also absolutely no context for ANY of the targets, beyong the mission briefing. One thing I really liked about previous Hitman games, and especially Absolution is how it made you really hate those targets. The story was delivered very well, with fantastic voice acting, cutscenes and in-gameplay dialogues, to really show how disgusting those people are, making those kills all the more satisfying. Hitman 6 doesn't do any of that, as your targets, except for the last one, are simply dossie's on a UI screen, all the context to them being given as in-game dialogue.
And of course since the story is basically non-existent, it's not reflected in the level design. There are no sections, where you feel like you are closer to the end, there are no changing art or layout styles. There are just huge hubs, with a single objective, that requires a lot of micro-steps to reach.
So yeah, I do think that I would have preferred a game that was separated into smaller more focused, but still open levels, each with a smaller objective that was relevant to the story, and the levels really being fully relevant to my goal, rather than having gigantic levels with a single objective for each, and a labyrinth of areas, items and objects to frustratingly navigate between, figuring out whether they have any relevance to my goals.
I do realize that these maps were designed for more than just "official" target, and that a lot of those objects could be used in player created contracts, however in my opinion that part of the game could have been sacrifised for more focus on the storyline.
Then of course you can read in all other reviews about the disgusting pre-order bonuses and the horrible release model, and the limited elusive targets and of course the damn always online DRM, that plaigues this game.
Nevertheless, I'd be a fool to claim this is a bad game. While I personally enjoyed Absolution more, Hitman 6 is a very competent sandbox stealth game, which many are sure to like. A recommendation for certain, although I hope the next game will not be episodic and give the storyline a lot more attention. I like my single player games to have one.

TLDR: Buy it.
I had no idea this game existed until I saw it released from early access today, and picked it up on a whim and have been very pleasantly surprised.  It's a very slick action oriented platformer that's a ton of fun to play.  If you have any interest in difficult platformers, pick this up, it's an absolute steal.
Positives:
Adaptive difficulty - I *love* this feature, if I'm playing well I get better rewards and things ramp up.
Refined movement - Double jump and and a dash with invicibility frames really lets you flit around and dodge like a madman, when you're in the zone it's a ton of fun.
No aiming - As weird as it sounds, I actually like the fact you don't have to aim, it makes concentrating 100% on movement possible.
Daily/Weekly challenges - There are challenges which reward high level upgrade items in game if you do well in the rankings, which keeps things interesting and provides incentives to keep improving.
Enemy/Item compendium - The pics/info on the enemies is really cool and helps provide some background to the story.
Negatives:
Backgrounds can be tough to differentiate - At times it's hard to tell if something is the ceiling or an opening you can jump through.
Unexplained mechanics - A lot of the mechanics in the game are left up to you to figure out, the loading tips are useful but there's no manual or any detailed explanations for what everything in the game does.
Summary:
I love platformers and buy a ton of them, this is one of the best I've played in a long time.  Highly recommended.

I had a lot of fun playing through BloodRayne 2. I remember playing the demo in the early 2000s when at the time this was one of the most demanding games on the PC. It was nice to finally play through the game past my memories of the demo stage! Despite being a dated DX8 engine, modders have released an "HD patch" for it that lets you set custom resolutions, increasing resolutions of the textures and even installing some HD ones. Besides some minor glitches in widescreen, the game looks great when applied.
The gameplay feels very "2000s action game" when every game was abusing slow motion with fast-paced action. The vampire twist is what makes it interesting, as your health is solely dictated by drinking the blood of your foes, including all your guns which are "reloaded" the same way. The game is very violent, with decapitations, impalement, burning, etc. Story is spoon-fed to you as you go along, with a few pretty FMV sequences thrown in to highlight major plot points. The combat is fairly simplistic, though the developers tried to liven it up by adding a "combo" system depending on the sequence of buttons placed in addition to directionals. The game also heavily uses the environment as a means to the combat flow, requiring you to launch enemies into environmental hazards in what otherwise would be endless enemies to progress the game. The game also contains some basic platforming, but nothing overly challenging or frustrating.
Difficulty wise, the game is easy, especially once you learn to abuse dodge in combination with your "blood rage" which essentially gives you infinite health and damage instead drains your blood rage meter. Replay value is also low with completion of the game just unlocking new costumes for Rayne. The game is by no means amazing and even for its time would be considered a typical action game, though Rayne's character and personality, as well as the gothic and vampire lore is enough for me to give it a recommendation!

Spec Ops: The Line holds an incredibly dear place in my heart.
I've played through this game a countless number of times now. It's not because it's a particularily fun game, or that the gameplay is notably immersive, or what most people would generally consider makes a good game.
But what this game has is a story. A story like no other game has had before. A story that perfectly weaves your actions and choices as a player into the tale, and pulls you along as you watch helplessly as the consequences of your actions unfold in front of you.
It is by no means a game that offers you comeplete agency, and the story is extremely linear. However, even though many people have analyzed this as a game that is supposed to be reflective of the player, I still like to view it as a story about the character and understanding why and how he makes the choices that he does.
Play it for the story, the experience is well worth it. And if you enjoyed it as much as I did (and still do), please consider nominating this game for the open category in the Steam awards for "Most Compelling Storytelling."

If you want a game that has that 'I'll play just one more level' factor, Seraph has that in spades. Easy to learn, harder to master, its beautiful simplicity belies a wealth of tactical choices and tough upgrade decisions. Whether you have a couple of wind-down hours to spare or just fifteen minutes of time, there is always a sense of achievement and challenge to be found.
If you want to just chill out and shoot things, you can. If, like me, the storyline compels you to battle on through sector lockdowns and multiple bosses, you are rewarded with an unfolding story with intriguing characters.
Twitch mode allows viewers to make your life hell or give you a reward, if they choose. Survival mode and daily/weekly challenges add variety and friendly competition if you want to push it to the limit.

The /short/ version;
It's a 2d platform/shooter with super powers and multiple weapons, the guns aim themselves which leaves you concerned with the (especially at higher difficulties) frantic avoidance of enemy attacks to focus on.
Miracles are those super powers (as well as blink to dodge/zip out of the way of enemies), they're varied some boost your  defensive abilities, knocking enemies away or putting a line in the side they will take heavy damage if they cross, others are flat out offensive monsters, damaging everything on screen that you stay near after a few seconds, or shooting out across the screen and returning like a boomerang causing massive damage to anything in it's path.
Really cool for what's mostly been a 2 or 3 person studio for it's development! Gives me the same sort of "this is awesome" feeling I got from Isaac and Super Meat Boy although out of the popular titles it probably plays most like Rogue Legacy (just faster and more twitchy skill than puzzle solving).

Spec Ops: The Line holds an incredibly dear place in my heart.
I've played through this game a countless number of times now. It's not because it's a particularily fun game, or that the gameplay is notably immersive, or what most people would generally consider makes a good game.
But what this game has is a story. A story like no other game has had before. A story that perfectly weaves your actions and choices as a player into the tale, and pulls you along as you watch helplessly as the consequences of your actions unfold in front of you.
It is by no means a game that offers you comeplete agency, and the story is extremely linear. However, even though many people have analyzed this as a game that is supposed to be reflective of the player, I still like to view it as a story about the character and understanding why and how he makes the choices that he does.
Play it for the story, the experience is well worth it. And if you enjoyed it as much as I did (and still do), please consider nominating this game for the open category in the Steam awards for "Most Compelling Storytelling."

I purchased this through Indigala's store after reading the blurb of the game and watching the gameplay demo/trailer video they had and I would greatly reccommend this game for those who love skill based games.
Having a game where instead of your having to aim on a 2D plain which during high paced combat and for others a sheer panic-fest becomes rather difficult Seraph actively picks her own targets during combat allowing you to focus more on the important things such as movement, evading and your placement through out the various levels.
You are given one of two objectives each level being either kill the lieutenant elite Deamon (A boss in simple terms) or destroy X number of beacons (the number increases as you progress) but here is the twist during play the game will alter the difficulty depending on your skill level resulting in either more Deamons spawning, adding extra attacks to the present level of Deamons or just be completely mean and just throwing countless waves of mutated elites at you.
Either way you're going to do one of two things. The first is die, get frustrated and try again and again eventually restarting your game (Good news upgrades unlocked remain unlocked. With Daily random challange and Weekly survival challanges available offering heft sums of materials and shards for buffs these too have various rules. The Developers too are active to your pleas of bugs and work dilagently to fix any bugs you encounter (Assuming you point out where and how you found them on the bug report part of the disscusions) and the more information you supply the better they can duplicate the problem and repair it.

TL;DR
All in all, the game is a valiant effort from such a small developement team. Solid, responsive controls, grounded, yet satisfying sound design, a visual style that, while needing some more oomph regarding level design, all work together in favor of the game. The replay value is high with daily challenges, upgrades that carry over through playthroughs, and a decent selection of game modes including Surival, SpeedRun and the first-of-its-kind TwitchMode.
The game ends in a way that could open itself up to a sequel and if one is in the works. I'll gladly buy it, just as I did this one.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!
Detailed Reivew:
------------------
So here is my take on the game after having played it since the Early Access launch in April this year.
The random level layouts add great replay value, but the constant repetition of the 'rooms' and their always-squared shape blurs away the occasional changes in themes (a theme being a color palette change, ammo crates looking different and various doo-dad's changing to match). With very rare exceptions, it's hard to tell one level apart from another. And after repeated playthroughs in the game, I still cannot tell how far into the game I am, unless I am watching character dialog for the plot.
The gunplay in the game is well done with generous hitboxes and the auto-aim mechanic almost being a necessity amongst the need to constantly be blinking, wall-jumping and sprinting through the often erratic layouts.
The daily challenges (though there could be more variety in this matter), Rebirth mechanic and upgrades persisting through consecutive play-throughs all give the game a high replay value. Further the lack of gore, or blood of any kind for that matter, makes this game for all ages. Further, there is no multiplayer or competitive mode (aside from the previously mentioned Challenges and a stand-alone Speedrun mode) so you can play the game as casually or seriously as you want.
One of the stand-out features though is TwitchMode. TwitchMode is a mode where viewers of a Twitch streamer playing Seraph, can alter the game difficulty in various ways by voting for or against the player. The game issues a vote to the audience, the audience votes in the streamers chat and the game reads the chat, automatically tally's the votes and bestows the winning boost or penalty to the player/streamer accordingly. I truly wish more games had this mode, but as of yet, this is the only game I'm aware of that has such a thing.
The only drawbacks to TwitchMode is that voting only happens between levels and there needs to be a far greater range of benefits/penalties to keep the audience invested and the player on their toes.
The music in the game is atmospheric, but since there are such a limited number of tracks, it does get repetitive as you fight through the dozens of levels to reach the end of the game.
Major Boss Fights are intense and long, as they should be, but the number of Major bosses are extremely limited and the interim 'level bosses' are far too repetitive (they are just bigger versions of existing enemies) to have any meaning. This compounded with the seemingly limited number of enemies (there are about a dozen or so types) makes for a game that tends to rely on the love explosions, the visual bliss of your holy powers and the solid sound design to carry it.
The story in the game has a few twists and generally the player is kept on the fence as to whether you should be rooting for Seraph or rooting against her. While this isn't the deepest story in gaming, and it's certainly among the least visual (plot is conveyed through hidden logs and text based dialog), it does at least keep a person interested and acts as a welcome break from the thumb-numbing gameplay.
TL;DR
All in all, the game is a valiant effort from such a small developement team. Solid, responsive controls, grounded, yet satisfying sound design, a visual style that, while needing some more oomph regarding level design, all work together in favor of the game. The replay value is high with daily challenges, upgrades that carry over through playthroughs, and a decent selection of game modes including Surival, SpeedRun and the first-of-its-kind TwitchMode.
The game ends in a way that could open itself up to a sequel and if one is in the works. I'll gladly buy it, just as I did this one.
RECOMMENDED!

Wow. Just wow. I spent the first 12ish hours just getting episode 1 to level 20.
Episodes have a xp system instead of money for unlocks each episode has set unlocks for each level with the max being 20. The weapon/gear unlocks cross over to other episodes and are unique for each, i.e. in order to unlock every weapon in the game you have to master every episode. This might sound like a huge chore and in many other games it would be, but in HITMAN it is executed masterfully.
The challenges are interesting puzzles that force you to learn the layout of the level and the path your targets take and what events they trigger. Many of these events only trigger if you are within earshot so you don't miss them but a few are scripted to take place with or without you.
I am only in episode 2 but so far I have not seen a single area/room where I said to myself, "oh this is just that other room from over there mirrored" or anything like that. Every area seems unique and detailed I find myself wanting to replay episode 1 again even though I have "mastered" it already.
Also when you "master" a level you unlock "professional" difficulty which moves many of the key items, places more guards in places there were none before and many of the useable items like rat poison or crowbars are now carried by an NPC that you will have to knock out to get rather than just pick it off the table.  On these missions it seems nearly impossible to do a silent assassin challenge unless you have items from future episodes but they show signs of knowing common stratiges by placing guards in areas that are key paths on normal difficulty.
All in all I am blown away by the quality of this game and the enjoyment I am finding playing it. I was skeptical and waited for the 50% off sale and I almost regret it. Definetly worth it.

EDIT: RIght after typing my review, a patch downloaded, and I just tested it - my Core2Quad issues have been resolved, and it's playing with very good frames on that system with the 1050ti!
GREAT job Devs.
Just played this for 6+ hours straight.  After trying to launch to play on my living room setup (and failing) - I moved onto my desktop, which is a much more powerful system.
Living room:  Core2Quad Q9550, 8gb DDR3, 1050ti = crashed right after launch (sometimes before).  Tried all the fixes, nothing worked.  Hopefully they iron it out. EDIT: They did and it's awesome, but the controller/camera needs a bit of tweaking.  Overall very happy!)
Desktop: i5 4670, 24gb DDR3, R9 290 =  crashed only on the first launch.  Never again after that in six hours of playing.
Overall, this is a very fun game, even solo.  I slowly figured out how to play as I went along, eventually building a rover, then skipping the truck and shuttle for a Spaceship.  Launched and landed on several planets, all very different looking, but like NMS, samey.  There are no enemies to fight, just a few plants that spew poison clouds (but can still kill you).  There's grass to be mowed and collected for use in generators, and there are many options to provide power and oxygen.  You'll struggle at first but it's a fun struggle.
I've had a lot of fun for 6 hours, and the game is worth 20 dollars, for sure.  That said, I played NMS for 60+ hours and I honestly really like that game for what it is, and similarly enjoyed GRAV for many hours.  This game feels like a cross between No Man's Sky, GRAV, and Scrap Mechanics, and in some ways is better than all.  NMS has more polish and feels like a more living universe, maybe. And GRAV's combat is a bit more fun.  But the environmental effects and hazards make this game a lot of fun.  There will be tense moments.  It definitely feels like an early access indie game.  But in a good way.
It seems the devs patched some things right off the bat (none of which helped my situation at first), and hopefully we'll see that continue in the coming days and months.  (EDIT: There was a patch waiting as I wrote this review that resolved my issues - amazing job Devs.)
I'm giving it a thumbs up, but steer clear if you're running an AMD CPU for now.  I hear there are some problems with those currently.  However, my AMD GPU had no issues running very nicely with my i5.
Even though the game is simple looking, graphically, it seems to be proceedually generated (the two starting planets I tested were quite different), so the look of the game from trailers fool you into thinking the system demands won't be high.  I expect there's a lot going on beneath the surface.  No pun intended.  I experienced a lot of frame loss especially on new planets, and when my base got pretty large.  I feel that on a game this simple looking (no/barely textures) it shoudln't be hard to run at max, but again, there's a lot going on, and weather effects, etc probably hamper that.  Unreal Engine is notoriously a glutton for resources besides.  (Re: ARK.) Hopefully we'll see some better optimization soon.  (Typically I was getting 40-80 FPS at 1440p, though - and the slow down wasn't enough to frustrate me much, as it only happened rarely.
It's very colorful, the music is a great match for the feel and look of the game, and the audio fx are suitably cool, silly and spacey as well.  I quite like it so far, going to try to talk my gf into playing with me tomorrow now that the Core2Quad issues have been fixed.
Good job, devs.  I'd love to see some creatures to fight, and some silly/fun weapons, perhaps a monitary system or something to save for in the long run.  I found that the drill for the truck really doesn't do a hell of a lot compared to your own multitool and it fell off my truck a lot.
At any rate I love it so far, and can't wait to play multiplayer.
I will certainy be putting many more hours into this little gem!

Wow. Just wow. I spent the first 12ish hours just getting episode 1 to level 20.
Episodes have a xp system instead of money for unlocks each episode has set unlocks for each level with the max being 20. The weapon/gear unlocks cross over to other episodes and are unique for each, i.e. in order to unlock every weapon in the game you have to master every episode. This might sound like a huge chore and in many other games it would be, but in HITMAN it is executed masterfully.
The challenges are interesting puzzles that force you to learn the layout of the level and the path your targets take and what events they trigger. Many of these events only trigger if you are within earshot so you don't miss them but a few are scripted to take place with or without you.
I am only in episode 2 but so far I have not seen a single area/room where I said to myself, "oh this is just that other room from over there mirrored" or anything like that. Every area seems unique and detailed I find myself wanting to replay episode 1 again even though I have "mastered" it already.
Also when you "master" a level you unlock "professional" difficulty which moves many of the key items, places more guards in places there were none before and many of the useable items like rat poison or crowbars are now carried by an NPC that you will have to knock out to get rather than just pick it off the table.  On these missions it seems nearly impossible to do a silent assassin challenge unless you have items from future episodes but they show signs of knowing common stratiges by placing guards in areas that are key paths on normal difficulty.
All in all I am blown away by the quality of this game and the enjoyment I am finding playing it. I was skeptical and waited for the 50% off sale and I almost regret it. Definetly worth it.

It all boils down to this:
Activision doesn't give a continental rat's elbow about their fanbase. They want us to buy their games. And we do. Because we're loyal CoD fans. But once you own their game, you are no longer any concern of theirs. Why should they care about us? We've given them our money already. They just move on and make the next "Call of Duty: Slightly Different Version".
I have 510 hours in this game, and over 200 in Black Ops III, so I think I can rate this game fairly. The game itself is good, fun, and an all-around good CoD game. However, if you go into this game, expect to never be able to play a single match without hackers ruining the game for you. This game is totally infested with them. And I'm not talking your "minor" hacks like perk-hacking or no recoil, I'm talking about no-recoil/aimbot/wallhack/VSAT hack combo guys. You know the kind, the ones who get 49-1 K/D ratios in every single match.
Recently, I was playing Black Ops III, but that game is a flop of a CoD game (Feel free to read my review, or anyone else's for the reasons why.), so I decided to revisit this game.
Sigh. I wish I didn't. Since I've began playing it again, I've played at least twenty matches. Zero out of those twenty matches were hacker free. I just kept playing different matches, hoping to find a single fair game. And, depressingly, I didn't find any. Not a single one.
But the worst part by far is this simple fact. The hackers are the same ones I saw way back when I first played. The exact same guys. Still hacking. Still ruining this game for everyone. Now THAT was a slap across the face. I've been playing Black Ops III for many months now and hadn't played Black Ops II once since. Now I did, and still see the exact same hackers? No. I've officially given up on the entire Black Ops franchise. Hopefully Infinite Warfare gets their act together, but I doubt it. Everyone's just buying it because they want the Modern Warfare Remaster. Call of Duty as a franchise is in trouble, and it can be fixed SO easily. Just... ban the hackers. I'd settle for a single game without hackers, but I just can't seem to find one.

Euro Trcuk Simulator is a driving simulator game developed by SCS Software, the same people behind the 18 Wheels of Steel franchise and the Bus Driver game along with many other simulation games
A bit of history as to how I knew SCS Software and why I love their games, I orignally discovered SCS Software's games with 18 Wheels of Steel, a trucking game which took place in countries all over the world
I loved the game so much that my family relatives would always get me an 18 Wheels of Steel game for Christmas or my birthday, all the way to the last game in the series titled: 18 Wheels of Steel: Extreme Trucker 2 which ended my love of the 18 Wheels of Steel series
I also played the bus simulator game known as Bus Driver and both the 18 Wheels of Steel games and the Bus Driver, I now own all of them on retail, however you can now buy them digitally on Steam
Now with the history lesson out of the way, let's go onto Euro Truck Simulator
Euro Truck Simulator takes place in the lovely continent known as Europe where you can drive and deliver items to all sorts of companies across Europe. From the United Kingdom to Germany and from Italy to France and so on
The game is extremely relaxing as you just drive on long highway roads travelling from one country to another. However, the game does also penalize you for driving incorrectly such as going the wrong way, through a red traffic light, driving on the wrong side of the road, hitting a car or a truck, no indicators, speeding and so on. So it's not all relax on the busy streets of Europe
You deliver all sorts of items from food to livestock to hardware and big bulky things across the European landscapes and deliver it to your next port of call. The game is extremely easy yet oddly satisfying, relaxing and a huge time waster
The game's graphics are okay but do show their age. Euro Truck Simulator came out in 2008 and uses an older engine that SCS Software uses on their games. I know because some of the graphical options, sound effects and even music is recycled from SCS Software's other games of the time such as the 18 Wheels of Steel series and the Bus Driver game which came out a year before in 2007
This may put off some people but for me I don't really care for graphics, however, if you want prettier graphics than I highly recommend the sequel, Euro Truck Simulator 2 or it's American counterpart, American Trcuk Simulator which has prettier graphics and better A.I.
When it comes to the recommendation of whether or not Euro Trcuk Simualtor is the game for you, if you like games that are simulation games and likes games where you just drive around and deliver stuff, then Euro Truck Simualtor is the game for you, otherwise, don't even bother
If you are going for graphical fidelity, I would highly recommend Euro Truck Simulator 2 or American Truck Simulator as they have prettier graphics, better A.I. and more content. If you want to have the SCS Software collection of games, then by all means, start with Euro Truck Simulator

I had no idea what to expect from Seraph. I saw it was a side-scrolling action game where you don't aim your guns and was like "How is that possibly going to work?" It turns out, it works really well.
The story of Seraph is a bit confusing (you're some kind of vessel for god, trying to escape a deep, undersea prison because...I don't know) but it's a framework for a great series of systems. You have to fight your way through procedurally generated levels where the focus isn't on controlling where your guns are pointing but the acrobatics around that. This focus on mobility is what makes Seraph feel familiar compared to games like Devil May Cry but is also enough of a mechanical difference to make it feel fresh. Movement is fast, fluid and dynamic and standing still will go badly for you, especially since the difficulty scales up the longer you survive. It will feel easy initially but becomes a challenge fast.
There's also a fairly deep crafting system, allowing you to create new and better secondary guns and buff charms that can appear in the levels. Utilising this system will be critical to surviving the harder levels. You also have up to three miracle powers you can use in tight situations and these can also be created and leveled. There's a surprising number of systems at play in Seraph and using them is critical.
Despite reservations I have on Early Access games in general, this is a rare exception. There is a ton of content here already, it's technically very polished and has working Twitch integration and the developer has said he doesn't need the money to complete the project, he just wants community feedback. This is a game that will get finished and even in its current state, still has a ton of features and content.
I will likely review it again and do a new video once it goes final but even now, this is a very fun and mechanically unique brawler.

Passing Pineview Forest is a weird title, while I don't find it to be the worst game ever, I don't really think it's that good as well.
Passing Pineview Forest is a prequel title to Pineview Drive. The main goal is to walk through the woods until you reach the pineview manor, but be careful to not make much noise, cause there is a spirit in the woods and it wants to kill you.
The games main focus is audio. The audio gives you notes when playing, like when to stop and when to start moving again. The audio design is amazing and definitely the best aspect of the game.
The gameplay itself is rather tedious to say the least. The entire time I felt frustrated when I got killed when I swear that I didn't make any noise.
But the game itself is quite nerve racking at moments. Some of the sounds really creep you out and they do wonders when creating atmosphere.
The graphics are nothing too special, you will want to use as less of your flashlight as possible, so you won't really see the environments.
The game lasted me 30 minutes and apart from the one playthrough there is no replay value.
Overall Passing Pineview Forest is a really fun horror title, even though it has very tedious gameplay it's still worth to play just to get a good dose of horror, not to mention it's free.
Final Rating:
7/10 - Alright

Very fun but challenging platformer. The way it's designed I think really helps make it challenging without being frustrating.  You have a lot of control over your character in the air as well as how high the character jumps and how fast they move in the air and on the ground. Once you play a bit it doesn't take long to get a feel for how much you can control the character  so it starts to feel kind of second nature. The levels have a really great tradeoff of shortness vs. challenge and they are always throwing new elements at you as you progress. Everything is very quick and responsive so you rarely feel like you're wasting your time waiting. There's no "lives" system, no "powerups"; the game is all about fun, challenging platforming all the way through with no unnecesarry stuff to bog the core gameplay down.
Compare this to something like Dustforce where, in order to progress, you have to play perfectly through a minute or two long stage and have to restart from the beginning if you make a mistake. That can tend to get frustrating as the stages get more difficult. Also, in Dustforce, some of the stages require an amount of precision that seems to require lots and lots of practice or just a fair amount of luck. In Meat Boy, the amount of precision required of you I think does a good job of being just difficult enough without requiring you to spend hours of your life practicing a single stupid jump or trying over and over again hoping you get lucky. Also, in this game, you can still beat it without collecting 100% of stuff, but that stuff is still there if you want to play more and challenge yourself even further.
If you like platformers, I highly recommend this game.

The Flaws of Gravity isn't a fantastic game by any stretch.
But it is free and therefore offers more value per dollar then even the best games. (Provided that the game at least somewhat fun.)
Everything functions as it should. Could do with a bit more polish, but it is made by a student development team and I see no way for this game to turn a profit, so who can blame them.
List of small things which could be "fixed":
-Clipping through various walls (can't go through, but can see through).
-The credits page background has black with black text, making that section useless.
-Movement system occasionaly bugs out and stutters.
-You can see through the player model.
-Crosshair/reticle is large and opaque.
-The trailer shows things that are not in the game (The level, the arrow on walls, the reticle, the background, shadows and lighting). I assume that this was somehow the goal but as all students have done, they didn't have time to make it want they wanted. To add to this, there is nothing to do with story here despite what the trailer description says on YouTube.
-Does not keep mouse centred, so I frequently would spin left (my second monitor is on the right) in order to make sure that the mouse doesn't click on something on my other monitor.
-The game has three levels. The Greenlight description says five. Idk if this is still in development, but it isn't what it says on the tin.
HOWEVER, there is an Itch.io version which does (mostly) contain these things shown in the trailer. Why is it not on Steam? There are only two levels in the itch.io version and it lacks proper textures. But it has nicer graphics, so that's nice.
---
Tl;dr Devs have shown something that isn't really there, pulled a graphical downgrade even Ubisoft could admire, but the game is short and free so it is still worth it.

For a game developed by students, I think they did a pretty decent job here.  The basic foundations of a puzzle game are in place.  Puzzles are simple and physics based with the core solving mechanic revolving around changing the direction of gravity.  Working in the mythology theme adds to the game, and gives it a bit of atmosphere.  Graphics are simplistic (but hey, student game, remember?) audio is good (music is not at all bad), and controls work just fine.
I like the idea of development students publishing games for free on steam.  It exposes student developers to real-life feedback from actual gamers.  But by posting a game on a real-life market, they should be prepared to face real life feedback.
Now for my criticisms:
-Missing textures on movable objects.  They look like carved cheese in their current state.
-I can see the seam lines in the skybox
-Textures are simplistic in areas, and have too much gloss in others (specifically the black/dark colors)
-Would be nice to be able to change gravity direction in air
-The character model looks glitchy at times.  I shouldnt see the top of my head when I look up.
-Loading times are very long.  1.5 minutes to get into the game from the menu screen.
-Smooth out the movement.  It feels a bit jerky and stiff.
-Short at 13 minutes to complete (I understand this is a student project, but realworld criticisms here)
-Why do you show levels and scenery in the steam store that are not in the game?

The Flaws of Gravity, a short but fun puzzle game, free to play and I enjoyed it. I recommend anyone who is interested just go for it and try it out.  Gameplay wise Flaws of Gravity has you manipulating Gravity itself to solve puzzles.

This works mechanically. It's a short, gravity changing puzzler; there aren't traps or challenging puzzles, the puzzles that it has are straightforward & decently implemented.
For a game by students, I would say this demonstrates the core compentencies of first person gravity puzzle games.
It would have helped if you could switch gravity in the air, but that is a minor critique.
The more major critiques, which don't really harm the experience because it's free, but are still worth noting:
There are 3 levels but the level select (which I can't get to actually select a level) has 5 levels in it, so I don't know if content got cut or what, but all the environments in the trailer aren't in this & I don't think I saw the first screenshot area either (the fourth & sixth screenshots are from the trailer I think, so they are also not present).
Hope this team either fixes the other environments (because they looked good) or works this into a more fully fledged game like Pneuma: Breath of Life or its gravity equivalent.

Congratulations to the student dev team.

I've been a big fan of DmC since the beginning, but they lost my interest after 3. I decided to pick DmC5 up (mainly because it was super cheap on the Steam sale) and I'm so glad that I did.
What's one sure fire way to keep people interested with yet another button-mashing, combo-chaining, gory death-fest? Make Dante younger. And wilder. And give him a total devil may care attitude that makes him rude yet charming. The character development in this game is really great; we get to walk with Dante as he discovers himself and learns what he truly is. The environments are amazing. The effects that Purgatory have are very reminiscent of Silent Hill and I freaking love the way that, as you move about the levels, things start decaying instantly.
The monster designs are so great and there's a lot of variety to keep you on your toes. It's not just a button-masher but it's also a game that makes you really think before you hit the attack button. Is this weapon going to be effective with this monster? Will this weapon work better on crowds? Why is this monster immune to my demon powers?!! It's a great take on the battle system and I really enjoyed it.
As a woman, I've come to extra appreciate the redesigns for the Sparda twins (I finally get the appeal Bayonetta has for men after watching Dante fly through the sky, naked, and putting his clothes on like some muscley god of gravity). Dante's redesign hooked me right away, and the nods and mentions toward the previous series made it very charming.
The only downside to this game is playing it on PC with a keyboard. As you get more weapons and abilities, you have to have at least 12 fingers to do them all at once properly. Get ready to contort your fingers in ways you never knew you could before.
All in all, it's an amazing game, and considering it's price, why WOULDN'T you buy it?

Not quite reaching the elegant fluidity of Bayonetta's combat, nor besting the endless combo possibilites of Devil May Cry 3, DmC is nonetheless a spectacular reboot that definitely ranks amongst the better offerings in the series and indeed the genre as a whole.  The presentation is polished to a mirror sheen and often dazzles with twisted creativity (a certain boss fight and the entirety of Lilith's nightclub immediately come to mind).
Yes the origins of the main characters have been significantly altered, and yes the story occasionally beats you over the head with clumsy edginess to drive the "message" home.  However, the new Dante isn't so different from the old, the one-liners are still cheesy as hell and the cutscenes are still ridiculously over the top.  Despite what some would have you believe, this isn't some massive change in tone.
One of my favorite games of 2013.  Highly recommended.

It all boils down to this:
Activision doesn't give a continental rat's elbow about their fanbase. They want us to buy their games. And we do. Because we're loyal CoD fans. But once you own their game, you are no longer any concern of theirs. Why should they care about us? We've given them our money already. They just move on and make the next "Call of Duty: Slightly Different Version".
I have 510 hours in this game, and over 200 in Black Ops III, so I think I can rate this game fairly. The game itself is good, fun, and an all-around good CoD game. However, if you go into this game, expect to never be able to play a single match without hackers ruining the game for you. This game is totally infested with them. And I'm not talking your "minor" hacks like perk-hacking or no recoil, I'm talking about no-recoil/aimbot/wallhack/VSAT hack combo guys. You know the kind, the ones who get 49-1 K/D ratios in every single match.
Recently, I was playing Black Ops III, but that game is a flop of a CoD game (Feel free to read my review, or anyone else's for the reasons why.), so I decided to revisit this game.
Sigh. I wish I didn't. Since I've began playing it again, I've played at least twenty matches. Zero out of those twenty matches were hacker free. I just kept playing different matches, hoping to find a single fair game. And, depressingly, I didn't find any. Not a single one.
But the worst part by far is this simple fact. The hackers are the same ones I saw way back when I first played. The exact same guys. Still hacking. Still ruining this game for everyone. Now THAT was a slap across the face. I've been playing Black Ops III for many months now and hadn't played Black Ops II once since. Now I did, and still see the exact same hackers? No. I've officially given up on the entire Black Ops franchise. Hopefully Infinite Warfare gets their act together, but I doubt it. Everyone's just buying it because they want the Modern Warfare Remaster. Call of Duty as a franchise is in trouble, and it can be fixed SO easily. Just... ban the hackers. I'd settle for a single game without hackers, but I just can't seem to find one.

In a nutshell, this is Hitman Absolution, with some great sandbox maps, good variety of scenarios and pickable objects, standard kind of Hitman executions and a godda*n lack of work put into voice acting.
*The game finally seems finished. I bought it in mid-december 2016 when they had released all of the planned levels, they allegedly had removed the always online feature and it had a nice discount at the time.
*The game plays similarly to how Hitman Absolution felt. The overall physics are very similar.
*The instinct feature is still here, yet it is cut down, which is good.
*The spotting feature is still here, though this time only several people will be able to spot you as suspicious, rather than in Absolution everyone thought you are a man in disguise, which was complete nonsense.
*When you have drawn too much attention to yourself, the people will run and alert guards. If they find a weapon, the guards will then deliver it to a safe area. If a dead person is discovered, it is then put into a body bag and delivered to a designated area. It is really nice and keeps the constantly changing interaction going.
*The maps are huge, with my favourite being Sapienza. It has amazing scenery, many places to go, many things to do and discover, with above and below sea level interactions.
*The game doesn't show your score getting higher or lower constantly, which is what I like to see. I don't want my immersion broken and attention interrupted by a constant score that shows "+X points" or "-X points" for this or that (Absolution did that).
*The game runs fairly well. The reason for the graphical quality being good, but not spectacular and me not being able to max it out on higher FPS, I think, is because of the size of the levels and the quantity of people. The levels are quite big and are loaded altogether and in almost every level there are multiple large areas with many people in them (quite a unique approach only seen in Hitman Absolution and this HITMAN).
*The movement and animations still feel a little too stiff, since this is based of the engine and physics in Absolution and it suffered from the same thing.
*They have really cut down on costs and not put enough effort in voice acting. Regardless of whether I am in Paris, in Italy, in a godda*n desert - 99% of people speak perfect english. And many even speak with a pure english accent. In earlier Hitmans, in some maps you did not even understand what people were saying, because you were in some country in Europe, where this biker gang or russian military did not even speak english, or spoke with a horrible accent. This really pisses me off, because everyone always speak perfect english, which is impossible.
*This game has a level for you to play and a cutscene between them. The problem is, that even if you just want to play the story mode, you cannot just play non-stop. After you finish the level and watch the cutscene, you then see how well you did, what achievements you got and then you exit to main menu and pick the next story mission. What the hell is that? Why do I need to exit to the main menu? FFS!
*Even though, you can prepare before each mission, it is put there just to try and shut up the people, that asked for planning before assignments. Because this approach is just a complete formality and doesn't blend together with how earlier Hitman games did this. You can only have one silenced pistol and two tools. In earlier games you had your silenced gun, your two Silverballers, a syringe, a fiber wire, a lockpick and maybe a coin.
Here, you only get a silenced gun, and choose between a coin/wire/syringe/lockpick/an explosive and
. It's nonsense. Why so restricted?
*You can have an item delivered to a location in the level, which you can then retrieve, to level this restriction out a little bit.
The major problem for me with this is, that if you choose a sniper rifle, then you retrieve the sniper rifle and you carry it around on your back. What the f**k is that? I so enjoyed walking around with a briefcase in Hitman Contracts, where it had a rifle inside of it. And when I needed it, Agent 47 actually opened the case and assembled the rifle. And put it back in the case if neccesary. WHERE IS THAT IN 'HITMAN 2016'?
Overall this game is fun to play. It has both elements from older Hitmans and from Absolution-(mostly physics, instinct and the variety of pickable interactive objects). It has expanded its horizons with massive levels and brought back the sandbox feel. But it also has several annoying elements, where most could be eliminated with a weeks or two work. I also despise the lack of believability, that everyone in the world speaks perfect english, even without foreign accents. The music is amazing, probably one of my favorite video game soundtracks, the graphics are just beautiful, and the mechanics are very polished.
That being said, not all games are perfect. The game is extremely hard if you don't collect most of the collectables (I making the mistake on my first playthrough to not collect ANY life cells), but it is possible. And I was bummed when I had to pay another twenty dollars just to buy the definitive edition. The only reason I actually forked up the money, was because I love this game and I wanted to play it on my computer (for my father plays on the Xbox all the time, leaving me little time to replay Ori).
I am also not sure if anyone else had any problems with the controls of the game. Unless you play with a controller, expect problems with the controls. This game requires quick fingers and reactions, whether during the Forlorn Ruins or Moon Grotto. And it may be just because I'm bad at the game or something, but I suffered greatly with the controls of the WASD layout. The controls didn't start to become an issue until I recieved the glide ability (Kuro's Feather), which required that you hold the shift key in mid-air. Now, this doesn't seem like it would be an issue, but when entire areas are centered around this mechanic and timing is crucial, I found myself often dying from stupid control mistakes. When quickly reacting, I found myself accidently hitting caps lock or ctrl, or even getting my fingers messing up and hitting space bar, causing Ori to jump, wasting his double jump or killing him. And when you throw in even more abilities (some requiring the shift key along with various other keys) and the mouse, the controls just seemed to get chaotic to me.
The game also seemed to severly lag in multiple areas, ESPECIALLY Black Root Burrows. And the music and sound effects didn't sync up with the cut scense for me. I don't know if anyone else had this problem, or if I need to do something to fix it, but the music and sound effects were sometimes multiple seconds AHEAD of the cut scene, causing the cut secen to awakwardly play in silence for a while. Some cutscense were only off by a second or two, some hit almost fifteen to twently seconds of delay.
But critisim aside, this is a great game with somewhat minor flaws. If you haven't bought the original one, I suggest purchasing this game, it is amazing. But if you are like me and you already own the original, save your money. Sure, the game made it MUCH easier to backtrack, and the new area is kinda cool (along with the new abilites) but it is almost the exact same game. Everything that makes the game great, is in the original one. I recomend this game to anyone who doesn't own the original and has a way to set up a controller to play the game.

This game is everything I could have hoped for an Hitman Game. After the (subjectively) bad Absolution, IO really proved they could go back to the roots of Blood Money and improve on it.
The levels are just gorgeous and masterpieces of level design (except Marrakesh), the gameplay is really great with tons of ways to achieve your objective (the replayability factor is above everything else I've seen so far), and the challenge is indeed present now that we have the very hard Professional Mode.
That is not to say that Hitman is without its flaws, as there still is a few bugs with the AI, most importantly some VERY rare (twice in 120h of gameplay), but VERY frustrating AI X-Ray vision, or their 6th sense when it comes know where you are when you are sniping.
One other flaw being the DRM. You have to be online to enjoy 90% of what Hitman has to offer. In 2017, that's ok 99.9% of the time, but when the servers are failing the last 0.01%, you feel really screwed.
What's NOT a flaw though is the episodic nature of the game. I know this will be frustrating to some, but the replayability of the levels in Hitman really fits with its episodic nature. In fact, I'll even say that people buying the game now and enjoying the full game, will miss out on some of the fun of the levels, as chaining new levels one after the other in the space of a few days/weeks, isn't the same as taking your time and only discovering a new level every few months.
From a financial perspective, it's also very customer-friendly, as you can spend a few bucks to try out the tutorial and the first level, and see if you like the game for only a fraction of the final price.
This means that IO has to make every new level interesting, because every level can potentially NOT be bought by their customers. That's why I say that the episodic nature of season 1 (and soon season 2) wasn't a bad thing.

It feels like they packed too many options into the same few maps. its cool to have many different ways of assassinating someone; but the sheer amount of options coupled with the lack of maps kinda gives me "map fatigue." For example, killing Caruso with the explosive golf ball was really cool, BUT after tens of times trying to kill the same guy on the same map via different methods (sniping, furnace, poison) just got boring after a while. And the opportunities for assassination feel too scripted - they're basically staring at us straight in the face. I miss the discover-as-you-go-approach of Blood Money.
Nonetheless, HITMAN is a huge step up from Absolution. Just that you still don't feel that you REALLY control Agent 47 unlike in Blood Money, where you can throw weapons, do human shields, actually swing your arm with left-click etc. Can't help but think that the franchise has been dumbed down and made more "arcadey." But what can melancholic gamers do? Developers gotta eat.
But to be fair; the level design is great. Though I can't help but feel that the Hitman (a cold, calculated killer-type) atmosphere isn't really there - it doesn't have the dark, menancing feel of the earlier titles in the franchise.

I'm a man god dammit! Why am I crying?! ;_;
To be honest, I never thought a game could touch me like this. The stroy is very emotional and if you don't cry then you are a heartless creature! I'll stop talking about the story now, because you should experience it blind.
Besides that there's only the art and mechanics I can talk about.
Let's start with the art:
To be honest, this is the most beautiful game I've ever played. If I wouldn't know that this is a videogame, I would hang this game on my wall. Because let's face it: It's simply gorgeous. The music fits perfectly too. The music is purely orchestral with a female singer, which not only fits perfectly with the whole theme of the game, but also sounds insanely well.
Gameplaywise this game feels pretty good aswell. The game is very dynamic and fast and every section has it's own atmosphere. The platforming is very smooth and precise and you have good control over the character. You get powerful abilities early on and the whole game is based around them.
Things I have to critizise are, that the difficulty ramps up only by increasing the damage spikes and enemies deal to you.
This is especially frustrating when you collect all the life pick ups. What's the point in having lots of lifes when you still die in 3 hits?
My biggest complain though is about the One Life Mode. You can choose the difficulty before you start a new game and one of them is the One Life Mode. There you'll get only one life and if you die, you need to start from the beginning. The problem I have with this is, that there are some obstacles in the game that kill you instantly. When you die, it sometimes feels like a cheap death and not really deserved. Then you need to play the beginning again and again. That wouldn't be bad, if the whole dialogues and cutscenes wouldn't be there. I mean when you play this mode, you already played the game like 10 times for the achievements. So why is there no option to automatically skip the tutorials, cutscenes and dialogues? You already know everything, which makes those things completely useless. This mode seems more timewasting and tedious than challenging.
All in all this game is beautiful with an amazing atmosphere. The story is great and the platforming is tight and precize.
My only real complain is the One Life Mode. I expected a challenging experience, not a tedious one.
Other than that disappointing mode, everything is very well put together!
