This is definitely an enjoyable game. Several reviews talk about how it's a test of your humanity and so on, since you'll be forced to choose between a quiet prison and a morally sound one, but I have to think they're just not very good at the game. Building a reform-centric carebear prison to suit the bleeding heart in all of us while remaining safe and profitable is both entirely doable and weirdly rewarding as you watch your carefully attended and mostly reformed murderers take their first steps into the world after parolling out with a 2% chance of reoffending.
That being said, the system is spectacularly easy to manipulate if you're willing to micromanage, and anything below high security becomes trivial to keep as quiet as a midwestern corn field. Avoid googling for tips and tricks, as there are a few big eureka moments that are (A) great to discover on your own and (B) almost game-breakingly effective.
It also has pretty severe AI stability issues in the Mac version as of 9/2017, and it simply will not run with Steam overlay. When (not if) you start having prisoners starving for no reason and nothing getting built, it's because your workmen forgot how to brain, and you'll have to save, restart, and hope the food starts going out again in time to keep the prisoners from burning the prison to the ground. The achievement system is also bugged pretty significantly, which is not a big deal unless, like me, you live your life by the number of chievos you get.
All in all, definitely worth a look. I made three full prisons from scratch to profitability in like 3 12-hour sittings and will no doubt come back to it in a few months' time.

I enjoyed the little time I was able to explore this game. Compared to Arkham City I noticed better lighting effects, finer texture and graphic details, a more immersive environment with greater architectural scale and a convincingly snowy atmosphere.

I was less impressed by the voice acting. In previous games Thug dialogue was very entertaining in part because the tone sounded genuine. Here it fell flat.

Then there were the glitches and choppy animation quirks. I ran into a number of issues within a very small amount of playing time. Most frequently I would experience interruptions in the flow from brawling to a final finishing move. Finishing a foe that was dazed on the ground would have Batman's character model swiped from one position to the next in a bizarre sliding levitation move. It seems the game would reconcile where it wanted Batman to be for a new animation, and where Batman actually was by just moving his model rapidly into place. Simply put, there are times when there is no animation between the movement A -> B. Usually the effect is quick but it is jarring, just visually wrong.

Aside from the choppy animation, on one occasion I bugged through a railing I wasnt supposed to pass. Luckily I was able to recover.

About 2 hours in I entered a room where two people were fighting off in the distance. The entire environment quickly disappeared leaving only some Thugs cheering and the two people fighting off in the distance on top of a pitch black void. I restarted the game, and when it loaded batman was falling through the void. At a great distance below me I saw there was a tiny little square. I dive bombed toward it, and kept falling for maybe a minute before the tiny square finally grew larger and appeared as a single light blue platform suspended in total emptiness.

Well I missed the platform - didn't quite land on it. And that's how the game will end for me. Restarting from the last checkpoint doesn't work. I see no way to load earlier saves.
TLDR ; Every time I try to play this game I just get Batman falling through an eternal abyss.

GTA: San Andreas is a game worth buying. It has the world that can't compete with that of GTA V's (in size, that is), but there are 3 separate cities which are pretty big, with different people, with different gangs, with different, unwritten rules.

+Open-world, no worries with the time
+Soundtrack variety
+Car customization, didn't happen in later GTAs until GTA V
+3 cities gives the player a better choice to live in
+Modifiable
+The patch added controller support for PC
-The patch ruined pre-patch saves, hopefully another patch is released to patch the patch that broke pre-patch saves (ay man, I heard you like patches...)

After watching Zisteau & Sl1p8r play this on YouTube, I decided it would be an entertaining break from Factorio and Minecraft.  From what I can tell, it released today in something called pre-alpha format, which I'm guessing means that it has just enough features enabled that the developers felt good about charging for it.
And I'm glad they did!
I can tell that it's not in final form as the graphics can get blurry when you're moving and the character is a little tough to maneuver.  If you ever played Spore, the controls feel very similar to the animal phase right after you come out of the water, but just a hair smoother.
The game itself is a ton of fun.  Exploring your planet, setting up a tether network so that you don't die, expanding your shuttle into an actual base -- it's all so much fun.  Since each world is procedurally-generated, I started 3 worlds tonight just to see what they were like.  The coloring was different on each one, the day/night cycle felt different, and the cave systems were located at different spots.  Each was entertaining in it's own way, but the third world looks like the one I'll be sticking with to see what else the game has to offer.
Conclusion: If you're looking for a feature-complete game, this isn't it.  This is pre-alpha, which means it still has more features to be added.  If you're looking for something with a few surprises (yes, there are things that can kill you!), but is almost cartoon-safe, this is the game for you.  I can't wait to see what else they add to it as time passes.

I got this game gifted to me by a very generous friend and was super excited to play it because I thoroughly enjoyed the previous installments (Arkham Asylum and City). I also have been a huge fan of the Assassin's Creed series, which shares overlapping gameplay mechanics with the Arkham series. I absolutely loved my gameplay experience.
If you like Batman, gritty/dark themes, being Batman, stealth/stalking, lots of side quests, and plenty of action, then you will love this game.
The aesthetics are fantastic - the amount of detail in the world and character models is very, very well-done. Details are so fine that there is a (quite popular in superhero games; ex: the later Spider-man games) "wear-and-tear" mechanic on Batman's outfit. As you progress through the game (specifically, after boss battles), you will notice different "battle scars" adorning Batman's costume. For example, you may see nicks and scratches on his arms, or tears in his cape. I think this simple, but salient feature helps show how much of a toll the events of Origins is taking on the caped crusader. The sounds, music, and voice acting are great and add a lot to the experience of being Batman. I frequently mute gameplay music in favor of my own, however, in Arkham's case, I enjoyed the complete experience until I beat the game (took 18 hours, doing a good number of side missions).
The controls are numerous, however, they are fairly easy to learn. I strongly recommend using a controller for this game. The tutorials help immensely, and there are practice/challenge modes that help you hone your skills. During your playthrough, there will always be tooltips (ex: press x during a scene) to assist your progression. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with the Arkham (and even the Assassin's Creed) series - intuitive countering system makes fights pretty easy on normal difficulty. When you play new game + (after completing one playthrough), you will be able to experience a much harder story - the "counter" icon will disappear, and enemies will be more aggressive/skilled.
Gameplay involves you moving around the city of Gotham, subduing criminals and completing side/main missions. You will frequently encounter enemies in groups, giving you opportunities to build up a combo chain - the higher your combo when you've cleared the immediate area of enemies, the greater your experience gain. When you level up, you can select abilities to do with Batman's more physical calling (combat-related) or his predatory nature (stealth- and stalking-related). The map is fairly large, and you can unlock radio towers to allow for fast travel. To move around, you will most likely be using Batman's grappling hook extensively (faster than running over rooftops).
Combat is very fun because the game is set up to make it reasonably easy for you (at least in the beginning). Whenever you land an actual hit, you build +1 to your score combo. As the multiplier increases, it will eventually allow you to execute special moves (one-hit knock outs) - for example, every 6x you get, you will be granted one special move. There are abilities you can select that make your combo requirement lower (I believe mine is at every 4x). Counter indicators pop up over enemies' heads whenever you can trigger a counter move - you can even do this to multiple enemies. The combat animations are very varied, ensuring that combat does not get stale too quickly. There are also a multitude of different enemy types - complete with their own attack patterns and weaknesses - to keep things fresh and interesting.
There are predator instances, where you (should) use stealth to beat your opponents - typically because they are all armed and/or have hostages. To complete these scenarios, you will have to use a lot of hiding and stalking techniques - like swinging to and from ledges, moving through vents and underpassages, etc. Batman has a "detective mode" that allows you to see enemy heat signatures and objects of interest (like switches, mission objects, etc). Later in the game, you will encounter jammers that impair your detective mode, and must be disabled before you can use it again.
One of my favorite parts of the game is the "detective" scenarios, where you must rebuild crime scenes. To do this, you will have to scan an area for relevant clues, then usually rewind simulations in order to discover more clues (like a basic version of L.A. Noire's detective mechanics). This component of the Arkham series really adds to the idea and experience of playing as Batman because it isn't just about beating up and stalking bad guys.
There are plenty of side missions to complete, and many involve finding x number of items (ex: Riddler packages, Black Mask's weapon caches). Usually, after completing these tedious tasks, you will be allowed to fight/capture the mastermind.
A common criticism of this game (the third installment, following Asylum and City) is that it borrows too heavily from its predecessors. While I agree, I still enjoyed this game immensely. If you are interested in this game, then I sincerely hope you will try to begin your experience with a fresh, clean mindset. Yes, you will see, do, and feel things that will remind you of the previous games (if you've played them), but I hope you do not let it subtract from a great playthrough. Something that the Arkham series does very well is slowly adding new elements to keep the game interesting. For example, you will have many predator encounters, but new challenges will be added like jammers on the wall - and, even later - jammers on enemies. Different areas of the game will require further progression to enable access because you unlock more gadgets as you continue the story. This is also a focal point for criticism because people wonder, "shouldn't Batman already have all his gadgets ready to go?" Probably better than the first 2 games (since this is the Origins story), this is explained by Batman having certain gadgets still in development; he also sometimes takes gadgets from enemies and fashions them for his own use.
Overall, the game is a fabulous experience and I implore you to get it if you enjoy the Batman series even slightly. It is a nice segue into Arkham Asylum (since Origins is a prequel) and even has some nice easter eggs if you take the time to look for them.
ABSOLUTELY RECOMMEND!

Grab it if you can.

**TO ALL WHO ARE HAVING MOUSE ISSUES WITH THIS GAME**
1. Run the game.
2. Start Task Manager (Ctrl+Alt+Delete).
3. Highlight the game then right click.
4. Click "Go To Process".
(should take you to the "Processes" page with GTA already highlighted)
5. Right click the game and click on "Set Affinity".
6. Then it's going to ask you "Which Processors Are Allowed To Run?".
with the options to check on or off:
_<All Processors>
_CPU 0
_CPU 1
_CPU 2
_CPU 3
7. Check <All Processors> off and only check on one CPU, doesn't matter which one, but I always just go with the first one: CPU 0.
8. Click "OK" when chosen, close the Task Manager and click back on the game and all should be well.
9. None of this will work if the game isn't already running before you open the Task Manager.
**Note: This is the fix for Windows XP, Vista & 7, I do not own 8, but I would assume it's very similar, if not.. there's always YouTube lol**

Campagin - I like how they have added choices in the game, not just meaningless choices but choices that affect the game and the ending, like choosing to kill a fellow Navy Seal or killing A BAD GUYYYYY. Balanced Create a Class - At first, I didn't like the 10 slots system but I came to like it because it balances out the game. It let's people create classes taking their playstyles into account but restricting them from going overboard. A level 4 could come out on top of a level 55 with weapons with higher damage thanks to the 10 slot system.

Knife detection - I love it when you're behind an idle enemy and you go straight through him yet you don't kill him.

OP shotguns - I swear to God, the KSG is a mid-range sniper with long barrel on... Almost every shotgun is a one-hit kill and it is incredibly annoying, especially when you're on a streak and you get killed with a camper using a remington...

Inspired heavily by Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" (same book that inspired "Apocalypse Now") this game tackles war, jingoism, and choice in a way that takes advantage of the videogame medium.
It's a very competent third-person cover-based shooter. You have the weapon types you know to expect, the well-known enemy types, the strategically placed turret sections. As the game starts you find yourself as the leader of a three-man squad sent to the heart of Dubai, after first a natural disaster and second a whole US military company going silent. Your squad starts as a bunch of by the numbers badass types. A small "band of brothers." They are "professional." They are there for "humanitarian reasons." It's not surprising that 10 minutes in you are mowing down brown people by the dozens. It is surprising though, when a couple hours later you find yourself mowing down US soldiers by the hundreds. And that's the first hint this game is here to subvert your expectations and face you with a giant mirror.
And as the game advances it all devolves more and more for the characters, emotionally and physically. It devolves for the game menu. It devolves for the loading screen tips. You are behind the wheel fot it all and hopefully will learn something about war and yourself too.
It's also important to note how the game handles choice. As in war, there are many times when you as a player have no choice and are being railroaded by the developers. There are times when the game telegraphs you clear choices (Hey, you can stealth this section or go in guns blazing! Hey, you can choose to save this character or that character!). But then the game has several points where the choice is entirely up to you, it's up to you to even think there is a choice, and this includes the multiple endings for your character.
I would recommend this as required reading in schools. Screw Scarlet Letter and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn - this is the thought-provoking and decidedly dark story they should be exposed to.

I could only find one serious fault to it, but it's so big it completely broke the game for me, here it is:
By nature this is a slow game. Some levels seem to take forever not because you're lacking skill, but because they're designed that way. So every time you die, it's refreshing you can get right back in and try again.
Except that's not what happens. Instead you have to watch the whole unskippable intro to the level again, presumably while you leave the game and go make yourself a cup of coffee or something.
Except that's not what happens either. Instead the game throws you back at some PREVIOUS level, forcing you to watch its intro and go through its lengthy gameplay even though you don't find it challenging or fun anymore.
Think of it this way: you're watching a show you like with your bff, episode 6 is about to finish and you can't wait for episode 7 because this one was kinda boring. But you accidentally ask your bff: "wait, is character XY with the bad guys?"
Unfortunately for you, to clear things up your bff is now forcing you to watch the entirety of episode 5 and 6 again before you can watch episode 7. Now imagine that happening many times over and you'll have an idea what this game is like.

This game is an extremely accessible modern entry in the metroidvania genre, with beautifully crafted environments. I absolutely adore the aesthetics and the way the levels make you use your various powers together. The few sequences where you have to escape places are particularly memorable and are an interesting way to really test your ability to use your combined powers instead of traditional boss battles. Some of the platforming sequences (specifically, the few escape sequences) can be challenging, but overall the game is not difficult. Unlike most metroidvanias, no collectibles or pickups in this game are hidden in hard-to-reach places that require you to really master some little-used gameplay mechanic. You can create save spots anywhere you want as one of your abilities, which keeps the game from getting frustrating. You have a plethora of powers and abilities by the end of the game that you can use to get by challenges in a variety of ways, which is nice, though some powers seem a bit superfluous once you get to the late-game. Enemies can kill you quickly, but once you get the "bash" power, you can easily bypass or kill any enemy in the game.
The graphical style, the escape scenes, and some of the late-game platforming sections remind me of Rayman Origins or Legends. The Rayman games are a bit better than Ori at distinguishing platforms from background graphics, and telegraphing to the player where you are supposed to go. Ori is still great, but some parts will probably kill you a couple times until you figure out where to go next during a chase scene.
The story is short and sweet, too, though it is mostly narrated by a tree that sounds like Jabba the Hutt with subtitles.
Highly recommended if you like Metroidvanias or platformers with beautiful graphics.

Being new to the Devil May Cry franchise, I can`t speak for classic fans. But as far as Ninja Theory`s, DMC is concerned I must say it was absolutely awesome the entire way through. I am definitely not normally into the fighting genre of video games, but I must say the story and world this game twisted and turned you through was action packed, and had me so hooked I actually had to go look up the plots from the original DMC`s.
As far as the combat goes the battles are beautifully fluid and almost make you feel like you`re in a movie, perfectly stringing together maneuvers. Throughout the entire game you encounter new Demons to go up against leaving you never bored. In addition, pretty much till the last few missions you will be constantly unlocking new weapons, whether it be ranged or melee. Also earning upgrades is satisfying, allowing you to unlock new abilities and moves with your weapons.  As well as increasing maximum health.  Even with all that the gameplay has more to offer; I would most definitely consider this game a platformer with the amount of climbing, jumping, and swinging that occurs.
Where this game shines in my opinion is it`s one of a kind world and story. Most combat will happen once you have been dragged into “Limbo,” a city controlled entirely by Demons. The artwork in this game, (especially in Limbo) is stunning and refreshing, often having vibrant colors and offering a unique look. The demons also look like serious creatures, but still leaving enough room for the game`s dark comedic tendencies. The plot I suppose is more personal opinion but I simply couldn’t get enough! The thought of exploring the afterlife and the backstory of Dante was really cool, and the three protagonists (Dante, Kat, and Virgil) all have their reasons for what make them to me, strong characters. In particular, Dante.  Plus the thought that the world we inhabit could have far more going on than meets the eye. The voice acting in this game is nothing but the best, every moment there was dialogue I always found myself drawn.
Overall this game is a must purchase, the world is one of a kind and the plot and characters were extremely engaging. DMC is on Steam right now for only $24.99, which is a steal! Just to back up my recommendation Metacritic gave this game an 85/100, IGN rated it an 8.5 also stating “This is exactly what the Devil May Cry franchise needed,” and Destructoid rated it an 9/10.
These are the reasons why I give Devil May Cry a very strong recommendation!
(And mission 20 is badass.)

I have played a substantial amount of Devil May Cry games in the past. I started with the first entry, and have successively completed each iteration as they have become available. I was beginning to fear that the series was headed for trouble, as I didn't think the fourth entry was as solid as the previous ones (let's just pretend Devil May Cry 2 didn't exist) had been. Lo and behold, a shimmering demonic light from the heavens (hells?) broke forth and a new Dante stepped forth to usher in a familiar, yet dazzlingly refreshing, combat and upgrade system.
In DMC, you are still tasked with finding and murdering scores of demons all the while guzzling down their nutritous life-force, but this time the combat mechanics have been changed to allow for more over-the-top and wild combos that previous iterations would be unable to offer. Tired of fighting on the ground? Excellent! Just start pulling demons to you from the ground and use the new mechanics that allow you to keep ascending higher and higher. Think more weapons are better than fewer? Super! There are now five weapons available for maximum murdering potential.
Overall, I love the balance of combat that this game offers. This Dante feels much like a happy cross between the Dante of Devil May Cry 3 and Nero from Devil May Cry 4. I couldn't reccomend this game enough to long-time fans of the series and think that there is plenty to love (and a slightly less harsh learning curve) for newcomers.
4.5/5

I’m new to the DMC series, and as an outsider I’ve always viewed the old DMCs as hokey and full of cheesy acting by unrelatable characters. Therefore, DmC astounded me with its intelligent combat system, engrossing story, hyper-stylish mood, vibrant visuals, and virtually flawless execution.
DmC is just an incredibly well-made game. DmC is so compelling that I started a new playthrough immediately, which is the obvious intention of the developers what with four (four!) unlockable higher difficulties.
All cutscenes are skippable, although the acting is so good I find myself rewatching most the cutscenes. Death is very forgiving, and the pacing never bogs down. I didn’t encounter a single glitch, and the HD textures make for a crisp, elegant world. The sound design is superb as well.
Basically DmC is a brilliant game that will last 20-30 hours if you desire to find all secrets and fully upgrade Dante. In my opinion Ninja Theory has taken DMC from niche-bizarro status to universal appeal through sheer quality of design. After 40 hours of play, I must conclude DmC is the greatest action game ever made.

Inspired heavily by Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" (same book that inspired "Apocalypse Now") this game tackles war, jingoism, and choice in a way that takes advantage of the videogame medium.
It's a very competent third-person cover-based shooter. You have the weapon types you know to expect, the well-known enemy types, the strategically placed turret sections. As the game starts you find yourself as the leader of a three-man squad sent to the heart of Dubai, after first a natural disaster and second a whole US military company going silent. Your squad starts as a bunch of by the numbers badass types. A small "band of brothers." They are "professional." They are there for "humanitarian reasons." It's not surprising that 10 minutes in you are mowing down brown people by the dozens. It is surprising though, when a couple hours later you find yourself mowing down US soldiers by the hundreds. And that's the first hint this game is here to subvert your expectations and face you with a giant mirror.
And as the game advances it all devolves more and more for the characters, emotionally and physically. It devolves for the game menu. It devolves for the loading screen tips. You are behind the wheel fot it all and hopefully will learn something about war and yourself too.
It's also important to note how the game handles choice. As in war, there are many times when you as a player have no choice and are being railroaded by the developers. There are times when the game telegraphs you clear choices (Hey, you can stealth this section or go in guns blazing! Hey, you can choose to save this character or that character!). But then the game has several points where the choice is entirely up to you, it's up to you to even think there is a choice, and this includes the multiple endings for your character.
I would recommend this as required reading in schools. Screw Scarlet Letter and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn - this is the thought-provoking and decidedly dark story they should be exposed to.

It seemed to register that I got squished, yet most of the deaths did not involve me even coming close.  Other than these issues, Super Meat Boy is a good game, and is even enjoyable with a keyboard, which I have used the entire time.  Most of the game is tough but fair.  About 90% of the time, if you die, it's your fault.  It really should be 100%, but most of the time, mistakes can be remedied on the 2nd or 3rd try.  I recommend this game to hardcore gamers ONLY, and I recommend the console versions if you have that option.  For its price, it gives a lot of replay value.  I'm about 10 hours in, and I've barely touched the Dark World yet, and I have 1.5 worlds to go.  Overall Score: 85/100.

SMB is a great platformer, since level design and controls (two of the most important aspects of this type of game, by the way) are really good. Levels always offer nice and different sets of challenges like traps, moving platforms or seemingly impossible jumps. They usually aren't too long, and this really helps in a game with no mid-level save mechanism whatsover. You'll find yourself doing certain levels over and over but that will always be your fault, not the developers' one. Controls are in fact really smooth and precise. Different characters have different featured moves and skills, which makes the gameplay quite variegated and gives you the chance to play each level with a suiting character. All this said, SMB is not one of those inexplicably difficult platformers; skill and practice will bring you far!

Having completed the prior two games, I think I'm spoiled. Arkham Origins isn't all in all a bad game, and it's especially not bad for a superhero game, but it pales compared to the earlier two. In short, if you want Batman, play Arkham Asylum or Arkham City. If you have played both, wait for Arkham Knight. I can't recommend Arkham Origins.
Compared to the earlier two games:
- The plot is inferior. Rather than the ride Joker takes you on, or the twists and turns of City, it's just "here's a bunch of 3rd Tier villains, fight them." Gone is the deep plotting of Hugo Strange. Gone is the long con of Joker. Now it's just a set of bosses to fight.
- The combat is more finicky. Combos break abruptly, attacks swing in the air instead of jumping to another target, commands occasionally just don't get recognized. Getting a high combo is harder than it was.
- The bosses are terrible. In particular, Deathstroke, Firefly and Bane are some of the most tedious fights in memory. I'd rather the repeated Titan battles from Asylum. Deathstroke more than anything is a sheer-cliff difficulty spike such that he's become notorious, and he even has an achievement for a perfect victory... which is next to impossible as countering his attacks is glitched and occasionally he becomes unblockable.
- The bosses aren't anyone we care about. I'm fine with Black Mask and Deathstroke appearing, but Firefly? Copperhead? Shiva? Electrocutioner? I miss Clayface, Two-Face, Scarecrow, Poison Ivy...
- The city layout is vastly inferior. Too many impassible buildings and invisible walls end up limiting you to a few ways to get around the city instead of freedom. The bridge is annoying and much too long considering how often you have to cross it. And hey, look, it's snowing in winter as goons complain about the cold again. It would be deja vu if it weren't so much worse of a layout.
- Besides layout issues, too many paths are restricted to the one and only way the devs wanted them passed. One ledge can be grappled, but not climbed up to otherwise. Another ledge the same height can be climbed, but not grappled. Another ledge much like the first two can only be accessed with the Remote Claw. What's the difference? Just which tool the devs liked that day. There's no flexibility.
- The challenges were not apparently tested. In order to obtain all the equipment (ex. Sonic Batarang), Batman has to complete 60 challenges, such as getting a 20x variation in combat, or completing a room without being spotted. Unfortunately, they must be done in order, so that 23x variation you got earlier won't count if you weren't up to that challenge yet. Worse, some of them can only be accomplished in one spot in the entire game, so you'd better be ready before getting there and you'd better accomplish it right there, or you can never go further in the challenges and can never unlock the remaining items. Terrible.
- Bugs. The major showstoppers have been fixed so the game can be completed now, but Batman still fails to glide sometimes, enemies still fail to spawn sometimes, interrogation prompts fail to trigger sometimes, enemies clip through walls sometimes, punches in combat fail to connect sometimes, combat button presses utterly fail to register frequently, and I've never run into a game that makes my PC run so hot before, including games with higher system reqs. But hey, at least we know the devs will never patch it again because they'd rather sell more DLC instead.
- Stupid DLC. Preorder bonuses and separate purchasable DLCs mostly give you extra costumes (even though they're mainly just alternate shades of gray), but you can't use them. You have to complete the game then start over a New Game Plus before you can wear the costumes you paid money for. Why? Arkham City allowed played to enter a code to access costumes in the first play through, but that has been removed in Origins.
I would like to include a list of improvements over the earlier games for the sake of fairness, but I can't think of anything it really does better than earlier titles. The Batcave feels more lived-in, but that's about it.
On the whole, yes there can be fun here. It's still an Arkham game, still has freeflow combat, still lets you punch goons as the Batman. But I can't recommend it when there are two better games available as GOTY editions and a newer game coming out soon.

This game is good & comparable to Arkham City in many ways.  In fact, a lot of assets from AC look like they were used in this game.  The downside is it's not AC & it's hard to say whether it's better or worse than AC in general because there are a lot of issues with this game that keep it from greatness, but it also adds a lot more to the game as well.
PROS
-Large open City to Explore (roughly 3-4x larger than AC)
-More Villains & Boss Fights
-Same great combat system
-Even more gadgets & upgrades
CONS
-Bugs & Glitches
-Performance Issues (DX10 Fix Needed)
-Feels Copy/Pasted from AC
-WB has no intentions of fixing what's broke
FEATURES
A good example of something good this game adds is the way you unlock certain abilities by completing challenges.  This may seem tedious at first & in the end it actually is, but it does add a bit more depth to how you earn & unlock certain gadgets.  The downside is all the gadgets in this game are all just carbon copies from AC with very few new additions.  The best new addition to your arsenal would be the Grapnel Hook which allows you to silently take out enemies from a distance or crowd control during combat.  Another new addition is the Concussion Grenade but I found it fairly useless.  It's only use is crowd controlling one target & it only stuns for about a second.  It's hot key is also set up in such a way that it's hard to quickfire so I never found myself using it.
There are also detective segments that are kind of interactive cut scenes where you rewind/fast forward to find clues hidden in the area.  These aren't a huge addition & don't really make you feel like a detective since it just feeds you everything you need to know.  It would have been more interesting to have actual puzzles or something to make you feel like a detective looking for clues at a crime scene like in L.A. Noire.  How is Batman the "World's Greatest Detective" if he just lets his computer do all the work for him?
The campaign in this game is done very well & is probably the only thing in this game that's better than AC.  It's set up around the period where Batman first meets The Joker & the main story is about Black Mask hiring all sorts of assassins to "Kill The Bat" during Christmas Eve, with a good plot twist near the end. It's extremely well done.  The voice actors are all A grade & the guy playing Joker does an excellent job of imitating Mark Hamill's Joker.  Honestly, you probably wouldn't know it isn't MH playing him unless you read the credits.
There is also a lot more to do in this game than in AC.  Well over twice the amount of content, with a city almost 3x (maybe more?) it's size.  This means more collectibles & many more Riddler items you will need to collect in order to beat him.  There is also a fast travel where you call your jet to pick you up & drop you off.  You do need to unlock towers that Riddler has locked down in order for your auto-pilot to find you & you can't unlock them all right away as some require gadgets that you unlock through the story.   The city is huge & full of things to find & there's also random "Crimes in Progress" that happen periodically that will keep you busy well after completing the game.
There are also several more enemies & boss fights in this game.  The downside is that all the boss fights are full of fake difficulty.  Pretty much every boss in this game (with a few exceptions) you fight along side his minion cohorts.  Now the other games did this as well, but when they did it they gave you opportunities to take out many minions at once either by controlling bane or a giant mutant, but this one is set up with little to no actual devices for that.  Sometimes the boss may hit a minion, but most of the time he'll focus on you & when he does actually hit a minion by accident little to no damage is taken & it mostly serves as a short stun effect.
GLITCHES & ISSUES
This game also has several glitches that WB has no intention of ever fixing & these range from minor failings to major oversights.  One in particular is in the beginning of the game in the first boss battle with Killer Croc.  When it triggers he will constantly flash invisible & most of the sound will stop working properly.
Another glitch involves interrogating certain enemies similar to Riddler henchmen in AC, except they can't be KO'd however this KO invulnerability will sometimes bug out & render the interrogates unable to interact with & requires a reload of a previous save.
Another annoying glitch is the 2x enemy speed that sometimes happens in free flow focus mode.  Enemies are supposed to be slower but sometimes they'll be much faster & nearly impossible to counter.
There's also a glitch that happens during gliding which seems to be an animation bug where you constantly go in/out of a dive.  It's not a huge issue but it should be noted.
Civilian faces are also very messed up looking with their eyebrows stretching beyond their forehead because of the forced expression that is on their faces.  First time I saw this I thought it was a glitch, but nope.  Every civilian seems to have high-arced eyebrows.  Also, they all seem to be men for some reason.  I guess WB didn't want to depict civilian women being attacked by male villains & then being saved by a male hero possibly to avoid SJW propaganda backlash.
PERFORMANCE
I found myself having to use a 'fix' to put the game in DX10 mode in order to actually play this game.  If you're experiencing any slowdown, long loading, or anything else you may need to do this as well.  This fix is mainly for those of us running older hardware.
You'll need to find BMengine.ini in your game files, open it with notepad, CTRL+F "AllowD3D11".
Set "AllowD3D11" to FALSE & "AllowD3D10" to TRUE.  This usually fixes several performance issues that people experience with older/lesser graphics cards while playing the game.  If you still experience problems try setting both to FALSE.  This will force the game to run in DX9 mode.
The only feature the DX11 mode adds is better graphics & shading so if you don't mind the graphical downgrade & rather have a playable experience on an older machine this fix
OVERALL
Overall this game is good, but not as good as AC imo.  It's got a lot more to offer content wise but at times it can be too difficult & it's lack of polish when compared to its predecessors shows greatly.  It's still highly recommendable & worth playing.  You may even like it more than AC as a lot of people do.  For me it's great but not quite better than AC due to it's technical issues & lack of polish when it comes to glitches & animations.  If this were a more polished game it would be better than AC, hands down.

If the debate over whether or not games can be art still exists for anyone, they need only play this game.
It is a brilliant example of minimalist storytelling and a treat for the senses. The soundtrack is not just background noise, but rather is at the heart of the emotional narrative. Gameplay mechanics are introduced in a way that feels organic, not through heavy-handed tutorials. It's also a game for gamers, providing interesting puzzles and challenging platforming.
And if you can make it through the prologue without getting a lump in your throat, you have no soul. It's the video game equivalent to the first 15 minutes of Up.
I am recommending this to ever gamer I know, and saving the streams of my playthrough so non-gamer friends and family can experience it in some capacity as well.

Ori and the Blind Forest is the most beautiful and challenging platformer ever created, hands down. I'm so glad it's getting a sequel! The music's just amazing, the level design is unique, all the way through, and the story warms the heart. Say what you will about Microsoft, but they knocked it out of the stratosphere with this one.

This game is absolutely gorgeous, but the controls are a bit loose; Ori moves like he's always a little bit drunk.  This is exacerbated by the fact that the game won't let you assign custom keys to control the little dude; the worst case is Dash, which is unfortunately mapped to CTL.  I wonder if the playtesters had malformed pinkies to make that more comfortable than CAPSLOCK?
The game's best and worst features do come from how much fun the core game is, trying to figure out where to go and then going there, because saving your game is extremely limited - it generally costs an in-game resource and can only be done in a qualifying location, such as not on  moving platform.  The end result is that, quite frequently, I found myself screeming in frustration as I had to lose all of my progress over and over again due to a part of the game I found particularly difficult.  This is the core of the Ori experience:  wanting to accomplish something difficult, but having to re-do  a lot of prep work first over and over to keep trying.
If you have a high tolerance for that sort of thing, this is definitely the game for you; if you have high blood pressure, maybe you should stay away.  In case you're wondering, the second hardest challenge I've faced yet involved moving Ori, who is small, white, and slightly drunk, around on an almost all-white background with some blue elements, while being shot at from all 4 directions with things that would kill me in one hit.  Fun times.
Anyway, I played it all the way through to the final level, but the final level combines all of the game's most significant flaws into one terrible package: you have an extended series of tests to pass based on moving Ori around, but you have to struggle with the terrible default (and only) control scheme, Ori is, as usual, always slightly drunk, and you can't save progress, so one mistake at any point means starting over entirely.  I ended up giving up in disgust.

This game is amazing.
I'm an old school gamer, brought up on classic 2D platformers like Sonic/Mario etc. Personally I never cared for the 3D platformer revolution - for a long time I wished for a modern 2D platformer with all the graphics and capabilities that modern computers allow.

Having just finished the game earlier this evening, I thought I'd take the time to write a proper review.
Ori and the Blind Forest has simply been an amazing game - one that I definitely recommend to everyone.
I'm not very good at platform games, thus, I rarely play them.  As a kid, I was continually dying in Super Mario Bro. and the 1990s era Prince of Persia games, which put me off platform games in general.  I'll admit to having pretty bad reaction times and hand-eye co-ordination.  However, the gameplay of Ori and the Blind Forest made it ok.  The frequent saves I can make meant that when I did, I didn't have to start the level over from the beginning (which was often a frustrating aspect of platform games).
The graphics is simply amazing, and the story very well written - I admit to having cried during a couple of the cutscenes.  The music fits the atmosphere perfectly.
The only issues I did have was the controls during late game.  The controls themselves are actually quite well done - they were pretty easy to use and after playing for a bit, every new ability unlocked was easily mastered.  The issue I was having was that my fingers were getting confused as to which botton was which, often pressing the wrong button during tense/high stress areas.  Then again, it really could be my lack of video gaming skills!
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game, especially all the extra and/or secret areas to explore!
To summarize:

Best platforming game I've played in ages. Is frustratingly difficult at times but usually that was down to me not knowing how to tackle certain challenges properly or being familiar with the game's mechanics. Great graphics and story!

This game is probably the best example of Pay 2 Win abominations. While the concept of the game is nice and the gameplay is pretty easy to get used to, it suffers from numerous very serious problems.
Graphics of the game is slightly above average. It doesn't really look bad, but you'll quickly notice that the optimization is rather flawed and the game is unstable and choppy.
When it comes to music, there are several radio stations to listen to, so you could say there's a bit for everyone. Even classical music, which was my personal favorite.

I'm quite picky with platformers, but Ori and the Blind Forest managed to completely charm me and convince me from start to finish. The games qualities are simply off the chart.
1) The incredible variety of cool moves you can do (triple jump, wall running, wall jumping, bouncing off enemies and projectiles, launching projectile yourself (that you can use to bounce just as well), dash, aerial dash, power jump (including horizontal when you cling to a wall), air slam,  swimming, gliding...) are all very well implemented and can be combined/chained for incredibly satisfying result. Special mention to the bouncing off enemy/projectile ability. The way the time stops to allow you to choose your direction is just a so damn good way to implement it, and surprisingly despite the time stop it never felt like you're interrupting the action itself.
2) I shouldn't even have to mention it considering just watching the trailers is enough to notice it, but oh boy this game is so beautiful. The various forest environment are so damn pretty, the various light effects are on point, such a mesmerizing sight at all time. And as if that wasn't enough,
3) The sound is gorgeous. The music, the various talks in an imaginary language, and the sounds effect themselves helps making this game's beautiful graphics a dream-like experience. Some of the game's soundtracks have such a wonderful tune to them, it's actually hard to forget them afterwards.
4) level design are well thought and really ask you to use and combine quickly the various abilities you unlocked. And like I said in the 1, this games has a tons of available cool moves that can be combined. It's a fairly hard game ImO, but passing each difficult part feels so really rewarding and enjoyable it doesn't really feel like a problem at all. Also, there's another reason the game's difficulty isn't really felt as a problem, and that's
5) there is no loading time. Like, at all. Not even a "you died" screen or anything. You die, you instantly respawn on the last save point. Speaking of save point, this is another of your abilities: you can create a save point on safe grounds whenever you want (costing you a bit of energy, that can be fairly easily be replenished) so it's up to you to save whenever you want, rather than depending on the devs' opinions on where the next save point should be. Of course if the whole zone is crumbling/being flooded/taking fire/whatever over time, that's not a "safe zone" so you can't save until you escaped that part, but it's fine.
It's fine because this really feels like you're just continuing to play the game rather than a frustrating feeling of "redoing a part you've already did". No load time, no failure message, very satisfying to use abilities, enchanting music and environment, everything makes it so enjoyable than dying just means enjoying it longer anyway.
Note that this game also contain the ultimate hardcore mode of "one life only" for those searching for more challenge. Errrr... Good luck with that one. I heard some peoples did it. I just can't imagine how, but I'm impressed. Like, seriously impressed ;O.
6) The story is simple but efficient, the plot twist are again simple but well built, and the main enemy is actually quite interesting. That was a beautiful tale, for a beautiful game.
-The game provides up to 15-20 hours of gameplay if you explore the map to find the various hidden/hard to access areas, which is more than decent for a game of that price.
-Ori has a skill tree with three different lines of progress and a lot of amelioration that will have a real impact . You can get every single upgrades by the end of the game if you search the hidden areas I mentioned above, but the choices you make early on will change the way you tackle the game on the first half of the playthrough. Utility, survivability, firepower, mobility upgrades, or  a mix of them, your choice.
-This games also was one of the most memorable gaming sequence I ever experienced (and I've played tons of games ) with that "escape from rising water " sequence. The music. The beauty of the tree environment, of the tumultuous rising water, the satisfaction of using that new cool ability that you just unlocked a few minutes ago (bouncing from projectiles) just makes that escape sequence so worth it. I died. A lot.( Especially because I didn't understood that you could bounce from enemies too. Despite the game clearly saying it earlier *SMH*). And I enjoyed every single seconds of it so much. Rather than retrying it, due to all I listed earlier, it felt like one gigantic escape that was continuing again and again and was simply tons of fun.
If there is one metroid-vania platform games that you should play, it's Ori and the blind forest. That game is a wonderful gem, and i'm looking forward to any future game that team will make. 10/10, really.

DmC: Devil May Cry gets some flak from long time fans because it does some things worse than other DMC games. However, it does several things better, as well. The story is about as good as you'd expect: It's nothing extraordinary, but it won't make you sick, either. Dante is young and immature and this is the basically the story of him reaching that level of maturity you're used to seeing in other games. Don't be upset when he's kind of a punk, because that's the point.
But this is also a great game for those just interested in exploring Devil May Cry for the first time because the story is a prequel and you won't have expectations set by the other games. In other words, you won't be missing anything and you won't have to know what you're missing.
Pros:
Some of the best keyboard and mouse controls to ever grace this genre. Powerful, satisfying sense of impact and flair in fights. Top-level combos have less to do with tiny enemy step exploits (like in previous games) and have a more normalized flow. Skill upgrades are tied to XP, not currency, and can be respecced any time between (or sometimes in the middle of) levels. The unlockable content is good, and bloody palace mode is fantastic free DLC. One of the boss fights is really creative and entertaining, but describing it would be a spoiler.
Cons:
Certain action-less sections of the game are unskippable and become a chore during subsequent playthoughs. Devil trigger has been reduced from an integral part of combat to a 5-10 second invulnerability button. Dante Must Die mode is significantly easier than in previous games. Enemies that can only be hurt while in demon mode or angel mode greatly reduce your combo options and suck all of the fun out of a battle. One of the bosses takes way too long to beat for the amount of variety in the fight (none).
Devil May Cry always lives up to my expectations , lots of action and great storylines!

Holy hell this game was depressing. Like most people these days I imagine, I went into this game already knowing it was a deconstruction of the modern military shooter. Hell, knowing that is the only reason I even bothered, since it's not normally my genre. But I don't think I was quite prepared for just how dark this game gets. Everyone knows the now-infamous White Phosphorus Incident, but that's really only the tip of the iceberg, the moment you're first made aware of the road you're going down. This game is one long domino sequence of poor decisions and horrible acts in which Captain Walker - a man who looks like a cross between Stephen Amell and a hawk - slowly loses himself in a desperate scramble to rationalize the increasingly ♥♥♥♥ed up scenario he's put himself into.
Gameplay-wise, Spec Ops: The Line is unremarkable. A perfectly adequate cover-based third-person shooter that mostly just serves as a vehicle for the emotional ride. A few petty criticisms (the heavy troops that can tank multiple grenades are a bit incongruous, for example) are all I can really muster against it. The game gets a fair bit harder in the final act, but given it's building up to the climax that's kind of to be expected. I might be inclined to argue that there's a bit too much shooting in this shooter if that made any sense at all, as by the end you've mowed down literally hundreds of rogue American soldiers and practically every scene is bridged between firefights with fifty opponents or more. I mostly take it as a symptom of the genre, even if I'd personally prefer harder fights against fewer enemies than take on constant swarms of Clown Car Soldiers.
Not much else to say, the game is a fairly basic package containing an emotionally intense story. Pick it up if you want to feel like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for a few hours.

By far GOTY 2016. If the devs keep up the same good work in season 2 this could potentially also be GOTY 2017 as well. Keep in mind that the devs are still working on this game and they add more content and improvements as you read this.
There is a lot to bring up and if I would have to do a full on review this would be a 20 page essay and I feel I don't want to dedicate this much time into a single review.
Game starts out with a prologue (which is played slightly after the introduction of the first tutorial level in the first game hitman: codename 47).
You are introduced to Diana Burnwood, your handler and you have to show them that you are the perfect assassin. The game will guide you through different mechanics and once you are done with that the game will give you a free run. Do whatever you want on this boat. Just make sure that you kill the target and get out alive.
The second tutorial map will introduce you to the oppertunity system. It's like the first level where the game guided you step by step to complete an easy way to get to the target but it will still let you do it somewhat more in your way. Once the training is complete you are hired by the ICA
Due to the game has the oppertunity system the game is telling you how to bypass every map without any troubles - which is a good way for a beginner to learn the maps and some mechanics. But for the more experienced player I would suggest to turn oppertunities off in the options under game settings!
Now we are after the events of Absolution (absolution was during 2013, Hitman is based during 2019)
You show up at a model show and now you have a full on sandbox level. Nearly anything is possible to achieve here as long as you have the creativity to pull it off. When the game was released I spent at least 14 hours ALONE on this map before I knew the level 95% inside and out. The only thing I didn't know by then was all the AI pathings but I knew enough to find my way around the map and where items were. You have 2 targets: Viktor Novikov and Dalia Margolis.
This map should have been the tutorial for the game instead of the russian staged base where the oppertunity system was introduced. The fashion show is HUGE, 3 floors and a basement! All rooms serves some kind of function as well.
This is a GREAT map, solid 8/10.
This is the gem of this game. Solid 10/10 map. You have 2 targets: Silvio Caruso and Francesca De Santis and you have to destroy a virus in a secret lab under their mansion. Not only is the mansion and its garden HUGE, but you also have access TO THE WHOLE VILLAGE OUTSIDE THE MANSION. Nearly every house has something of interest and the map shows great potential for a true sandbox experience. I didn't like the lab section of the map myself but still; the map is great for contracts mode (seperate game mode where you can kill nearly any npc as you want and then let your friends or others try it out). This map also has 2 seperate bonus missions, landslide and the icon.
This map doesn't hold the same standards as the previous ones. The 2 targets (Reze Zaydan and Hugo Strandberg) are way too far away from each other and they feel seperated. They are in highly secured areas which requires a lot of sneaking around if you want to get past this level in suit only. It feels like the game is kinda forcing you to use disguises on this map and yet even then the map has so many enforcers (npcs who can see through your disguise) so you still have to sneak around. Most of the map is empty as well and the map itself doesnt serve any real purpose. I can't recommend this map enough BUT the seperate bonus mission A house built on sand is based on this playground that is so empty on the normal map and now suddenly Marrakesh is great. Small but yet so great.
The devs unfortunately didn't understand how horrible marrakesh was so they did the same mistake again. 2 targets here as well (Jordan Cross and Ken Morgan). The targets are way too far away from each other and one of them is in a very guarded area. Getting up to Jordan Cross is a pain in the back rear during suit only runs. Most of the rooms in the hotel don't serve any purpose and the map itself just feels... bland.
Full on stealth map. Looks like the devs wanted to go back to Absolution standards on this one. The whole area is a hostile area and you have 4 targets this time (Sean Rose, Penelope Graves, Ezra Berg and Maya Parvati) so you have to sneak around or grab a disguise. The visuals of the map just looks depressing and it feels like the map itself lacks creativity unlike the 3 first maps at least.
This map is a gem. You are now in a hidden medical facility in japan with 2 targets (Yuki Yamazaki and Erich Soders). The map is run by an AI named KAI and doors are locked based on what disguise you have. This is an interesting way to force players to try different routes as some are locked. You are not allowed to pre plan any equipment either until you reach level 20 in mastery on this map which is kinda stupid. But once you get to 20 this map is clearly one of the best. It's a small map but it's very good.
You have the story based 6 missions and the bonus episodes on paris, sapienza and marrakesh and then you have the following:
(somewhat loved) Game mode from absolution is back: Contracts mode: where you can make your own contracts.
Escalations: A new game mode which has 5 different difficulty levels. After you complete the first level you have to replay it again but now with more rules or changes to the map. This goes up to level 5 (or in one case level 3 - I'm thinking of the Kotti Paradigm). It just gets worse and worse and it will just be annoying in the end. I personally dont like these.

Elusive targets: A new unique target will appear on one of these 6 maps (paris, sapienza, marrakesh, bangkok, colorado or hokkaido) nearly every 2 weeks. They will stay on the map for about a week and then they disappear for good!!! If you die you lose and you can't replay the mission. If you complete 1 objective on the map you can not restart this at all so you have to finish it or die trying. People don't like the elusive target system due to they have missed 20 targets already so they have missed out on "content". The reward you get for completing these elusive targets are new suits as you can choose as you start a mission.
The AI can be very manipulated by the player
Content is locked behind a DRM system. You have to be online to complete challenges and unlock new items. Once you have them unlocked you don't have to be online anymore.
AI can't notice blood stains
Professional mode (which is locked behind level 20 mastery on each map) has some things that should be in the base game already (footstep detection, cameras dispatching guards when you are spotted or if it gets destroyed)
Professional mode just gets stupid, way too many more guards and most items you hold in your hands are suspiscious.
So conclusions? It's a very very good game, with a potentially even better season 2 by the end of 2017/start of 2018 (most likely that is the case since no date is confirmed). I would fully recommend this game even at full price. This game is all about trial and error. Imagination and execution. The replayability in the game is HUGE. 100+ hours is guaranteed if you are a completionist that will probably end up on 200-300 hours. Do I recommend this game? Yes. Defenitely.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is the 6th game in the series and one of the best.
The player takes the role of Carl Johnson, an ex-gang member that just heard that his mother was killed and comes back for home for answers. He is almost instantly brought back into his old gang and for the rest of the game he goes on trying to take over his neighborhood and later that whole state.
Players that have played GTA3 or GTA: Vice City know what the game is like; killing, shooting, racing, and just running a muck. And nothing really has changed since the previous games other then a couple little things like the player is able to swim and not die instantly, flying is easier and parachutes are added, lock on isn't perfect but better then before, and the game adds a fat-fitness part where the player has to watch what Carl eats and exercises so that he isn't too fat and slow or too skinny and weak.
One major thing over previous installments is the shear size of the state of San Andreas which it is about 2 to 3 times as big as Vice City's layout and is full of things to do.
The music is a mixed bag for me as most of the soundtrack is full of rap/hip-hop and the only stations I would listen to was the talk and rock stations and sometimes those got boring so I was glad I could mute the game and listen to my iPod.
The voice acting in San Andreas is awesome as all the characters from Carl to Officer Tenpenny all sound like they are real people in this faux world.
Now unless someone was living under a rock for the past couple years, San Andreas came under fire for having a "hidden" sex game but was only unlockable if the player owns a cheat device or has the PC version and unofficially patched the game so really the game got a little more heat than it should have. And in this edition that part of the code has been removed totally so players wanting to see the "hot coffee" are out of luck.
Added into the special edition is The Introduction which chronicles the events leading up where the game starts.
In whole the game is a blast to play and if you own a PS2 you shouldn't be caught dead with out it.

Allow me to start with the main reasons why I in fact, did not like this game:
- Lag. The trailers look promising, 30+ fps, but in the game, that's downgraded to about... A 15 fps. at best. If you're thinking: "Oh, he uses a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 80's computer" No, no I don't. I have 16 gb of ram and this STILL RUNS at 10-15 fps. I have no idea why.
- Pay 2 win. It's bad enough when a game has barely any balance at all, yet... You put in p2w elements? Maybe not p2w, but still, you're paying for stuff that basically makes you more powerful. Maybe "pay-2-cosmetic" is the thing i'm looking for, but in my eyes, it's "pay-2-variety", as in, you must pay or the game will get boring within 5 minutes.
- Imbalance. It might not be as bad when everyone plays the same class (which they all do, by the way. It's some kind of weird "engineer from tf2" kind of class, but has a grenade launcher that kills sentries in 2 hits, and they can build up to THREE SENTRIES. However, this is semi-balanced by the fact that they can't turn around, and they do barely any damage.)  but when there are 3 engineers, sentries everywhere, drones flying through the sky that you can barely hit because of the stupidly low range of the grenade launcher, and everything just becomes insanity, all while you only have 5-15 fps.
- NO COMMUNICATION WHATSOEVER. For a team-based game, it's terrible. Well, I mean, there ARE "rally here" and "attack" and "Defend" commands, but... Would it REALLY be that hard to put in a simple chat system?
- Leavers. If you join a game, it's likely 1/2 of the team will exit the game by the time the giant robot is done.
Now, the good things:
- THIS CONCEPT, OH LAWD. It's very good for just a simple variation on the "multiplayer shooter TDM bangbang" genre. When you kill enemies, they drop scrap. Depending on your character, you carry them different ways. For example, if you're an engineer-type class, you have a drone to pick it up and fly it away. If you're the bland soldier class, you just carry it. Once the drone reaches your spawn/you carry the bucket of scrap to your spawn, there's a big recycling machine. Standing near it heals you, and putting scrap into it starts building a giant robot. Upon collecting however many peices, your giant robot comes along from your spawn and walks in the background until A: finding an enemy, at which point he will bomb it until he dies or the enemy dies, or B: walks straight to the enemy base and starts smacking the enemy recycling machine. Upon the machine exploding, you win. The main problem is that if he sees ANY ENEMY AT ALL, he will chase them down until they die or it dies (again), even when smacking the machine. Since the spawn timer is 6-3 seconds, there's not a lot you can do to help make your robot destroy the machine.
Overall, 4/10, needs work.

This is a really great game. The developers have combined mechanical elements from games like the Smash Bros series and arcadey 2-D shooters, and polished it off with a nice clean graphical style, akin to something like Team Fortress. In a first play through, the game may seem a bit simple, but the joy of the game really comes in the way the various classes can be utilized for great teamwork. In particular, I feel like there is no better feeling than chain passing the scrap of an enemy back to your base JUST before the player can respawn. Snag the scrap with the sniper's claw, toss the scrap farther along with the big spikey guy, and then dash the scrap into the base just before it respawns with the ninja character. Feels good! There's actually a fair amount of strategy and complexity there for the players that are willing to dig in and discover the nuances of the classes, and how they can interact in the game.
Some reviewers have talked about connectivity issues, but I haven't had any problems at all. Played plenty of games.
I think there's some polish that the game could afford in the future, but it's absolutely worth playing right this second. Recommended!

Well, here we are again. My YouTube subscribers want something other than Minecraft, and so do I. My friend's playing Don't Starve Together, and I want to play Team Fortress 2 with him. He says no, TF2 is getting boring, so naturally I find an alternative.
Rustbucket Rumble is basically two-dimension Team Fortress 2. It is set in a world where humans have left to go murder another planet, and Robots (and possibly trees) Rule the land. Apparently, Earth was deemed unsafe to live on (Again, Trees and Eco-Friendly Bins), so Robots were left to slowly take over. The aim of each team is to collect enough scrap (Yay, let's murder our friends) to create a giant robot. Why do they need to make a giant robot? I dunno. What's the aim of the giant robot? Possibly Politics..?
RbR has good visuals, ranging from trees that I've always wanted to design like that to trigger-happy robots. It's sort of cartoonish, which suits the game. I found it a little odd at first because I thought that left-click was the only shooting mechanism, and I couldn't get my head around hitting L to pick up bins, when I could press another closer key. Then I discovered J. Haha, that was a good time.
I have a good enough computer, to say the least. I however have a few problems with this game.
Number one being that sometimes when playing the left side of my screen turns into a blue tint, with some visuals in that area disappearing entirely. Another thing is the server connection. When I go to join a server, occasionally it won't allow me to connect. And then I have to restart the game, because the game won't let me connect ever again during that play session. I get lots of server-wise lag when hitting Play Now, but when I play on a custom server most things go without a two-second delay.
To conclude, RbR is a good enough game when looking for something small, fun and free when playing with friends. I can see how it can develop further, and I am going to follow it for a little while. Though laggy and sometimes a bit weird, at least I know how the controls actually work, how to shoot, and how to laugh at my friend while he's being helicoptered to my recycling plant.

Pros:
-This game is fun as hell.
-The art style is fitting and in my opinion enjoyable.
-The classes despite some TF2 inspiration are mostly unique in their own right and have very strategic uses.
-There is a unique death system where enemies have to drag your carcass back to their base and throw you into a scrapping machine before you can respawn (and run off) in order to gain points. This makes the mechanics surrounding death and gaining points more interesting than just about any other shooter. (As well as leading to some comical situations.) I wish more games would be inspired by this mechanic.
-There is no mouse use and the shooting functions much more like a classic shooter, which is a nice change and controls well.
Cons:
-Holy ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game has the worst netcode of anything I have ever played. This game should have released in early access because its netcode is beyond broken. 99% of games will lead to nonsensical disconnects in matchmaking and custom games, the 1% of games that do work will generally lead to either everyone jumping around the map due to lag or the enemy team will quit when you are beating them.
-There are no options to party up with your friends in matchmaking. You can only play with friends in custom games which will never work, and you will barely see any listings. The matchmaking is automated trial and error and at least succeeds some of the time. So in short if you do download this, expect to play by yourself.
-There is no chat box anywhere. In lobbies to determine if a host is AFK and promptly yell at him for being the host of the one game you could actually connect to, or in game to co-ordinate strategies with your team.
-You cannot invite people to games in progress. While this in a way is a good thing it means players wont fill places when someone rage quits, or if you enter a rarely functional custom game and someone starts the moment they see another player join the other team then too late! You're stuck playing by yourself without the friends/anyone you planned to play with.
In Conclusion:
Extremely fun when it works with massive potential, but whoever is behind the netcode deserves to be shot. This game was not ready for full release and they have probably killed their long term player base by releasing the game fully with the multiplayer in a multiplayer only game in such a downright unacceptable disgusting state.
If the developer has the competence to actually fix this I would highly recommend playing the game as it can be brilliant, but so far (10/05/2015) the only developer responses regarding this issue have blankly said "we're working on it" with absolutely no eta on when the issue will be fixed with zero public announcements regarding the issue.
TL;DR: Multiplayer is ♥♥♥♥ed and rarely works, nobody knows if it will ever be fixed, otherwise really fun game, check it out if the multiplayer gets fixed.

There are two things this game is: near impossible and amazingly fun/frustrating (choose one or both). Made by a two man team, this game sends players across a selection of environments, each with plenty of hand-melting button-mashing as you attempt to guide our hero Meat Boy safely to Bandage Girl.
The main campaign isn't too long, I beat each level within it within six hours. This is not nearly halfway through all possible playtime. Each level has an "A+" time to beat. If you manage to beat this time, you unlock the "Dark World" variant of it. If you can't guess from everything else about this game, the Dark World levels are significantly harder than the Light World versions.
On top of that, many levels have a hidden Bandage to collect. There is no way of knowing which levels have these without actually finding them. They are always tucked away in the most infuriating places. Catching them isn't enough; you must get to the end safely to collect them.
Besides these, there are also bonus "Warp Zone" levels and "Glitch" levels. Warp Zone levels change the appearance to a more retro look, and sometimes force upon you the use of lives. Others feature a series of levels you must complete with a character from another game (e.g. Commander Video) to unlock for use elsewhere. Each different character has its own unique gimmick, but true hardcore players and speedrunners cannot forego Meat Boy, since he is the fastest character.
As if that wasn't already enough, there are plenty of achievements, a nice little storyline with cutscenes both horrifying and hilarious at the same time, a very nice art style, and a level editor. Yes, you too can be the bane of someone's existence or the existence of which someone shall bane by making and playing user made levels, straight from the Interwebz.
It also has a certain nostalgia factor to those who played the original Meat Boy (
) and/or Meat Boy Map Pack (
) by the same duo. I had played both well before Super Meat Boy and it was nice to see the revamped environments, music, and visuals as well as the much smoother control scheme and interesting new mechanics. If you do not yet know whether to buy Super Meat Boy or not, I'd recommend checking those two flash games out first. Expect all that is good from those games and more in Super Meat Boy.
Oh yes, and one final note: one of the most satisfying things in this game is finally beating a level after hundreds of deaths, sitting back, and watching the replay where all of your runs go at once.

I originally wrote a negative review, but upon trying out this game again, things have changed.
Attempt #1:
This game was recommended to me by some friends. Upon downloading and launching, the game crashed on the title page  after the menu (which doesn't have a heck of a lot of options now that I think about it.) I looked up things that might solve the issue to no avail. Uninstalled after that.
Attempt #2:
I got bored earlier tonight and decided a second try wouldn't hurt anything. This time, the game didn't crash a single time, despite several launches, alt tabs, and a friend spectating.
The game overall, is pretty simplistic. The music can be a bit much at times and can obscure some sounds, but definitely adds to the atmosphere.
Here's what you need to know in order to play:
1. Do NOT go into any buildings. There is nothing there for you and it's kinda easy to get turned around with all the doors and stuff.
2. Do NOT use your flashlight.
At times, the creature, whatever he or she is, will be directly behind you. You do not need to give your location away any more than what they already figure out during your gameplay.
3. Do not sprint.
When you sprint, you won't be able to hear the smaller noises (which I will list) and your reaction time will be slower. It may not seem like a big deal, but some sounds are nearly back to back and not all of them are super obvious. Walking slowly and regularly will also help you figure out when the creature is following directly behind. (Which for me, was the absolute most cringe worthy part when it happened.)
4. Do not play in a loud environment. I was in a Skype call which made hearing the sounds very hard and killed me the first two tries.
SOUNDS:
If you hear these sounds, STOP and DO NOT LOOK AROUND.
1. Breathing.
2. Footsteps besides your own.
3. Squeaky noise/toy
4. Owls hooting.
5. Bushes moving or twigs snapping.
6. Laughter.
Once the noises have passed it's safe to continue on.
This game is -all- about patience.
One cool thing about the game is that they never tell you what creature or horror is that's following you. There's no real lore to it, but the atmosphere of the music, the mood that is set, and the general surroundings are enough to put the player on edge until the end, whether they are caught or pass through the gates.
If you do choose to download this game, know that it is a good game, but does have a rep for crashing upon starting (which seems to have been voiced by several other reviews). If that happens to you, it seems like a complete uninstall then reinstall fixes the issue.
