I'm quite picky with platformers, but Ori and the Blind Forest managed to completely charm me and convince me from start to finish. The games qualities are simply off the chart.
1) The incredible variety of cool moves you can do (triple jump, wall running, wall jumping, bouncing off enemies and projectiles, launching projectile yourself (that you can use to bounce just as well), dash, aerial dash, power jump (including horizontal when you cling to a wall), air slam,  swimming, gliding...) are all very well implemented and can be combined/chained for incredibly satisfying result. Special mention to the bouncing off enemy/projectile ability. The way the time stops to allow you to choose your direction is just a so damn good way to implement it, and surprisingly despite the time stop it never felt like you're interrupting the action itself.
2) I shouldn't even have to mention it considering just watching the trailers is enough to notice it, but oh boy this game is so beautiful. The various forest environment are so damn pretty, the various light effects are on point, such a mesmerizing sight at all time. And as if that wasn't enough,
3) The sound is gorgeous. The music, the various talks in an imaginary language, and the sounds effect themselves helps making this game's beautiful graphics a dream-like experience. Some of the game's soundtracks have such a wonderful tune to them, it's actually hard to forget them afterwards.
4) level design are well thought and really ask you to use and combine quickly the various abilities you unlocked. And like I said in the 1, this games has a tons of available cool moves that can be combined. It's a fairly hard game ImO, but passing each difficult part feels so really rewarding and enjoyable it doesn't really feel like a problem at all. Also, there's another reason the game's difficulty isn't really felt as a problem, and that's
5) there is no loading time. Like, at all. Not even a "you died" screen or anything. You die, you instantly respawn on the last save point. Speaking of save point, this is another of your abilities: you can create a save point on safe grounds whenever you want (costing you a bit of energy, that can be fairly easily be replenished) so it's up to you to save whenever you want, rather than depending on the devs' opinions on where the next save point should be. Of course if the whole zone is crumbling/being flooded/taking fire/whatever over time, that's not a "safe zone" so you can't save until you escaped that part, but it's fine.
It's fine because this really feels like you're just continuing to play the game rather than a frustrating feeling of "redoing a part you've already did". No load time, no failure message, very satisfying to use abilities, enchanting music and environment, everything makes it so enjoyable than dying just means enjoying it longer anyway.
Note that this game also contain the ultimate hardcore mode of "one life only" for those searching for more challenge. Errrr... Good luck with that one. I heard some peoples did it. I just can't imagine how, but I'm impressed. Like, seriously impressed ;O.
6) The story is simple but efficient, the plot twist are again simple but well built, and the main enemy is actually quite interesting. That was a beautiful tale, for a beautiful game.
-The game provides up to 15-20 hours of gameplay if you explore the map to find the various hidden/hard to access areas, which is more than decent for a game of that price.
-Ori has a skill tree with three different lines of progress and a lot of amelioration that will have a real impact . You can get every single upgrades by the end of the game if you search the hidden areas I mentioned above, but the choices you make early on will change the way you tackle the game on the first half of the playthrough. Utility, survivability, firepower, mobility upgrades, or  a mix of them, your choice.
-This games also was one of the most memorable gaming sequence I ever experienced (and I've played tons of games ) with that "escape from rising water " sequence. The music. The beauty of the tree environment, of the tumultuous rising water, the satisfaction of using that new cool ability that you just unlocked a few minutes ago (bouncing from projectiles) just makes that escape sequence so worth it. I died. A lot.( Especially because I didn't understood that you could bounce from enemies too. Despite the game clearly saying it earlier *SMH*). And I enjoyed every single seconds of it so much. Rather than retrying it, due to all I listed earlier, it felt like one gigantic escape that was continuing again and again and was simply tons of fun.
If there is one metroid-vania platform games that you should play, it's Ori and the blind forest. That game is a wonderful gem, and i'm looking forward to any future game that team will make. 10/10, really.

This is a fairly charming and playable platforming and puzzle game, with a satisfying difficulty curve and a decent variety of puzzles. The controls are simple to master and the platforming is mostly forgiving, due to Beep's high degree of mid-air manoeuvrability and tendency to stick to platforms with its treads. Deaths were infrequent and usually fair, so frustration never really crept in.
There are often a number of ways to deal with enemies and solve puzzles, mostly due to the games somewhat wonky but effective physics engine and the gravity gun. This tool allows you to sling objects (and enemies) all over the place and is the basis for most of the puzzles.
Ultimately, its not the most polished game you will find, but its a steal for $2 and I enjoyed it to the end.

Prison Architect offers an incredibley in depth game.
Not only do you need to build a secure, Well thought out prison you have to take in to account of and plan for the tiny details from guard patrol routes to drug rehabilitation programs.
Run the prison with an iron fist and expect riots.
No kitchen and expect your prisoners to slowly starve to death.
Educate the prisoners and help them become fully functioning members of society less likely to re-offend.
Build all the key elements of a prison, cells, solitary, visiting rooms, kitchens, workshops, classrooms and much more.
Sim-type games are always overlooked,
Within the first few minutes of playing, The cartoon-like prisoners and environments set you up for what you think will be a fairly lighthearted game but the first few tutorial levels soon contrast this and turn fairly dark (you need to build an execution chamber).
There are cut scenes of a fashion covering with plenty of swearing in the dialog (hence the age 16 rating).
The soundtrack is also well suited with atmospheric music kicking in at all the right times in the missions.
By this point you already know if this game is of interest to you.
It's a rare simulation game.

First 5 minutes of the game:
You pick your astronaut model, there's 5 choices I think.
Your astronaut and his/her pod fly down to a planet and land in, usually, a good starting area.
That pod becomes your 'home', you can save your game by entering it, as well as escape dangerous weather.

DMC Devil May Cry is a phenomenal action game with a decent story to boot.
1. Gameplay-
Controls are tight and responsive with the added "PC only" benefit of a constant 60 FPS, provided your hardware meets the recommended specs. The diversity in Dante's move set allows the player to flamboyantly rain death and despair upon his demonic adversaries. I truly feel that this game is highly underrated and is deserving of much more fan attention. While this might not be the Devil May Cry that people remember, it is definitely one worth giving a shot.
2. Presentation-
Let's just skip the obvious- this game does not have top tier graphics. However, the graphics engine (Unreal) is tried and true; allowing the developers to focus on art direction and technical proficiency over sheer eye candy. This ultimately works in the game's favor since it runs at the aforementioned 60 FPS while a large number of enemies and graphical effects are on screen simultaneously. The facial animations and voice acting are superb due to developer Ninja Theory having extensive experience in those departments from their previous titles.
3. Story-
I don’t like to spoil things, but I will say that the story for me was very captivating. Dante and his brother Virgil are basically two sides of the same coin fighting for the same reason throughout most of the fame. But anyone that knows Devil May Cry at all should see what inevitable outcome will come to fruition.

Well, after 15hrs of gameplay, I still haven't even scratched the surface of everything this one can do, and am SUPER surprised that it actually runs on my computer (with a horrid graphics card.. long story).
As an older player, I'm a bit too old school and a bit too much of a 'trial and error' type to read many wikis or watch Let's Plays on games.. so although I agree the intro portion of the game (really meant to teach you the ropes, NOT to give you quest lines) is a bit short, if you are like me.. don't let that scare you off. It will STILL take you awhile to get through each one.
Absolutely reminds me of Bullfrog-type 'theme' games, but I'm actually finding it a bit more self-explanatory than those.  And the level of time and attention to detail the creators of this game put into is really mind-blowing.. they thought of pretty much everything, and then some.
My only complaint is that the game CAN be buggy... and that makes it a bit frustrating.  Bits of wall don't get built, then get concealed by open doors, so you can't figure out the issue.  Power lines from multiple generators cannot be connected together.  And in one of the very first scenarios, if you built a separate room for the 'quest' (the one with the chairs), it absolutely would not work.
Overall, though, those issues are tiny, and don't affect gameplay overly much.  You adjust to get that stuff fixed, or done... or hunt up an answer if all else fails.  And super pleased to see the creators didn't dumb down the disturbingly violent aspect of prison... as your max security prisoners dole out fatal blows to your workmen.. and as a single hole in the wall (while you are trying to be nice and upgrade your facility) results in mass escape attempts.
I bought this one on sale, because I'm sorta tight like that.. but well worth the full cost as well.

Don't get this if you're trying to improve your aim. You're unable to move in any of the training modes, hence the only kind of aim you can train in Aim Hero is 2D aim. Most games, on the other hand, require 3D aim, which is why Aim Hero is of very limited use. It might be somewhat useful for CSGO aim (where the shooter usually doesn't move much), but your common aimbotz map is a much better tool by comparison (since it also accounts for recoil etc).
The best training modes are probably the reflex and fast aiming modes which work similarly to Aimbooster (which is free, by the way). Both suffer from one fatal flaw though, namely the impossibility to scale the target area to full screen size (i.e. to reduce player distance to zero). In games, however, you typically need to be able to flick to any point on your screen, not just to some point in a limited area of your screen, which is why those modes aren't that useful either.
Overall, it is a better idea to spend your time in-game than in Aim Hero.

Games consist of 5 vs 5 competitive matches (2 vs 2 option as well), casual 10 vs 10 matches, deathmatch free for all and arms race (kills gains a new weapon to win with). Two teams play, Terrorist and Counter Terrorist; in competitive and casual, the Counter Terrorist (CT) must stop the Terrorist (T) from planting a bomb on one of two bomb sites; no respawn or health gain for each round. Deathmatch you are still in T or CT and can only kill the other team, but the player with the most points at the end of 10 minutes wins; instant respawns. Arms race is similar
This is not like CoD - real skill is needed.

Performance:
For real experience, 60fps+ is needed throughout all gameplay; lower graphics is recommended for better performance. If your rig is not very powerful, about four of the main maps run quicker than the rest: Dust2, Mirage, Overpass and Cache (learning a couple maps very well will be better than not knowing a lot and trying to play).
If your rig is powerful, top graphics can be played with no problems. Mess around with what settings there are to optimise gameplay. If you can get 200-300 fps, then again that is better than a better looking game.
My computer has i5 quad core cpu, 960 4gb gpu and 8gb of ram and I get 200+ fps on max settings.
Hope this is helpful; enjoy

ONE SENTENCE REVIEW:
Rustbucket Rumble is a 2D team based shooter with dated visuals, poor controls, and overall bare-bones gameplay that does not bring anything new to its genre and lacks content when compared to others in its genre.
LONG REVIEW:
Rustbucket Rumble feels like an Early Access Game. Don't get me wrong this isn't a rant on Early Access Games (fairly enough some of them are really good...*cough* Don't Starve Together *cough*), but sadly it does feel like one. First off when you start the game you're greeted with a tutorial explaining the mechanics of the game. Now the game has 1 mode, and its basically this: Kill Bots, Grab their Recycled parts before they turn back into bots, so you could make a Big Bot. Sounds fun? Believe me it gets stale really quick. As the two free characters of the week quickly lost its flavour (currently its Clancy and Daisy at the time of this review) as you are completely stuck with them for the rest of the week. Now most you MOBA players might be used to this already as every MOBA I have played it has a weekly character rotation. But here's the thing, with this game, unlike MOBAs which has at least a dozen characters, this game has only 6. And to top it off unlike MOBAs where you can get you're character by grinding for coins, the only way for you to get the characters PERMANENTLY is to PAY the DEBUT BUNDLE which includes all Characters at launch which is roughly 300 PHP (which is around 5-10 USD). Meaning you can only get these characters permanently by paying, if you don't want to pay then you can always win around 10 matches (if I'm not mistaken) to unlock the character... FOR A WEEK. Yep after that week the character "expires" and you have to wait for the game to make them free again. Albeit you can argue that the game is just trying to make you play all the characters, but that just not the case. I found Daisy to O.P. since players just put turrets everywhere and kill you, and Clancy to be your generic dime a dozen soldier. Nothing special about him.
My second and overall problem with the game are the controls. Since the game does not let you utilize your mouse either from shooting, it feels awkward to shoot with your keyboard (W and S to shoot up and down? Not jump and crouch? that's weird), maybe if you guys use a controller then you might be able to get through the controls. But at the moment of writing this review I DO NOT OWN A CONTROLLER. I play with my keyboard and frankly because of these controls it feels like a Console Port even though this game was created for PC.
So overall Rustbucket Rumble is a bare bones 2D side scrolling shooter with little redeeming value.
Do I recommend it? NO.

The first time I wrote a review for this game all I wrote was "Very interesting" I figured the words of the other reviewers would be enough and that I didn't really need to add much to the bucket of "Overwhelmingly positive" reviews.
But I've come to the realization that maybe it's not entirely fair to the developer to not give them the praise they deserve. That being said I still think there's no use typing a novel so I'm going to keep it as short as I can.
The definitive edition is better no real doubt about that. It has more story more levels more powers all things that make the game more fun. The increased price really doesn't bother me that much since it gave me more entertainment than the normal version. I think it's worth it but I should clarify it's only really worth it if you follow the advice I'm about to give:
Play the game once just doing whatever you want to at first. Feel free to skip some of the deep hidden secrets or even some of the parts of the map in general when they're not necessary. Don't murder yourself over points you don't get or powers you haven't unlocked just explore a little with most of your focus being on the main story.
Once you've finished the whole story, and have recovered from the emotional trauma you might experience if you're a weak soul run through the game a second time. This time carve through every single inch of the game get 100% completition. Once every part of the map is 100% and you've completed every objetive, achievement, you've unlocked every single power and all hidden areas have been discovered you will have gotten MORE than your moneys worth out of the game and I doubt you'll get bored the entire time.
Finally play the game a third time. Your third save slot should be dedicated to a "no death" run where you start on the "one life" difficulty trying to complete the entire game without even dying once. It will be pretty easy at first, you might die by accident one or two times just because you did something stupid. But this should provide another 20-30 hours of gameplay if you're a half-decent player.
Overall doing all of those 3 runs should land you at 60~ish hours of gameplay depending on how long you take on the first and third run which more than makes up for the cost.
Oh and don't forget to enjoy the visuals and the music. If you're like me you mute the music the moment you start a game and play your own stuff. Don't do that for this game it's not worth it.

This game is absolutely wonderful. I was skeptical because of the episodic format and the quality of Absolution, but I shouldn't have been. I bought it after all the levels came out. I was very much against the episodic format, but it really does make sense: each level is designed in a way to make you spend days in it. A huge amount of content is crammed into all levels, which means you have 2 ways to play the game:
The levels are very atmospheric, they have a very James Bond-esque feeling. The only exception is Colorado, it's the only one really moving the story forward, but it's also the most boring.
There's tons of content beside the main missions. I expected them to be low quality, but they are actually close to being as good as the main missions.
Especially ellusive targets. I expected these to be a gimmick, and again, I was wrong. The fact that you can't save, and can only try the assassination once has a huge effect on how you play them. Giving the player a single chance actually causes them to spend an evening carefully planning the perfect murder, then finally execute it while sitting on the edge of their seat. This is a genius idea.
The overarching story is average. The backstory of each target is good and very atmospheric. It's surprising to see that many seemingly random NPCs have their own story going on in the background (especially seen in Paris and Sapienza).
The game looks very nice and framerates are OK, but not great.
Controller support is perfect. I tried PS4 & Xbox One controllers, switching between controller and mouse is seemless, the button hints switch too right after you start using the opther input device. When using a controller, the menu gives you a layout for your specific controller. I recommend using a controller for this game.
Ultrawide support is not too bad ingame. Using the instinct view only shows up NPCs in the middle of the screen, but this could be intentional. The map is 16:9, and has an overlay problem. Cutscenes are both pilarboxed AND letterboxed (small ultrawide cutscene in the middle of the screen...).

Arkham Origins is an interesting beast. A game that probably no one asked for, a quick fix for the Fall gaming season upon release and a title that is and always will be foreshadowed by "big brother" Rocksteady's Arkham City. It is a case of mapped out goals that are selected just right enough as to not upset what came before. And as a result, it ends up not really having an identity and being a stop-gap before the next big instalment that has now turned out to be Batman: Arkham Knight.
The
here isn't particularly bad. It's simply serviceable. It's Christmas Eve and a fledgling vigilante Bat finds himself having to deal with a group of assassin's hired by a certain Roman Sionis (discovering alter egos is part of the fun) who want him rather dead. This motley crew has to kill this particularly grouchy incarnation of the Bat in one night.... Try not to think too much about the logistics of the plan and the hours required to fulfill it. It truly doesn't make sense, but semantics be damned. All this culminates in a twist that fans especially will see coming from MILES away. To add to the main story experience, the Game of the Year (GOTY) edition goes further to include one story DLC that has you revisit the game's locales and challenge map scenarios that are simply battle arenas.
Arkham Origins is a clear case of "...if it ain't broke don't fix it". It's more of the same old same old with very slight changes in the combat animations. Having come from completing Arkham City myself (review incoming), I feel that the combat rhythm here is slightly "off" with the Bat's animations being very slightly sluggish between frames. This is especially apparent when you are maintaining high combo strings and he has to move a tad faster between enemies when surrounded. That aside, all other traversal mechanics are present and correct from the previous installment of City, but if you've been used to the routine before there isn't much new to see here save for one particular tricky class of fighter and some new gadgetry (including the Shock Glove and EX Suit that just lovely cop-outs). The detective work has also been tweaked somewhat to provide a bit more narration. Here WB Montreal did a good job.
this game performs really well especially after the raft of patches that came post release. Includes some extra DX11 features with regard to ambient occlusion and tessellation that really helps bring out the best the Art team at WB Montreal had to offer for their game. Only really applicable and apparent when you enable ULTRA settings. It certainly looks and runs really great post GOTY.
is not really memorable in that you probably will not end up latching onto a favorite audio track in your head when done. I suppose all the audio work was meant to do was simply set the tone in certain areas while providing some ambiance to the experience albeit with a very limited track selection.
So is this title worth getting? Yes. With a caveat... Wait for a sale. Treat this as a quick romp (if you're an old hand at the series) and if you're a new fan? Probably start here then play all of Rocksteady's work back to back with the proviso that Arkham Origins is not a complete necessity but an appetizer to the main event. Be advised that if you are knowledgeable in your DC Comics lore you'll enjoy your Easter Eggs like a certain "Queen Industries" Shipping Container.
Parting Shot: "It's Christmas Eve Sir..." ~ Alfred Pennyworth.

Well, after 15hrs of gameplay, I still haven't even scratched the surface of everything this one can do, and am SUPER surprised that it actually runs on my computer (with a horrid graphics card.. long story).
As an older player, I'm a bit too old school and a bit too much of a 'trial and error' type to read many wikis or watch Let's Plays on games.. so although I agree the intro portion of the game (really meant to teach you the ropes, NOT to give you quest lines) is a bit short, if you are like me.. don't let that scare you off. It will STILL take you awhile to get through each one.
Absolutely reminds me of Bullfrog-type 'theme' games, but I'm actually finding it a bit more self-explanatory than those.  And the level of time and attention to detail the creators of this game put into is really mind-blowing.. they thought of pretty much everything, and then some.
My only complaint is that the game CAN be buggy... and that makes it a bit frustrating.  Bits of wall don't get built, then get concealed by open doors, so you can't figure out the issue.  Power lines from multiple generators cannot be connected together.  And in one of the very first scenarios, if you built a separate room for the 'quest' (the one with the chairs), it absolutely would not work.
Overall, though, those issues are tiny, and don't affect gameplay overly much.  You adjust to get that stuff fixed, or done... or hunt up an answer if all else fails.  And super pleased to see the creators didn't dumb down the disturbingly violent aspect of prison... as your max security prisoners dole out fatal blows to your workmen.. and as a single hole in the wall (while you are trying to be nice and upgrade your facility) results in mass escape attempts.
I bought this one on sale, because I'm sorta tight like that.. but well worth the full cost as well.

If someone was to ask me what one of the most interesting and fun games to play is, they might think me crazy if I told them it was Euro Truck Simulator 2. I'm not sure what made me buy it in the first place but it is not a decision I regret as I have now put over 100 hours into this game. The amount of depth is surprising and keeps you hooked for a long time. Visually the game looks fine, I don't think it needs crazy graphics and the trade off is that performance is great able to maintain a flawless 60 fps, the only thing worth mentioning is that I do experience a bug where the screen will just freeze whilst sound continues, this requires me to restart the game. Luckily the games saving system means that I never lose much progress. As for sounds whilst fairly basic, the sounds you expect to hear such as the engine which can get repetitive,  windscreen wipers, horn as well as ambient sounds are all present. The in game music is a pleasure to listen too as it gets stuck in my head and I find it quite endearing. As for gameplay itself, there is more then just making deliveries. When you start you don't have your own vehicle. So you'll find yourself doing basic deliveries whilst you earn the cash to get your own first truck. Once you do the amount of customisation available for each truck is awesome and you can really make each truck look unique from another. Once you have your own truck i'd recommend taking out a loan to start building your own company. Earn enough to buy another cheap truck and then hire a driver to work for you. You can then keep earning until you can upgrade your first Headquarters and fill it with your own drivers. Once that done you can then start to expand purchasing new headquarters around Europe whilst getting to explore the landscape in the process. There is also a leveling system in which you can develop your own license such as being able to take explosive or corrosive products to taking heavier more important loads and even being able to carry goods further. Which allows you to start earning more per delivery. You also have to watch you own vehicle as you need to keep it topped with fuel as if you run out you need to get it towed which can cost you a lot, and their is also a fatigue system which can be turned of in the settings which requires you to have to rest after driving for so long. The map is huge, and will take a considerable amount of time to fully explore.  That's the only downside however most towns in the game look almost identical giving you very little reason to want to go and explore them. Same for a lot of roads as they can lack variety which can make driving feel dull after some time both issues that were worked on in American Truck Simulator. However seeing as I've played this game for so long the management side of the game as well as just cruising around in general is fun enough to keep you playing for years to come.

I got BEEP in a puzzle-related game bundle so hard to assess the value vs fair price for me. However, I think I got what I paid for.
I love a good platform puzzle game and while BEEP is such a game, I only like it.
To start, I had to play in windows-mode only (alt-enter to exit fullscreen) because the fullscreen mode would not cooperate. I spent a good amount of time trying to make it work in fullscreen that I should've just played it in windows-mode the whole time. The graphics are indeed nothing to boast, but cute to a degree. The micro-expressions the beep does when underfire, firing, jumping/etc is amusing (if noted during gameplay). You are given a mini-background story as to why the BEEPs exist and then you appear in a galactic map. It isn't clear where you supposed to go as I ended up flying the ship around the 'galaxy' wondering what to do. It's also funny to me how the ship comes to an abrupt stop when you stop clicking a direction for it to fly to (unrealistic, but in a game were Wall-E's cousin has a better job than him, it doesn't matter).  While the design is fairly easy (WASD/Arrow in combination with the mouse),  the game can be both unforgiving and lenient. If you over-jump even a slightly bit, you are most likely falling to your death. However, if you are jumping and your wheels are able to touch a surface (along the side of the walls or where-ever), you are allowed another chance to jump again to make it (granted, you have to be pretty quick with your reactions to do so). The goal to collect the anti-matter and little gems (25) to get another anti-matter makes it more than just a puzzle platform. Especially so since you do need to collect them to progress the game. Some of the puzzles are very simplistic at the beginning and I believe it'll be so throughout the game since there isn't much combination the game can do with the gravity gun besides just moving the objects around freely/around a pivot piece.
Overall, it's a decent game and if you get it in a bundle or stand-alone, you will have some fun time with it. Not a game to finish immediately, but I suggest on the side. 7.5/10.

The game is absolutely awesome, and more than a worthy successor to Blood Money. The levels are fantastic, huge, complex, full of ways to reach the goals.
IO understood that Absolution, while a good game on its own, made a mistake by trying to be a story-driven stealth shooter. Blood Money never was a real stealth game, or a story driven game, it was first and foremost a puzzle game. The puzzle being: "here are the things you can do and take in the level, here are the NPCs, now find a way to achieve your objective." This is what made Blood Money so excellent, and this game brings that back.
(Also, no more save points, but proper savegames. THANK YOU IO. The savepoints ruined any experimentation in Absolution, because you had to rush  from savepoint to savepoint.)

Standard but fun side shooter, with a brilliant concept that makes this game great! Classes actually feel balanced so far in my opinion (this coming from a player that played the so-called weak rifle character). I'll refrain from commenting too much on the character availability issue at this time, as my experience there is limited as of the time of this writing. What I can say, is that I don't mind a rotation system as long as the classes are balanced and fun, which they so far seem to be.
One of the best parts? It's free. Can't go wrong with free. If you like Contra-style side shooters, then perhaps you should give this game a go, and perhaps you'll find this to be a hidden gem.

Finally! A quintessential Hitman release. They seemed to address (at least at a glance) all the shortcomings of both Absolution (there were many) and Blood Money. Disguises work without arbitrary "instinct", but not around people who they logically wouldn't work with (i.e. half the cops recognize you as not one of them while wearing the uniform; the ship's captain will know if you're not a real ship mechanic, because he knows his crew, but deckhands won't necessarily, etc); the game's difficulty is extremely adjustable without a "brute force" approach to difficulty -- if you want the game harder, turn off all hints and pay a *lot* of attention to your surroundings; the levels are much more open-world, and the short bit of story I've seen focuses on Diana and 47's relationship, which is really the core of the basic story there is; etc. So far, an excellently made game. As an aside, the online issues seem to have been addressed as I haven't run into any.
I can't give a solid recommendation from having beaten the game (I haven't yet), but initial impressions would be at least 9/10.
However.
They seemed to go for a more...retro vibe with the soundtrack. While it's well done for what it is, it's missing Jesper Kyd. The tone of the game is completely different: it's a lot less dark and "heavy" than Blood Money or Contracts. For me, the previous games were largely about atmosphere, and I'm afraid the score just doesn't do it for me for a Hitman game. The retro vibe is certainly appropriate to a certain degree, as the beginning of the game is more or less a "47 joins the ICA" story, and it's certainly a well-done retro vibe. But Kyd's very particular trademark just isn't on there. If I had never played Hitman before, this may not have mattered as much to me. This unfortunately drops it down to a 7.5/10.
TL;DR:
Game: Actual Hitman game for a change. Combined good elements of Blood Money and Absolution, largely getting rid of the poorer elements.
Initial impressions: 9/10
No Jesper Kyd score: 7.5/10

We all hate DRM, most of the negative reviews are about♥♥♥♥♥♥DRM and the new never before seen episodic release system, where the game releases maps every now and then l ike a TV series releases episodes (Except it's every few months instead of once per week, but hey these american TV series guys can never stick to a weekly schedule anyways, so it's basically releaseing new levels like a tv series, yeah.)
Now, on the DRM, the game now has an offline play option so don't you worry too much about that, (I also never had any issues with it, Just Cause 3 had similar issues, my only issue with it was how long it took to start the game because it had to connect to the DRM service to let me play but that's off topic here, I experienced zero issues with the DRM in this game, didn't even notice it was there.) but hey, DRM is♥♥♥♥♥♥ I get it, I agree. But it is what it is, if we wanna buy games instead of pirate them, we have to live with the DRM, that's just how it is.
Next up on the Episodic release and this is where it gets interesting... I had nof aith in this system when I first saw it, I thought it was just a stupid money grab to release maps as 'dlc' and add more transactions to the game so that they can get more money out of it. But really? It's actually not like this. The entire season 1 is out now making this a full fledged game, so it's not a bother to anyone here anymore I guess, but I was so wrong about this. This is basically a Triple A method to release a game early, as in 'early access' in order to fund further development and I know that's not what we all want to pay for, but what we do get in return for this weird release model is... Amazingly, mind blowingly friggin incredibly never before seen levels of detail on every single map in the game, and I don't just mean the graphics I also mean in the map design and well, the scale of the maps, the possibilities on each map to take out a target, you basically get a huge playing field with at least a dozen (probably usually a lot more than a dozen) different ways to take out your target using the environment alone, events, etc, instead of just shooting them in the face.
And I do think that this makes the episodic level release system worthwhile, we don't get the full fledged game on day 1, no. But we give them the resources to make increasingly better and more creative levels and the time to build each map with incredible finesse instead of just building the whole thing rather well all in one go. The episodic release system allowed this game to have significantly more quality than it would otherwise have had by giving the map designers time to think carefully through the map many times over before finally determining the final layout, and the modelers and texturers time to do the very best they can (and it is GOOOOOOOD) so that not a single object in the entire game lacks detail.
As for the gameplay, it's classic hitman. You select your tools and the starting point on your map where you get dropped down into a massive playing field where you can take out your targets however you want, you also have a little info on who your targets are and a few tips on where to look for ways to exploit their dirty little habits. Like absolution it has an achievement/challenge system for each map (like never wearing a disguise, or killing people in specific ways, wearing specific disguises, etc) and you also get points for finesse (like only killing your target). I had all sorts of fun in this game, never went guns blazing but I tried up close and personal neck snapping assassinations, sniping (it was a challenge to find a vantage point and a clear shot every time. Choosing the right one is half the fun) and letting people die in terrible, terrible accidents. I was just bummed that I couldn't select 47's iconic silverballers until after I finish some challenge, I'd prefer to always have these silverballers, they're some OP♥♥♥♥♥♥
Now that the episodes for season 1 are all released the anger over the episodic release system has died down, and lots of issues and bugs the game used to have have been ironed out providing you, the late buyer, with the ultimate experience.
Buy it, if you're a hitman fan it's worth every penny and more, if you're not a hitman fan, you'll be one soon enough if you buy this.

Artificial game prolonging: The Game.
It is a typical modern open-world game which prolongs time played through meaningless animations/cutscenes, an obscenely large and empty world, copy-pasted "go kill/collect" missions and a meaningless set of collectibles.
Vehicles:
There's no joy in building your Archangel (your primary vehicle), as it is simply about completing the game and upgrading the parts - there's no valuable customization. You don't trade top speed for acceleration or anything of the like, you need to complete objectives in a given region to unlock the ability to buy an upgrade for your car.
You are able to steal, save and drive NPC cars and even race in them. The races have different objectives and rules, but are usually quite easy by shooting your opponents until their cars explode.
Outposts: Similar to Far Cry, simply kill or destroy whatever opposes you. There are optional objectives which don't seem to contribute much else than getting you closer to that 100%.
Some of these have bosses, which are all alike in mechanics.
Story: There is barely any. Mad Max wants to get to Gastown, he encounters a dog, a mechanic and people who vary in hostility. No characters to get attached to and no feeling of the Mad Max movies. This isn't the tale about a traumatized ex highway-cop.
This game has fun for 4-8 hours depending on the person, but it is just an empty WB licensing cash-grab. The most fun you'll get is from harpooning stuff from your car, but the few variations in this will shortly become bland and grey, just like the wasteland we're set in.

There's an enourmous jump in physics between everything you do. Running, jumping and sliding feel like different games altogether, and you are constantly being forced to switch between them. The result is that you can't get properly used to any of them.
Most people will have brains that function with clear sets of rules and being able to anticipate when these rules will change, and compensating for that. This is impossible in Super Meat Boy, since your brain will not be able to anticipate when your reflexes are going to kick in, and since the rules change majorly every time you click a button, the result is LOTS of memorization.
People praise this game for its difficulty. Is it difficult? Hell yes. Perhaps to such a degree that it's poor learning curve design.
I would have been ok with that if it wasn't for the nature of the difficulty.
People praise this game for its old-school difficulty, bringing the feel of the old platforming classics back. Is this correct? Not at all. Using the difficulty of the classic megaman games as a standard, I will explain the differences. Note that all my points will not be true for ALL the other classics, since megaman's difficulty is nearly perfect. But lets assume that they are more or less correct, at least much more so than SMB(this game, not super mario brothers).
Megaman has distinct and accentuated hazards that will first appear and signal their arrival, then begin their attack or function. This allows your attention to be directed towards said hazard and allow you to focus on how to use your abilities to avoid it.
Super meat boy allows a lot of its difficulty to be due to hidden hazards or sudden patterns that come at you too quickly for you to make it out before death. Some levels even taunt at your ignorance as a main game mechanic(the levels where a button will make something timed happen at the other side of the level or drop a key somewhere off screen where you are supposed to catch it before it disappears).
Megaman has controls that feel analogous to your efforts to press the button(it's funny, but surprisingly true). When you jump or run, it feels like YOU are making him do that. It is very difficult or impossible to die due to unresponsive or counterintuitive controls(though there are exceptions, like the water levels with spikes in the ceiling).
In super meat boy, you feel like you are telling the keyboard to tell the processor to do something to make the engine cause super meat boy to make some general movement in some direction. Many, many of my deaths were because I felt like the character was doing something I didn't try to.
Megaman can take some hits before he's out. In any difficult platformer it comes natural that completely new challenges will take a few shots to learn to tackle. Megaman has the ability that you are allowed to learn and progress simultaneously, making it feel absolutely wonderful to master. It is hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it lends you a hand and tells you to believe in yourself. It allows you to make a mistake, and if you keep making that same mistake, it punishes you to hell.
Super meat boy punishes you. Period. The main mechanic for learning the patterns that arise in this game is by dying and being forced to repeat the level over and over and over. Every new challenge will kill you, probably more than once for every single element that make up the pattern, and will shame you every time. You are not allowed the freedom of mastery through intuition, and combined with how you will only be able to get past a hazard by luck until you have gotten past it enough times that your brain can ignore the physics altogether and just get past it like if it was a sequence of button pushes that made a green light go "good job", this makes a game that is 10% skill and 90% luck, where the luck portion can be converted to 90% muscle memory with extreme amounts of grinding and practice.
In conclusion, no. SMB does not use old-school difficulty by any means other than the fact that it's difficult.
It is in fact more punishing than it is difficult, which results in a feeling that beating a challenge is not worth it. If you are like me and get a feeling of reward proportional to the difficulty that has been overcome, you WILL be punished far more than you will be rewarded.
I hate this game. I hate it utterly and completely. It left me feeling depressed and angry, no fun involved.
Other than that, if you've played the first world, you've pretty much played the whole game. All the remaining levels will be more difficult reskins of the first stuff(with a few exceptions). It feels very repetitive, and this might also be due to the fact that there is no variety in the hazards you meet except their trajectories. Everything kills you, so everything in the game translates to "sawblade moving right", "sawblade following you", "sawblade beam", "sawblade that bounces".
All in all, this is NOT an old-schooly platformer, and does not reward you based on your skills from about the moment you finish the salt factory.
It is, however, a perfect tool for masochists to get off with. And it is also the perfect way to demonstrate how dedicated you are to the Super Meat Boy™ brand. You can practice this stuff for weeks and brag about how you managed to teach your hands to do complicated sequences of actions. As a matter of fact, with the amount of muscle memory involved in this game, it might be the best chance humanity has to achieve sentient hands.
I despise this game and hate it and want to burn Edmund McMillen for making it(only slightly, like with a matchstick or something. I wouldn't do it though, I love the Binding of Isaac and Time ♥♥♥♥, and I don't want to go to jail), but I have endless admiration for the people who managed to get good at it despite the amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥and♥♥♥♥♥♥it flings in the players face. You know what? This is a good game. I didn't really expect to like it...I'm not much of a platformer guy, and I originally only had a license because I bought a bundle. But the graphics were interesting enough in a oddly appealing way, and it looked as if it wasn't just constant Mario moments with a bunch of hidden crap that you had to memorize, so I decided to add it to my library instead of trading or gifting it. And man, am I glad that I did.
What I got was a thinking man's platformer that includes some really interesting mechanics (especially the many variable ways that your gravity beam can be applied). As the environments change, so do many of the challenges for those levels, so the environments aren't merely eye candy. Everything was achieveable, even if getting to 100% completion on some levels required some pretty diabolical thinking.
The controls are tight, graphics are original, and gameplay is solid. I ended up playing every level, and hanging in there to the very end (many platformers make me rage quit 20% of the way through the game, and I have enough other stuff in my library to play that I will often just dump the platform game to play a FPS/RPG/adventure game, which are my primary genres).
The only downside to this game? You're left with a bit of a cliffhanger at the end -- an obvious set-up for the next game -- but, to the best of my knowledge, no sequel was ever produced (this game was released in 2011, so it doesn't seem very likely that will ever happen). That's too bad, because I would gladly pay to play the sequel as well.
At two bucks, if you like platformers at all, you'd be kind of dumb to pass this one up. This is a really solid game from an independent developer, and I'm happy to hand him my $2 all day long. Great game, Big Fat Alien, and I hope that you decide to follow up BEEP  some day with a sequel. I'd pre-order just to support you. Nice work.

I have been following this game for a while and instanly bought it when I had the chance. I have been playing the game for a couple of hours now and I have been enjoying the game from the second I started it.
Once you open the game, you are greeted with a beautiful loading screen with all the planets orbiting the sun. After the loading is done, you can select your character and you're instantly 'launched' to your first planet.
When you get out of the pod, it's the best feeling in the game. you can walk around in this vast world full off colours and vegetation. There are mountains, raveins, caves and lots more.
After you progressed a bit and have some basic machines running, you can look into all the diffrent modules. You have options like a solarpanel or a wind turbine for power generation, but there are also things like storage racks and batterypacks. You can snap these modules everywhere, don't like them there? move them somewhere else.
But the best thing in this game: the vehicles. Trucks, rovers, landers. They are compatible with all the modules and you can even daisy chain them. You can jump to other planets and start bases there, the posibilities are endless.
Sure, there are some performance issues, especially when your base is getting bigger and bigger, but that's to be expected with a pre-alpha game like this.
Really like where this is going, looking forward to the updates!

Finally! A quintessential Hitman release. They seemed to address (at least at a glance) all the shortcomings of both Absolution (there were many) and Blood Money. Disguises work without arbitrary "instinct", but not around people who they logically wouldn't work with (i.e. half the cops recognize you as not one of them while wearing the uniform; the ship's captain will know if you're not a real ship mechanic, because he knows his crew, but deckhands won't necessarily, etc); the game's difficulty is extremely adjustable without a "brute force" approach to difficulty -- if you want the game harder, turn off all hints and pay a *lot* of attention to your surroundings; the levels are much more open-world, and the short bit of story I've seen focuses on Diana and 47's relationship, which is really the core of the basic story there is; etc. So far, an excellently made game. As an aside, the online issues seem to have been addressed as I haven't run into any.
I can't give a solid recommendation from having beaten the game (I haven't yet), but initial impressions would be at least 9/10.
However.
They seemed to go for a more...retro vibe with the soundtrack. While it's well done for what it is, it's missing Jesper Kyd. The tone of the game is completely different: it's a lot less dark and "heavy" than Blood Money or Contracts. For me, the previous games were largely about atmosphere, and I'm afraid the score just doesn't do it for me for a Hitman game. The retro vibe is certainly appropriate to a certain degree, as the beginning of the game is more or less a "47 joins the ICA" story, and it's certainly a well-done retro vibe. But Kyd's very particular trademark just isn't on there. If I had never played Hitman before, this may not have mattered as much to me. This unfortunately drops it down to a 7.5/10.
TL;DR:
Game: Actual Hitman game for a change. Combined good elements of Blood Money and Absolution, largely getting rid of the poorer elements.
Initial impressions: 9/10
No Jesper Kyd score: 7.5/10

We all hate DRM, most of the negative reviews are about♥♥♥♥♥♥DRM and the new never before seen episodic release system, where the game releases maps every now and then l ike a TV series releases episodes (Except it's every few months instead of once per week, but hey these american TV series guys can never stick to a weekly schedule anyways, so it's basically releaseing new levels like a tv series, yeah.)
Now, on the DRM, the game now has an offline play option so don't you worry too much about that, (I also never had any issues with it, Just Cause 3 had similar issues, my only issue with it was how long it took to start the game because it had to connect to the DRM service to let me play but that's off topic here, I experienced zero issues with the DRM in this game, didn't even notice it was there.) but hey, DRM is♥♥♥♥♥♥ I get it, I agree. But it is what it is, if we wanna buy games instead of pirate them, we have to live with the DRM, that's just how it is.
Next up on the Episodic release and this is where it gets interesting... I had nof aith in this system when I first saw it, I thought it was just a stupid money grab to release maps as 'dlc' and add more transactions to the game so that they can get more money out of it. But really? It's actually not like this. The entire season 1 is out now making this a full fledged game, so it's not a bother to anyone here anymore I guess, but I was so wrong about this. This is basically a Triple A method to release a game early, as in 'early access' in order to fund further development and I know that's not what we all want to pay for, but what we do get in return for this weird release model is... Amazingly, mind blowingly friggin incredibly never before seen levels of detail on every single map in the game, and I don't just mean the graphics I also mean in the map design and well, the scale of the maps, the possibilities on each map to take out a target, you basically get a huge playing field with at least a dozen (probably usually a lot more than a dozen) different ways to take out your target using the environment alone, events, etc, instead of just shooting them in the face.
And I do think that this makes the episodic level release system worthwhile, we don't get the full fledged game on day 1, no. But we give them the resources to make increasingly better and more creative levels and the time to build each map with incredible finesse instead of just building the whole thing rather well all in one go. The episodic release system allowed this game to have significantly more quality than it would otherwise have had by giving the map designers time to think carefully through the map many times over before finally determining the final layout, and the modelers and texturers time to do the very best they can (and it is GOOOOOOOD) so that not a single object in the entire game lacks detail.
As for the gameplay, it's classic hitman. You select your tools and the starting point on your map where you get dropped down into a massive playing field where you can take out your targets however you want, you also have a little info on who your targets are and a few tips on where to look for ways to exploit their dirty little habits. Like absolution it has an achievement/challenge system for each map (like never wearing a disguise, or killing people in specific ways, wearing specific disguises, etc) and you also get points for finesse (like only killing your target). I had all sorts of fun in this game, never went guns blazing but I tried up close and personal neck snapping assassinations, sniping (it was a challenge to find a vantage point and a clear shot every time. Choosing the right one is half the fun) and letting people die in terrible, terrible accidents. I was just bummed that I couldn't select 47's iconic silverballers until after I finish some challenge, I'd prefer to always have these silverballers, they're some OP♥♥♥♥♥♥
Now that the episodes for season 1 are all released the anger over the episodic release system has died down, and lots of issues and bugs the game used to have have been ironed out providing you, the late buyer, with the ultimate experience.
Buy it, if you're a hitman fan it's worth every penny and more, if you're not a hitman fan, you'll be one soon enough if you buy this.

Don't listen to the haters.
DmC is by no means perfect. I don't think anyone will ever recreate the magic that was DMC3, but for all the negative hype that the game received, DmC really does its best to impress.
Mechanically, the game is fantastic. For veterans of the series, it is a breath of fresh air. Dante retains all his abilities (similar to his appearance in DMC4), and through five different toggle buttons he's able to quickly access any of his tools. Perhaps most notably, almost all of the tools in DmC are different and useful. Each attack sequence has a unique purpose for which it is best-suited, and while you'll probably come out with some favorites that you rely on, you'll almost certainly use every tool in your kit to play on the harder difficulty modes.
Also, DmC is hard! For people just wanting to experience the story, the easier difficulties are quite easy. However, even the Nephilim difficulty is fairly hard on one's first time through the game. Series vets who want a challenge will find it, and unlike DMC3, the DMD difficulty is pretty fun and rewards aggressive play rather than the tedium of DMC3.
The story is a mixed bag, but it is two stories in one. The surface story -- the one most people comment on -- is rather contrite. It's a story of revolutionaries fighting against evil governments and corporations, and makes a lot of overt social commentary on modern culture. DmC throws this message in your face over and over, and honestly I was turned off by it. Fortunately, there's another story behind that one.
The real story of DmC is its commentary on freedom versus order, or chaos versus slavery. It's also a story about the little people, and not about the godlike characters (Dante, Vergil, Mundus) who move the plot. In the end, even though one side does triumph, it is supposed to be a hollow victory, as though something of great importance was lost. DmC has a lot of message beneath its very blatant and shallow surface, but because the social commentary is so loud and obvious, it tends to be obscured.
Perhaps most noteworthy about the story is that, other than his appearance, Dante is still Dante. While he's young and a bit inexperienced -- allowing him to grow as a character  -- he retains all the elements we're used to with Dante. He's a brash, arrogant jerk with a heart of gold, fundamentally the same Dante we've known and loved.

Wow. I just beat the game and that's all I can say. Wow. This game is stunning.
For those of you who don't know, Ori and the Blind Forest is a Metroidvania game where you control an orphan on his journey to restore the land. It's such a simple idea of paper, but the execution of it is mindblowing.
Let's talk about the obvious attraction to the game first. This game is beautiful. There are multiple times where I got frustrated at a platforming section, but when I was finished my frustration instantly vanished because the visuals, along with the music, blew me away.
Then there's the story. The beautiful cutscenes and intense moments are what make this story so great. I don't want to spoil anything because this really should be played 100% blind.
As for the gameplay, I only have one minor problem. You can't rebind controls. The default controls are great, but I got a low quality third party XBox controller, and the keys don't bind correctly. There is a way to rebind in the game's files, but you can't change the trigger buttons, and those are vital for many platforming sections. Since mine don't work, I had to have my pinky on the shift key of my keyboard and use a mixture of keyboard and controller controls. It was as uncomfortable as it sounds, but I'd rather that then full keyboards, especially since I was already used to using the controller by the time I needed to make this shift. However, I don't blame the game for my broken controller, but the feature would be nice.
Everything else feels great. This game can be hard at times, but it never felt unfair. I had no problems controlling Ori except for the occasional issue with one of the abilities you get later in the game. I was immersed in the world the entire time. The gameplay, in my opinion, is perfect.
When I see people talk about games as art, they usually point to Journey. Journey is a fantastic game, but it was mostly just walking and observing. It wasn't as replayable as other games. Ori and the Blind Forest, however, has the art syle, atmosphere, music, and story to be considered a fantastic piece of art. The gameplay that goes along with it is what turns it into a fantastic game.
I was able to beat the game in 7.8 hours, but I still feel like it was worth $20. If you don't have a controller that maps the buttons correctly, or you don't like the keyboard controlls, then get this game on console. Otherwise, get it on Steam. Either way, this game is one everyone should at least try. I'm sure it's not for everyone, but even though I don't see myself replaying it often, I consider Ori and the Blind Forest to be one of my favorite games.

HITMAN:
+ Superb stealth game, you'll need to use all your skills to eliminate targets. Patience is a virtue and will allow you to strike at the right times. Distract guards by tossing coins, turning on faucets, switching off fuse boxes, planting specially designed audio devices which emits noise and much, much more. By breaking patrol patterns you'll be able to sneak into restricted areas, where new disguises can be found or another path to your target becomes available.
+ This game has the most diverse methods of assassination in the Hitman series. It's very fun to replay multiple times. Dress as a waiter and spike your targets' drink with rat poison, then drown them in the toilet. Weaken the structural integrity of a lighting rig with explosives, so that it collapses on your target during a Fashion show presentation. Perhaps you'd like to impersonate a Psychologist who has a meeting with your target, giving you personal access - then suffocate them with a therapy pillow. This is just a fraction of the options available, truly incredible.
+ Very good graphics, really atmospheric, lovely colour palette and attention to detail.
+ About 150 hours of gameplay for completionists - tonnes of challenges to complete and unlocks to acquire.
~ The story is pretty light in HITMAN. At the end of every episode more cutscenes will explain the plotline, but it's not a super interesting story - in fact it's rather basic. Despite that, it's not terrible either.
- A few key AI issues plague HITMAN. There is no explanation on AI line of sight, so sometimes you think you're clear to conduct an illegal action, but suddenly the AI is alerted. On other occassions the AI should be able to detect you, but apparently they can't. For example, I jump the fence to an off-limits section in plain view of security, but beause I am a certain distance away they don't see me, even though it's obvious in real life they could. This inconsistency creates uncertainity for the player who is always unsure of what they can and cannot do. Very frustrating.
- Game stutters unjustifiably on high graphics, despite my gaming PC being far beyond requirements (GTX 970 4GB GPU, 8 GB RAM, i7 CPU). Dips in FPS range from 20-30 depending on crowd size. With the PC I have it should be consistent and stable, unacceptable!
8.5/10

Mad Max
Don't let my playtime fool you, I bought this game for Playstation on release and fully played through it and even then I was more, "Meh". Its not a horrible game, but its far from a good one. The following is the review:
-Unique Idea as far as games go
-Open World
-Decent out of car combat
-Decent car combat
-Big map
-A few charming characters along the way
-You're called "Saint" by your trusted hunchback, which helps the ego a bit.
- The open world is more of a forced open world. Majority of it is empty as you might expect given what the setting  of Mad Max is, and it's post-apocalyptic type. By saying the open world is forced I mean that you have to grind to get a lot of things. You have to search around the map for "scrap"  which you find often, but only normally in quantities of 4-5; while upgrades normally always require upwards of 300 scrap. So you HAVE to go around the open world getting scrap in order to progress.
-The grind. When I say grind, I mean driving around in a desert raiding small/medium  sized bases that are few and far between looking for 200 scrap to stick 4 very small spikes on each side of your car. I wouldn't mind the grind as much if I felt I was getting something that proved to be worth it all. But I didn't. At any point.
-Considering majority of the game is driving through desert/apocalyptic lands, this scenery gets old pretty fast.
-Longevity. The game is long when I did my full play through on the playsation, but yet again, the length seemed to be almost entirely due to
.
-Story. If you know the story of Mad Max (which lets be honest isn't a very strong one, but it isn't supposed to be), then its pretty much the same as this. Except you have to upgrade a new car from scratch because your original was stolen.
-Characters. Relatively forgettable other than Hunchback.
If you like the grind and not feeling as if it was worth it and the Mad Max storyline, then I would maybe pick it up if its on major sale. Other than that though, it was a cool and interesting concept, but it focused too much on the boring emptiness of the world and didn't have enough "Holy Sh*t that was awesome" moments to make it worth it.

Been playing for an ~hour and it's looking quite good.
I'm thinking this is going to help me build up my mechanical aim quite a bit.
Once thing I would like to see is a "Automatic Fire" option. Right now you have to click for each shot... There is no "reload" or "delay", your firing speed seems to be restricted to however fast you can click.
For people who want to train their mechanical aim for Automatic Weapons this can get quite tiring on their fingers since they want to fire like an Automatic Assault Rifle.
There is the "Lightning Gun" mode; however, it's still quite different.
Pretty good for warming up and for training in general. One thing that should be added is the option to practice y-axis movements for the strafe training mode since Overwatch is pretty big on that.
In FPS games, I let opponents get into my head and start fumbling. In Aim Hero, I don't have to worry about that at all, so I can just focus on my own raw aim. Extremely useful.

For $5 this is a no brainer if you're interested in improving your aim in FPS.  The reflex mode is really nice for practicing flick shots and the strafe/lg modes are good for hitscan.  You can change the background/target colors to something you're comfortable with, and customize aspects of the different modes to change difficulty.
I'd recommend finding a sensitivity you like (you probably already have one you're comfortable with in whatever your main game is) and then using the various mouse sensitivity calculators out there to use it across all games you play.  Then go nuts with this and ingrain that muscle memory.
It's also great for a 10-15 min warmup before you hop on.  In the little time I've used it I've noticed I'm more confident my first game after a few minutes on here.  GL HF.

I'm a Modern Warfare (yes, the original one) fan who thought it was about time to upgrade after nearly a decade playing that game and the most positives I heard was for BO2. It is currently $60 -- I heard the reasoning for Activision pricing like that, though I don't buy it (pun intended). A while back, it was discounted to $30. A much better deal, but I still couldn't really justify it at that price. Then Humble Bundle had a deal where it was $20 and I decided to go for it.
...to be honest, I kind of regret it now.
Don't get me wrong -- BO2 is a good game and I do recommend it. The campaign is really fun, the multiplayer is great and is as you remember from other CODs, and zombies seem to be a half-decent mode. I kind of regret it though because primarily because of multiplayer's matchmaking shtick.
Due to matchmaking, I'm unable to really play the kind of matches I want to play and it does get aggravating at times. Not only do I often get into matches where there aren't enough people, too many people, or people far too skilled for my level, but the problem worsens because I'm often forced to play maps I dislike. One time, I was put into a match where there was a huge map but only a small amount of players. The result was that I literally ran around the whole map for several minutes before even encountering a single opponent.
NukeJacked 24/7 mode solves this problem somewhat, but the game really could have been improved by a server browser that lets you pick what kind of matches you want to play. It could have also made a few other improvements to making the game easier, e.g. a drop-down menu allowing you to choose game settings instead of clicking up/down arrows or allowing you to save settings for bot choices.
Well, BO3 has already been released and the complaints I'm making now are well known, so there's no point in dwelling over it. If you can get BO2 for $20 (or, better yet, $10), I'd say go for it because, again, it is a genuinely good game. Just be aware that it can get a bit restrictive.
If nothing else, the bots in this game is one of the best things about it and a big reason why I bought BO2.

NANANANA BATMAN

Going into the game with the a new developer at the helm of this legendary franchise, I was extremely nervous, as Arkham games captured not only the essence of the Dark Knight himself, but also the dark sinister world in which he casts his shadows. I was expecting the developer will stick to the comfort zone and will follow closely if not completely copy the blueprint of the gameplay and structure perfected by Rocksteady (the developer of the previous two Arkham games) while coming out of the comfort zone with a captivating origin story that drops the first dominoes towards the build up to the next two games in the chronological sense.The good news is they indeed managed to keep the solid gameplay intact, in fact they didn't make any changes to the fight and gadgets, just with different variations of the same gadgets used in Arkham City like Glue Grenade over Freeze Grenade. There was a much greater emphasis on Batman's detective skill-set. As as you found more evidence, the crime scene slowly builds and is illustrated in a hologram. You sometimes had to rewind, pause to a specific spot to find a clue that you might have missed. It was really cool, and perhaps the only new thing this games does that was not done in the previous game. Although, I wish it was much more deeper and instead of just looking at the spot and pressing the 'X' button to scan and tag. Oh well, there is always the next Arkham game right?
So I never expected the developer to re-invent the bat wheel for the series, that sort of task is best left to Rocksteady and good thing they didn't as results might have been catastrophic. However, I wished they had done better with the narrative flow of the game as well as the plot. The story felt disjointed and felt like different pieces of awesomeness attached to one another in hopes of making one giant awesomeness instead of melding pieces of narratives that complement each other and make one big awesome narrative like Paul Dini did with the previous two games. I was hoping the Christmas background of the game would add to the atmosphere, but apart from some radio of random christmas songs and some Christmas decorations here and there...it hardly felt like a Christmas Eve, sooner than later it felt just like another long night for Batman. The Another thing that caught my eye was the city itself. The game is supposed to take place in Gotham City, or some part of it. However it hardly feels any different from Arkham City. With virtually no one out in the street instead of hundreds of thugs and random police here and there. This further kills the Christmas vibe, seriously I don't care if it is snowing like crazy, people go out during Christmas Eve, at least some do. At times I felt like I was back to Arkham City, or even worse, considering from the number of thugs out on the streets and rooftops far outnumbering the country's soon-to-be biggest criminally Infested Zone.
The story is not at all bad, where Arkham Asylum was a great batman story, Arkham City later became perhaps one of the best (personally the best) Batman story I've witnessed; Arkham Origins comes out short and tends to be a good story. Then again, it is sometimes hard to blame the Warner Brothers Montreal because the legacy left by the first two games were so great that I doubt any developer would succeed leaping over or even matching it.
The new voice actors did a solid job and overall the performance of voice actors were on par with the previous games. I thought I would dearly miss the Conroy/Hamill duo of Batman and Joker. I did, but the performance of the actors were amazing, especially Troy Baker's Joker, the way he captured the insanity, the horror and the comedy of Joker only Mark Hamill previously understood.
I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, I will post my impressions as soon as  I dive into it. But from what I've heard from people who played it, it is not really worth spending a lot of your time on.
So there you have it, its a very good game and a worthy game to add to the Arkhamverse. If the previous two games were masterpieces from a renowned artist. This game comes out as a masterpiece from the artist's best student. The student will only get better as long as he/she comes out of the comfort zone more often.

There's two kinds of art in this world.  There's art that becomes deeper and better the more you experience it (ex: the movie Fight Club), and then there's the kind of art that doesn't and the more time you spend with it, the more you realize it's not actually that good (ex: every song by Smash Mouth).
Unfortunately, Arkham Origins falls into the second category.  My first playthrough was just great and I really liked the story and characters - but on my New Game + run, everything started falling apart.  I started noticing things about the plot that made no sense, minor grips about the combat system became major annoyances, and doing the detective parts a second time made me realize how much of a useless time waster they actually are...
So would I recommend this game?  Yes - but only play through it once, and don't bother with the achievements or challenges.  Do this and you'll love it!

It's Hitman! :)
In the beginning, all the possibilities and the huuuuge size of the levels are overwhelming.
The game takes you by the hand, revealing so called 'opportunities' that guide you. But only if you wish, you can turn this feature off, of course.
Same goes for instinct mode. While you CAN use it, you can turn it off in the settings.
All in all it's a HUGE game. Due to it's episodic release I started playing it only after all episodes were released. I don't want to play 1 level and then wait for two months. That's a bit on the 'minus' side, that episodic release model.
It's like a campaign that you experience in slices every two months. Buy it now abd you're good. Also, you can buy episodes seperately. Buy the first one to give it a go, if you're not sure.
The story - so far - is WAY LESS cool than Absolution's. This one here is more James-Bond-Like. Faceless corporations and syndicates with generic villains to kill. Nothing like the deep background story of the marks in Absolution (Lenny for example - what a great sidestory).
You don't really connect to the villains here, because the missions are spread allover the world without any real background story that makes you 'feel' the game.
Absolution made you save a little girl form a crazy cowboy, it had everything. Touching story, fully fleshed characters, a believable universe.
Here, it's really more James. Bond. It's more sterile if you will.
However, I really like the game overall, it's mechanics work fine, and as I said, you can tweak EVERYTHING in the settings, making the game punishing hard.
I think they nailed the stretch between casual and hardcore players this time, with the ability to adjust the game to your skills.
Yes, the game has online DRM. You HAVE to be online. What's the fuzz? Steam _IS_ an online DRM if you will. ;)
All in all, as a fan of the franchise, it is what the community asked after Absolution: It's more like blood money gameplay-wise, but it keeps the cool mechanics of Absolution.
It's a definite buy. And if you only buy ONE episode, you will have fun for several hours - I guarantee it.
Give it a go. ;)

Perfect tool for building muscle memory and improving response time.
As far as I know you can rig up somewhat similar aim practice in Counter Strike with a custom map. But Overwatch players only have the training range at their disposal with no customization available... So you stand there landing headshots on hitboxes as big as houses thinking you're a hotshot. In a real match you find your self looking at a healer in the distance with a head the size of a dust speck and can't hit a damn thing. Destiny 2 players get an even worse deal, no training range and limited ammunition in the actual game - you get a few sniper bullets once or twice every 10 minutes if you're lucky, absolutely horrible.
Options are exactly what you would want and need to match the aiming sensitivity and aiming conditions to your FPS games. There are preconfigured mouse sensitivity scales for Overwatch and other popular games so you can use identical numbers for simplicity. VSync is not forced on you and FPS limiter is included, that way you can match the input lag conditions. Even more importantly field of view is adjustable. Just keep in mind that the FOV setting is for the vertical axis so to match Overwatch/Destiny2 100 FOV you use 68, to match 110 you'd use 78.
Honestly it could use a lot more features, but right now at its price it's a good warm up every day.

Having logged nearly one-thousand hours into APB:Reloaded, during the many updates, I can confidently say: This game has me forever. APB:Reloaded caters quite well (Thanks to the more recent updates) to new players, but still has a fair learning curve, and rewards the more hardcore gamers like myself.
APB:Reloaded hosts two Factions: Enforcers and Criminals. Whichever faction you choose, you're signing yourself up for the most brutal Cops vs Robbers shooter you've ever played.
Just like with any shooter, no matter how meshed it is with Online play, the tedious dying and respawning will sink its teeth into any gamer and steer them to the point of aggravation. Team up with friends or acquaintances, however, and you'll be the one enjoying the sweet taste of Raging Gamers.
APB:Reloaded incorporates teamwork as well as common sense and intense strategy. Playing against opposition, you need to spend your time wisely; rushing straight for an objective is the best way to feed the opposition kills and points. That being said, retreating to cover behind a vehicle after snagging a briefcase, you had better pray said vehicle doesn't explode if it takes too much damage.
All this reviewing, and I haven't gone over the character, vehicle and weapon customization yet. Needless to say, the vast majority of options given to you, the player, is quite overwhelming and will keep you playing for hours.
All aspects considered, I'm giving APB:Reloaded 8/10. There is room for some improvement, but that will not stop me from playing.
