I will mark this game on 5 topics:
-graphics
-gameplay
-horror value
-sound
-replay value
Introduction
Five nights at freddy's sister location, like all the other FNaF games, is a sit and survive horror game where animatronic characters come to life and hunt the player. When the first game came out, it was like slender all over again, every youtuber was making a video on it, it's popularity spread like wildfire. It was a different concept, and a lot of game developers made clones of the the topic, some were good, some were bad. In 2017, it's still happening, but not as much. many more games were made after the original FNaF was released, including a spinoff, and within 3 years, Scott Cawthon, the creator of FNaF, was able to publish 6 games related to FNaF. Sister Location is the fifth main FNaF game to come out, and the newest in the franchise. I will base this game's review on five topics, if the overall rating is 5 or above it's recommended. Let's get to the first topic.
Graphics
The character designs for sister location is kind of different to most FNaF animatronics besides the toy characters. But what really makes them horrific, is the endoskeleton inside the plastic-like costumes, if it manages to scare me than that's a pass. Some of the things i have noticed during my time playing Custom night, is curves on both sides of the screen and unreal static showing at the edges. It ruins the atmosphere and horror aspect to the game, and looks ridiculous, it can be an easy fix. When fighting ennard in the fake ending, I noticed that when typing 1983 on the keypad, it showed a simple easter egg in which the moniters were monitering rooms which seemed to be from FNaF 4, but when this easter egg is activated, a scrumpled up sheet of paper shows static along with the moniters, that tiny setail dropped the horror factor a bit. There are more to cover but i'm pretty much done with graphics. I would give graphics an 4/10, there were too many design glitches which could be easily fixed, the animatronics almost saved it.
Gameplay
Unlike the previous main FNaF games, every night is different, you need to do something unique on every night and that really dragged me into this game. The difficulty on most nights was too much for me, it ruined the horror experience. On night 4, the only time i was scared was when ballora got scooped (literally) and when i was jumpscared for the first time. there were some fun parts of the game and the feeling of beating a challenge/night was amazing (besides the first night). There are some fun and difficult aspects to the game which adds to the gameplay, but ruins the horror aspect. 7/10
Horror value
I've mentioned this in my previous topics, the game doesn't give the scary feel it should have. After the first jumpscare, it's more swears than scares. There are some things which ruin the horror like difficulty and design glitches. I'm not going to talk much on the horror aspect since I've mentioned it too many times in the past topics. Also F.Freddy's voice is too quirky. I'm going to have to give the horror a 2/10, sorry Scott.
Sound
I don't know why but I love it when sound is implemented into a game in which you need to use it to survive. Especially for a horror game. It uses it well, if you don't listen, you die, so you must keep your headset on. there's not much horror to the sound, again, taking away the horror factor. Sound was obviously worked on quite a bit during the developent process and he got other people to voice the characters. overall i give the Sound aspect an 8/10, really well done, I like it.
Replay value
There are hidden things within the game making you want to turn back to night 1 and look through it all. Some of the challenging aspects of the game makes me want to replay them and feel that same emotion that rushed through me after beating it the first time. there's not much else i can say about the replay value. 7/10
CONCLUSION
topics: 5.5/10, There are many good things about this game like the sound and replayability, however an almost even number of bad things too like the horror aspect and graphics (kinda). It's more fun and challenging than horrifying which is good for the gameplay but not for the horror. You'll find yourself screaming more swears than being scared and if you are a completionist, you're in for a ride. The game is definately different from the other FNaF games and that to me earns a bonus point for origninality. The story for this game is too complicated, -0.5 points, and the final bonus is my overall opinion of this game. I think that this game is really fun, if you have came for the horror than i'd suggest you should go back, but if you want a real challenge (which I like) Than this game is for you +1.2 points my overall score for this game is 7.2/10 i would recommend it

Rust is a game of patience and persistence, and you experience that the moment you start the game, and that turns a lot of people off. As of recently, updates have been kiling the game, but I have hope for this wonderful game. This game attracts the player who enjoys sitting down and grinding and having their work pay off (most of the time), but it also attracts cucks, so watch out. I reccomend playing this game with a veteran if you're new, but once you get the ist, I reccomend playing solo, to better understand the game. Overall, I rate this game 7/10.

While Rust is an early access game, the developers and designers are constantly making updates and changes not only to the functionality of the gameplay, but to the graphics and perfomance as well. While the constant updating can be an upside to the EA norm of getting greenlit and then never touching your game again, the updates have also been a headache to those that loved the game at a specific stage of development and would rather it not change.
It's a fun game with a really fun premise of survival and base building. PvP is constantly being tweaked and PvE is having its ups and downs as well. If you get this game, don't settle in for how it is at any given point and expect things to change from week to week each Thursday.
I would recommend this game to anyone that likes PvP survival games with crafting and building elements. I would not recommend this game to anyone wanting a finished game that won't change. Please believe me when I say this game will change. The hings you love may be deprecated while the things you hate may be promoted.

First of all, the game begins with an amazing intro, followed by one of the best soundtrack in the game industry, Soul of a Man by Steven Stern.
Speaking of sound, the voice actors are very good, the cars are realistic, but the fighting sounds can become pretty monotone, which is a sin for such a great game.
The story is very well written, even though it's a bit short, with an anti ex-machina ending, a sad one, but it's in the Mad Max films' spirit. The characters are also well written and the locations are beautiful, with wonderful landscapes where you can spend so many hours without realizing.
The gameplay is good as well, but I would say the game is fairly easy if you max everything you can ASAP, just like I did. I didn't have any problems in destroying convoys or overtaking camps, dying like twice in the whole game.
The controls are the best ones in a Warner Bros game, which I love as a keyboard and mouse user, many games suggesting playing on a controller.
The achivements are easy to get, one or two being a little bit harder to unlock, but in 60-70 hours you can make a perfect record.
In conclusion, if you like open world games, like Far Cry or Middle-Earth, you'll love this. The game is pretty cheap these days, but even at the full price is worth.

Besides I highly recommend trying to explore as much as possible, since the map is really huge and you should always come back to early parts after getting different powers in order to get cells to make your life easier.
Also the graphics are beautiful, everything, from the scenery to the animation blends really well, leaving you breathless while playing the game, especially in the escape parts.
The story is pretty simple, yet very touching. I'm not going to spoil it, but I will just say it gets sad pretty fast.

To say I was surprised by the quality of this game would be an understatement.  The game, while being very short (it took me maybe 5 hours on my first playthrough), is extremely engaging and extremely fun.  The controls are tight and movement is incredibly fluid.  Combat is "meh", but the way it ties into the rest of the games movements and abilities, it doesn't get stale.  The art style in this game is absolutely phenominal, and was one of the things I was surprised by the most.  The landscapes are just ridiculously good..  I'd say this game is worth it at full price, but if you're the type who waits for sales, it does go on sale quite frequently.

I rarely binge complete games anymore, but I made an exception for Ori and the Blind Forest. It's really good. Reminds me a lot of Metroid but it has its own art style and story that's reasonably captivating. It's a beautiful game.
Pacing in terms of introducing new game mechanics is perfect. It starts off like a straightforward and behaves like any familiar platformer should, but then you progressively get new abilities that drastically change the way you navigate around the environment, unlocking new areas while you do so. By the end of the game I was able to perform a wide variety of moves, but I never felt overwhelmed. The game is very good at ramping up difficulty while also giving you new abilities at just the right times.
There are a few "platforming gauntlets" in the game that really test your platforming proficiency for an extended period. That is, you have to input a long series of precise moves and attacks, and if you fail you have to start from the beginning. While they are tough, the feeling when you complete them is just great.
I completed it 100% on normal in about 11 hours. If you've ever liked Metroid, you're in for a good time!
Beautiful art, music, animation, and design at every turn - I can't recommend it enough!

Ori is an absolutely gorgeous world. I found myself bawling within the first five minutes of the intro -- the characters are very easy to become attached to. Gameplay and controls are smooth, absolutely beautiful scenery and story. One of my favorite games by far.

WARNING: This game does crash sometimes, there is a bug regarding a loop with Sergei that will crash the game sometimes, and some random crashes may occur, however I find they tend to be rare. See the Note at the bottom for help on some crashes.
Pros
-Replayability
-Different take on RTS
-Unique factions make for very diverse types of play
-Scenarios and Adventures offer decent amount of content
-Editor is easy to use and can change gameplay dramatically
-AI is challenging although it can be a drawback in other ways
Cons
-Graphics are alright but nothing spectatcular
-Voice actors are absolutely awful (some are comically bad though)
-AI can make dumb and simple mistakes, positioning troops in the weirdest of places
-Crashes sometimes on newer operating systems (although there are workarounds to make it better, as well as quicksave button)
-The way combat is calculated is somewhat convoluted and explained poorly, albeit the basics are easy to grasp
-Some errors in spelling and grammar as it is not a AAA title
Despite the cons, the game itself is quite solid, and offers a different expierence than most traditional RTS titles like AOE and Starcraft. The game only has two resources, food and gold; gold being used to purchase and upgrade units, and food being used to keep troops healthy. The game has a larger emphasis on unit compositions and supply lines, rather than micromanaging workers and your economy balanced with military battles. Heros act as generals in the way that they grant better stats to units under their command, and make organizing armies better. One upside to having average graphics is the ability to having thousands of units on screen at once.
Overall, I'd give the game probably a 8/10, only taking off points because of the horrendous voice acting and average graphics.
NOTE: If you are having trouble with the game crashing frequently (namely windows 10), try running task manager when you start up the game, going to the Details tab, finding the tpw.exe, right clicking it, and setting the affinity to run on only one of your CPU's (You will need to do this every time you start up the game). This tends to help older games such as this one run on newer systems.

I played this game for many years in starting in junior high.  It came via one of those book order catalogs the school gave out.
The main reason I bought it was my love of history.  On that front, the game has a decent amount of actual historical information in it.  However, it also has a lot of inaccuracies.
This is a great game to kill time.  I'm no expert on RTS games (this is the only one I've spent time playing), but it feels fairly balanced.  Oh, sure, there are ways to cheese the AI, but to do that you have to play for a good amount of time to build up the resources.  You can play the campaigns (two of which contain five missions; the other four or five are single mission) or play 'scenarios.'  The campaigns have interesting logistical restrictions (i.e., you have only a certain number of soldiers and no way to create new units until capturing an objective; sending gold to a certain shipyard, triggering your home city to send reinforcements a few minutes later; etc.) and force you to think carefully.  The scenarios do not have any plot to them, though there are about twenty custom maps that can make for interesting strategic situations.  Two of them (one of Western Europe/North Africa and one of Spain) are based on historical landmasses.  If I have to criticize the scenarios for anything, it would be this; the game depends heavily on resources.  As long as you have the population to conscript soldiers, the gold to pay for them, and the food to support them, there is no real limit on the size of your forces.  On the other hand, limitations on any of those three things severely hampers you.  This means that it can be a long and drawn-out process of conquering the finals enemy city or cities (there can be up to 8 at a time), even though the eventual outcome is not really in doubt.  This kills the suspense a bit.
The music is generally pretty good.  A few tracks are quite catchy.  It helps pass the time.
Another great thing about this game is the map editor.  Suffice it to say that you can create very complex and interesting maps and missions with this thing if you put the time into it.  This is a game that works for people who just want to sit down and play (that's what the premade campaigns and maps are for) or for someone who basically wants to create his own game.
I've greatly enjoyed this game.  If you're into historical RTS games, give this one a shot.

Not bad, but didn't fix any of the problems. Let's start with the good things. The story isn't bad, as well as the graphics or city. There are a lot of side quests as well as a lot of enemies, which keeps things interesting. They add a few new items, as well as a few combat tricks which keep things interesting. Now the problem. There wasn't much done new. The combat is basically the same, its in the same city, you fight penguin, joker is the main enemy, killer croc, and bane. Fighting the same enemies every single game gets boring. Take a risk guys. They didn't fix the biggest problem with the last game, the platforming. You will be moving around the city and for some reasons tons  of ledges won't be able to be used for grappling. You will even be looking at something you've used before it and won't let you, only to let you once you've looked at it in a tiny different angle. Half the time you grapple something behind you instead. They really screwed up navigating the city like this. Then there is combat/stealth. They make things not intuitive and not easy to use. To use a smoke pellet you can press a button, but only if you've been found does it work. Then later it won't work that same way, and you have to press a button to switch to it, then press 2 buttons at the same time to use it. I would constantly start getting shot but there would be nothing I could quickly do, which is just dumb.  Most of the abilities in stealth are like this and require weapon switching and 2 button pressing, which aren't helpful in the moment. Same goes for dropping spray bomb. There is a quick use button, but to detonate you have to switch weapons to use it then hold 2 buttons (why?!).  There are times with takedowns that just don't make sense. Like how when grabbing a guy from a gargoyle and doing inverted takedown, you can't cover his mouth, making it a loud takedown, which is dumb. When you try to grapple to ledges it automatically makes you get up and over, which is dumb if you want to do ledge takedowns. Same goes for grate takedowns, as he could easily grab them into the vent, but he jumps out into open for no reason. Multiple times you get stuck on the environment and the game just flat out doesn't work correctly. I would sly down from a stoop and land on a ledge right next to a guy standing there.......but you can't do a jump tackle from that close or do ANYTHING....I would press the attack button and my guy would just stand up on the ledge and try punching the air in front of him, instead of doing something productive like he should do, and I would ultimately get found out.  Blade dodging and the shield run-up smash move both are spotty and unnecessarily hard to complete, due to direction and pressing the buttons and doing everything correctly, but them not working.
The camera could not be worse in the game. When you dodge or run in circles, it stays put and looks behind you instead of the way you are facing. You can turn it but it is a pain. Constantly in boss fights or in regular combat I would dodge out of the way and it would turn the camera in a way I couldn't see the people in front of me or the person coming at me, and let to me getting hit very often. It has to be one of the worst camera's in a 3rd person action game that I've seen in a while. It just doesn't move intuitively and always seems to be looking a way that doesn't help you. There are a few bad boss fights (2/2 Bane fights) where the mechanics don't work well by overcrowding with guys, and the advice the game gives you is wrong. Sometimes the game is unclear where you need to go or whether or not you can grapple onto something or use something, leading to you getting lost. This is annoying when you sometimes have to backtrack and other times don't. The game does a lame rip-off of assassins creed by having you do eagle-eye towers (sorry, called comms towers in this). They still love to do missions and things with 100's of collectibles, which should only be for art or something for those tryhards that want to waste time. Also costumes should be able to be used in first game. So due to the combat and stealth mechanics and button problems not being intuitive, or well done, the terrible platforming, and other smaller things, the game is a solid 7/10.

I am not generally one for platformers on the PC, but Ori was recommended by so many people I got it in the last wave of the summer sale.  I cannot recommend this game enough (unless you hate playing platform games, then you should get it for someone you love that does, and watch them ;).
The writing, puzzles, skills, art, music, are all exemplary. I really like the Shinto storytelling lore and style, and Ori uses many of the same nature and spirit trappings, so I was hooked very early on :)
I really like the use of saves, and the rewards for exploring the map, which forces you to master the skills available (or waiting until you do have them) to reach them, which pays forward to the one part that is really hard about this game, the escape sequences.
Some reviewers have complained that there aren't enough clues as to where to go during these sequences.  That is a true statement, but the real lesson is one of focus, you are being forced into a panic/flee situation, with both the environment and monsters in your way.  It forces you to know the controls well so you can just pay attention to what/where and now how.  However, it also punishes you for using a keyboard and mouse, sometimes heavily (the door fragments near the top of Sorrow Pass especially).  This is the only thing I will take off of a 10 on this, is the lack of key remapping.  Shift, Control, R, S. W, all do important very specific things, usually chorded, or in rapid order.  If I could have remapped one or 2 of those to my Naga (especially dash), this game would've been much less frustrating, especially in the 1.5-3min all or nothing escape sequences. I imagine with a full XBOX controller, it would likely be fine, but I don't use one with PC games (and I never got around to buying an xbox :P).
FWIW, I played through on Normal. I haven't tried any of the other difficulty levels, though there are achievements for that sort of thing available for the die-hards out there.

The Celtic Kings RTS franchise from Haemimont Games has a few mechanics that are true throughout all 3 titles: Celtic Kings: Rage of War, Celtic Kings: The Punic Wars (aka Nemesis of the Roman Empire) and Imperivm III: The Great Battles of Rome (which was only released in Italy and Spain, has no official english translation).
The mechanics are as follows:
- When game starts, there are neutral buildings and villages to take.  Some are defended by neutral oppositions and some are not and can be yours when one of your units gets close enough.  When you press space it opens are really well designed level map that is generated just like the level.  In this view, you can direct the buildings you control to supply resources back to your base, if you so choose.  Some buildings train units to be higher level, some generate gold if you supply it with 2000 gold to start off it's "business", some convert gold into food.  Putting units into a building does the age of empires thing and sends arrows flying from the fortification.  The more men in building the more arrows get thrown.
- There is no actual construction of buildings in this franchise.  It's military-based, the buildings all start fully constructed.  It's about conquering them to use them to overpower the enemy, eventually taking their camp for the win.  You hire a hero, attach units and try to progress the hero (and hopefully the units) to have field experience that levels them up to be stronger.  What doesn't kill them, makes them stronger after a fight.
- Buildings cannot be fully destroyed.  They can be damaged and repaired, but mostly, buildings stay alive.  What gets destroyed/killed are the units inside the buildings you are trying to invade.  When you bring ur hero or unit to a building taken by enemy, you have to right-click on it to "intimidate" the building back into your color.  If there is enemy approaching and is a substantial force/army, the intimidation will fail and the enemy color numbers will regenerate to 100%.  If it's not as substantial as the intimidating force, the building will succum to changing colors/teams, although slower, if there is enemy military presence nearby.
Those are the mechanics that stay true throughout all 3 titles of the Celtic Kings series.
That's the gist of it.
I'm a long time player of Celtic Kings: Rage of War, Celtic Kings: The Punic Wars (also known as Nemesis of the Roman Empire aka, this one) and  Imperivm III GBR.  Both Celtic Kings games were more polished even pre-steam release then Imperivm III GBR;  Nemesis of the Roman Empire and Imperivm III GBR introduce extremely unique game-play elements (like unit and hero skills) that make this RTS franchise standout for me and are even more interesting in Imperivm III: GBR.  Nemesis is the transition game from the CK1 mechanics into the full GBR mechanics.  It's the in-between game and rightfully so, as it's the 2nd of the 3rd installment.
To those not familiar with the Celtic Kings series from Haemimont Games, know this:
The skill-based mechanics offer unique RTS precedent.  They are historically and relligiously modeled after the civilizations of the time.  It really feels empowering, commanding an army and setting up formations to best utilize the skills against the formation and unit types of incoming enemy army;  However know that Celtic Kings 1, Nemesis, and GBR all have very different mechanics between them.  CK1 is stat-based units, Nemesis is hybrid of skills and stats (doesn't have hero-based skill sets tho), and GBR has stats, skills that give very unique gameplay mechanics to -each- unit and even hero skill sets to level up that give bonuses to hero and/or army.
Variation examples:
Example (GBR): Roman Hastatus has 10 points of stamina-based, called "Deflection".  Each deflection costs the hastatus -1 stamina.  Britannian swordman has the skill "Tripple Damage".  The swordsman does x3 damage, costing -1 stamina per hit.  What will happen in this case is the Roman Hastatus soldier will tank -1 point of stamina (which will recharge slowly in fight, as long as the unit is fed) and recieve 0 damage until stamina runs out, while the Briton swordman will still be losing health trying to tire out the roman's shield since the hastatus is continuously attacking the Briton swordman.  An army of only hastatus versus an army of only briton swordsmen will absolutely annihilate the Brittannian swordmen army.  The Britannian hero and units would have to severely out-level the Roman hero and hastatus army to even stand a chance in that match up.
Example (Nemesis): The units have special skills that boost stats.  The hastatus shield's "Defense stance" gives bonus stats when unit is holding ground while in combat, instead of absorbing all damage for a block and not losing any health at all.  The hastatus was later changed in GBR to have "Deflection" instead of "Defensive stance".  Swordsman to swordsman, the roman hastatus vs the gaul duel will play out in a more stat-focused fashion.  The roman hastatus with "defensive stance" will take damage each time, but just less of it.  It still will win against a gaul swordsman, but the gaul swordsman will, at least, do damage to the hastatus before he dies, ergo in Nemesis there is leeway in being able to be more worthy in battle against a non-compatible unit.  The gaul swordsman in GBR has learning ability.  Each successful hit, it gets +1 experience point, eventuall gaining a level (until hitting the max level researched in the Gaul arena).
In short, GBR formations require mixed armies and then insuring that units designed to counter other unts are matched in combat, better then your opponent is doing against you.
In Nemesis, this is much more lenient.  There are still units that counter other units better, but overall, you successfully deal damage to the units, allowing more leg room.  I'm not quite a fan of that, I prefer the GBR mechanics more, it's the more unique one, with no RTS on the market having such an interesting skill-based counter-unit mechanic emphasis.
Formations are incredibly important.  Each formation gives a certain kind of bonus stat to each unit under hero's regiment.
It has a level editor that allows some C++ scripting, randomly generated terrains and levels (like age of empires) a polished AI and even to this day, excellent graphics and sprite animations.

The Devil May Cry franchise has long been one of my favorites. The games hold a special place in my heart and memory, they were the most cathartic way to get rid of frustration and anger in my angst-filled teen years. Now even as an adult I enjoy popping in one of the originals and battling demons for an hour or two with the wise-cracking Dante. I was in love with the story, riddled with holes as it was, and helplessly in love with Dante.
Upon hearing that the current DMC universe was being abandoned you could not find anyone else more upset about it than I was. I was angry and felt betrayed by Capcom, who were cutting short a story I had spent years in. The new Dante character design was bad, his attitude was at best childish. Stubborn as I am, months turned into a year and I began to realize that change was indeed needed. Ninja Theory seemed to be at least listening to what the fans were saying and with the release of the first player footage my mind began to slowly turn from general hatred of the game to feeling that maybe it would not be so bad.
I personally feel this game to be somewhat of a prequel to DMC3. There's a lot of interaction between the brothers in this game. And in the end I believe is the reason vergil despises his brother dante in the classics. Now the game revolves around propaganda and a group of revolties. Very similar to the antics of V of V for Vendetta. Mundus makes an appearance as once again the antagonist of the game. They even gave him the 3 eyes just like his DMC1 counterpart as a reference. If you played DMC1 than you know Mundu's wants to rule the world and our hero has to stop him, but it's more than that. All this little things really help build up the story till the very end. I don't want to spoil anything so I'll leave it at that.
The gameplay is awesome, very smooth transitions from the sword swings. You only get around 7 weapons, 3 guns, 2 angel, 2 demon weapons which is a downer for us who like to have more in our arsenal. If you are expecting dante to give us a little exhibition like he did in DMC3 when he acquires new gear than think again. Now for the DT (Devil Trigger), you do more damage, are faster, get white hair and a vibrant red coat. To me it's not as cool as the other DMCs but again this is a reboot so it's expected.
The sound for the most part is pretty much what you would expect. Voice acting is top notch, music is metal and screamo. It's alright imo.
There are a few little things that could have been done better, but when it comes down to what's important, the game was extremely fun. Metroid: Other M.

Rating 8/10
Overview: Action/Adventure
The Good:
+ The story takes place over the course of Christmas eve. Batman has a contract on his head and has to take down multiple assassins out to kill him. The story is very well written and more cohesive than arkham city. The pacing is also excellent as the story begins to unfold the game gets more interesting.
+ Crime scene investigations have been improved by adding a holographic video of the crime taking place while you investigate. It is a small addition to an otherwise mundane activity but it does add a lot in terms of the feeling of solving a mystery.
+ Combat once again remains mostly the same with a few added enemies for good measure. There are however 2 big differences compared to the other games. The first is that more powerful combat techniques are locked behind main/side quests and challenges, making them much harder to get early on (and in some cases missable) and thus making combat more challenging especially in the early parts of the game. The second is the addition of the electric gloves, another item obtained later in the game. These gloves charge up as you punch enemies and once fully charged you can toggle the option to become nearly unstoppable: punching through any enemy regardless of what they are carrying or doing. It is practically a "win" button if you find combat too frustrating. The difficulty curve for combat goes from hard to frustrating to ridiculously easy.
+ Every boss battle is unique and fun to play. Granted some of these bosses are more flash than substance but it still feels epic to take one of these bosses down.
+ Once again Riddler collectables are scattered across the map for you to find. You can (once again) find riddler informants to 'interrogate' to reveal the location on your mini map. Although I liked collecting these I also found the puzzles associated with them to be simpler than Arkham City. So long as you had the right item, it wasn't very difficult to collect any of these. I was a bit disappointed with the riddler trophies this time around.
+ Predator/Combat maps are available for those who want to play some post game content. Both combat and predator maps are MUCH easier than the previous two games.
+ Although the voice actors are not the same they do an excellent job of representing their characters
+ Great soundtrack
The Average:
The games biggest 'fault' is that from a design standpoint it is almost identical to arkham city. The game doesn't do anything particularly new, if you played arkahm city then this game offers little surprise in terms of its gameplay, you've done it all before.
Christmas Eve in Gotham means nobody is outside, no people, no cars, no...anything, just criminals looking to terrorize the city. Arkham city was able to get around this by saying this was a section of the city solely for criminals, it just feels weird in this game gliding around a city with nobody in it.
Surprisingly the multiplayer is still active, even more surprisingly the multiplayer is actually fun. There are only 2 game modes and 4 maps and only one game mode is still active, it was still a lot of fun to play and it is definitely worth checking out. The problem is the community is slowly fading away and it is getting harder and harder to get a good game going. A lot of achievements are for multiplayer as well.
The Bad:
- The game crashed on a few occasions and I experienced a few glitches, nothing a restart couldn't fix however the game clearly lacks polish.
-Missable upgrades for combat may frustrate players or completionists.
Conclusion
The game starts off slow and it wasn't really doing much for me. It wasn't until the story really starts to pick up that things start getting interesting. Locking important upgrades for combat also soured me a bit in the beginning but does make sense given the story and for gameplay reasons. One problem with Arkham City was that you could obtain some of the best combat upgrades early making combat feel very trivial for the rest of the game. The boss battles are excellent but also the gameplay/build up to the boss battles as well. Every boss battle you face feels climatic.
You could argue that this game is a cash grab however its a damn good cash grab. If you loved both Batman games by Rocksteady, especially Arkham City then more likely than not you too will like this game, hopefully you are not burned out by the same gameplay.

I've always loved platformers, have been playing them since the Spectrum era.
Having said that, I strongly dislike this game, mostly due to the controls/phyics of the main character, and the "humor"/personality infused in it.
I found the jumping mechanics, controls and character physics to be pretty unintuitive, hard to get into, and frequently felt the game didn't even respond to my commands (they either feel like they're ignored by the game or that there's a delay). This was playing with an xbox gamepad, as recommended by the game itself.
The character's hitbox feels bigger than visually apparent, which leads to frequently running into instadeath traps that you felt like you otherwise would avoid.
The other thing I dislike is the "humor" or "personality". This is of course subjective, but most of it is either references to older videogames (with no humor itself, just a reference), references to memes, or "it's funny because it's extreme violence against cartoons", Happy Tree Friends style juvenile humor. I'm all for use of extreme violence for a joke, but it just falls flat in this one. I ignored it at first but it keeps getting pushed into your face to the point of grating.
The positives for this game are the visual polish in the menu areas, even if the art style is mostly monocromatic and bland, there's lots of little animations in the menus (unfortunately, the game itself looks fairly flat like a flash game, which it initially was, clashing with the high contrast of the game menus).

One of the most difficult and challenging platformers in the market, and has been for a while now. This game does so many things well as a platformer. The game is designed with player convenience in mind, especially when it comes to ameliorating frustration. You may die over and over again, but when you do, the game disregards already-seen cutscenes and dialogue so you can get back into the fray without delay. It also avoids looping music upon death so you don't get annoyed at the amazing sountrack. This is further improved by fast-paced gameplay and short levels. Good game design, check.
By far the most attractive part of the game is the soundtrack. Danny Baranowsky's compositions belong in a McMillen game, with hard rock riffs and dramatic choirs composed to mimic the kitsch melodrama of blockbuster movies against a backdrop of flying meat cubes and buzz saws. Bad♥♥♥♥♥ to say the least. Awesome soundtrack, check.
There's also a ton of content in the game that will definitely keep you busy, with over 300 levels divided across seven worlds (and their darker counterparts, providing an even harder challenge for harder players) and 25 characters, many of which must be earned and all of which are uniquely designed to enable players to replay the game differently. For fifteen bucks, I would say this game is a steal. On top of all that, you can edit, publish, and play levels of your own or of others around the world. Tons of content for sure.
I will say, the visuals aren't the strongest part of the game. Most of the cutscenes are wrought in the archaic Flash program, and thus are very simple in their rednering and animation. However, Edmund makes good use of the medium to convey a queerily whimsical world through bouncy styles and thick, cutesy linework. Decent visuals, sure.
The story isn't much to remember honestly. It's a classic damsel-in-distress type of story that has hit its peak in interest eons ago. That said, it's wrought through such ridiculous renderings and strange characters that the experience is still somewhat of a novelty. Some would argue it's a parody of that classic plot trope, but I would not. In any case, you won't be playing this for the story, and it isn't like it will turn you off. Quite the opposite actually. Okay story, yeah.
But overall, this game is well worth the fifteen bucks and more. I also really suggest purchasing the soundtrack, it's too excellent to not add to your video game soundtrack playlist. Five out of five chicken nuggets.

Spec Ops: The Line presents a really interesting idea, but fails to execute it in a believable way.
I can't understand the praise this game gets. I appreciate what this game is trying to do by tackling the stress and horrors of war, a subject most games skim over, but it fails to tackle the subject in and engaging way and only supported by mediocre gameplay.
To its merit, this game does have some good Call Of Duty action movie style set pieces, a great, but sparingly used soundtrack, a couple of really good characters, and good voice acting to go with them. The game is about 5 hours long, which is a little on the short side to me.
However...
The third person cover based game play works, but really has nothing that makes it particularly exciting or even interesting. The opponents AI is predictable and tends to only charge the player, which seems strange since they are meant to be a professional military. Many of the guns feel very similar to use, and the game is rather easy if you stick to cover (although I only played on medium difficulty). There is a lot of big action sequences in this game that while really cool, are not very realistic. I think that perhaps a different approach to gameplay could have helped convey the story better.
I was recommended this game because of its story, but I found this to be its biggest let down. The story just isn't believable and player character is annoying.
I'll try to avoid spoilers.
Spec Ops is advertised as a game that will "challenge players' morality by putting them in the middle of unspeakable situations," however this never really happens, because in these 'unspeakable situations' you have no choice at all. Failure to perform whatever horrible action will cause the mission to fail, and you must load a checkpoint. I think this idea would me much better executed if instead the player was forced to choose between two bad options, rather than being simply forced to do something or the mission fails.
The player characters scripted decisions further detract from the believability of the story with him very quickly disregarding his original mission, and instead deciding to try and fix everything himself. His two companions realise that he is making bad decisions and comment on it, but for some reason never actually do anything about it and just follow along.
However there are some pretty cool action movie bad guys in this game, however their placement is what is meant to be a realistic war just makes the story less believable.
Perhaps I just don't see what everyone else does, but this game just didn't do it for me.
Spec Ops: The Line isn't a bad game, it's just not anything special. If shooters are really your then, then you might want to pick this one up when it's on sale, but if you're looking for a deep and harrowing story then you had best look elsewhere.

The new game steals music from users who legally purchased the game while the license was still active. This is not okay nor is it legal. Putting up a new copy of the game online so that new customers don't get the expired songs music is how this should have been handled, but they had no right to remove the songs from copies that were legally purchased by the end user while the license was still active. It's no different than if they illegally hacked your X-box to remove access to the songs from the hard copy of the game or if a music company hacked your computer to erase some MP3 files that you bought and downloaded because the publisher lost the license for some of the songs on it.

Not a bad game, but it certainly tests your limits. It's rather clever in it's execution, imho. Hear noises? Footsteps coming up behind you? Stop! Whatever you do, don't run...or walk. It's our natural instinct to run from things that scare us. But this evilly challenges that instinct and makes you yield to your fear. Very clever, indeed.
My only real gripe with the game is that the music tends to get too loud and you can't hear your surroundings. Let's be honest, if you were actually walking in a forest there wouldn't be any scary music playing in the background. I wish I could at least turn it down or completely off. To me the music really spoils the mood and takes something away from the game. Yes, it's spooky but that's not my problem with it.
Another problem with the game is that there's no save button or automatic save from your last death. It can get tedious to have to start all over again especially if you don't die by "it". If you die by "it" then I can understand starting again, but the way I kept dying was getting annoying.
My last concern with this game is that there's no instructions about what keys to use. Even clicked on the info button on the first screen and all it brought up was a bunch of specs. Nothing about how to turn a flashlight on or how to run. Both of which I only found out that existed because I visited the forum. You're not suppose to use those things, of course, but then again shouldn't the developers tell you so they can trick you into using them? That would seem like dirty pool and I'm surprised they didn't. (By the way, F for flashlight and shift for run. Use at your own risk.)
All in all, I'm really liking this game and I'm determined to make it to the end. My main cause of death most of the time is falling off the beam whilst trying to make it to the other side of the cliff. Is "it" pushing me off of it or am I really that bad at crossing it? Most likely it's the latter.

DmC manages a fantastic balancing act between accessibility and depth -- the first time through, weapons, moves, and enemies are introduced at a measured enough pace to make it possible to keep up with them, but there's still a massive scope for building your skills and racking up massive scores with SSS combos in battles that used to be a struggle just to survive, just by mastering the systems and weapons. Different weapons are swapped in instantaneously using the triggers as a modifier, and it results in a really wide toolbox of attacks that can be strung together in very satisfying ways.
The combat is the real reason to play, but this is also a fantastic-looking game, particularly in terms of the imaginative environments, which make heavy use of ripped and distorted versions of real-world locations. And being on PC running 60 fps helps a lot too. The story and dialogue is a bit less successful -- it has enjoyable moments, but is on the heavy-handed side in terms of its satire.
Despite going into this with no expectations or background in the series or genre, I liked it enough to play through the game and the DLC on four consecutive difficulty settings, going up to Dante Must Die, and would name it my Game of the Year for 2013. It also inspired me to seek out more in this genre, which I had mostly ignored previously.

I've decided to rewrite my review as the complete version of Episode One is finished. I would strongly recommend Hitman to any fans of stealth action, as it is a remarkable game that will leave you immersed in a beautifully designed world. At least until one of the 3 voice actors they have spoils the mood cause you just killed the guy who sounded just like him. Everything about the game feels refined (except for the voice acting) with each mission being a gigantic sandbox full of exploration and small details.
The episode release format you likely heard the drama about is now over, but the way they released games was a solid idea allowing them to focus on one specific map at a time and then moving on to the next after releasing it. The game is very good and any fan of Hitman should certainly get it. When you get this game, just go ahead and turn off hints, Instinct, and the Mipmap to see this game in its true glory! Also, as of this review, the hardest difficulty is behind a mission lock where you have to get a certain ranking to unlock, I hope to see that changed asap as this mode is the quintessential Blood money feel (aside from getting a newspaper about your hit at the end)

This review (more of a salty rant than a review, actually) focuses on gameplay ONLY. I don't care about the graphics, I don't care about the always-online DRM or whatever, if my third-world internet connection of 10k can handle never crashing once during 90+ hours, you have no reason to complain. Go away.
Oh. Great. Yet another patch that penalizes creativity in favor of adding crappy scripted nonsense and completely shutting down any attempts at recreating Blood Money's gameplay. What's that? The community found out that shooting somewhere makes guards suspicious? Nah, too realistic. Gone. What? The gameplay is too inconsistent, you say? Well, let's add in head movement for no reason! That's what everyone wanted, right? Oh, so the community found a way of dealing with two people at once without having to wait around for 16 months? Nah, removed by replacing the way the "compromised" feature works with a completely asinine "unconcious witness" stat. Basically, as soon as anyone even REMOTELY SLIGHTLY MAYBE catches a GLIMPSE of you doing ANYTHING, they're a witness and you might as well restart. Add in the fact that basically nothing anyone's ACTUALLY asked for has been implemented or fixed, like 1. fixing head movement, 2. fixing the inconsistency with silent attacks, where if you're standing behind someone but you're 4 degrees off, you won't silent attack them but instead punch them in the face and get spotted, 3. fixing the lock-on mechanics, 4. not nerfing everything that's even remotely fun into the ground? and you'll find out that IOI just doesn't give two ♥♥♥♥s (anymore?). Also, the new "Professional" difficulty is the cheapest, laziest attempt at a difficulty spike imaginable. Move or remove every item or disguise that's there in "Normal" difficulty, make every melee weapon practically useless, add cameras and enforcer guards at every corner and you have the uninspired mess that is "Professional". Clearly just advertising for getting more people to buy the "Full Experience" for another 50 bucks.
The game itself definitely has the potential to be better than, or at least on par with, Blood Money, but as it stands right now, with all the crap listed above and a lot, LOT more quirks and annoyances worthy of complaining about that I couldn't be bothered to write down, it's just a little better than Absolution. Which, needless to say, is not very impressive. But, I assume IOI won't put down the nerf gun anytime soon, if ever, so unless you like following mindless "Opportunities*" (at the current pace, in a few months there won't be any actual gameplay left, just opportunities) and annoying everyone with your 12 hours of gameplay time and statements such as "wow good grafiks!!!", save your money until this game takes its (rightful?) place as the successor of Blood Money. However, I'm not holding onto too much hope there.
*Opportunity: Highly scripted tutorial-esque solution for completing certain levels that literally tell you what, when and how to do something in order to beat the mission.
TL;DR: Fun things get patched, bugs, glitches and restrictive gameplay get enforced or ignored.
Edit April 9, 2017: Last patch has brought back legshots as well as other qualify of life changes. Maybe IO has started caring?

Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Just got my 100% Completion after 105 hours (on/off for 2 years). Recommend with warnings. Summary below pro/cons.
Pros
+ Amazing graphics, beautiful lighting and skybox.I played at 1440p and this is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.
+ Vehicle combat and satisfying progression systems
+ Unexpectedly good story and world. More-than-serviceable.
+ Hot air balloons
+ No missable achievements
Mixed
+/- loads of content here, still about 40% of content was remaining for me after story completion.
+/- Repetitive. If something is good, repetition isn't all that bad. Vice/versa.
Cons
- excessive collectibles
- "overly specific" challenges ("Let's be overly specific" being the name of an ACTUAL challenge)
- some gameplay systems work against each other, especially apparent after story completion
Summary: The pros of Mad Max greatly outweight the cons and I would recommend anyone at least complete the story content. There will likely be a great deal of content remaining after finishing the story. There will be a crossroads once you finish the story and I can't entirely recommend continuing at that point.  I will elaborate below so read if interested.
Elaborating on post-game
1. POINTLESS LEVELS - Max continues to level up, I was level 191 and all points will already be allocated by level 100. The problem is that I am continually reminded of this each time I level up. It's better than gaining no levels or upgrades at least.
2. GAMEPLAY DESIGN FLAWS/QUIRKS -There are challenges requiring Max to clear all areas of enemies, yet there are also challenges requiring you to defeat enemies in particular ways. The game can become a huge grind if you clear all areas before completing the combat challenges. This is due to enemies becoming very rare. I remain very grateful that all challenges are still possible to complete without missing.
This was a far, far better game than I thought it would be. I have always been a Mad MAx fan and this game truly does the franchise justice.

I've always loved platformers, have been playing them since the Spectrum era.
Having said that, I strongly dislike this game, mostly due to the controls/phyics of the main character, and the "humor"/personality infused in it.
I found the jumping mechanics, controls and character physics to be pretty unintuitive, hard to get into, and frequently felt the game didn't even respond to my commands (they either feel like they're ignored by the game or that there's a delay). This was playing with an xbox gamepad, as recommended by the game itself.
The character's hitbox feels bigger than visually apparent, which leads to frequently running into instadeath traps that you felt like you otherwise would avoid.
The other thing I dislike is the "humor" or "personality". This is of course subjective, but most of it is either references to older videogames (with no humor itself, just a reference), references to memes, or "it's funny because it's extreme violence against cartoons", Happy Tree Friends style juvenile humor. I'm all for use of extreme violence for a joke, but it just falls flat in this one. I ignored it at first but it keeps getting pushed into your face to the point of grating.
The positives for this game are the visual polish in the menu areas, even if the art style is mostly monocromatic and bland, there's lots of little animations in the menus (unfortunately, the game itself looks fairly flat like a flash game, which it initially was, clashing with the high contrast of the game menus).

One of the most difficult and challenging platformers in the market, and has been for a while now. This game does so many things well as a platformer. The game is designed with player convenience in mind, especially when it comes to ameliorating frustration. You may die over and over again, but when you do, the game disregards already-seen cutscenes and dialogue so you can get back into the fray without delay. It also avoids looping music upon death so you don't get annoyed at the amazing sountrack. This is further improved by fast-paced gameplay and short levels. Good game design, check.
By far the most attractive part of the game is the soundtrack. Danny Baranowsky's compositions belong in a McMillen game, with hard rock riffs and dramatic choirs composed to mimic the kitsch melodrama of blockbuster movies against a backdrop of flying meat cubes and buzz saws. Bad♥♥♥♥♥ to say the least. Awesome soundtrack, check.
There's also a ton of content in the game that will definitely keep you busy, with over 300 levels divided across seven worlds (and their darker counterparts, providing an even harder challenge for harder players) and 25 characters, many of which must be earned and all of which are uniquely designed to enable players to replay the game differently. For fifteen bucks, I would say this game is a steal. On top of all that, you can edit, publish, and play levels of your own or of others around the world. Tons of content for sure.
I will say, the visuals aren't the strongest part of the game. Most of the cutscenes are wrought in the archaic Flash program, and thus are very simple in their rednering and animation. However, Edmund makes good use of the medium to convey a queerily whimsical world through bouncy styles and thick, cutesy linework. Decent visuals, sure.
The story isn't much to remember honestly. It's a classic damsel-in-distress type of story that has hit its peak in interest eons ago. That said, it's wrought through such ridiculous renderings and strange characters that the experience is still somewhat of a novelty. Some would argue it's a parody of that classic plot trope, but I would not. In any case, you won't be playing this for the story, and it isn't like it will turn you off. Quite the opposite actually. Okay story, yeah.
But overall, this game is well worth the fifteen bucks and more. I also really suggest purchasing the soundtrack, it's too excellent to not add to your video game soundtrack playlist. Five out of five chicken nuggets.

There were times in the game that i honestly was so mad that i wanted to post a negative review giving it 0/10, it's that annoying. The game is unforgiving, there are all kinds of traps in places you can't possibly expect. You'll have to repeat certain areas time and time again, moving one step at a time to find out what traps lies on the next step. It's almost like the ones who made this game want you to die repeatedly, which is bewildering. However, if you decide to go on with the game and reach the end you'll realize that it was worth it. I'm a fan of the Arkham games and their blend of open world looting, fluid-fighting encounters and linear story polished to an expert sheen by developers Rock Steady.
This time around we have WB Games Montréal in control. And unfortunately it shows that they are no Rock Steady.
We're given a prequel because really that's the safest route to take before Rock Steady resume control. However this process of exposition and discovery (Who's the Joker? Who's Batman?) is incoherently handled. The story is supposed to take place over the course of one night and to shoe-horn all of these villains, Batman, his relationship with Gordon is just asking too much.
If the plot isn't much cop you'd expect the game mechanics to be solid. And they are. Mostly. WB Games Montréal haven't sought to change much. They've added weapons and have a slightly different unlocking system which works in conjunction with the challenge modes. If you're not into those, like me, certain things won't unlock as you play the campaign.
It feels overly complicated and you can't help but feel that the designers wanted to provided a padded out package that would last for a long time. Having completed the game and only unlocked 33% that much is clear. After a while solving the Enigma puzzles or pursuing side objectives can wear thin.
The main problem with gameplay is a headfirst dive into the world of extreme button prompts. Boss fights are half normal scrapping and then after a certain point in the health bar, we are prompted to press X to repeatedly beat someone up.  This allows fights to be presented very cinematically but you become a spectator more than a integral part of the action.
The campaign eventually focuses on the Joker who manages to be an annoyance rather than a dark malevolent terror. His pitbull Bane is someone you have to fight repeatedly and the only reason for that I can think of is padding.
Throughout the somewhat underwhelming campaign there are still moments of thrills, excitement and achievement. It would help if the complexity of the combat controls was better communicated and Bats could benefit from more fluid movement in general. Sometimes he slows to a plodding walk with fists braced when you really want him to dart into the shadows.
Finally bugs. Oh WB Games Montréal. I'm usually lucky enough to play AAA games whose bugs are either completely benign or mostly invisible to me.
But Origins has far too many obvious ones where fights don't trigger and Bats is left wandering around staring into the eyes of his foes or disappearing into walls or sinking into the floor when fighting Bane.
You can restart and all will be well but it's disappointing to see. WB Games Montréal also decided to not fix these bugs in favour of problems which would stop you completing the game. I understand the prioritisation but not the lack of committment to making the best game they possibly could.  Bear their name in mind the next time you see a WB game.
If you're a Batman completist then go for this but otherwise you're not missing much and can safely skip to Rock Steady's Batman game due in 2015.

In this review I will go over the basic gameplay and explain the Pro and Cons to this game. For a shorter review scroll to the bottom and read the summery.
APB is a MMO third person shooter based on the idea of Cops vs Criminals. Players queue for matches in district servers to do mini pvp matches against each other which take place in various parts of the map. There are 2 "PVE" maps and 2"PVP maps currently. The two PVE maps are the Finacial and Waterfront, each hold their own factions alliances in the district. Players either pledge to a specific contact to level up their standing with them or just play at random leveling up whoever is available.

Both Criminals and Enforcers (Cops) get their own specific gameplay that they can do while in the game. Criminals can operate burgleries by ramming into stores and storage units to steal the items inside,or robbing civilians on the street, then fence the items at their closest contact. Once the items are turned in the criminals are then required to go to the "Money Launder" to collect the cash. Enforcers can participate in this as well, it is called "Wittness Mode". While a Enforcer is driving about he can patrol for Criminals commiting crimes and when he finds them he presses the Wittness Key, default Alt, and him and the criminal are now put into a mission where the Enforcer needs to get the evidence to the lock up while the Criminal needs to get it to the fence. This is a very unique system that is very entertaining and always present in the game. Enforcers also get a unique gameplay choice which is Less Than Lethal weapons. LTL weapons are the games way of making it more interesting and putting a twist on the game. When using LTL weapons, the Enforcer stuns the enemy and then arrests the Criminal. Criminals are able to free their team mates from handcuffs but only if they can make it there in time. The advantage to LTL is it makes the spawn timer longer, with the disadvantage that the LTL have a shorter range and require time to arrest Criminals putting the Enforcer in danger of enemy fire.
Being that the game is a third person shooter, the game is less about skill and more about placement. Covering corners and knowing the range of your weapons as well as how they fire can give you a large advantage over players who are simply pointing and shooting. The starting rifle both Crims and Enforcers start with is incredibly good, both in accuracy and power but it must be fired with control burst instead of full auto otherwise it loses it's strengths. That being said the game is incredibly unfriendly to new players, it has such a large learning curve that it causes most people to give up and stop playing. Because of that the playerbase is reletively smaller and all the players tend to merge into the "Silver" districts which can cause unfair match making. New players should be recomended to play on the "Bronze" servers until they learn the ropes better and are ready for the big servers.
One of the biggest gripes about the game is the cash shop, yes the cash shop sells weapons. Before you drop the game though you should know the weapons in the cash shop have very little difference compared to the "free" weapons. Most CS weapons are infact reskins of the free ones, with the exception of the few that are special/unique weapons. One of the most powerful weapons in the game is also one of the first ones you unlock for free. Most of what comes out of the cash shop is cosmetic items that are for cars and clothes.
So now that we went over the basics and you have a little bit of an understanding of what you are getting into, lets get into the good things about this game. Number one of all time is, the customization. Free players are limited on how much customization they can do in the game, but even then I've seen amazing things come from free people. You can style everything from the clothes you wear to the logos on them, from the tattoos on your body to how fat you want to be. Customize your car, it's color, the model, the decals, the lisence plate, body kits, even interior design on some of them. Your weapons can be modifide depending if you unlocked guns with open mod slots. Do you like your gun shooting faster, more accurate, longer range, better zoom, better hipfire, bigger magazine, or maybe you like to carry more ammo. You can use mods to change that. Even with your car too, Nitro, Steel plating, mobile spawn, mobile ammo supply, or even have a brick that can be used when you jump out of your car to launch it at enemy players. Players can add mods to their character as well to carry ammo, be able to survive hits from vehicles, reduce fall damage, or even ride ontop of cars without falling off. The game has endless combinations and possiblities that you can take advantage of and have fun with.
The conclusion, if you can get around the very steep learning curve, get over the cash shop selling weapons and just have fun with the game, you will enjoy it. This game is one of the few games where customization is literally at your command. Dress as a business man, or run around half naked, it's your choice. Alter your weapons to your play style and make your dream car, it's all in your hands. The game is definately worth a try for people who like shooters, but remember that the game can put you in unfair match making at times. This is because of the size of the playerbase, the more people play the better match making gets. Those of you who just read the bottom and are thinking of trying the game, I suggest you give the whole review a once over to understand what I'm talking about completely and half some understanding of what you are going to be doing ingame.

The AI is much better than in recent installments, but isn't as unforgiving as in Blood Money, or the earlier titles. This shouldn't deter long-time fans, because a difficulty increase is easily availible in the form of Escalations.
Speaking of Escalations; they're the reason I keep playing this game. Hell, I haven't finished the main story, and don't intend to until I have unlocked the mastery levels for each location. I have a feeling that doing so will make the storyline missions much more enjoyable, and make me feel like an elite assassin.
Buy this, if you liked Blood Money.
Buy this, if you like stealth assassin games.

I've decided to rewrite my review as the complete version of Episode One is finished. I would strongly recommend Hitman to any fans of stealth action, as it is a remarkable game that will leave you immersed in a beautifully designed world. At least until one of the 3 voice actors they have spoils the mood cause you just killed the guy who sounded just like him. For those worried that this game would be Absolution 2.0, it most certainly is not and I would dare to say this is the successor to Blood Money. Everything about the game feels refined (except for the voice acting) with each mission being a gigantic sandbox full of exploration and small details.
The episode release format you likely heard the drama about is now over, but the way they released games was a solid idea allowing them to focus on one specific map at a time and then moving on to the next after releasing it. The game is very good and any fan of Hitman should certainly get it. When you get this game, just go ahead and turn off hints, Instinct, and the Mipmap to see this game in its true glory! Also, as of this review, the hardest difficulty is behind a mission lock where you have to get a certain ranking to unlock, I hope to see that changed asap as this mode is the quintessential Blood money feel (aside from getting a newspaper about your hit at the end)

This review (more of a salty rant than a review, actually) focuses on gameplay ONLY. I don't care about the graphics, I don't care about the always-online DRM or whatever, if my third-world internet connection of 10k can handle never crashing once during 90+ hours, you have no reason to complain. Go away.
Oh. Great. Yet another patch that penalizes creativity in favor of adding crappy scripted nonsense and completely shutting down any attempts at recreating Blood Money's gameplay. What's that? The community found out that shooting somewhere makes guards suspicious? Nah, too realistic. Gone. What? The gameplay is too inconsistent, you say? Well, let's add in head movement for no reason! That's what everyone wanted, right? Oh, so the community found a way of dealing with two people at once without having to wait around for 16 months? Nah, removed by replacing the way the "compromised" feature works with a completely asinine "unconcious witness" stat. Basically, as soon as anyone even REMOTELY SLIGHTLY MAYBE catches a GLIMPSE of you doing ANYTHING, they're a witness and you might as well restart. Add in the fact that basically nothing anyone's ACTUALLY asked for has been implemented or fixed, like 1. fixing head movement, 2. fixing the inconsistency with silent attacks, where if you're standing behind someone but you're 4 degrees off, you won't silent attack them but instead punch them in the face and get spotted, 3. fixing the lock-on mechanics, 4. not nerfing everything that's even remotely fun into the ground? and you'll find out that IOI just doesn't give two ♥♥♥♥s (anymore?). Also, the new "Professional" difficulty is the cheapest, laziest attempt at a difficulty spike imaginable. Move or remove every item or disguise that's there in "Normal" difficulty, make every melee weapon practically useless, add cameras and enforcer guards at every corner and you have the uninspired mess that is "Professional". Clearly just advertising for getting more people to buy the "Full Experience" for another 50 bucks.
The game itself definitely has the potential to be better than, or at least on par with, Blood Money, but as it stands right now, with all the crap listed above and a lot, LOT more quirks and annoyances worthy of complaining about that I couldn't be bothered to write down, it's just a little better than Absolution. Which, needless to say, is not very impressive. But, I assume IOI won't put down the nerf gun anytime soon, if ever, so unless you like following mindless "Opportunities*" (at the current pace, in a few months there won't be any actual gameplay left, just opportunities) and annoying everyone with your 12 hours of gameplay time and statements such as "wow good grafiks!!!", save your money until this game takes its (rightful?) place as the successor of Blood Money. However, I'm not holding onto too much hope there.
*Opportunity: Highly scripted tutorial-esque solution for completing certain levels that literally tell you what, when and how to do something in order to beat the mission.
TL;DR: Fun things get patched, bugs, glitches and restrictive gameplay get enforced or ignored.
Edit April 9, 2017: Last patch has brought back legshots as well as other qualify of life changes. Maybe IO has started caring?

If you are a fan of previous Hitman games, this is absolutely a buy for you.
At first I was curious how the episodic nature of this game would work out, and I am a fan because of how it was handled in this game. (not a failure like in other games) Each episode/level is large, has a lot to do, and tons of replay value. So many different ways to play each level. You have different challenges, if things get stale after an episode try an escalation or some of the user made contracts which can be very fun, forcing you to think and plan. Unlock the other gear if you haven't, try beating a level as a chef only, or knife only, so many options for you.
The always online has been fixed since I got the game, you can play offline with things you have unlocked, this should have always been the case since release, at least they realized the problem with the always online DRM and made this fix. If a game does not do this (allow offline play) it has always been a huge red flag for me.
All aspects of the game, graphics, gameplay, re-playable, a solid amount of content are all pros for me, if you like the stealth/action type stuff this is a 10/10.
Cons -
The things I feel ehh about are the elusive targets, time sensitive fine and great if you log in and see it, play it. They feel thrown together, NO REPLAYABILITY, and are forgettable. I would rather not have these and instead have had an extra bonus mission or 2. Also these elusive targets are only good for unlocking custom suits/outfits, which look cool, but are not as cool as a bonus level in my opinion. Be prepared to see the elusive targets as a DLC you can buy in the future, at least that seems to be general concensus on the forums.
A few bugs here and there, enemies see you or notice you through a wall, this is especially bad when on the first day of an elusive target before they do a hotfix (the next day or 2) because you failed the target because of this, and can't replay it with the fixed version of it.
Leaderboards for a single player game based on how you score, it just doesn't make sense. Either you enjoy the missions and levels or you don't. Beating another guy on a mission by 1 second just doesn't matter to me.
All in all, a solid buy and one of the best games I played during 2016.

A brief review on one of the best space games in recent memory:
TLDR:  Grade A : Game is very fluid, with simple but intuitive mechanics that lead to a really smooth experience. Game is noticeably missing aspects but many are on the road map; except npc creatures. A great pickup to play solo or with friends.
Mechanics: B+
+Fluid systems of storage and creation.
+Power and Oxygen systems are very fresh
+Future hunger and thirst systems will add to this experience
-Some storage systems are a bit clunky when trying to put things in specific spots
-Camera is clunky at times, colliding with walls
Graphics: B
+Very "cute" graphics that many will be appealed towards
+Simple design of compnents leads to easier recognition and simpler gameplay
-Some variability in zones is apparent but needs some more terrain variability (on roadmap)
Sound: A
+Soundtrack is amazing, very fitting for the type of game
-Sound may not work for some people right now because of certain glitches
Overall: A
+Good game mechanics leads to overall good experience
+Mystery of game intrigues me as it will many
+Component system is unique and refreshing
-NPC creatures would be a great addition (hopefully gets solidified on roadmap)
