In this review I will go over the basic gameplay and explain the Pro and Cons to this game. For a shorter review scroll to the bottom and read the summery.
APB is a MMO third person shooter based on the idea of Cops vs Criminals. Players queue for matches in district servers to do mini pvp matches against each other which take place in various parts of the map. There are 2 "PVE" maps and 2"PVP maps currently. The two PVE maps are the Finacial and Waterfront, each hold their own factions alliances in the district. Players either pledge to a specific contact to level up their standing with them or just play at random leveling up whoever is available.

Both Criminals and Enforcers (Cops) get their own specific gameplay that they can do while in the game. Criminals can operate burgleries by ramming into stores and storage units to steal the items inside,or robbing civilians on the street, then fence the items at their closest contact. Once the items are turned in the criminals are then required to go to the "Money Launder" to collect the cash. Enforcers can participate in this as well, it is called "Wittness Mode". While a Enforcer is driving about he can patrol for Criminals commiting crimes and when he finds them he presses the Wittness Key, default Alt, and him and the criminal are now put into a mission where the Enforcer needs to get the evidence to the lock up while the Criminal needs to get it to the fence. This is a very unique system that is very entertaining and always present in the game. Enforcers also get a unique gameplay choice which is Less Than Lethal weapons. LTL weapons are the games way of making it more interesting and putting a twist on the game. When using LTL weapons, the Enforcer stuns the enemy and then arrests the Criminal. Criminals are able to free their team mates from handcuffs but only if they can make it there in time. The advantage to LTL is it makes the spawn timer longer, with the disadvantage that the LTL have a shorter range and require time to arrest Criminals putting the Enforcer in danger of enemy fire.
Being that the game is a third person shooter, the game is less about skill and more about placement. Covering corners and knowing the range of your weapons as well as how they fire can give you a large advantage over players who are simply pointing and shooting. The starting rifle both Crims and Enforcers start with is incredibly good, both in accuracy and power but it must be fired with control burst instead of full auto otherwise it loses it's strengths. That being said the game is incredibly unfriendly to new players, it has such a large learning curve that it causes most people to give up and stop playing. Because of that the playerbase is reletively smaller and all the players tend to merge into the "Silver" districts which can cause unfair match making. New players should be recomended to play on the "Bronze" servers until they learn the ropes better and are ready for the big servers.
One of the biggest gripes about the game is the cash shop, yes the cash shop sells weapons. Before you drop the game though you should know the weapons in the cash shop have very little difference compared to the "free" weapons. Most CS weapons are infact reskins of the free ones, with the exception of the few that are special/unique weapons. One of the most powerful weapons in the game is also one of the first ones you unlock for free. Most of what comes out of the cash shop is cosmetic items that are for cars and clothes.
So now that we went over the basics and you have a little bit of an understanding of what you are getting into, lets get into the good things about this game. Number one of all time is, the customization. Free players are limited on how much customization they can do in the game, but even then I've seen amazing things come from free people. You can style everything from the clothes you wear to the logos on them, from the tattoos on your body to how fat you want to be. Customize your car, it's color, the model, the decals, the lisence plate, body kits, even interior design on some of them. Your weapons can be modifide depending if you unlocked guns with open mod slots. Do you like your gun shooting faster, more accurate, longer range, better zoom, better hipfire, bigger magazine, or maybe you like to carry more ammo. You can use mods to change that. Even with your car too, Nitro, Steel plating, mobile spawn, mobile ammo supply, or even have a brick that can be used when you jump out of your car to launch it at enemy players. Players can add mods to their character as well to carry ammo, be able to survive hits from vehicles, reduce fall damage, or even ride ontop of cars without falling off. The game has endless combinations and possiblities that you can take advantage of and have fun with.
The conclusion, if you can get around the very steep learning curve, get over the cash shop selling weapons and just have fun with the game, you will enjoy it. This game is one of the few games where customization is literally at your command. Dress as a business man, or run around half naked, it's your choice. Alter your weapons to your play style and make your dream car, it's all in your hands. The game is definately worth a try for people who like shooters, but remember that the game can put you in unfair match making at times. This is because of the size of the playerbase, the more people play the better match making gets. Those of you who just read the bottom and are thinking of trying the game, I suggest you give the whole review a once over to understand what I'm talking about completely and half some understanding of what you are going to be doing ingame.

I've been a fan of the Hitman games since Codename 47 and can easily say without a doubt in my mind that this is THE Hitman game.
Each level is absolutely brimming with content and feels like a mini sandbox game. The gameplay is fluid and the game is visually stunning, even on low settings. It's everything I've ever wanted from a Hitman game.
The game is ridiculously replayable. I've personally spend at least 400 hours on Blood Money alone on a variety of different platforms including Steam, and Blood Money isn't even half as replayable as Hitman 2016. I can definitely see myself putting idiotic hours in to this game.
A lot of the negative reviews are because of the episodic release, which I was skeptical about at first and didn't end up purchasing the game until Bangkok had been released. I really think the episodic format worked though as it gave you time to digest each level completely instead of rushing through to get to the next one and missing out on things. I've never been a part of any kind of episodic game and I genuinely found entertainment in being in on the hype and discussing what could be coming in the next mission and what went right or wrong afterwards.
Another thing that puts people off is the always online thing, which has been more or less abandoned and shouldn't be a problem for the majority of players. If you don't have a stable connection then it could definitely be a problem. You need to be online to unlock things when you complete a mission, but you can still use all your unlocks offline which gives me some reassurance that the game won't just be abandoned when it comes to an end and that you will still be able to play completely offline. It has been said that the always online thing is also used to generate heatmaps to see which areas players spend most of their time so they can drop an Elusive Target in a zone that doesn't see much use.
The game does have it's downfalls though, as any game does. The fact that you can't garotte/subdue NPC's that are on stairs or sitting is very irritating and I can only hope that we will be able to melee sitting targets in the future. A briefcase has GOT to be coming too seeing as you are now suspicious if you walk around with a sniper rifle in a guard outfit on Professional difficulty. There are still some X-ray guard vision bugs that need to be ironed out but personally, I've never had it happen to me, though I've seen it happen to other people. Metal detectors, elevators, and blood pools are also troublesome to the developers but I have faith that these things will be added/fixed in Season 2.
Elusive Targets are a bit of a disappointment though and feel as though they're little more than player made contracts with a few extra NPC's and a cinematic. They are way more leanient than they seem and allow you to spend as much time as you like scouting out the area, then reload and do it for real. You can easily ammend mistakes by either restarting very quickly as soon as you realize something is wrong, or pulling your Ethernet cable. Elusive Targets were made to seem like you had a time limit and had to kill the target quickly before they left the area, but this is not true. The targets will just do their usual routine over and over, practically waiting for you to spot the window and make a move. You can spend hours on an Elusive if you really want to and the target will never leave.
The new Professional difficulty is fantastic and has totally shattered every fool proof tactic I had and has added so much more replayability to the game. Maps have been tweaked, more guards have been added, some items have been taken away, holding things like hammers and crowbars is seen as suspicious, bloody disguises can't be worn, and a few other conditions. One of my favourites is the fact that guards now react to what cameras see, if you're caught trespassing by a camera then guards will flock to the area to hunt you down and it's absolutely fantastic. Cameras affect your score in Normal difficulty but nothing else, and nobody responds if the camera records you doing suspicious things. Guards have been given a ton of extra brain cells too and instead of giving up chasing you if you break line of sight, they will sweep the entire area like they really want to find you. I was spotted trespassing in the morgue in Hokkaido and decided to hide in the room with the guy in the shower near the staff cafeteria. The guards ran upstairs in to the resturaunt, cleared all the civillians and used a different set of stairs to come back down and close in on me from the other direction. If it was Normal difficulty then guards would've abandoned the search as soon as they left the morgue.
TL;DR - A must have for any fans of Hitman or stealth games, but it does have it's quirks. It's a rough diamond at the moment but devs are constantly listening to suggestions and complaints and are working hard to give us what we want, and the episodic release allows them to do this while giving us new content at the same time.
Also a tip to new players - turn Opportunities off right from the beginning. They hold your hand way too much and suck all the fun out of finding scripted kills on your own.

I remember back in 2015 when Mad Max first launched. I loved the movie but the price tag of 60 dollars was out of my budget. I finally purchased it 2 years later during the steam summer sales and it was nothing short of fantastic. On hindsight, I would have gladly paid the full price for this amazing game.
The vehicular battles is one of the attractive aspects of this game. Ramming, crushing, tearing wheels off, shooting harpoons loaded with explosives, there are just so many ways to destroy the annoying post apocalyptic thugs chasing you at every corner.
There are also occasional weather pattern changes which are considered dangerous events, such as sandstorms and lightning storms where you could try to salvage additional materials the storm brings, however the risks are great. That said, I feel that these weather events are relatively infrequent and their level of occurence could be increased, but I was extremely impressed and pleased by this additional game mechanic.
Vehical customization is relatively limited to colours, signs, and the parts you plan to put on the Magnum Opus, but the level of depth was just right for me. There are also collections to complete such as the vehicles from each faction and little historical notes that shed light on what used to be before the apocalyse. This forms much of the gaming time and it might not be for everyone but it was rather enjoyable for myself.
Quick travel is available once you unlock certain areas of the map, however I have never used them since I prefer driving around in my car to get to places (so that I can crush more people with my harpoons).
All in all, Mad Max is a great and graphically pleasing game. I would definitely purchase the sequel if WB Interactive decides to make it. I would like to thank WB interactive for creating Mad Max and Middle Earth:Shadow of Mordor. These 2 games would always be in my personal favourites for a long time to come. You have earned yourself a loyal customer!

Clear an area and leave it for more than about 30s and it respawns, meaning if you try to retreat from an enemy in front of you, the stuff behind you in all likelihood will have come back.  The 'bash' mechanic they seemed to fall in love with coupled with stupid mobs that only pop up when you're in a certain proximity range - not too close, not too far, and then you have to rely on their firing - based on your triggering of them, to be able to make it through areas. This game is just astonishing for how much I have come to hate it.  If it were just a poor quality game that I simply don't find interesting I would just set it aside and that would be that, but this game makes me rage at it. This is a very nice little puzzle platformer where the highlight of the game is the Box2D physics engine. The game is one big physics playground. Every world adds a new gameplay element, mostly physics based, that usually isn't used later, so it keeps the challenges and puzzles fresh. Some of the levels are quite big and it is unfortunate there are no secrets to find or achievements. The music is very nice and relaxing, and every world is not just visually unique, but has its own music theme too.
One negative about the game are the mouse controls. The cursor doesn't move completely free, but "sticks" to certain objects and stuff, so it often feels clumsy. It takes some time to get used to. Other problem is the framerate which is quite unstable and drops below 60 FPS even on a powerful PC. I think I had more stable framerate in Crysis 1 than in this game.
The game is not very challenging, just enough to keep your brain busy without the danger to get you stuck or get frustrated. I would highly recommend this for kids, to work on their problem solving and logic skills, or for casual players.

Overall, I recommend this game -- though there's still a fair bit of work that could be done to improve it. The various game modes are useful in helping to develop mechanical skills that give an advantage in games like Overwatch, but some of the games themselves still feel 'off' in what they provide. The clearest example is the "lightning gun" game, which should be an ideal choice for improving tracking. The problem is that the target is reactionary to the cursor, so rather than learning to train tracking on a randomly moving object, we have one that seems to actively repel itself from wherever the crosshairs happen to be. It loses the feel of genuine tracking (or so it seems).
However, for its price it's a fair product, and seems to be doing the job in helping to improve aim in game.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a metroidvania title which shows a giant middle finger to "critics" claiming that games are not art.
I'll try my best to have this review at least somewhat organised:
I almost guarantee that your first playthrough will be very emotional... That's basicaly all I can say. I don't want to spoil anything. Just watch the videos from the store page. You should get the general idea of what you are doing.
Challenging as if you were playing Dark Souls... Okay maybe not as challenging. How can I even compare these two games? Well either way the game is not just for beautiful sights. It is going to test you. Precision is key, especialy near the end, where you rarely even have ground to step on before something is going to shoot you.
As in every metroidvania you are rewarded for exploring the forest. The different collectibles include:
- Life cells - which increase your max hp;
- Energy cells - increase you max energy. It is used by some of your abilities and most importantly, in creating Soul Links, which are basically save points. You are going to need them;
- Ability orbs - varying in size, though you gain "experience" by killing enemies, dostrying blue rocks and the like. You gain ability points from these, and can spend them on different upgrades, such as "reveal specific collectible on the map", or "attack two targets at once".
These are the most essential, there are some other things to collect though.
Getting to most of them usually requires having specific move, and there are plenty of those to discover.
In short you do things like bashing different enemies until they die, jump between walls, throwing projectiles back at the enemies or using them to launch yourself into previously unaccesible area or blowing up everything around you.
There are also run-for-your-life segments. You know, the ones where something really big is behind you and isn't safe to touch? Yeah, and they make me feel like I am playing in a cinematic movie. Adrenaline will surely kick in when you get to them, and they are not easy, but so satisfying when you finish them.
Ori and the Blind Forest is just gorgeous. The graphics, artstyle, animations, effects. And the music. It makes you feel just like devs intended. It will make you cry during a cutscene, and make you excited and full of adrenaline in the previously mentioned run-for-you-life segments.

Have you played the previous Arkham games? No? Then do yourself a favor and don't start with Arkham Origins.
If you played the others and liked it then you'll likely enjoy this one as well. It is inferior in many ways though, and I'll try to make a comparison of the most pertinent aspects below.
Did you enjoy the story hinted on the trailers? If so, I'm  sorry to say this but you'll be disappointed. I won't spoil the surprise (even though I find it hard to believe it's a surprise to anyone by now) but there's a very obvious twist that simply negates the whole story advertised in the trailers. After the disappointment with the story passed I actually quite enjoyed it though! there are some interesting moments and characters. Nothing fantastic but it does its job competently.  Considering this is a prequel they certainly made some strange decisions reagarding the story. We know the villains, we know Alfred never dies, we know Batman doesn't die etc. These things can't really be used as tension effectively, but they certainly tried. They should have used the opportunity to introduce some new characters and put some real tension in there, but that's my opinion.
But the true problem with this game is the obvious lack of polish. Bugs, glitches, freezes,crashes, performance drops... you name it, Arkham Origins has it. The lack of polish also shows on most of the gameplay features. A few examples: when in combat mode, the camera will be your worst enemy, showing the wall, hiding behind light posts, losing sight of batman or, when not being completely against you, just sitting the least helpful orientation possible with every enemy on the wrong side of the camera. Other example of lack of polish in gameplay is when gliding accross the city. You'll find yourself frustrated by the grapple's edge detection system. It has the habit of not detecting obvious edges you can see right in front of you, sometimes detecting edges you have no intention of grappling to etc. It's a less satisfying experience to say the least. These examples just illustrate the way the game was rushed to the shelves. It lacks polish, the kind of things solved by tweaking of parameters until everything feels right.
My last complaint is the zipline feature. This was one of the fun things in other games, all you needed was a wall behind and in front of you to zip accross it! Fun and a gameplay element that opens up so many possibilities. In this game they ditched that for a zip line you can attach to nodes that are put on the map by the level designer. It's so boring. It's essentially a door/key system in disguise. A very similar dumb move was made by Thief developers when ditching the freedom of rope arrows in favor of predetermined nodes where you can put your rope. It's just a fancy key to a door.
It's hard to find something they did better than previous games. I like the graphics a lot! but it's not exactly better, it's just different, more realistic style. But I do welcome the different approach, it looks very nice.
If we weren't comparing with previous Batmans (which admittedly is a difficult position for any game to be in) I would say the bugs are the main problem with it. Some of them are absolutely game breaking! but if you can endure that this is a great game. It has my recommendation.

WB may have patched the bugs that everyone is complaining about (or maybe I'm just lucky) but I just finished the rather short campaign and never hit any bugs that affected gameplay. The occasional FPS drop and unresponsive counter attack, yes. There felt to be a lot of loose ends with the main story that aren't addressed by the end of the game. Without giving too much away, there are certain villains that take a back seat as the story goes on and the game never revisits them, instead pushing the Bat towards one or two of them until you start to forget about the others. Overall, it's your basic Arkham game: smooth combat, strong storyline (except for the previously mentioned issues) and lots of bonus objectives after the completion of the story. Overall rating: 8/10

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I'm glad I bought this game after letting it sit in my wish list for two years. I had not played an open world game like this in a while and it was a refreshing experience. The driving and combat system of the game feels great. The look, sound and feel of the world is equally nice and holds up well. There's a very minor ability to customize Max and his car's appearances which reflect on cutscenes - always something I like. The story of the game is simple but sufficient: Max kills a warlord, sets out on revenge to get his old car back, kills everything in his way and makes some new friends along the way.
Enemy camps and locations aren't procedurally generated but rather fixed, however they are all 100% unique which makes exploring areas and clearing them very satisfying. Despite being a desert, the world has enough locations and enemies spread across the entire game to not feel empty. In fact, there is so much in the world that to attempt completing this game to 100% would be insane. If you're looking for a new open world title to play, this game is a great candidate for your money.

Just as a note I bought this game for a few dollars in the Humble sale. It was for sure worth paying this for 50 hours of gameplay. If you like driving games, especially when you can smash into and wreck other cars, buy it. The first section of the game up to the starting base is a lot of fun as you get to grips with the game but after that you get a sense of been there done that.
Visuals look great and make you feel the world is desolate and lacking in hope
Super storms are amazing to drive in
Upgrading Max and the car is fun
Locations such as enemy camps and weather baloons all have a unique layout
Very atmospheric in places (you can drive underground in the dark while red-eyed enemies await you)
Taking on convoys is really challenging and fun
It's interesting to hear Max's view on the world when he finds photos of the past
Takes too long to quit the game (you will probably want to Alt F4)
Enemy cars will always catch up to you
The car spins out of control like it just wants you to fail a race
All characters even Max are weak and 2D
Missions are fairly mundane and repetitive
Build up 4 bases in the same fashion (not fun)
Final race mission is frustrating
It's worth the price! Story ,action gameplay and atmosphere in this game is very nice. One of must-play game in my opinion.

Mad Max Fury Road.  WHAT A MOVIE!   And here's a Mad Max game, it's definitely going to suck right?
Well no, actually first off this is Mad Max NOT Mad Max Fury Road, the timing is the same but this is an all new story and that's kind of surprising.  Even better while it has clear connections with the movies (Immortan Joe's War boys) this is an all new story, all new characters and while similar looking characters appear there is minimal connections.
So the story is interesting and good, so it's an easy sell?
Ehhh maybe not. The story is good when it's there, and the game definitely has some VERY good parts.  The car combat is great, the upgrades for the car are great, and there's a helper character who you'll learn to love.
But Mad Max is a bit of an average game posing as a great game.    The fact is the combat is solid from Batman, but not perfect like Batman.   There's a bit of fluidity and sometimes the attack icons seem to come too fast.  This increases the difficulty which doesn't have a selector, but doesn't make for a better game in my opinion.
In addition this is NOT the game for achievement hunters and collectors.  There's a LOT to do in this game, and I mean 60-70 hours of content.  There's so much to do that I got burnt out after 30 hours or so of playing.  That's not necessarily a bad thing, but only 10 percent or so of the content is extremely interesting and good, and that's like maybe 2 hours out of 18 hours of exploring the wasteland.  There's 191 scavenging locations, most of them just scrap hanging around.  There's scarecrows that you have to drive to and destroy, and snipers you have to do the same with.  There's races, and collectibles, and buildings to make.   And so much more.
But the thing is it feels like a treadmill keep doing X so you can complete more of the game, and overall.  I just finally stopped not because I was bored, not because it was too hard, but because I just didn't feel that interested in continuing.  I left the story unfinished because I had gotten so burnt out on the rest of the game that I didn't really want to continue a solid but not outstanding story.  Kind of sad in my book.
Yet I got 30 hours out of the game, and I have to admit, at 20 bucks, you will get your money's worth.  Just don't expect AAA blockbuster, or don't do the side quests if you can avoid it.  It's not a awful game, but if you make the game into a chore of trying to do everything you get burnt out fast, and this is a game that could have been excellent with half the content or less, instead we get a game that's long on content because it can be, but the content isn't as exciting as it could be.
A shame, but still I did play about 30 hours before I got dragged down.

I'll preface this by saying I may be a somewhat sentimentally inclined person. So if you consider that a bias, then, well this review will be a bit biased.
I'll get straight to the point though. I'm in love with this game. It is without a doubt my number one favorite platformer now, and I think it's totally worth a much higher price even. I'll tell you exactly why, if you want to know more.
The easiest thing to notice is the visuals of course. The entire game looks like someone manipulated oil paints into a moving, living, breathing dream land. Everything looks smooth and clear, yet there is a gorgeous, soft, colorful and playful nature in the art style. The animations look sleek, organic and well done. The whole thing will leave you gasping several times throughout. To go with that, a top-tier soundtrack. It fits in perfectly with the visuals. Don't be surprised if you end up wondering if the developers had angels come in to their studio from heaven to orchestrate some music for them.
Ori and the Blind Forest doesn't just look and sound like a dream though; when you play it, you'll be in awe at how it
like a dream, too. The physics are nearly perfectly tuned to hit that sweetspot between realism and the freeing feeling of a floaty platformer. There are tons of creative new platforming ideas here that kept me engaged and thinking. And, the further you get into the game, the better it gets. With plenty of awesome abilities to unlock, there becomes a number of acrobatic ways to get through each situation, and you'll feel amazing when you see Ori pull off just the right moves. However, it's only fair if I tell a little more to that end.
This is by no means an easy game. It can be difficult to learn and understand how to use all of the abilities at your disposal at once, too. If you are easily frustrated, or are looking for an entirely relaxing experience, then I can't completely reccomend Ori and the Blind forest to you. (However, this definitive edition does add an easy mode, which does help some.) But for me, I didn't mind this at all. Each moment was so exhilirating, that as soon I lost I just wanted to immediately jump back in for more. At no point did I ever feel that a death was cheap or unfair, either. Every death felt like something that was a result of my lack of skill and adaptations. Nothing more, nothing less. That kept me going.
Finally, I should probably mention the narrative here. Ok, I'll admit it. I wasn't kidding when I said I was a bit sentimental. This game had me tear up at least three times, and one of those times became full blown sniffling and tears running down my face. ... but let's move past that for a moment. I won't claim that there is a wholly original and intricate story here. It's something you might expect from a children's fairy tale. But, the characters are simply so lovable, so special, that you can't help but feel their pain and joys. (and, for those of you who are interested, the definitive edition adds a sort of packaged in DLC to a special area in the game that will go further in depth with one such special character) The overall experience was very touching, and heart warming.
You know what? That's how I'll sum up my feelings about Ori and The Blind Forest. It really touched me. It left a lasting impact; one that I will not be forgetting for a long time to come. Well, that is, if I ever stop playing it first.

First impressions: This game is HARD AS HELL.
Allow me to go into more depth. This game is the successor to a 2008 flash game (which i wasted countless joyful hours on) made by team meat. The games both have an identical setting: You are a boy who is a cube of meat. You have a girlfriend made of bandages, and there is a fetus in a jar in a suit who hates your guts, so he beats you up and steals your girl. As any decent gentleman would do, you roll up my cuffs and set of to rescue your girlfriend and beat the ever-loving CRAP out of that Dr.Fetus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (does he even have a PhD? if so, in what?).
The gameplay is very simplistic, it could be played on an NES (not that that is a bad thing). Furthermore, it has a difficulty level very reminescent of those classic titles from the earlier eras of gaming. You can move forward and backwards, jump, and sprint. As you progress through the game, you may find a few purple swirly things in a few levels. If you can reach them before they dissapear, you will be greeted with either a retro style level set which you have 3 lives to complete, or a level set based on another indie game, in which you play as that games main character and if you beat the level set, you unlock them for regular play. They all have extra abilities, either related to the jump or sprint functions. There are also a few characters unlocked by typing a code into the character select screen WHEN ENTERING FROM THE MAP. 'outatime' unlocks a character with a reassigned sprint button, and 'petaphile' unlocks BY FAR the best character in the game. There are also bandage collectables through the levels, some of which are only collectible by a certain character. Every time you get a set amount of bandages, you will unlock another new character. It's a very intriging way of doing things, and it lends the game an absolute metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of replay value, further increased by the dark world levels, harder versions of levels unlockable only by beating the original level within a set amount of time and getting an A+. All in all, a wonderful game, faithful to its predecessors, its sister games, itself, and the community.

First of all, this game is absolutely gorgeous both visually and aurally. The characters are very well made and it is easy to understand why all of them are acting in a certain way (including Kuro, the vilain).
So, why should you play Ori and the Blind Forest?
The controls are nice and smooth, even with a mouse and keyboard (which I actually prefer to a controller)
The story is beautiful and I know a few people who actually cried (or almost cried) with the intro alone, myself included
It is fun and it includes interesting mechanics for platforming and battling (Especially the Bash)
It is challenging and does not become boring because it is too easy.
Why should you not play Ori and the Blind Forest?
I've seen many people complaining about the game being too hard, even on easy mode. If dying over and over at one place frustrates you a lot, then I would say not to get this game since you would probably only break your keyboard/controller while having a bad time. Other than that, I do not see any reason someone would not play this game.
Overall, this game is now one of my favorite games and I regret not buying it earlier.

If you have been holding off on this game for a while the whole first season is now out and it is worth the buy. The gameplay itself is great hitman fun with all the classic tropes. They took out the ability to slow mo mark targets like you could in absolution but instinct is still around if you would like to use it. There is an incentive to play each mission over again multiple times this time around where you gain mastery on each level and you can get new locations to start the mission, weapons, gadgets, and disguises. Elusive targets are also a new thing that are amusing though they are still buggy. The most recent one "The Blackmailer" got bugged for me and he was stuck in line waiting to enter the catwalk in Paris but because he was not coded into the normal script the other models all kept passing him and he never walked the runway leading me to be forced to eliminate him in plain view. I was able to pull it off but it was annoying for those of you who don't want to save scum or restart.

Absolutely fantastic game, a worthy successor to 2006's Blood Money. Hours of fun with interesting locations; targets; and ways to kill said targets.
That said:
The same 5 American and British voice actors for all NPC's is a let down. Hearing EXACTLY the same NPC voices (with no hint of location appropriate accent or attempt to change tone or delivery) no matter if you're in Morocco, Italy or Japan can be very jarring. One woman's voice is particularly recognisable and is prominently featured as the voice of general female NPCs #1-5 in every damn level.
As I don't get a great deal of free time to play elusive targets before they fade back into the ether, I would like to see these contracts become available to play again in the near future. This is something IOI have stated they would not do, despite the contracts having already been made, leaving me a bit bewildered as to their reasoning behind this decision.
Personally, I have had very little issue with the 'always online' DRM, but I can see why it frustrates. Though apparently this is now improving somewhat.
8.5/10 please hire more diverse, location specific voice actors for Season 2, IOI!
This is how micro-transactions were meant to be.

Been playing Rust for a year now, seen it go through XP system, components and now to a BP/ component hybrid. It's definitely had its ups and downs but I think Rust is at a point now where this is the system that takes it out of Early Access. The last few months have felt like a PVP death match rather than a true survival game. People are complaining that it's too much of a grind now, but it's a survival game, it shouldn't be easy to find a gun within the first hour. The new system completley removes that, and with the newest update make it even harder for clans to rush AKs. People have become normalised by how Rust was, getting guns and being raided within the first couple of hours was a very real threat. It's back to how it should be and a huge step in the right direction. The guys at Facepunch do an incredible job of listening to their fanbase, updating the game every week without fail. Ignore the new negative reviews, it's just salty kids who want something different to what Rust is destined to be..

This is very nice for an Overwatch player, specifically McCree players. Counter Strike players may have practice maps made by the community, but Overwatch has only the sub par Practice Range. Set the FoV to 71 to mimic Overwatch.
The different modes and maps are nice. You can customize the size and speed of the targets, as well as the crosshair to mimic the Overwatch dot, and short crosshairs. I set the dot to .70, and the short crosshair to .3 to mimic Overwatch crosshairs.
The game mimics Overwatch's sensitivity pretty accurately. It has modes for shooting at random targets, strafing targets, and doing flick shots. There is a lightning game mode that mimics Zarya's gun, but I found that the target moves too much randomly on the Y-axis to be good practice.
This program was instrumental in improving my McCree play at a higher sensitivity than I was using before. I was able to quickly test and experiment with different sensitivities and grips, and the feedback stats you get at the end of a round were very helpful to compare my method's effectiveness.
I would like to see features added for customizing the rate of fire of your weapon, shooting projectiles over hitscan, and the amount of shots it takes to destroy a target on the "Simple" game mode. More maps and modes would also be welcome.
All in all, I highly reccomend this program in its current Alpha state. The price tag is as much as a cup of coffee, and the training is zen-like. I really enjoy training on this program.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a fun little game.  I say little because it's short: I finished the game, with a 76% completion rate (as in, visited all the sites of power and opened all the doors and such) in as few as 8 hours.
Artwise the game is very well done, it picks a style of nature-fantasy and implements it wonderfully with a dazzling array of vivid color.  This is great stuff.  I won't say that the art direction is a master's stroke.  I could nitpick some little details, like how I felt the backgrounds of the different map zones would often blur into themselves (I knew when I'd switched map zones, but then inside of those map zones it didn't seem like there was a wealth of variety), or how you don't travel through the game as the combo of characters you see on the promotional image for the game (the brawny biped with the smooth-mask face and the cute little cat-like creature).  You play the game solely as the latter - Ori - and Ori's purelight color, to a point, is at least a little monotonous.
But beyond the nitpicking, Ori and the Blind Forest *is* a very visually gratifying game.  It's just, the game has a reputation of being awe inspiringly gorgeous, or beautifully stunning - a reputation that I don't think it fully upheld for me.  There's nothing revolutionary about the style, nor is it the pinnacle of the style that it adapts.  As I said, it's not a master's stroke, but I would say it's above the mean.
In terms of its actual gameplay, Ori and the Blind Forest is actually quite fun.  I'll admit that there's a short part of the game at the beginning - before you actually acquire some of Ori's needed skills, like walljumping - that I found unnecessary a little boring, but beyond that nearly everything else in the mechanics of the game was very fun.
I'll draw a comparison that I doubt anyone would've expected coming into the reviews of this particular game: Dark Souls.  The pattern of attacks from the enemies in the game had me feeling like I was playing Dark Souls, where each enemy is a puzzle waiting to be solved.  This comparison is apt not only for the combat (which is fast and fun, if slightly repetitive - luckily you can avoid many enemies if you so choose), but also for some of the "action sequences" where your goal is to escape a rising tide, or a lava flow.  You'll die, but eachh time you'll make it a little further along in the action sequence, getting better at each piece of the physical puzzle as you re-do them until you can make it all the way through without error.
I will say that one of my few complaints about the gameplay had to do with these action sequences.  Occasionally one piece of the puzzle would be a bit unintuitive, and since these sequences must be performed quickly you don't have a lot of time to explore your potential options, so you'll die and have to re-do the entire sequence only to get back to the confusing part and you'll have to make up your plan of action in the 1-2 seconds you have to then execute it.  Very frustrating at times, but luckily these action sequences do not make up the bulk of the gameplay.
As you explore the game you are able to collect skill points to unlock perks in a three-pathed skill tree, but many of these were unfulfilling (e.g. your charge blast now costs less mana, you now collect additional mana from mana drops) and I beat the game without unlocking any of the highest tier perks available.  The more rewarding and useful skills in Ori and the Blind Forest are instead collected from ancestral trees as you explore the areas in the game, which is a fairly cool system and has some serious impact on what I consider the crowning achievemennt of Ori and the Blind Forest:
Level design.  One of the coolest things about this game is that some sections of map zones are inaccessible until additional skills have been acquired from the ancestral trees spread throughout the game.  And the game doesn't exactly hold your hand in terms of indicating what's current inaccessible, you just have to decide on your own if your character doesn't have the capabilities to reach something yet.  So sometimes you'll have to forge on ahead without fully clearing an area (something that can be painful for some gamers!), and then double-back once you've acquired an extra skill that lets you reach a higher platform, or break down a wall or burst through the floor.
This may sound a bit tedious, but on the contrary: you end up having to do the physical puzzles or action sequences (like navigating through an area with spikes using aerial manuevers and wall grabs) in reverse, which is cool because you now have some mastery over the puzzles, and have renewed motivation to go through them!
The soundtrack to the game was perhaps the biggest letdown.  The music was just fairly boring and generic, which seemed a bit out of place for a game on the verge of greatness.  The characters don't have voice overs, except technically for the Great Spirit Tree - but his voiceover is in an unkown language, and we then read the translated dialogue. I thought that was kind of a dumb move.
One upside to the soundtrack was the sound effects, which I took no issue with.

While Batman: Arkham Origins offers more of the same as the previous (and overall better) Arkham games, it does manage to improve on one aspect - the story. Origins has a well-crafted plot that elevates the game from a derivative sequel to a surprisingly great experience. This is in no part thanks to the terrific voice acting throughout as well as the writing, which offers a number of genuinely memorable moments.
Yes, it isn't as good as the previous games, because yes, it isn't made by Rocksteady, but that doesn't mean Origins is bad. On the contrary, its story is worth the price of admission alone. While Rocksteady's "proper" second sequel will be released this summer to what will undoubtedly be much fanfare and (hopefully deserved) praise, Origins is still a good experience on its own.

Feels like the proper sequel to Hitman: Blood Money we've been waiting for. The levels are huge and very open-ended, and there's a bunch of new modes adding more replayability to the game. The Elusive Targets are especially a highlight as they pose a unique one-time challenge. The AI is a lot more interesting and fun to mess with compared to previous games in the series, and for better or worse, no less exploitable.
There's a couple of downsides however. I think embracing the mayhem and trying to improvise when things go wrong is a big appeal of the game, but the more familiar you get with the maps, the less likely things are to go wrong (Elusive Targets are a great addition for this reason as they help mix things up a lot). A couple of the modes are a little bit lackluster. I like the idea of creating your own challenges, but they should allow for more freedom. And the Escalations can feel tedious to do. But there's still a lot of content go through, and throwing rubber ducks at people's faces never gets old.

After bouncing off the Hitman series a few times, completely failing to see its appeal as I floundered around trying to understand what on Earth the game wanted me to do, this one is so, so great.
It helps a lot that it's absolutely NOTHING like the advertising suggested - that's all "Be Mr. Evil Sniper ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, look at the cool pornographic violence you can do! You lot love GTA, right? Well, here's something without all that driving to the mission stuff!" Instead, it's like some demented cross between Groundhog Day and Mission: Impossible, where instead of Simon Pegg's impractical CG blueprints your detailed knowledge of the infiltration setting comes from your past lives.
It also helps a lot that the world is clearly in on the joke - whether that's the surprisingly large number of people who just so happen to look like Agent 47 in a ridiculous outfit that covers their hair (and your lack of), targets' propensity for standing under chandeliers, giant horse statues and lighting rigs, or the amazing opportunity to spend 20 minutes manipulating events so that you can push one target off a balcony at just the right moment to land on the other, 50 feet below.
But possibly the greatest moments in the game are the badass walk away from the scene. For example, on my second go at the first tutorial mission I managed to figure out where the right set of toilets were so I could:
1) Rig up the relevant bathroom stall with a remote explosive.
2) Find, subdue and switch clothes with a waiter.
3) Tend bar, discreetly putting laxatives in the target's wine glass.
4) Once they've taken it off me, switch to a different outfit.
5) Stroll nonchalantly down the gangplank, blowing up the entire bathroom just as I'm about to be noticed by the guards at the bottom, giving them something more important to worry about.
Damn, if you don't feel like the best Secret Agent in the world when it all works.

First impressions: This game is HARD AS HELL.
Allow me to go into more depth. This game is the successor to a 2008 flash game (which i wasted countless joyful hours on) made by team meat. The games both have an identical setting: You are a boy who is a cube of meat. You have a girlfriend made of bandages, and there is a fetus in a jar in a suit who hates your guts, so he beats you up and steals your girl. As any decent gentleman would do, you roll up my cuffs and set of to rescue your girlfriend and beat the ever-loving CRAP out of that Dr.Fetus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (does he even have a PhD? if so, in what?).
The gameplay is very simplistic, it could be played on an NES (not that that is a bad thing). Furthermore, it has a difficulty level very reminescent of those classic titles from the earlier eras of gaming. You can move forward and backwards, jump, and sprint. As you progress through the game, you may find a few purple swirly things in a few levels. If you can reach them before they dissapear, you will be greeted with either a retro style level set which you have 3 lives to complete, or a level set based on another indie game, in which you play as that games main character and if you beat the level set, you unlock them for regular play. They all have extra abilities, either related to the jump or sprint functions. There are also a few characters unlocked by typing a code into the character select screen WHEN ENTERING FROM THE MAP. 'outatime' unlocks a character with a reassigned sprint button, and 'petaphile' unlocks BY FAR the best character in the game. There are also bandage collectables through the levels, some of which are only collectible by a certain character. Every time you get a set amount of bandages, you will unlock another new character. It's a very intriging way of doing things, and it lends the game an absolute metric♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of replay value, further increased by the dark world levels, harder versions of levels unlockable only by beating the original level within a set amount of time and getting an A+. All in all, a wonderful game, faithful to its predecessors, its sister games, itself, and the community.

DmC: Devil May Cry
Tears will be shed
When you think of Devil May Cry you think of the iconic character that stands at the front of it, the nonchalant protagonist who remained a core part of the franchise and its image. A lot of gamers would see his white hair and red jacket and know it was Dante, from Devil may cry. Dante as a mascot could be considered more prevalent than the series he originated from, with several crossovers including a role in Marvel vs. Capcom 3. DmC: Devil may Cry does away with all of this, rebooting the entire franchise, all of its characters and it’s universe to try to appeal to more gamers, with a contemporary storyline written by the guys at Ninja Theory, you know, the guys who made Enslaved: Odyssey to the west, an amazing game. Unfortunately, while DmC: Devil may Cry may have some of the looks of a DMC game, it’ll never have their fire.
DmC: Devil May Cry is a complete shamble. Something went wrong at Ninja Theory when these designs came together, and it’s unclear how such a mess could’ve occurred, but at least there’s something salvageable here, it’s just a question of whether that something is enough.
You start off with a pretty off taste main menu, with Dante surrounded by near naked Angels, where-in you can start a game in a few difficulties, with more unlocked later down the line.
The opening cutscene is more than enough to make you sick. To put it into simple words, Dante goes to a club, picks up two girls, and takes them to his camper van to have sex with. Classy, Ninja Theory, Very Classy. After this, the first main game cutscene starts off with a naked Dante in his camper, waking up to a disturbance as he’s pulled into Limbo, a Plot gimmick that allows Dante to fight Demons in broad daylight while unsuspecting people go about their day. When gameplay starts after a brief cutscene with the forgettable love interest, you’re taught some basic combat moves as you fight some lesser demons, it plays well, it works and looks good. At 60 FPS it definitely fills its role as a spectacle fighter. Unfortunately it doesn’t get any better.
The games story progresses in a linear manner as you’re introduced to characters like Vergil, Kat, Mundus and the other antagonists. The Dialogue ranges from acceptable to messy. When the best your character can follow up a ♥♥♥♥ you with is a ♥♥♥♥ you, then followed by a successive ♥♥♥♥ you, you lose a lot of my respect for the integrity of your story and it’s writing. Also, “You can call me Dante the Demon Killer” sounds like an 8 year old in a playground, which is pretty much what our new Dante can be equated to. Vergil is also a disgrace of his former self, but I don’t think you need to look further than his fashion sense to know that.
Gameplay consists of the usual combo fighting expected from a DMC game and it plays very well. From my experience it felt robust and fun to play, and using the weapons was fun, unfortunately, even the best parts have their issues. Most enemy designs are well made and fit with their roles, but the main problem comes from the inclusion of Demonic and Angelic weapons, and the inclusion of enemies that can only be hurt by specific weapons. Limiting your arsenal to specific weapons (Until you get 2 of each weapon, which can be quite late in the game, this limits you to literally one weapon) in a game about performing a variety of combos makes no sense to me.
Later into the game you also acquire abilities such as a chain to pull yourself to places and pull things to you, which seem to provide a similar function to Nero’s arm in DMC4. The utility of these in combat makes it quicker and less frustrating to engage enemies as quick acquisition of an enemy is no more than a chains pull away. Along with a glide, these mechanics make movement and combat a lot more exciting and streamlined than previous instalments, and they don’t take away the depth of it either. Some ‘hardcore’ players will argue though that the game doesn’t provide enough weapons or combos to suit their tastes, and this is a valid argument, but for those who aren’t interested in the ‘hardcore’ aspect of the DMC games, the combat in DmC:DMC is good enough to entertain most players looking to do one, maybe two playthroughs.
The accompanying soundtrack to this game is questionable, employing such talents as Noisia and Combichrist, one known for making Dubstep and the latter for making “aggrotech”. One or two tracks are acceptable and give a good fighting feel, but a good majority of it resides in the realm of sounding like every other Dubstep track out there, or some loud vocals partnered with unfitting techno.
DmC: Devil may Cry features really beautiful environments, some of the best of its generations of games. Not once did I see a texture and think it was stretched or low res, or a model that looked a bit jagged. The Art style for most of the assets is really nice and colourful which is a contrast to previous games in the genre, and although some of the old, dark and spooky areas from previous games are missed, the new ones are a welcome addition. It could be argued that they take away from the atmosphere of the game but it’s a hard argument to make considering the plot surrounding that atmosphere.
Overall the plot and handling of the characters is the most controversial topic here and needs some going over. There are some serious issues with the way the reboot was handled, including the defacing of the franchises main character. Many would argue that it's a small price to pay for a good game, but a lot of what made DMC good was the connection with Dante as a nonchalant cool character that broke a lot of normal story telling conventions. Dante wasn't a mopey protagonist who hated being a half demon who had to kill people and had a burdened past or whatever. He was cool, he didn't care, and he was having fun doing what he did and the players were in on that too. At the same time, there was a sense of delicacy with the plots of the original games, which was not taken into account here. The plot feels scrambled together with names taken from the original but not much more care put in past that. Mundus is some kinda weird Corporate Boss that doesn't fit his original representation, Vergil is the new Anonymous ringleader and the ending twist is poorly done and easily predictable.
DmC:DMC has some issues and is an insult to the original fans who craved for another iteration of their beloved franchise. It's not bad though, and it has some appeal and fun aspects, but don't expect a DMC game. Expect a game with a poorly mashed together 'contemporary' plot, some awesome spectacle fighting gameplay, terrible Dubstep music, and gorgeous environments.
If you're still interested buy it on sale but don't pay more than £10/$20 for it. If you're a fan of the original series and are interested in similar games that could scratch that itch, try Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising Revengeance (Slated to come to Steam in the near future).

Batman: Arkham Origins is an interesting beast, given the two excellent games that precede it. While some may cite the recycled environment from City (with the addition of South Gotham) and items (with the addition of the Shock Gloves and Remote Claw) as reasons why this game should be skipped, looking at the full package, this game is worth playing. It boasts a compelling story as a rougher, younger Batman confronts a number of assassins who attempt to kill him on Christmas Eve, some of whom have never been featured in the "Arkhamverse" before. He also must deal with Black Mask, and more importantly, a sadistic, psychopathic criminal known only as "The Joker." This "forging of key relationships" that the game sells itself on is consistent throughout the game's narrative, helped by some excellent CGI cutscenes and voice acting from Roger Craig Smith and Troy Baker. There are some bugs that might hinder one's playthrough, and the number of collectibles do have the tendency to make the side quests drag on, but Origins remains a solid game hampered by relatively minor problems. These problems don't prevent the best moments of the story from feeling like an unhinged, flaming roller coaster ride.

Just a tip, if you're playing this game right after Arkham City, don't. This game is essentially a slightly expanded Arkham City. Very similar structure with more or less the same kind of gameplay.
Tip #2, if you want this to be your first Batman arkham game, don't make it so. This is an alright game, i'll get to the reasons shortly, but Arkham Asylum and Arkham City are so much better, and you don't really need to know much about Batman to understand what's going on in any of the games.
Arkham Origins is a prequel to Arkham Asylum, 2 years into Batman's crime-stopping career, back when the people of Gotham thought the existance of the man was merely a myth. There'a simple way to describe what's going on in the game, Batman goes around beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of villains.
The majority of the gadgets from Arkham city are back, Batman's as versatile as ever during combat, and for the most the game plays it safe. You got a city, with a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of things to do in it, mainly involving the Riddler, who is as much of a pain to get as he was in Arkham City. There are datapacks spread all over the game, collecting 10 datapacks of the same type grants you a little info about a certain character, through some sort of interview tape, or just a random voice message recorded for no real reason other than to give the player some exposition. They're interesting to listen to, but i never could be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to get all of them because there's so many, and some of them are hidden in places that i can't find for my life, even if they're pointed out on the map.
One thing that was introduced in Arkham Origins, is the Dark Knight System. The game presents you with a big set of challenges, which encourage you to use your entire moveset. Like for example, the system would like you to hit at least two enemies in a row with a slide attack, and for doing so you're awarded experience points, as per usual used to upgrade your character's defense, or your gadgets. Every few challenges you're also awarded additional gadgets, so while i never got around to finishing the entire list, it's a very nice addition and gives me an excuse to try different strategies to take out enemies.
The story is probably the best part of the game, definitely some of the best writing that the arkham games received. I don't wanna spoil anything however, so i can't get into much detail why. But overall, i found the villains much more menacing and threatening in this game, due to how they were presented, and there are loads of good moments found across the single player campaign.
So, here's the low points of the game. Arkham Asylum and Arkham City were developed by Rocksteady, while this game was developed by WB Games Montreal, as something to keep the fans at bay until Rocksteady finishes their next and final Batman game, Arkham Knight. Something went a little bit awry during the development of the game, because it can get quite buggy. I had a few instances where the enemies ran against walls, ragdolls started spazzing out as they got stuck in walls, the worst offender was my first playthrough where i wasn't able to climb up a vent (It's a very simple thing to do so there's no way i was being stupid), and i literally got stuck and had to restart the entire game for the problem to be fixed.
A more minor instance was when i wasn't able to beat the game 100%. There was a side quest in which i had to take out all enemies except one who i had to interrogate for information. Normally, the game never allows you to knock out an enemy you have to interrogate, but in this case it let me do it, and the side quest was literally not completable. I tried coming back later, seeing if they'll respawn so i can try the interrogating thing again but they were gone.
What really pisses me off however, is that WB Games literally stated they won't be patching the game because they're working on DLC. Oh yeah, of course, because patching the game won't ♥♥♥♥ing earn them money, will it? How greedy.
And like i said before, the game doesn't really try anything new. Arkham Asylum and City are two entirely different beasts with significant differences, Arkham Origins looked at City and said "Good enough." And i suppose it makes sense why it turned out that way, this was a game that was made in about 1 year, and it usually takes much more time than that to create something fresh. That's why Rocksteady's taking their sweet time to get Arkham Knight done, they wanna make it different from Arkham City. And i can appreciate that. I mean ♥♥♥♥ it, if Arkham Origins wasn't made, i wouldn't care, i would wait patiently for Knight to come out if it meant they're taking their time to create a really good game. And i'm sure that's the case.
So, is Arkham Origins worth getting? Debatable. Definitely the low point of the arkham Batman games, but for what its worth, i had a good time playing this. It's not an awful game...it's just an alright one at best. The story was awesome, but it doesn't make the game. If you're still skeptical about buying it, wait for a price drop, and then i'd say it's fully worth it.

I have always been an avid fan of the Hitman franchise. As a kid, one of my favorite games to play was Hitman 2: Silent Assassin on the Playstation 2. Then Contracts, then Blood Money...and Absolution happened. After seeing the rewarding open-world format massively scaled back and simplified, I felt that the franchise was doomed. It would surely become a victim of a cruel and unforgiving death like many of Agent 47's targets. Then, HITMAN was released. Although many new features are present in this installment, HITMAN presents itself with classic open-world gameplay on large levels that allows players to decide when and how each mark will meet their fate. While it is typically plausible to dispatch your targets with a well-placed pistol shot to the back of the head, players who observe the world around them will find Opportunities that allow Agent 47 to lure victims off of their routine or even draw them into an accident. This could be anything from causing an faulty gas line that would engulf the target in flames to dropping a massive chandelier on an unsuspecting victim. More subtle approached could involve dirty tactics such as rigging a chess game so that the target, sastisfied with his victory, goes for a shot of vodka that you have previously spiked with lethal toxins, or disabling a computer hard drive so that the target leaves her heavily-guarded office to reboot the system. Overall, I would highly recommend this game to veteran Hitman fans and also to those who are new to the series. It is a wonderful point to start at, and if you like it..check out the other titles, except Absolution. ♥♥♥♥ Hitman:Absolution.

Is this woth playing or recomendable...
I think the managed to get the tone of the newest film quite good, but it does not work very well as a game I think.
Though I kinda find the simplicity of the story fun. "My car is gone. I need a new car, but it has to be cool and powerfull." ... well that's it. Sorry for the spoilers :-D.
But the whole mythology arround te cars in the world is very nicely done! And it works well.
What does not work so well is getting a big game out of that concept. You need help with your car, so you make "friends" or better put aquire "sponsors" to get some stuff and shelter.
These sponsors are the political powers of the world, who struggle with enemies of their state, economy and internal defense... so they rely on Max, a shady dude who just came by and needs help with his car.
Well, it is the postapocalypse, so that is normal behavior for the heads of state, but how does Max solve all these complex political problems?
By driving to the bad dudes and beating the crap out of them... that's it! Nothing more... OK, it is still the postapocalypse and the beating-the-crap-out-of-them-part is actually quite enjoyable. It always looks natural, and it has a good balance of challange and fun.
But it gets boring way to fast. You drive to a place, destroy all outer defences, enter, beat everyone up and then leave to repeat that somewhere else... I think that's wasted potential of my beloved Mad Max World.
There could have been more variation or even interactions...
To give you one example:
One enemy-category would be a dude hanging on strings with a drum. His job is to alert his companions and boost their strength with his passionate drumming.
The game wants you to kill him first, so that the others are more easy to kill. Well I don't care, because it makes almost no difference in the fight. So often the poor guy keeps hanging arround (literally) after I killed his colleques.
Then he starts talking with me. And lays out his skills in drumming and describes his references, to apply for a job. That is a nice touch, but do I get any options on what to do with him? No! I can only kill him and I have to, or the place would not have been cleaned...
In the movies Max always makes friends and can show kindness... why not in the game?
The most fun for me are the convoys. Dealing with them is the only situation, where your car has a purpose beyond getting you from place to place.
Are they as awesome as in the movies?
No... no they are not. They are just little groups of cars (always the same type) and can be finished quite fast. That is a welcome contrast to the raids, but... well... a wasted opportunity.
So can I recommend it? No.
It is fun for a short time, But that time is too short for a recommendation.
I would recommend it, if there would be more debth or if it would have a coop-mode, because beating the crap out of people is such a nice activity done with a friend :-).

I had mixed feelings when I bought this game. I saw many reviews saying how bad it was yet I saw some saying it was good. I would like to say that DmC: Devil May Cry is my favourite game of 2013 and in my top 3 games of all time. The graphics instantly hit you when you load with their many colours and what seems to be some of the most realistic graphics I've seen in a video game. The combat system is very easy to use, besides a few late registrations. The new and improved Dante is a blend of "Super-model pornstar" and "Popular comedian" with a slight hint of mystery to him. The variety of enemies to kill and weapons to kill them with is even better with the huge number of combo moves that you can unlock. The collectables are easy to find and a challenge to get to, yet very satisfying when you get them. The secret side challenges are amazing, ranging from easy to hellishly hard.
Pros:
- Dante has been highly improved
- Funny and subtle hints to previous games get you ammused instantly
- Easy controls
- High number of enemies and weapons
- Large number of combo moves to unlock
- Side challenges to do when you want a rest
- Amazing stroyline
- Jaw dropping graphics
Cons:
- Some minor glitches
If you have some spare cash lying around, I would highly recommend this. You will not be disappointed.
Overall, I would give this game a well earned 10/10!

No matter how much I like the original, white haired Dante, this new one is a delight in his own right. So what if his hair is short and black? His personality and wit are a pleasure to observe throughout the entirity of the story, which also is the best in the DMC universe.
Simply put, DmC: Devil May Cry is a game worthy of any fan's time of the hack and slash genre. It's intoxicating gameplay can't help but draw me into play over and over again.

Astroneer is a wonderfully unique and fun exploration game.  Much in the vein of games like Minecraft and Subnautica, it has you exploring, gathering resources, and crafting items, vehicles, and modules to help further explore and discover what the world(s) offer.  Eventually you can build a spaceship or shuttle to visit other planets and moons in the solar system and explore even more to your heart's desire.  There are unique plants to look under for research material, crashed space debris to plunder, and caves to explore for special resources you'll need for your base.
The game uses a unique method of interacting with the world, yet has no user interface to speak of.  It is seamless and helps to immerse you into the world that you explore and create.
The visuals are simple, yet not in a bad way, but in a surreal, vivid, and imaginative way that has you staring in awe at your first sunrise and sunset and enjoying them long after the novelty has passed.  The music and sound effects are both well done, and in the case of the music, subtle yet memorable.
In its current state, Astroneer is an early access title with a ton of potential, yet is already fun and exciting.  With more content, optimization, and TLC it could easily become a classic in the genre.  I'm very much looking forward to the continued development of Astroneer and what it has in store for all of us that enjoy this kind of game.

Frankly, GTA: San Andreas is the game which got me interested in the franchise. Extremely well-written, expansive, innovative and incredibly fun. CJ is one of the strongest characters Rockstar has ever developed, along with the rest of the character list. The voice acting is incredibly well-done, the music selection is (or was) second only to GTA: Vice City in my opinion. The variety of things you can do in this game is arguably second-to-none in the entire franchise, which helps Rockstar in its portrayal of a truly open world.
The graphical stylings, while outdated by today's standards, still please the eye and many parallels can be seen between this game's environment and that of Grand Theft Auto V's more recent version of Los Santos which I can't help but think about as I play this game. GTA V's environmental design would undoubtedly have suffered in my opinion had Rockstar not made GTA: SA previously.
Overall, I'd consider it a must-play for anyone interested in sandbox games, GTA as a franchise or... hell, historically notable games. This game is widely considered one of the best of all time, which makes sense, considering it was the best-selling PlayStation 2 game ever.
However, the Steam version has just been updated (after several years with no updates whatsoever), and there are a few unfortunate setbacks I have to point out for people who are considering buying the Steam version.
Years ago, Rockstar updated GTA: SA for Steam with version 3.0. Among some bugfixes and miscellaneous improvements, the patch somehow inexplicably broke 16:9 resolution support entirely.
This problem is still around in the latest patch, which, if you're like the majority of PC owners these days and have a 16:9 widescreen monitor, will mean you will encounter letterboxing and a lower resolution than your monitor is capable of rendering. Only with an unofficial modification can you get around this, and it's deeply disturbing that Rockstar still hasn't noticed this problem yet.
Alongside this, Rockstar, apparently pressured by music publishers whose tracks they licensed for GTA: SA's soundtrack, has removed somewhere around 20 tracks from the game entirely. This was done retroactively, meaning that previous owners of the game before the latest patch, like myself, have no choice but to play the game now without musical content they purchased.
If you don't play GTA games for the radio stations, this may not impact you as much, but regardless, Rockstar's approach to enforcing licensing restrictions with this patch was in my opinion heavy-handed at best, criminally deceptive at worst. It can set a precedent for AAA publishers to unilaterally remove content at will, and while the change of content with/without notice is disclosed in most games' EULAs these days, that just doesn't work in an economic system where one pays for the ownership of a good.
Some of the artists in this game I first found out about thanks to GTA: San Andreas, including Helmet, Rage Against The Machine, NWA, Eazy-E, Ice Cube and Public Enemy, and it's a little heart-breaking that the game no longer reflects my childhood memories of it after a decade, with some of my favorite songs conspicuously absent. These are songs everyone who bought the game before the update paid for.
Rockstar hasn't even mentioned the update at all on their website (par for the course, though, they're very sporadic with their PR), or on the News page on Steam for the game, so I'm not sure whether or not they were even going to announce this. We shall see what happens.
I will be fair and include the latest patch's implementation of (apparent) DRM-free implementation and XInput control support, however. The XInput implimentation is not perfect but still playable and hopefully it is beneficial to people accustomed to GTA console controls.
Basically, if you try using an Xbox 360 controller's triggers for throttle control for vehicles similarly to GTA IV you've got your work cut out for you, as all inputs besides the thumbsticks are treated as digital buttons including the triggers. This makes it very difficult to regulate the speed of your vehicle in my personal experience, which is extremely important in multiple missions. Other than performing steering with thumbsticks, I gained absolutely nothing in playablility because of this but was still capable of beating the game.
It's due to these less-than-ideal changes to the game, as playable as it still is, that I cannot recommend you purchase the Steam version of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, because at the end of the day you get less content than you would have had a week ago for the same price (at the time of writing) and have no choice in the matter. You owe it to yourself to find an original retail version with the soundtrack and resolution compatibility completely intact, at least then you won't be forced to update the game according the whims of music industry executives.
(As the update to the game was very recent and may change in the future, I will accordingly update this review if things develop further.)
