This is the script for the review portion of my review video (I have a small thing at the start)  You can watch the video here:
Or you can read the review here.  This review goes over all current modes in the game then my overall opinion of it, with a short list of suggestions at the end to improve the game.
The goal of Aim Hero is to help people improve their aim in First Person Shooters, particularly Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, Overwatch, and Paladins with their sensitivity settings, and particularly CS:GO as the developers have tried to recreate various positions on Dust 2.  This in particular confuses me but we’ll get onto that discussion shortly.  First I want to talk about the actual game.  The game is split into currently seven modes with a total of four maps, so let’s go through them one by one.
Numero Uno is Classic.  Serious question here how is it classic if this is the first game using it?  Also you spelt Lifes with an F, when Life is plural it’s Lives with a V.  Sorry inner spelling grammar legionary came out for a second.  This mode is seriously weird though, basically targets slowly appear, enlarge, then minimize, and you have to break them before they minimize to oblivion.  What this is to help you with, I’m not sure.
The second mode so far is Strafing, a simple concept.  There’s a target moving back and forth almost constantly and you have to hit it.  Not a perfect representation of CS:GO which I think this is primarily for but again WE’LL GET TO THAT LATER.
Third or should I say Penta is Pentakill, on one of three maps based on Dust 2 you shoot for targets moving into the site.  Each takes one shot and you have limited ammo.  Simple enough.
Speaking of Simple, Simple is a mode that takes place on three maps like Pentakil but is merged with strafing, you shoot a target and it starts strafing somewhere else.  Go for high scores.
Reflex is a reflex testing thing where it has a target for a second or two and if you hit it or not it appears somewhere else for a second or two, rinse repeat.  Done better IN WHAT IM SAVING FOR LATER.
Fast aim is similar to classic except they don’t expand, minimize, or anything.  They just keep appearing.  Shoot em, whatever you get the idea.
And finally and most recently added is Lightning Gun.  If you’ve played quake or a quake like, maybe doom im not sure.  Unreal Tournament?  Yeah the lightning gun shoots completely straight, normally like a sniper.  You just follow a target with it.  The target moves and that’s about it.
Now that I’ve briefly described what this game is, you might wonder what do I think of this game.  Well… I have been mentioning how CS:GO has things, and not much else.  If you’ve played a lot of CS:GO competitively and have tried to get better, like what the target audience of this game is supposedly doing, you’d know that workshop maps exist, and within that large array of maps are maps to help you improve your play  Maps like Aim botz  by uLLetical and various others made to practice nade throwing.  And as for Overwatch or Paladins, I don’t seem to understand those either.  If you really wanted to have people practice those games, wouldn’t you try and set up challenges based around certain mechanics or abilities?
While I might not understand the point of everything in this game, and know for a fact that almost everything, if not everything is already available for free elsewhere, if you have a reason to pick it up or find a mode appealing, by all means try it out.  As for me, as I personally don’t understand nor really enjoy this ‘game’ (I’d rather use ‘tool’ but whatever) I wont be recommending it.
Also since this is in Early Access (even though their store page said a final version within 2-4 months, and its currently the fifth to now sixth) I’ll be stating some basic things to focus on:
1.	 Import settings directly from games.  This is somewhat possible by allowing the user to set paths to files such as config INI’s.  This will assure 100% accuracy of mouse controls.
2.	Add specific challenges for heroes of Overwatch and champions in Paladins.
3.	Here’s an idea, create a mode that cycles you through various already implemented modes, a couple of times.  Make it targeted for daily use, and have statistics of how the player improves day by day, similar to Wii Sport’s Training mode and statistic tracking in their mini games.
These are only a few ideas, as I’m not some professional hired QA, but hopefully this feedback will be used well.

Before I get started on the review, I just want to say that I already have a good amount of hours in Quake live, Team fortress 2 and Overwatch bot games just practising over and over again. This is something I do for
and feel that practise does make perfect.
So when I saw that this game was recommended for me, I was thrileld by the idea and instantly bought it. However, just after 10 minutes I can already list out what this game is lacks and how to improve them, because honestly, this is a great concept for players that want to improve but unfortunately does not have the level of polish to pull it off, (especially since this game has a price tag for a service that is practically free).
- This is a no-brainer, everygame has a FOV slider which does impact your aim, so having this in an aim practise game is a MUST. Scopes also has different FOV so they also impact your aim/ sensitivity.
- For example, in Overwatch alone, Widowmaker and Ana are both snipers that uses scopes. However, what many people might not know is that they both uses different FOVs in addition to their hipfire/ default FOV. The exact FOV for the scopes are not known, so that's why many people don't mention it (at least until Blizzard releases this info). So ProGames Studio, do your homework.
- This might be a minor pet peeve but if I'm dedicated enough to fork out money for this game, you should have a cm/360 OR inch/360 sensitivity setting in the options.

- Every game has their own multiplier for sentivity but if I was serious enought to get a game like this, I would know my cm/360 and would do my best to keep this number consistent across different games. Telling me to visit
in your annoucement just isn't good enough, especially when I'm spending money for the convinence of an aim pracitse service that I could get on a free game like Team Fortress 2 (or aimbooster if i'm desperate). Plus, it is virtually impossible to keep it to an exact number across games, so the closer the better.
- I love that you have applicable maps like bomb site A on dust 2 and the targets rushing in, just like in the real game. However, you also have maps while you're just standing in the center of an empty room looking at a 'screen' and keeping targets. If I wanted to do that, I would go to
and do that exact same thing FOR FREE. Not to mentioned that aiming on a 2 dimensional plane is drastically different from aiming in a 3 dimensional plane, this is the reason why playing games like Osu! doesn't improve your aim because they are two completely different concepts.
- So for example, instead of having a target move around on a screen in your 'classic' training map, why don't you have life-sized targets based on the game map you're playing on. Besides the obvious "different characters have different hitboxes" arguement, it goes back to the fundamental concept that aiming on the 'screen' is dfferent from practising in, say, quake live against bots. Unless you're going to port literally every single map known to the FPS world, having 3 dimensional targets are the next best thing.
- Please let us move around, this goes back to my arguement that you're basically aiming at a screen. Also in a real game, you would be able to move around, and reposition yourself to better suit the situation. If you're worried that many players might move closer to make aiming easier to get a better score, they aren't your target audience.
- Again, if you're using maps based on popular FPS games like CS:GO or Overwatch, have targets based on the models in their respective games.
- Have weapon models relevant to the game they're pracitising for. This is both because it does affect gameplay and also because the current models are just atrocious.
- Hit markers/ Hit Sounds; Having an arbitrary number on the top of the screen that is both out of the way and distracting is not the way to help the player improve/ indicate to the player that they're doing well.
Now I'm not saying this game doesn't have potential, I mean this is a fantastic idea that caters well to players who are looking to improve their aim game, and I
it. It's just that this game lacks so much polish, given that this is an early access review. So I would strongly advise that you
buy this game until a content patch that meet most of these requirements are met. Otherwise, just go to the game you're practising for and load up some bots and practise exclusively on what you're trying to improve (be it trace, flick or projectile)

A very enjoyable entry into the Devil May Cry series, even if not as conventionally brow-beating as the rest of the series.
Dante's characteristic bravado and wit are somewhat subdued here, and he is much less campy and over-the-top. And yet, I find it an enjoyable break by providing some much-needed character development.
While I was very skeptical at first, the gameplay and art style went through a few revamps and I was sold. When I began playing, I was immediately engrossed in the drop-in gameplay and the interesting new mechanics borrowed from DMC4's Nero and his Devil Bringer.
While a stark contrast to the previous entries in the serious, I would recommend DmC to fans of the series and newcomers alike, as long as you don't hold your breath for some of the same old.
Critiques I do have are mostly based on the style change (which I got over) and the ease of difficulty, which seems less masochistic than the more current entries.

I have always been an avid fan of the Hitman franchise. As a kid, one of my favorite games to play was Hitman 2: Silent Assassin on the Playstation 2. Then Contracts, then Blood Money...and Absolution happened. After seeing the rewarding open-world format massively scaled back and simplified, I felt that the franchise was doomed. It would surely become a victim of a cruel and unforgiving death like many of Agent 47's targets. Then, HITMAN was released. Although many new features are present in this installment, HITMAN presents itself with classic open-world gameplay on large levels that allows players to decide when and how each mark will meet their fate. While it is typically plausible to dispatch your targets with a well-placed pistol shot to the back of the head, players who observe the world around them will find Opportunities that allow Agent 47 to lure victims off of their routine or even draw them into an accident. This could be anything from causing an faulty gas line that would engulf the target in flames to dropping a massive chandelier on an unsuspecting victim. More subtle approached could involve dirty tactics such as rigging a chess game so that the target, sastisfied with his victory, goes for a shot of vodka that you have previously spiked with lethal toxins, or disabling a computer hard drive so that the target leaves her heavily-guarded office to reboot the system. Overall, I would highly recommend this game to veteran Hitman fans and also to those who are new to the series. It is a wonderful point to start at, and if you like it..check out the other titles, except Absolution. ♥♥♥♥ Hitman:Absolution.

This game was very anticipated! the last Big hitman game was absolution way back in 2012 and it wasnt the game to bring back the series since its best game (Through public opinion and rating) Blood money (Which was 2006!, this proves that old games can beat the newer games purely from features alone.) The freedom of the levels in blood money was particulary liked by fans of the series. Absolution was played in small levels in contrast. Time for a change? IO-Interactive thought yes! Thats where this game comes in. It brings back many of the loved traditional hitman features while modernising and polishing it with good graphics and a clean HUD to name a few.
I personally love this game and think its what the series needed to bring old players back in and get many new ones in the same action!
Heres my Ratings of the aspects that make this game better or worse.
Story 8/10
The Story is great, although its biggest weakneess is that it progresses in episodes which slows dow the story a lot, and the cutscenes where the story parts are is only at the beggninng and end of missions. which gives about 10 cutscenes of storyline. The Story itself is suberb and has an amazing cliffhanger at the end that leaves players begging for season 2! which cant come soon enough.. The Targets themself throughout the campaign serve as "connections" to piece together this massive conspiracy of a puzzle that 47's handler is unearthing, with the help of 47 himself of course! But no spoilers here.
Environment 9/10
Paris, Sapienza, Marrakesh, Bangkok, Colorado and Hokkadio are the 6 locations you will be visiting in season 1. My personal favourite is Sapienza because its the largest level with the most replayability. They did a great job swith the variation but there is still a ,lot of destinations to be used! Hopefully they use a few new ones for season 2!
Tools 8/10
The Variation of "tools", weapons and Gadgets are amazing, although thre best ones can only be obtained if you master a level, which means doing almost everything it has to finish enough challenges. This isnt a problem for completionist players like myself, but people that only play the game once through will miss out heavily on these features.
Voice acting 2/10
Somehow everywhere where 47 visits, everybodies voice has been replaced with 5 different amercians and 2 englishmen..
Maybe this part was overlooked! but its super frustrating to have your immersion broken because you were gazing over the japanese Mountains and a japanese guard next to you starts speaking with a suspiciously heavy American accent.
The Best voice acting obviously comes from 47 himself, he is voied by
, The Same Awesome South african that has voiced  47 is every game that he has spoken in! Except absolution. which hardly mattered anyway. PLus he doesnt speak much which adds to his character greatly.
Graphics 9/10
Obviously with environments as ambitious as they are, good graphics hve to go hand in hand with it. Which they do! Seeing the details in the distance is particualry well done. playing a level and looking past the playable area to the Paris skyline, The Hokkaio Mountains and The Colorado Countryside is very detailed and it hardly makes you feel like you are "trapped" in the mission because there is so much to see outside the borders!
Gamemode Variation: 10/10
Apart from the story, it has 2 other modes to keep you occupied. and 1 special feature to keep players coming back..
-Escalation mode is a challenge mode where you have to take down one or more chosen targets for 5 levels and each level it gets harder. Each level adds a smart complication to hinder your progress! (such a no pacifications, extra cameras, delete all evidence within 1 minute, time limits and more.)
Its a pure test of skill ands patience! I definetely recommened that you master the level you play this mode on so you can navigate a lot more efficiently, knowing where that backdoor is could help you a lot!.
-Contract mode is where you can create your own target(s)!, pick anyone on the level and you can just select them and then play the level out untill you complete it! You can find the hardest people on the map in the weirdest places and select them so people can have a massive challenge when playing your level!
You can play other people featured contracts to get some of the well made Contracts, normally very hard though!
Its as close to playing with other people well get! Although this gake isnt built for multyiplayer so i dont really mind
-Elusive Targets Im not the biggest fan of this, though i respect wy its in the game and why it can be as hard as it is.
Ill explain the premise first so my opinion doesnt "dampen" your view of it.
Basically its a target that arrives every week or so, they have about 72hours to be found and eliminated. If you die, kill him/her or fail the mission in any way you CANT try again. this difficulty is unique to any other target in the game and i respect that, however what i dont like if you buy the game late you have missed countless targets (There has been 19 so far). If you have a busy life or log on to finds that you have 5 minutesw left to complete it, it can be very frustrating. Now i dont hate this feature of the game, i think its very unique and smart of the devs to put it in, but for casual players its very hard and if the elusive target is on a map that you havent beaten/mastered yet, there is a stressful rush to learn about the "ins and outs" of the map before the elusive target expires! (although you are given quite adequete time to do this.
3 Major Cons:
The Stupid punch glitch wehich hasnt been fixed since the day this came out.
Broken mission objectives. its horrible to be stuck inside a mission with no clean way out.
This game tries to be open world but fails badly, once you play levels enough they feel super confined and boring with no extra surprises which eventually kills the experience overall.
Overall this game has the features from blood money. (Open map, many tools, basicaly more freedom.)
And the story or an intense Crime drama. (But much better.)
I hope that Season 2 continues this interesting Story with longer cutscenes and/ or more characters.
This is a great game and the many reviews of this game have been unfortunelty affected by too many people complaining about the always online DRM (Although the fact that your progress on a level
be lost if your net gos down for 10 seconds will frustrate anyone.), but if you afford to look past that mistep this game is a solid Hitman game.
If you dont mind the patience required and the effort youll have to invest to unlock the kickass gear avaliable for 47 then this is the game for you!But dont make my mistake and buy each episode at a time! Then you wont be able to get the bonus episodes included.
And thats the review! Thanks for reading it all. Its  a big game if you consider the scale of replayability that it has!

Astroneer is a wonderfully unique and fun exploration game.  Much in the vein of games like Minecraft and Subnautica, it has you exploring, gathering resources, and crafting items, vehicles, and modules to help further explore and discover what the world(s) offer.  Eventually you can build a spaceship or shuttle to visit other planets and moons in the solar system and explore even more to your heart's desire.  There are unique plants to look under for research material, crashed space debris to plunder, and caves to explore for special resources you'll need for your base.
The game uses a unique method of interacting with the world, yet has no user interface to speak of.  It is seamless and helps to immerse you into the world that you explore and create.
The visuals are simple, yet not in a bad way, but in a surreal, vivid, and imaginative way that has you staring in awe at your first sunrise and sunset and enjoying them long after the novelty has passed.  The music and sound effects are both well done, and in the case of the music, subtle yet memorable.
In its current state, Astroneer is an early access title with a ton of potential, yet is already fun and exciting.  With more content, optimization, and TLC it could easily become a classic in the genre.  I'm very much looking forward to the continued development of Astroneer and what it has in store for all of us that enjoy this kind of game.

The short summary: no matter how you feel about Asylum/City, this game is pretty much just a couple of good boss fights surrounded by warmed-up leftovers from City. Skippable.
The long version: the game begins pretty strong, and having one of its best boss fights early (hi Deathstroke) was a really good foot to lead with, but that's basically the peak of things, and it's kinda downhill from there on. Almost every bit of the game just feels like a lamer Arkham City, and some of the city actually seems to be directly copied from the last game, or real close. (It feels to me, and I have not reinstalled to check, like there are less grapple-points in the world. Which makes travel sorta lame even before the story-gated fast-travel checkpoints.)
Similarly, the combat has a couple of steps up (I enjoyed remote-clawing things onto people as an extra layer), but these come early and then you're out of new tricks for the back half. In another "was it always this way? I swear not" moment, a lot of encounters take place in the-seams-are-visible invisible boxes. More than once I tried to start an encounter with a gadget or trap and then discovered I had clawed or bataranged a man into a wall that kept him from actually moving where I wanted. (Try it sometime!) The enemy 'groups' are strangely seperated. I would occasionally beat up two of three men on a roof and get rewarded for the fight, while the other stood there oblivious because he wasn't part of the same team.
The prequel conceit also hamstrings the game really, really hard. On the one hand, kudos for going "heck with it, he's going to get new tricks and we don't care that they aren't in the other games". On the other, the barely-reskinned stuff that shows up in here but is telegraphed from miles away (looking at you, "glue" grenades that still come out as blue platforms...) if you've played the last games is lame, and oh my god there are too many batarangs. You have seperate multi-target batarangs. That's a real design decision someone made. And to circle back around: you throw in a bunch of villains you haven't used in other games and then expect us to believe that three dudes who all show up in every other game are in danger? For god's sake, at least fake us out with someone we KNOW isn't going to appear 20 more times.
Speaking of design: this game is buggy. I only had it crash to desktop the once, but the volume just FLATLINES randomly on area-swaps, at times I had to restart the game because triggers stopped working/responding, and at least once an entire encounter had to be redone because a man fell through the world. This is apparently miles better than the game at launch, as friends pointed out to me, but man, it's not what I call excellent.
I don't recommend this unless you're really, really hard up for some more City-style action but don't want to replay that, and even if so... maybe just save a few bucks up by not buying this and put it towards Arkham Knight? I mean, there's still the chance that could be a debacle, but at least it'd be a much more interesting debacle than this rehash of a title.

Batman Origins is the third installment and is the weakest of the three. It lacks the polish that made the other two games fun and is plagued by glitches that rather subtract from the overall challenge at times.

The game might be open world but the main missions are still in a series of events. There will generally be places you are unable to access due to the lack of gadgets, which results in being restricted at first when trying to get all the collectibles. Once you get further in the game you will end up revisiting places to either get the collectibles or access other parts of the level you were unable to before in order to progress further down the story.

The bosses themselves are quite fun though they tend to be easier than the minion fights. The bosses do vary from time to time in how exactly you go about defeating them. There are times where you have to stealth alot in order to take them down and there are other times where you simply have to dodge their charges and stun them. It’s of similar quality concerning the last two installments nothing less and nothing more.
There are two different types of bosses, the assassins which are the main plot enemies out to kill you and the side mission criminals.

The side mission criminals are still interesting and fun to actually go after, most notably the mad hatter takes notes from the scarecrow section of the first installment batman arkham asylum and creates fun environments with puzzles and obstacles to overcome though sadly it only happens once.
There is stealth and combat sections you can play outside of the main story. It’s in the challenge mode which works the same as the previous two games, you can unlock more of them by simply progressing through the main story and accomplishing certain requirements to unlock them.

+Several Collectibles (Data Packs,Tags,Plaques,Network Relays)
There are collectibles scattered throughout the city to find that reward you with exp bonuses. Some of the collectibles like tags can only be detected in surprise detective vision while the other ones like network relays require alot more gadgets and maneuvering in order to hack the security consoles and reveal more elements of the map within the radius of the tower.

-Gloves really break the balance of the game
+The combat is fluid and with great arsenal of gadgets
Batman combat remains fluid as the previous installments. The tendency to also use alot of slow motion from one takedown to another remains. With every installment in the batman series this was no exception from introducing new tools. Most notably the addition of the shock gloves which is just a get out of a bad situation for free card. The gloves really dominate most bosses and difficult situations you will come across. The difficulty up to that point is somewhat proper then simply plummets, as a result of these gloves.

-Glitchy compared to previous games
+Tools are still useful to take out enemies in multitude of ways
Batman is no stranger from taking out his enemies while remaining in the shadows, or watching enemies become more paranoid as their allies fall Batman goes through vents and hangs on statues in order to take down his enemies, while at first they are calm, they start to feel the tension as their partners start to disappear. This results in them guarding each other more closely and grouping up together into search parties, for the batman.The Matrix seems to have interfered this time around, for enemies tend to glitch out more and run into walls, before you know it batman will be making a choice between two pills before proceeding to punch Morpheus in the face, but I digress.

The word “origins” is the wrong way to title this game, yes its about a young batman dealing with the trauma of facing foes for which the likes he has never seen before. However you don’t really go through any training montage unlike the first movie, or anything to really show him growing up to be the batman. It would have been a better game if it was centered around him and growing his persona to the bat rather than the same old song and dance that batman installments have already done. The game takes no real chances with its characters, gameplay, or stealth and perhaps that’s why I ultimately cannot recommend the game to people who owned the previous two installments. Yes, this game is fun but it really lacks anything that sets it apart that would make it enjoyable from the other two.
The city wasnt as good as arkham city's, but I found the story to be more interesting and the gameplay more fun than the previous installments.

This game is inferior to the other two, but they were so good that even an inferior version still is a good game. The combat is still as good as the others and with a few additions, such as the shock gloves you can use to enhance your attacks and the fact that you can stack special moves if you deal enough hits. The predator encounters are also good and the enemies react really well as they adapt depending on how you deal with them, and it also has a new addition: a hook that you can shoot, like the batclaw, except that you can choose where both ends will go. This means you can hang enemies onto gargoyles from afar, or make them hit each other, or even use it to throw objects at them without exposing yourself. They tried to make it not too easy for the player, placing some new, stronger enemies (such as the Venom-user thugs), and they can also put mines on the gargoyles on predator encounters that will explode if you touch them. I won't lie, though: the game still felt a lot less challenging than the others. Boss fights aside, because those were actually pretty intense.
The bosses are really cool, but they feel like a worse version of the Arkham City ones. The final boss, for exemple, is pretty much the "stealth battle" against Mr. Freeze, except not as well made. The battles against Deathstroke or Copperhead felt like the one against Ra's Al Ghul, but again, not as cool. They can feel a bit repetitive (I lost count of how much time I spent only pressing the punch and counter button at specific moments over and over again against Deathstroke), but they still look pretty cool and are also a nice challenge, so that keeps you on edge and you basically forget that you're just doing the same thing over and over.
The atmosphere is still good, specially when you go inside somewhere, and the awesome soundtrack really helps. The city's scenery felt a bit dull, though. It's basically an expanded Arkham City covered in snow, except that the expanded portion has nothing to offer. You go gliding around and thinking "oh, that building was in Arkham City! It's a really cool building", but then you look at the new things and you see nothing worth noticing. It's also a bit frustrating that you can't get on top of the tall buildings with the batclaw.
The story is actually good. Again, not as good as the other two games, but still good. The highlight of the plot for me is the interesting take on the relationship between the Joker and the Batman, specially when the Joker himself talks about it. I also liked that they portrayed Bane as he should be portrayed this time. The sidequests, on the other hand, are pretty boring (the only one I liked was the Mad Hatter's), and the Riddler one was a real disappointment. Gathering all the collectibles is really not worth it, so thank god they didn't have 400 of those again (and, might I add, keep it that way and never do that again); the end of the quest is just a little joke of a reference to the other games, and all you get are a few tapes that are so uninteresting I almost gave up on getting the hidden data just for that: I thought I'd get tapes about the villains and listen about their psychological traits, like the other two games did so well (specially Arkham Asylum), but instead, most of the tapes were related to police officers that barely show up during the game, and all they do is show how corrupt Gotham is. Wow. What a surprise. Just let that sink in. Who could've imagined right?
Now, the biggest con are the bugs. There are a lot of them. I never experienced a game breaking one, but it might happen. One time I was trying to do a sidequest and I couldn't get on top of the building; if I touched it, Batman went right through and fell into infinity. Luckily, when I chose "Retry" on the menu it was fixed. I also saw enemies that stopped moving completely, and NPCs I couldn't interact with, even if the game demanded it (like interrogating an enemy after you beat him; the option to interrogate him just wouldn't appear). I fixed everything with the "Retry" option, but as some reviewers mentioned here, this could turn into a game breaking thing.
With all that being said, would I still recommend it? Yes, I would. A "bad" version of really good games is still at least a good game, and I had a lot of fun playing it. So yeah, specially now that you can get it for a low price, I'd totally recommend it. Not really a "must play", though, so just take those things into account and decide if you'd like to play it or not.

If you want a very short review of this game, I think one of Chumbucket's lines in the game perfectly sums my experience up with this game: " Whatta blast!"
In a nutshell this is an amazing open world game, I will now proceed to list some good and bad aspects to be more specific:
Good:
*Amazing graphics, and well optimized to boot! Has some of THE best if not the THE best explosion and fire effects I have ever seen.
*Very good story, I've always loved the world of Mad Max for it's grittiness and in a way, realism. The story is really great and a very interesting exploration into the Max character and the ♥♥♥♥ed up world he survives in. Also beatufiul cinematics, it has probably my favorite cutscene/dream sequence in any videogame EVER.
*Interesting lore and backstory. The history relics give a great look back at the world that once was, and Max's commentary over some adds even more.
*Gameplay is fun! Honestly some of the better melee combat in WB games, feels better than the Batman games, to me at least. Punches feel really powerful and an upgraded shotgun is something to fear, specially for your ears since it sounds the way a shotgun should. Driving (the best i've ever felt driving in a game) and vehicular combat is great, even tho in the beggining you will die a couple times, once you start getting serious with your upgrades, it becomes really fun to just blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up with your Opus.
Now to the negative stuff:
*Repetitive gameplay, even tho it didnt reach the level of being repetitious to me. You will be doing a lot of the same in this game, punching, making♥♥♥♥♥♥blow up, collecting scrap (oh boy will you be collecting scrap), liberating camps, but it's always fun, but I see why some people wouldnt be happy with that.
*Busywork feeling activities, I'm looking at you minefields and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ intel encounters.
All in all, this is an amazing game, and an absolute MUST for any Mad Max fan, and a very big YES from me to any open world lover. I paid 5 bucks for this a year ago and honestly it's worth even the 20 bucks it goes for these days.
pd: also a bit of advice,
*unless you're an achievement freak, don't sweat if you can't 100% loot every little camp and scavenging location. There are literally hundreds of these to go, there's enough scrap to get all you want without losing your mind over that one damned scrap piece you just can't find in that one damned place.
*driving around can get pretty boring, so I really suggest putting some tunes in the background and just chill. I listened to a lot of Jinsang and lo-fi beats while doing it and honestly i bet i'll have some fond memries of this game while I listen to those songs in the future. Also while you engage in road wars be sure to listen to the MADDESt and  MAXEST of all songs, Road Rage by Miracle of Sound, i guarantee it will improve your experience at least 3.5 times.
Now, go and have fun Wastelander. Until death.

I recommend this game only on the condition that you really like the Mad Max franchise, and you'd happily play a Mad Max themed game even if it's not a particularly inventive game. I'd recommend getting it when it's on sale, as it's a fun game for the most part.
I'm surprised it has so many glowing reviews though, because...
Overall though, it's a mediocre game imo, and frustrating because it could have been so much more. It feels like little imagination has been put into making it feel like a unique game or a living world. It's just 'Fury Road' aesthetic and design meets generic open-world game. It's not bad, it's just... really average. A little more work at original gameplay ideas and believable AI and this game could've been really good.
The pros:
- Nice environment and settings
- Good ground and vehicle combat
- Attacking convoys can be challenging and a lot of fun
- Did I mention that vehicle combat is a lot of fun?
- Car customisation is cool
- Decent playing time
- Authentic Mad Max/Fury Road feel to enemies, camps, vehicles etc.
The cons:
- The world has so much stuff in it that you never feel a sense of isolation
- Not very immersive. The world does not seem 'alive' but rather 'setup for you to discover'. What the game tells you about the world you're in is very different to the world you witness. e.g. Convoys do not make supply runs between enemy camps and Gastown, they just drive around never-ending loops waiting for you to attack them. In most regions of the map, Stank Gum's crew do not terrorize other wastelanders, they stay in their camps waiting for you to attack them. Besides, the other wastelanders and 'allies' don't really seem to exist in the world anyway
- No settlements other than enemy camps/bases and a handful of allied strongholds. No 'neutral' survivor settlements or camps.
- Repetitive quests and gameplay
- All the 'Top Dog' bosses look and behave the same
- Cars can't roll over
- No soft body physics (although the crashes and damage aren't bad)
- No semis/articulated-vehicles/lorries
- No pole-cats or ploughboys
- Mediocre story that's fairly short, most playing time is in side-missions which are repetitive
- Poor story ending that's out-of-character for Max. Also, the ending results in a different world to the one you're actually left in after the ending. I know that sounds like nonsense, well, it feels like nonsense in the game too.
- Only the Magnum Opus is customisable
- Predictable and repetitive AI and in-world experiences
I'd love to see a Mad Max themed game built more in the style of The Forest. Now there's an immersive and creepy game with fantastic and hard to predict AI.

This new Dante feels like an old friend.
I'll admit, I was skeptical of this series re-launch, especially when it was first announced back in 2010 and the first promotional image was this:
My gut reaction to seeing that image back then was "You just ruined Dante and the DMC franchise." and to an extent, that gut reaction sort of stayed with me until I finally had a chance to try the game for myself.
Thankfully, the end result was far from my initial fears.
DmC does a good job of managing to reinvent the so-called "origin" story of Dante and Vergil, and yet by and large once you manage to get used to the new face and very different attitude (at least at first) of the new Dante, you'll discover that the gameplay itself is nothing short of the classic DMC style you've come to know.
Controls have been somewhat re-imagined in a way that neither takes too long to get used to nor feels terribly unfamiliar. By and large they are handled well, and a lot of the familiar signature aspects that the franchise is known for are still here as well.
For example, orbs and the time statues for "shopping" are present here. Dante still has Ebony and Ivory and they still get unlimited ammo. Signature abilities like Stinger make their return with a new control schemata. Devil trigger is of course also present, though it works in a slightly different way than in most of the past entries, it nonetheless manages to impress just as it always has.
While I did have some initial complaints about Dante's voice acting (the lines seemed really flat early on in the game) once you give it some more time it fleshes itself out better, and that also gives you a chance to get adjusted to the new Dante as well.
And it IS an adjustment. Gone is the super confident whimsical and snarky don't-take-life-too-seriously Dante of yore, for the most part. This new Dante is younger, more apathetic and less enthusiastic, but to an extent this new attitude is plot related as well, and for what it's worth I think it is a convincing way to show character growth and progression.
Gradually as Dante begins to open his eyes to the situation around him through the plot events, he starts becoming more empathetic, and discovers his own true nature in the process.
I won't spoil the details too much, but it was good to see his character maturing over the course of the game. And while I do feel like he never reached the same height on the badass meter that classic Dante manages to capture, by the time all is said and done it's clear to see he's squarely on his way to becoming more like his platinum haired alter ego.
Take away from this what you will, but if you're willing to brave the initial storm and wait for the seas to calm, as far as the new Dante goes, you'll see this is another great entry in the DMC series. It takes a bit to get used to the changes, but change can be good sometimes.

It would be awesome if this could be played grand-theft-auto style, but it's a truck driving sim.
I don't like it, but I'm recommending this game to anyone that wants a truck driving sim.

This game will make you feel like you are on the road for long stretches of time... watching the daylight and weather and scenery come and go, pulling out of truck stops in the middle of the night, and rolling into town as the sun is rising.
There is a pretty serious time commitment here for such a simple game. Things like truck upgrades, unlocking new territories, and hazmat licenses are expensive relative to the amount you get paid for driving. You will be doing a lot of time-consuming long hauls to get a halfway decent truck and open up a few countries.
My recommendation would be to load some music files or even audiobooks into the game folder so that you can listen to them through the truck radio, or at least have something going in real life while you play. Otherwise you might get bored before too long just sitting there forever keeping your truck in the lanes... since you're not actually getting paid for it and all. But if you can find a way to multitask it can be a relaxing and fun time.

The story Arkham Origins tells is superior to previous games, but they somehow managed to nearly break the combat system. Coming directly off a third or fourth Arkham City playthrough, it was immediately apparent that timing during combat was tweaked slightly, which is especially frustrating when trying to time a Counter. Capcom and Dante got a lot of crap for this one. A superfluous decision to reboot a franchise that wasn't in need of rebooting and a grittier, almost 'emo' new look turned a lot of fans off. On top of that, many see Ninja Theory as a rookie developer that still haven't really hit their stride. Games like Heavenly Sword and Enslaved: Odyssey to the West were both great efforts that slightly missed their mark. I'm glad to say that DmC their best work yet. While I have no qualms over the new art direction, I even enjoy it, I can understand where most fans are coming from. The whole 'emo' look is frowned upon (I, personally, don't think he looks all too emo) and Capcom wanted to reboot the series with a more modern, gritty, western feel. They achieved that. The aesthetics are beautiful in this game, down to the UI and HUD. The style retains a little bit of old Devil May Cry while dabbling in a newer, sleeker look. As for story, it's nothing special. Where Enslaved, I feel, had a great story, DmC takes a step back for Ninja Theory. However, this doesn't detract much from the game. While I can spend time talking about how the game looks and describing why it's story is lackluster, I wouldn't be doing a review of this game justice. The fact of the matter is this game is pure, unbridled action fun. This new entry in the series clearly simplifies the DmC combat/combo system. DMC veterans may not enjoy the main-streaming of the combat. However, anyone who wants to play an explosive action game and feel like a total badass will enjoy this title. The combat, while still holding true to a steep difficulty curve and high skill ceiling, is exhilarating. When you grasp the basics of weapon switching mid combo and using the pull/grab feature this will be some of the most fluid, smooth and rewarding combat you've ever enjoyed. No word epitomizes the combat system better than 'butta' (as in 'smooth as butter'). The combat system definitely lends to the games replay-ability. Die hards will want to work for a better final score on chapters or work to unlock all aspects of the system by unlocking new skills for Dante's weapons. Masochists will get a kick out of the several difficulty levels above the traditional normal mode. This is something the Devil May Cry series has always prided itself on and it hasn't disappeared. Collectors will want to go through each level and play every clever and increasingly difficult secret mission or collect the many Lost Souls scattered throughout the game. A combination of all of those archetypes will find hours of enjoyment in collecting concept art from defeating large amounts of each enemy type and beating the game on the highest difficulty setting. I could truly put this game in the running for Game of the Year 2013. While the game stands mostly on it's combat system, there is definitely more there be enjoyed. For anyone who has bored of Sparda's favorite son, the Vergil's Downfall DLC is also a worthy investment. Playing as Vergil is almost a completely different experience. They do the character justice and it feels fantastic. Anyone who enjoys a good hack n' slash or action game, and anyone who is holding back because of the new decor, take the time and give this game a chance.

Where do I start with this game?
In a Vacuum this game is a solid 7. "Why a 7" Is probably the question you're asking. Well for starters, the script; while workable and functional leaves something to be desired even though it gets you through the game. I know you've probably heard the outcry for the "F*ck you-F*ck you" back and forth between Dante and the Succubus; though I guess you could look at that  as Dante's such an♥♥♥♥♥that he has the innate ability to♥♥♥♥♥♥off demons without trying. No, being an♥♥♥♥♥is not necessarily a bad thing. Then comes the voice acting. I have to give it a pass simply because the only real cringe worthy lines in the reboot, won't scar your brain like the original (look up "fill your dark soul with light" on youtube, you'll see what I mean). The voicework is on par with the script. Passable, no stellar performances, some hitches here and there (hitches as in cringe-lines), but it's not bad. For an example of bad, look at the original resident evil, or Sonic Adventure.
The combat is decent. Hell when mastered it's practically on par with previous games, though there are still things that I personally wish they kept. For one, royal guard is no more. That got replaced by the parry system. This system is good and bad, because you can use it intentionally to make enemies kill/damage themselves, but at the same time you'll get a bunch of free points just by accidentally parrying enemies you had no intention of parrying. The H/H weapon is just plain boring to use; effective against certain enemies, but still boring. Sorry but Beowulf was just too damn good to not miss it.
Taunts are missing even though there's a free button that's not used while playing with Dante. This was a fun mechanic for funzies that is definitely missed.

Another issue with combat is that it's so loose that when you try to cancel certain moves it causes conflict with the animations which leads to certain abusable bugs or Dante Jerking around. I honestly can't recall previous DMC's having this particular combat bug, though the "fair play" bug seems to be shared.
What I mean by fair play is that enemies usually won't attack you unless they're in the camera's view, or are already in the middle of an attack when the player points the camera away from them. Though sometimes while looking at enemies they behave as if the camera isn't looking at them and they'll just stand there in one spot, confused. This is usually fixed by turning the camera away and turning it back, but at the same time, why would a player want to do that? >.>

As this is more or less an audio/visual test that became a game, I was pleasantly surprised by how engaging it was to play. The gameplay is beyond simple - you can walk, run, turn your flashlight on and off, and jump (seems to only be a couple inches). The audio is the superstar here so play with headphones on.
It's designed to be played with the Occulus Rift, but if like me you don't have that, a darkened room and stereo headphones - or a surround sound system haha - would work for playing.
Pros:
+well-lit atmosphere (there seems to be a trick that after your flashlight is turned off, slowly the area brightens as your eyes adjust to the darkness)
+and genuinely creepy music and sound effects.
Cons:
-some performance issues - the game froze multiple times on only "medium" video and texture quality settings on my computer
-weird audio glitches upon first load
-Unintuitive gameplay (though this is forgiven in that it was a sound test and not really a game)
-Uneventful ending sequences
-Weird warning not to play if you're pregnant.
Overall if you're a fan of suspense, or just an audiophile who likes to let sound effects creep you out, it's worth downloading. The price is certainly right.

Okay, so this is a bit different for me. I watch scary movies and play scary games, I usually laugh or sing to cope if I feel uncomfortable. I decided not to do that tonight and wore my headphones seeing as to how this appeared to pull mainly off of sounds. I play through confidently even commenting, "Walking Simulator 2015 10/10" and of course the sounds are creepy but nothing alarming. I finally reach a house with a creaky swing and I hear footsteps. These footsteps are not mine, I hear them getting closer as the leaves rustle and the swing keeps creaking. Closer. My heart is starting to race. Footsteps are gone. I hesitantly turn around and there's nothing. I go inside house and explore, there are cockroaches and they make their own sounds (BTW developers make it easier to go through doorways, stairways etc. I got stuck several times.) After exploring upstairs I go back to the path and continue my adventure. I run most of the path until I reach another building. A church, I stop because I heard a new sound, it sounded like a squeaky toy. The Footsteps begin again, I nearly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥myself, and then continue until I reach another fork in the road where there is a scarecrow, a very detailed scarecrow with a face that appears almost...human. I keep my eye on it, then run like the wind with no intentions of stopping. I start noticing piles of hay on the sides of the path and it's becoming narrower. I hear the squeaky toy once more... I stop dead in my tracks waiting for the ominous footsteps. I didn't listen long enough, I panicked and ran, I kept running even when I heard the footsteps, I heard a scream, IT got me. Pros:
-Beautiful art style
-great soundtrack
-intuitive controls/smooth
-fun abilities
-smart puzzles | while tricky, they are not unfair and the sense of accomplishment is great
-tense moments that made me hold my breath and culminated in a satisfying victory that allowed me a breather afterwards
Cons:
-backtracking | there was a good deal of it, and after awhile, especially with tricky platforming, it got a tad annoying. Fortunately, if you can find them, there are some shortcuts in areas, however you have to have the right ability to unlock them.
-inability to really 'zoom out' in a way, or look around | this would have helped me avoid several unfair deaths where I died as a result of not being able to see where I was landing. While such deaths can mostly be avoided by exercising caution, dying because you literally did not see it coming will still occur (and it sucks). I wouldn't have minded if looking around only worked when I was standing still. I believe even that much would have helped in some situations. I'm not asking to be able to see the whole board, but at least to see just a little more of it.
misc. :
-Manual save points | I put these here because people see these differently, but I felt it was something to be aware of. You have a set amount of energy that you can replenish with pick ups, or at special areas. This energy is used to place a save point where you want it. If you have no energy, you can't create a save point, and should you die you will return to either the last save point you created, or the most recent special area.
-map icons | there are special zones called wells that act as fast travel points and replenish your health and energy. Unless you spend skill points to unlock icons on the map though, there is no indication of where said wells are.

Most people would think this is just another platformer, but what Moon Studios has created is nothing short of a masterpiece.
You play the game as Ori, a white spirit like character who fell from the Great Spirit Tree as a baby. As the story develops, you learn what happened to Ori after her fall. Who raised her and how she lived up & till a cataclysmic event causes Ori's life to change forever, and  with that the world plunges into darkness.
As you start your journey, you meet a companion by the name of Sein, who acts as the will of the Spirit Tree. Sein both guides you and gives you access to tremendous powers. From powerful jumps to using light as defensive weapon in various forms.
This is all necessary to defend yourself against the corrupted world and the nasty creatures waiting in it for you.
You are tasked with restoring the various elements throughout the world (Wind, Fire, Water & Earth) but I can't really expand any more about the story without spoiling it so I'll leave the rest for you to discover.
The game has some very unique mechanics, for a platformer. Being able to create your own projectiles or launch yourself off of objects was quite an interesting experience, especially when time gets added as a factor.
In terms of abilities, you have a total of eleven "powers" that allow you to explore the world and defend yourself against it. The monsters are the one part where it kinda falls a bit (for me at least) as the game doesn't have the greatest variety and there are a lot of re-colors, same enemy just a different color but with that being said the monsters are a bit creative, from monsters that
use roll attacks to leaping creatures that can one-shot you.
As expected the game has a decently sized map, with a bunch of unique areas to explore. Enough to keep you busy for at least six hours if you are just flying through and not collecting or exploring anything. I encourage you not to just blast through as this is where the game shines brightest. Navigating this amazing world by solving puzzles and exploring every inch of the map is so worth it.
As if you couldn't tell from the cover, this game sports some amazing art. Stunning graphics all around, from the area designs to the characters that inhabit it. It is such a beautiful game that words really don't do it justice, its something that has to be experienced to fully grasp it.
This game is worth every penny of its asking price, even better if you get it on Steam Sale :)

There is a lot to love about Ori. A couple of the more unique platforming mechanics are really interesting and fun, the story is great and the art is gorgeous.  Frequently (though not always), the platforming puzzles and challenges are super fun and feel rewarding.
Unfortunately, I think the bad cancels out all the good. The controls and platforming in the game are much more physics based than a traditional platformer, giving you less control in the air and to me feeling kind of sluggish (this is probably up to personal taste though). The various elements of the environment are frequently unclear because the screen is so busy. The level design and geometry of levels has at various points made me get stuck where I wasn't supposed to or made jumps seem possible or impossible when they were meant to be the opposite.
The enemy design is about half great and half terrible.  The first enemy you encounter is this dumb blob that shoots three projectiles and is annoying to fight rather than fun, but that enemy is probably the most common enemy in the game.  The annoying enemies wouldn't be so bad if combat didn't take way too long. You do tiny amounts of poke damage that requires you to get close to enemies but not too close because then you can't dosge their very fast moving projectiles! It makes for a tiring dance that has to repeat for every single enemy. Alternatively you could waste a save by using a charge attack that doesn't even one-shot most of the enemies.
Upgrade system is BLAH.  I mostly upgraded to alleviate the things I didn't like like limited saves and having to collect experience when it falls out of enemies.  Mostly I felt like upgrades had no impact until triple jump.
The metroidvania style results in both an annoying antiquated save system (this game would be way better with frequent checkpoints) and the possibility to get lost and be confused where to go next. Not to mention, death is a true restart from your last save, meaning you have to face all the annoying enemies you already beat all over again, you lose any experience or power-ups you gained, and you have to watch all the cutscenes over again. God help you if you save right before a cutscene and then die several times.
If the game were a straight platformer with checkpoints, and faster platformy enemy combat (like jumping an an enemy kills it) I would have liked it a LOT better.  As it is, I am glad I have played it, but I cannot possibly recommend it to anyone.

A worthy successor to Blood Money, HITMAN combines the sandbox of previous games with Absolution's mechanics.
PROS:
- Agent 47 is as deadly as always
- The game is constantly supported, bringing new contracts, updates, escalations or Elusive Targets each week
- Replay value, as there are plenty of ways to eliminate targets and tools that can help you with it
- Large, beautifully crafted, unique locations
CONS:
- Stupid AI
- Random glitches
- Clones in every location
- A really small number of voice actors, no matter where the missions will take you, NPC will always sound, and look the same
- I should also mention that the game requires constant internet connection, but to be honest I haven't had a problem with it, as now you can use starting points and gadgets while being offline

This game made me realise the disturbing fact that, I love killing people. I would normally go to see a therapist about these violent thoughts, but what if he's actually a hired assassin in disgusie? I can't afford to take that risk!
HITMAN follows the continued adventures of everyones favourite sociopathic bald murderer (yes, continued, despite the name, one opening cutscene make it very clear that this isn't a reboot.) as he preforms a series of seeming unrelated hits on people, but it soon becomes clear that someone is manipulating the ICA into preforming their dirty work for them. The plot is definitely intresting, but since this is only season one, it sadly feels like alot of build up but no pay off... But I still really want to see where it's all going, so it succeeds in that department. However, what the plot fails at, the gameplay passes with flying colours. Agent 47 controls great, every action feels smooth and simple, but it's the level design that makes this game. Maps are either massive or densely packed, with tonnes of options for taking out your targets in cool and memorable ways. The six maps presented are all unique locations and can be played through over and over again, not just the main story, but also escalation and contracts mode. However, the fact that this single player game requires online to access most of its content and that escluive targets can never be redone if you miss the deadline are both major grips for me, though i don't mind the game being episodic if the quality of each individual map is this good.

In my opinion, they did right by the series when they came back to the open world and less linear gameplay in this one. I really enjoy the large variety of methods to eliminate your targets. Even using the same methods there are plenty of routes to take to alter the experience. You could play one map for hours and not get the exact same method twice (unless you can't figure out any others) but to me its just the perfect balance between hidden paths and more obvious ones. I enjoy this game and its one of my favorite in the series. I highly recommend it.

DmC
The Look - The game's visuals are all top notch. The developers were clearly able to put a lot of time and effort into the environments and character designs. Dante and his cohorts all have a unique look and interesting attire. The game received some flack during its reveal for ditching the classic white-haired Dante but I think that there is a strong, fun, and unique visual style that permeates the experience. You will see some recycled enemy designs but there are enough minor differences between types that I never felt bored by their appearance. The main visual treat is the environment, which has a habit of transforming as you move through it. Walls rise and fall and floors will turn into stairs, pits, and stepping stones, as familiar environments often get twisted into a more hellish version of their former selves.
The Sound - No real issues with the audio quality. That said, the music tracks might not be for everyone. I don't have prior experience but I felt that the musical stylings of Combichrist had the potential to be somewhat polarizing. If you don't like heavy metal or death metal (or precious metals?) you might not be a fan of the audio tracks. However, I'm not a huge fan of the genre but I was never really put off by it so I think most people will be fine here. Great use of sound effects with some nice visceral slices, slams, and crunches during combat. Additionally, the voice acting, which you'll be exposed to frequently, is very strong on all fronts.
The Gameplay - Despite some claims of oversimplification, I think this game is tons of fun to play. It follows the basic 3rd person action trends with all of the combos, dodges, and power moves that you'd expect. What makes DmC stand out a bit is the variety of weapons and the diversity of each. Heavy, Medium, Light, and Ranged weapons are all on display and all offer something fun and new when unlocked. The game's grading system (a genre staple) is also a fun way to compete against others and yourself while trying to unlock things like concept art and new costumes. There are a number of hidden collectibes that can be found in the game, but these often veer into the dangerous territory of tedium when you try to seek them all out. Also, despite the fast and fun combat, there are some levels that feel overly long or overly short so don't expect that each new chapter will take the same amount of time as the last one.
The Story - DmC's story is a simple but fun affair. You are Dante, half-angel/half-demon, and you're out for revenge on the demon who orphaned you and is currently trying to take over the world. There are some fun twists and turns along the way but nothing jaw dropping or genre defining. While Dante's brash attitude may seem a bit obnoxious, the character grew on me and by the end of the game I found myself eagerly awaiting his next quip or shocking turn of phrase. The narrative has just enough momentum to keep you interested in learning more about Dante's past and to see what steps he'll take to get his revenge. You'll never be moved to tears, but you'll probably get a few laughs out of this yarn.
Other Thoughts - There's not a lot to say here. This is not a game of great thematic depth or complexity. The combat, on the other hand, has both in spades. I think this is a great first chapter in what will hopefully become a new series of games. Oftentimes, 3rd person action games will lose their footing somewhere. The story may be obtuse or boring, the combos may be too tough to pull off, the enemies might be too easy or difficult, etc. DmC does a great job of walking this line and not overstaying its welcome.
Score - 4/5 (A solid game. Genre fans should love it, while others will probably really like it. Check it out!)

So I read a review on Steam about this game and it wasn't very flattering, so I wanted to write my own review because I loved this game.
First of all, this is Mad Max.  If you know anything about the Mad Max universe, you should know what to expect.  It's based on a post-apocalyptic world where everything is a desert. Don't expect ocean, urban, suburban, forest, swamp, snowy or mall environments.  You should be expecting a consistent environment which follows the narrative of the story.  Having said that, there is a repetitive feel to your missions and the overall progression of the game.  However, if you really like Mad Max and you want to be a part of that universe then, you'll love this game.
There's an upgrade system to the game for your vehicles, your person, and your "worshipper."  Is it an in-depth extensive upgrade system?  No.  Is this a game where you'll find developing characters and elaborate plot twists?  No, it's not All My Children.  Is this a game where you'll have a million quests to find with numerous endings?  No.  So you might be thinking, well that kinda sucks, but I didn't think so.
For me this was an enjoyable game, so much so I finished it.  It really felt like the crappy, cut-throat, dog eat dog world I imagined Mad Max living in.  You have 1 primary goal in the game and everything moves you to that direction.  To me it made sense there wasn't a million things to do, because well everything was destroyed in some unspoken world event.
So, if you want to be Mad Max and just straight kill and blow stuff up for a while, try it.  If the Mad Max story-line, is only kind of appealing to you, then don't.  I really like the game though.
I played this game using Linux Mint btw.  It worked flawlessly.

A magnificient game marred by a worse than mediocre ending.
The gameplay is basically two layers.
The top layer is a strategic game resource management game where you engage in a struggle against Scrotus minions (the main antagonists). You gather resources, take over strategic sites, gather support among Scrotus enemies and in general fight off the influence of Scrotus warboys.
Below that we have what is basically two separate but integrated types of gameplay. Driving and on foot. Both types of gameplay are fun and engaging. The on-foot gameplay is reminiscent of Shadow of Mordor or Batman: Arkham Asylum. You climb things, you fight enemies through a maneuver/strike/parry system with unlockable special moves and you manage special weapon resources (in mad max, shotgun rounds and fury meter).
The driving portion is probably the games best feature. Pretty much everything about it is a joy, especially once you realize how to utilize your vehicles strengths against the enemies weaknesses (maneuverability on road and in sanddunes, weight, ramming power, armor, method of attack etc). Everything from open vehicular battle, convoy attacks and no-holds barred vehicle races to using the on-board harpoon to tear down defensive structures. The driving portion gets even better through the vehicle upgrades system where some (like upgrading the engine) are a no-brainer, while upgrading armor, ramming grill and certain vehicle weapons adds weight which affects acceleration and maneuverability, all catering to individual preferences and the mission in mind.
The only critique against the gameplay (and this is a minor one) is that too few of the games major confrontations are vehicle based. Too much of the strategic portion of the game is about taking on enemy strongholds on foot. The game map is divided into regions, and a significant part of the effort in taking these regions involves taking oil rigs and defensive strongholds; where the inner defenses require you to get out of your vehicle. While you're constantly challenged by enemy vehicles the only real vehicle combat obstacle are the convoys, of which there is only one to each region (compared to two to four or five strongholds). These convoy battles though are usually some of the best moments in the game.

If you have played City, and thought to yourself "That was really great, but I wish the story was a bit more interesting", then this is the game for you!
It is pretty much City, but re-skinned, and a bit buggy.  Bugs, you say?  How can they just re-skin and end up with bugs?  Well they did.  Not too many, but still annoying.  I have played 33 Hours when I wrote this, and I have had enemies half clip into terrain and get stuck about six times.  Luckily I have been able to knock them down to bring them back out of it each time, but that is still pretty weak work.  I have also had trouble with the odd interrogation not triggering at the end of a fight too.  Ground takedowns seem easy to miss as well.
Anyway, bugs aside, the game is pretty much the same as City.  Fighting and Stealthing are pretty much the same, with a couple of different gadgets in the mix.  You go around collecting "Enigma Data Packs" (Villians don't have their monikers yet), solving pretty much the same puzzles as in City.  You have a series of scattered objects you have to destroy.  The Hatter messes with your mind.
The crime scene stuff looks pretty cool, but really boils down to, find a red triangle and hold down spacebar.  Find the next red triangle and hold down spacebar.  Repeat until no further triangles are evident.  You get a hologram of the crime that you can move forward and back in (to find the next triangle) but it is not much of a minigame.
I had hoped that, being set several years earlier we would see a difference in tech level, but no.  Everyone has touch screen smart phones, Batman has the same cryptographic sequencer, and so on.  I think they missed an opportunity to look at the speed of progress of technology there, but oh well.
The other annoying thing they have done in this game is make the skill system into a kind of tree.  So you can't just get the upgrades that you want, you have to follow a sequence.  Or you may have to complete a particular side quest to unlock a move.  I finished the story without unlocking disarm and destroy, which was pretty annoying.  I did not study the tree to see who I had to defeat to get it, so just kept on wondering when I would it would pop up.
Oh yeah, one other gripe, Batman is just a little bit cross-eyed.  He glances around weirdly during cut scenes and it is just a bit off putting.
I liked seeing some different villains in the game, even if one was hilariously ineffective (one hit defeat on hard. I thought it may have been a glitch, but the same thing happened on New Game+ hard too.) and most of the boss battles were interesting and different enough to be fun.
Now, the point of difference: Multi Player.  I have only played a couple of hours of this, but it seemed pretty cool.  It is an eight player, three faction game, with Batman and Robin on one side, three Joker thugs, and three Bane thugs.  There are two game modes, but I only tried one.  The two thug gangs battle it out for control of objectives and the heroes just run around griefing the others.  If the heroes take out enough thugs without getting killed too much themselves, they win.  If a thug gang take all three(?) objectives then they win.  The Joker and Bane turn up late in the round to be taken over by whover opens the door for them.  I did not do that in the time I played, figuring their buffs could be used better by a more experienced mulit-player.  I found the game play pretty fun, either as thugs or heroes.  The lobby system seemed pretty clunky, and the requirement for eight players exactly seemed a bit limiting.  I was quite often sitting there wondering why the game was not starting, and not seeing what I could do about it.
So after reading that you may be wondering "why the thumbs up?".  While disappointing in a few ways, all of the other Arkham games have been so great, this one only fails by comparison.  If this was the first one I had played, I would love it.

This is the best "metroidvania" style platform game I have ever played.
The controls are very responsive, there is a constant well paced sense of progression with the new abilities you unlock and the level design is very clever at many points. This is a very movement based platformer, it's all about jumping, wall jumping, dashing, gliding and boosting your way through puzzles and hazards in clever ways. There is some combat as well, but it's very secondary and not nearly as interesting or as important to the gameplay.
PROs
* Absolutely gorgeous graphics.
* Suprisingly good and emotional story.
* Tight controls and a unique and interesting move set.
* Good level design.
* Great soundtrack.
CONs
* There are some places where it's not clear what is foreground and what is background, leading to stupid deaths.
* The enemies visual design is a bit underwhelming, they are all mostly various purple-ish blobs. With a certain own being a major exception.
* There are a couple of chase sequences where you have to outrun some enemy or environmental hazard. They are awesome in many ways, but sadly become tedious since they are too long with no intermediate checkpoints and you have to start over when you fail.
* Combat is underwhelming. Most enemies are either no threat at all or are there to be used as movement puzzle elements.
Over all, this is a must buy if you like metroidvanias and especially if you like games with a high focus on mobility, acrobatics and speed over combat.

Being surrounded by such vivid imagery constantly throughout game play is a definitive plus for feeling compelled and having a desire to keep going. Every new area always feels new and fresh to play through. The story also adds to the experience and world of Ori as it an emotional one that adds to the tone of the game and makes it that much more of a wholesome experience to invest in. Lengthwise, Ori is around 8 hours but compelling enough and has much to explore making it ideal and never a repetitive experience. Ori and the Blind Forest is a challenging game that is worth playing for amazing visuals, compelling and fun game play, as well as featuring a beautiful story.

Overall good fun. The Loot-n-Shoot formula is consistently rewarding and moving and maneuvering feels nice and smooth. The guns are quite satisfying as well, and there is a looot of variety.
Where this game excels in steadily good gameplay, it falls short in the writing department. There are some good bits, like the villain of the game, who's written pretty much as a middle-management ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and Roland's and Lilith's awkard relationship which feels pretty down-to-earth, considering the circumstances. But the bad bits, ewwww the bad bits. Right off the start of the game you spend quite some time chasing around Claptrap, who I thought was the most annoying, try-hardy, unfunny character I've ever seen in any media.
And then I met Tiny Tina.
They try so hard to up the ~WAKKA WAKKA SO WACKY AND EDGY~ ante, but it just falls flat and ends up being frustratingly unfunny. I think the problem I have with Tiny Tina's (and Gaige's) writing is that it feels really forced, and you can't do wacky humor if you have to force it. I hadn't even completed the first quest with Tina when I was already hoping she would just go away forever.
Another grievance that I also had back in the day with BL1, is that the difficulty curve... it's not really a curve at all. It's more of a zig-zag pattern; most of the time you'll be rolling over most mobs and bosses with no problem and then BAM the game throws at you an enemy that pretty much one-shots you. But then you do a couple of sidequests, get a level, maybe a better gun, and then all of a sudden that hard enemy is an absolute cakewalk.
All that said, they are in the end only smaller things in an otherwise very solid and satisfying game, with some pretty cool ideas (You even get to heist, not one, but two trains!). After thoroughly enjoying BL1, BL2 lived up to my expectations and a little more. It's a solid shooter with flawed attempts at contemporary humor, and well worth the purchase.

HITMAN follows the continued adventures of everyones favourite sociopathic bald murderer (yes, continued, despite the name, one opening cutscene make it very clear that this isn't a reboot.) as he preforms a series of seeming unrelated hits on people, but it soon becomes clear that someone is manipulating the ICA into preforming their dirty work for them. The plot is definitely intresting, but since this is only season one, it sadly feels like alot of build up but no pay off... But I still really want to see where it's all going, so it succeeds in that department. However, what the plot fails at, the gameplay passes with flying colours. Agent 47 controls great, every action feels smooth and simple, but it's the level design that makes this game. Maps are either massive or densely packed, with tonnes of options for taking out your targets in cool and memorable ways. The six maps presented are all unique locations and can be played through over and over again, not just the main story, but also escalation and contracts mode. However, the fact that this single player game requires online to access most of its content and that escluive targets can never be redone if you miss the deadline are both major grips for me, though i don't mind the game being episodic if the quality of each individual map is this good.

In my opinion, they did right by the series when they came back to the open world and less linear gameplay in this one. I really enjoy the large variety of methods to eliminate your targets. Even using the same methods there are plenty of routes to take to alter the experience. You could play one map for hours and not get the exact same method twice (unless you can't figure out any others) but to me its just the perfect balance between hidden paths and more obvious ones. I enjoy this game and its one of my favorite in the series. I highly recommend it.
