Arkham Origins is another entry in the Batman Arkham series, and it offers more of the gameplay you've come to expect in this francise. It does very little new, but it refines the gameplay through small tweaks, more varied groups to fight, and more abilities and gadgets that are practical and meaningful to use.
On that note, if you are looking for something new, Origins will do very little for you. However, if you just want to play more "Batman Simulators", this title is probably the best to date mechanically.
While the story this time around is a lot less atmospheric than Asylum was, it is immensely more cinematic. It starts off and follows a very predictable path, but then throws a bunch of curveballs to keep you second-guessing what will happen next. And in the end, it is a very well-done narrative to show how Batman became who he is today.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a commercial release of a total conversion mod for Batman: Arkham City.  That is not to say the game is bad by any means, it is however absolutely devoid of any innovation and serves as little more than a reskin with an altered map.
By setting the game years earlier than the previous two Arkham titles one would expect less gadgets and more low-tech solutions and puzzles in the game, instead all the same tools present in City have returned in Origins, even Mr. Freeze's ice grenades, which are retextured to be glue grenades instead but function identically.  The exact same hacking, the exact same remote controlled batarang...  It is all more of the same.  Some of the Riddler's puzzles are taken directly from City and used over again with only minor tweaks.
Again, not a bad game, but when you put out a new game the player should be able to expect a few interesting new things to see and do.  There are a few new bugs that I had not encountered in City present in Origins, so they got that going for them, which is nice I guess.
Yes, it is a game worth playing, but no, it is not a full game, so don't ever get it for a full price.

This is an absolutely gorgeous game with a great soundtrack, a heartwarming story and a great feeling gameplay as well. I rarely replay or even finish games, but I managed to finish this game several times and I’m planning on doing more because of the harder achievements. The controls feel great and the gradual improvement you get in your mobility and abilities by progressing with the story feels rewarding (a’la a classic metroidvania game). At first you start out with only the ability to jump, but later on you become an agile little wisp deathmachine. It might be a bit tough to beat it at first, but it’s not that long and a worthwhile effort to push through it just to experience the gorgeous art, music and story or even replay it for the challanges that the achievements can give you.
One bit of criticism I would give it is the gamepad support on PC. It took me a small bit of a setting up to work properly with my old Logitech Rumplepad gamepad, but there's a solution on the discussion forums which adressed the issue. It's a small tweak though and my gamepad worked without any problems after the fix. Also I did my first two playthroughs with a keyboard and it felt perfectly fine to play, so don't give up on it if you don't happen to have a gamepad.

There is only one thing about this version that I dislike, apart from that it is without a doubt superior to the original in every way I can think of. What kinda annoys me though is the way Ori moves, not that it's awful or anything, but compared to the original game the controls aren't as airthight in my opinion. Maybe it's just me, but the movement in the Definitive Edition feels "floatier" and less direct. This isn't a big deal as I got used to that eventually, but it still leads to unnecessary deaths from time to time.
However, I think this little complaint is heavily outweighted by all the improvements that - as many have said by now - should have been in the original version to begin with. The new areas and abilities fit perfectly, teleporting saves alot of time and nerves, and of course the game runs more smoothly now. It's not like the original had a lot of performance issues that the average player had to worry about, but it affected speedruns (especially the last part of the Ginso Escape tended to create a lot of lag for me and more than once led to an undeserved death).

With its art style, animation and music, Ori and the Blind Forest is definitely one of the greatest metroidvania action-adventure platformers of all time. A must-have if you enjoy any type of 2D platformer games.

I think the roots of zombies from World at War were still present in the first Black Ops and mostly in this one, but they are fading.
Overall great game, worth the money I believe. Possibly the only decent future call of duty game in the franchise.

San Andreas is one of my all-time favorite games, and for very good reason. It's a fantastic entry to the series, with enough content to keep you occupied for weeks. That's not even including the highly populated and still, very much alive multiplayer mod (SA-MP) and the plethora of other mods you can obtain for this amazing game.
However, since Rockstar is so hell-bent on ruining the PC user's experience, I can't recommend the Steam release of this game. The latest patch has removed a number (18, to be specific) of key songs from the once fantastic soundtrack. There is still no 1080p support. Previous save files will no longer work and you -will- more than likely crash if you are playing this game with a dual-monitor set up. Although despite these downgrades, at least they were 'kind enough' to implement very basic Xinput support, so you can play it with a controller. Woo.
Rockstar has all the right to do this. The removal of once available songs makes sense due to copyright reasons. You can't exactly sell your product when it contains content you no longer have the license to use, let alone monetize. But when the game is deliberately patched to take away content that users have already paid for, and to hinder the experience once again, you're just hurting your PC fanbase. Which, I suppose is nothing new if you've played any PC release of Grand Theft Auto post-GTA3.
The best way to enjoy this game is to purchase a retail copy. It'll probably be cheaper, it'll look good on your shelf, you can mod it by default all you want, and you won't have any of your content patched out without warning. With that said. Don't bother buying any other GTA games on Steam either. If they've already removed content in one title, then expect it again in the future from other installments of the franchise when licenses inevitably expire, or can no longer be obtained.
TL;DR: Great game but ruined by Rockstar's anti-consumer attitude. Go buy it elsewhere for the full experience.

Warning: Spoilers Ahead
If you want to know what I think of the game without spoilers, just know that: It's a great entry point for people starting the series, and still an enjoyable romp for veterans of the series despite the overall uninspired level design and combat. The story and performance of the characters is what sells this entry, and in my opinion is a must play/watch for any Batman fan.
This game gets lots of flack, and only some of it is deserved. I agree with people who say the game itself is uninspired, borrowing practically every element of their game from Rocksteady's preceding games. I also agree that when it first released, it was a buggy mess. Thankfully most major issues are all fixed now, and I didn't run into anything game breaking (a far cry from when I played it at launch on the 360).
Now, despite Origins' lack of innovation, I still think it's well put together. The actual design of the game, which admittedly lifts much of Arkham City's design, is very well done, and despite some reviews I've seen that say they added nothing of their own, there are TONS of added easter eggs and content that reward Bat-fans. Furthermore, Origins adds one cool new thing that is original and adds a much needed kick into Arkham's aging combat system; the shock gloves. The shock gloves alleviate some of the tedium of combat that veterans of the Arkham series are likely getting a bit tired of, if only because they mastered it two games ago. It is essentially a temporary super powerup, allowing Batman to do even more damage to enemies and therefore ending fights even quicker. They are also incorporated into a few puzzles, but aren't actually that clever despite looking pretty cool.
Speaking of puzzles, one thing Origins does better than any of the other Arkham games are the crime-scene reconstructions. They have multiple steps, and are a lot of fun to figure out. Yes, it may be scifi mumbo jumbo, but it's engaging nonetheless.
Most importantly, I feel that Origin's story is overlooked completely by most critics. The story of Origins is objectively the best in the series. It isn't overly convoluted, and doesn't contain any out-of-character moments like the Titan-Joker fight in Asylum. While I truly appreciate the comic-book style storytelling in the first two games, and I certainly don't think Batman needs his origin retold ever again, the Arkham games nonetheless are not good entry points to casual Bat-fans. Despite it being common knowledge amongst many comic-readers, most gamers had no idea who Oracle was in Asylum, and the fact that there were many people online legitimately trying to figure out who Azrael was supposed to be in City only cements that most players are casual Batfans. Despite my personal appreciation of Rocksteady's willingness to jump into the deep end of Batman lore, I can't help but think that it hurts various storytelling elements and opportunities.
Origins, on the other hand, tells a concise Batman story, where motivations, plot twists, and themes all come together and really impress on a more universal level.
It should also be noted that while I don't think Roger Craig Smith did a bad job as Batman, he certainly doesn't have the range nor depth of Conroy. Troy Baker as the Joker, on the other hand, is in some ways even better than Hamil. Don't get me wrong, I LOVE Hamil's Joker, but unfortunately for Hamil he was never really given an opportunity to cut loose with the character until much later in his career of voicing him, and his vocal chords at that point simply couldn't take that kind of strain. Baker is in his prime, and takes Hamil's version of the Joker (indeed, it is still Hamil's Joker, and I know Baker wouldn't deny it) to new levels of gritty realism and black humor that Hamil's Joker never got to really experience but a handful of times. It could be argued that Arkham Origins' plot is centrally about Batman and Joker's relationship's Origin. There is a brilliant section in the game that takes the classic Bruce Timm/Paul Dini story Mad Love, and somehow makes it even better by taking Joker's manipulation of Harley to another level completely. After being asked to describe fate by Harley, Joker begins rattling off his origin in typical dramatic fashion. The thing that's brilliant to me is that it's unclear if Joker even realizes that he's manipulating Harely; his romantic description of fate and everything it entails is [from the player's perspective] clearly concerning his relationship with Batman, but to Harley, it sounds like Joker is spilling out his feelings for her. This whole section plays out from a rather dramatic and abstract thought-plane from the Joker's perspective, with the player controlling Joker, maneuvering him through this surreal landscape while he describes how important fate is to him. It's all done so well, and Baker's performance really shines.
Another point that shines in the game overall are the new boss encounters. The assassins out to kill Batman are all capable, and in my opinion the real standout is the fight with a female Copperhead. While similar to the R'as fight from City, Copperhead's hard-to-read, snake-like movements make for an intense fight. Certainly, the boss fights overall in Origins are more varied than Asylum by far, and even City in my opinion, although nothing tops the Mr. Freeze fight from City.
Speaking of Mr. Freeze, the one extra DLC story mission is concerning Freeze's origins within the Arkhamverse. It starts out in Wayne Manor, and the player gets to control Bruce for a long while, which I always enjoy. It tells more or less the same story as the classic animated series tale, but modernizes it in a few key ways. For one, Batman reconstructs the fateful moment concerning Freeze's tragic origin, and this reconstruction is by far more engaging than the Animated Series original version where Batman simply sneaks into a security room and watches some easily-accessed, surprisingly well edited security tapes. Beyond that, though, there really isn't a substantial departure from the original tale, and like other elements of Origins, simply seems uninspired. It's done well enough, and it's worth playing through just to hear Marice LaMarche's performance as Mr. Freeze.
So overall, despite its uninspired gameplay and in certain cases storytelling, Arkham Origins is still quite well made, and certainly worth a playthrough for fans and non-fans of Batman alike. Just because it's uninspired doesn't mean it's bad, and now that it has been patched for a non-glitchy experience, there's no reason not to give it a play. The music is well done, if again, uninspired (it's mostly Gothic renditions of Christmas themes, since the game takes place during Christmas Eve). The voice acting is overall quite great, as well as the digital acting. The story is well put together and stands out as the most accessible and arguably well-written entry in the Arkham series. So play it if you get a chance, I don't think you'll be disappointed.

Given how many casual games are out there, I can't imagine that the casual-game marketplace has less competitive pressure than the AAA-titles do.  So I must conclude that the casual marketplace just isn't as picky or discerning as the more "hardcore gamer" market is, because few casual developers seem to bother striving for excellence; they develop their games to the point of being "okay," call it a day, and publish.
is yet another drop in that vast ocean of "okay" casual games.  The graphics are clear, cheerful and cartoonish.  The music loop gets a bit irksome over time, but is not offensively bad.  The gameplay concept is understandable, and reasonably interesting, involving trying to find the largest rectangular configuration of four same-coloured squares on a grid.  It's not a unique gameplay concept, but it's not nearly so overdone as "Bejeweled" or "Farmville" clones.  The use of a farming theme, conversely, is about as overdone as it can be in casual gaming.
There's an upgrade store, but while the upgrades make you more succesful, they don't make any real change to how the game is played.  Play well, and you'll have every item from the store bought by the time you've completed half the levels.  There is an "oil drilling" element to the game, which acts as nothing but a random drawing of bonus cash.  Bonus levels offer a form of gameplay that differs from the core levels, which would add some variety, if it were not for the fact that the bonus levels are both easy and mindless.
Bottom line:
avoids a thumbs-down only because it has no serious flaws, but it has no virtues, either.  It's a bland, forgettable, generic piece of shovelware.  It will fill an empty hour as well as the next casual game, but there are many better games out there that you should really consider first.

San Andreas is one of my all-time favorite games, and for very good reason. It's a fantastic entry to the series, with enough content to keep you occupied for weeks. That's not even including the highly populated and still, very much alive multiplayer mod (SA-MP) and the plethora of other mods you can obtain for this amazing game.
However, since Rockstar is so hell-bent on ruining the PC user's experience, I can't recommend the Steam release of this game. The latest patch has removed a number (18, to be specific) of key songs from the once fantastic soundtrack. There is still no 1080p support. Previous save files will no longer work and you -will- more than likely crash if you are playing this game with a dual-monitor set up. Although despite these downgrades, at least they were 'kind enough' to implement very basic Xinput support, so you can play it with a controller. Woo.
Rockstar has all the right to do this. The removal of once available songs makes sense due to copyright reasons. You can't exactly sell your product when it contains content you no longer have the license to use, let alone monetize. But when the game is deliberately patched to take away content that users have already paid for, and to hinder the experience once again, you're just hurting your PC fanbase. Which, I suppose is nothing new if you've played any PC release of Grand Theft Auto post-GTA3.
The best way to enjoy this game is to purchase a retail copy. It'll probably be cheaper, it'll look good on your shelf, you can mod it by default all you want, and you won't have any of your content patched out without warning. With that said. Don't bother buying any other GTA games on Steam either. If they've already removed content in one title, then expect it again in the future from other installments of the franchise when licenses inevitably expire, or can no longer be obtained.
TL;DR: Great game but ruined by Rockstar's anti-consumer attitude. Go buy it elsewhere for the full experience.

The game is an action slash and shoot style game where you will spend the majority of your time in senseless combat. The combat system in this game is actually quite good, there are several weapons which can be used and you can toggle between them almost instantly for insane combos. The combat feels fluid and the controls are solid when you are using a controller, yet the keyboard and mouse controls are less than stellar. There is however almost too much variety and you will sometimes struggle to perform the correct action as you fly from button to button mid combat. The cinematics are actually well done, and although the story is poorly written and predictable at best, the cinematics give it a movie-esque feel. The game is relatively short but offers a decent amount of gameplay and variety of enemies. Overall it is a decent buy if purchased on sale, and one of the better DMC games.
While I find this is a very good game overall, just like older DMC games the complex combat/combo system is still the best part of it.

This Hitman is like Blood Money on steroids. The amount of freedom you get to play however you want is amazing, the maps are gorgeous and huge. And you're encouraged to explore all of it, as parts of the story will be revealed from civilians/guards having conversations around the map.
Each target can be killed in several story related ways, many of them hillarious, if not brutally gory. And exploring the map will reveal to you the weaknesses of your targets, as the guards tell rumors about their bosses, and laugh into the sunset as they're about to get fired.
You're also given the option to play loadouts of different weapons and tools, that will allow you to approach each mission in a different way. Alot of these ways are also highlighted in the challenges section of the game, giving you some clues to all the easter eggs hidden around the huge maps that you've been given to roam.
Never have any game given as immersive an experience of the Hitman/James Bond lifestyle. As you roam around in hostile territory, hiding in the open with various disguises that you've aquired from stealth or brute force, whilst you walk through rooms with 10+ if not 100+ people in em. All the cities and buildings have alot of life to them, with people who work or shop there, and having real conversations with eachother. It all adds to the immersion of just walking around in the game, and feeling like this could be a real place.
The shooting is fantastic aswell. Not too easy, neither too hard, it's sitting right in that sweet spot of a good challenge that's still fun. Aiming is critical, and spraying will almost always result in 90% of your bullets missing. At this point i can headshot 4 people before they even pull out their pistols, but then again i've been going on killing sprees in every single map for that chamelleon challenge. ;)
The game also offers a game mode called "Elusive Target", which offers perhaps the toughest challenge in the entire game atm. This target is a win all or fail all, one mistake can cost you your only chance to succeed your mission. Each target will have a kill condition, like "Must be killed in what looks like an accident" or "Must be killed with poison" and so on. So far i've lost 3/3 that i've attempted, and everytime i was incredibly close to winning it. And in my opinion, that is exactly the way it should be. (also i'm rather impatient, and someone always walks in on me when im hiding their collegues, and starts screaming... rather troublesome really...
The game also has plenty of replayability, as the general experience of the game is fantastic, and just a joy to play through. There's plenty of challenge to be had, even if you know how to kill each target. And making challenges for yourself is easy, as the game offers so many ways to kill each target.
And if you don't wish to make your own challenges, you can always do player made contracts. These contracts will add new targets, in new places, that will require you to kill them in specific ways. Things like this will keep the game alive for long, and even more so since they're gonna add even more content to the game in 2017. Can't wait!
This game is truly a must have, i'd recommend it in a heartbeat.
Edit: I do disagree with the always online part of the game, but i also get why they do it. It's the 15 of January 2017, and the game has still not been cracked yet. Whether or not they lost or made money off this DRM is quite hard to say, but they did stop their game from getting pirated. I also never experienced a disconnect in my entire time playing this game, so that might also have something to do with why i wasn't bothered as much as some. But i won't put down the entire game because of Always Online DRM, i understand why it's there.
Also, if you do disconnect, the game autosaves constantly. So it's not like you lose a ton of progress, you more likely lose 5 minutes of progress.

Pros
-consistent yet diverse art design.
- locations feel self contained and distinct; with no direct correlation with one another.
- levels are massive and highly replay-able.
- engaging writing, where each npc has a story to tell.
- physics system makes killing both satisfying and amusing.
- a large array of visual and gameplay configurations allow the player to change the interface and difficulty to their liking.
- not a reboot, with deep and subtle ties to previous titles.
- rewarding; the game revolves around a reward system - encouraging further play.
- fun and relatively complex Easter eggs
- developers listen to fan feedback and evidently respond quickly and openly.
Cons
- the tone is less universally foreboding and more inclined to be shaped by the tone of each individual location; making the central storyline somewhat lighter in comparison to previous entries.
- the soundtrack, although decent; is a lesser contribution compared to Jesper kyd's use of electronica/ choir/ orchestra.
- online DRM
In conclusion, this game is confident and cohesive; the most consistent video game in quite some time. If the next season tackles the current cons, it can be a very, very easy "10/10". Making the third and conceivably finale season, a true and genuine magnum opus for not only hitman, but the stealth genre.
Final verdict.
9.5/10

Arkham Origins is an enjoyable game to play, unfortunately it doesn't stand up to its predecessor Batman Arkham City (which in my opinion was one of the best computer games I've ever played from many point of views). This review is directed for those who have played both Arkham Asylum (AA) and Arkham City(AC).
Story.
This game, as the title suggest, takes place earlier in Batman's career (so to speak :-P ) as a vigilante. A time before the asylum was created, a probably even darker time when Batman is not recognised by the public and often perceived as yet an other lunatic in Gotham City. Basically, Batman doesn't even know who the Joker is at this point. The story is pretty good, although the plot twist in the middle gives itself away too quickly and in general it is very fast paced making the game disappointingly short.
Gamplay.
Some new cool gadgets and some classic reoccurring ones. The gameplay is pretty much identical, it has a few new additions due to the more varied type of enemies. All the rest remains pretty much the same and you shouldn't have any troubles getting use to the game. In this game you don't just unlock abilities by levelling up but also by completing small (some of them are actually satisfyingly hard) challenges, that are listed on the menu together with the map etc. ( nothing to do with achievements and other account related stuff), and by finishing the secondary missions.
The Riddler is also back with his challenges (no riddles this time around though). I'm glad that this time around they made it so you accidentally knock out his informants and not get any info out them.
There's a new detective mode which is quite cool, although could have clearly been made more challenging. It was a good addition though as it added to the fact that Batman isn't just a vigilante with high tech gear that beats up people but also a detective.
The boss fights are well made, some of them are actually hard (especially if you play with the hints turned off so that you don't get attack warnings).
Oh and now there's fast travel too, which was quite useful as the map is even bigger than AC (contains the same areas of Gotham as AC and some other ones in other side of the bridge).
Spoilers from here onwards!!!!!!
Picking from the boss topic, fighting Bane 3 times was probably a bit boring and the final encounter which is also the final boss of the game was a bit of a let down.
I thought the Joker appeared too quickly in the game, and I really hope they will revert back to the previous voice actor as this one was not as good in my opinion. Actually the Joker shouldn't appear on Arkham Knight (AK) (I think at least he's meant to be dead at the end of AC right?)
If there was one highlight in this game, a scene that was really memorable, it was probably the scene the Joker first meets Harlequin and tells her about batman and how they have somehow so much in common. Really dwells deep down in the psychology of both Batman's and Joker's character. Really dark, thoroughly enjoyed it. I hope they will have more scenes like that in AK.
There's no other playable character on the main story mode which is a bit disappointing.
To finish off, if AO came out before AC, then it would have been a pretty damn good game with loads of new additions compare to AA. Since it's the other way around, AO origins was just a variation of AC, with a few new cool stuff, some annoying bugs (which is rather strange as AC had not a single bug whatsoever for me) and a much shorter life span. If you're new to the game series I'd say go and play AA and AC although if you start from this one you won't miss anything story wise since it's set back chronologically. If you've been following the Arkham series then you'll probably be a bit “meh” in the end of it, you know like “yeaaaah I've had better” kind of feel. But still do play it, as it's Batman and Batman is cool.
About to play the DLCs I hope they're worth the money.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a prequel to the Arkham Asylum and Arkham City games. The story takes place in a pre-Arkham Gotham city, staring a young and inexperienced Batman. The police force of Gotham is corrupt and mostly not better than the mobsters and criminals that run Gotham. The game takes place on Christmas eve, where Black Mask has hired 8 of the worlds greatest assassins to kill Batman.
The gameplay is smooth most of the time as it was in the previous Arkham games. Moving around is easier than ever with the new fast travel. The city is about the same size as Arkham City but is divided between old and new Gotham.
The combat system from the previous games returns. It is all based around timing and the rhythm of the fight. The stealth is a lot like Arkham City. You have the same structure of the last two games. New type of enemies and gadgets are introduced to add new elements to the game. There is a new addition to the detective mode. There are parts of the game where you use it to analyze a crime scene and piece together the crime. It is no longer just find something to trace and follow it to from point A to B.
The boss fights are improved and feel more serious but are repetitive. The story felt weaker compared to the other games. The main story could also last longer. There are also again side missions, again you have to collect the Riddler trophies. The challenge mode also returns in Arkham Origins.
Arkham Origins comes with a multiplayer mode. In my opinion it was not really necessary to implement a multiplayer.
Batman: Arkham Origins does enhance the visuals of the Arkham City engine and it is a very great looking game on max settings. The visuals are not a massive step above the already great looking previous game.
There is not much music to listen to but the overall theme sounds nice and fits with the whole story. All the characters do sound great. You have plenty of younger versions of characters seen in previous games. The new voice of the Joker sounds really a lot like the Mark Hamil voice.
Overall, this game is fun. I enjoyed it almost as much as the other two games.

APB: Reloaded is a unique game in a era where most games feel like every other one.  While the game may have some technical problems, the developers are working hard to remedy them and overall improve the quality of the game.  I've played the game since its first beta under Real Time Worlds in 2009, and there is good reason that it hasn't faded into the past as so many other games have.
The mission portion of the game is structured so that it seems different almost every time, and you don't get that feeling of repetition that you get with a lot of arena-style shooters.  (CoD, Battlefield, Blacklight)  You may get the same mission objectives, but the game randomizes the locations, your opponents and your teammates (if you don't have a premade group) throughout the zone each time.
Combat works as intended, and while it may not be the most modern shooter the game has a lot to offer on the battlefield.  The gunplay is smooth and tactical thinking and teamwork can win over even the most skilled opponents.  Having a good team working together is one of the best parts of this game.
There is also, of course, the customization.  There is no game on the market today that allows you to be unique in the way that this game does.  From making stylish threads, music and cars for yourself to making uniforms and patrol vehicles for your clan-mates, you can truly create your own identity here.
The game is a bit old, granted, with a somewhat outdated version of Unreal Engine and a lot of custom code at its core.  I'm hopeful, however, as the developers have an overhaul and upgrade planned for the game's engine.  According to the timeline it should be ready for testing by the end of the first quarter 2014, and all reports state that development is currently on schedule.

Astroneer offers little on it's plate, but what it does offer so far is really fun with a great aesthetic. Like all other survivor titles you're shoved into the world left to figure things out (mostly) on your own, tutorials are sparse but it's half the fun. Luckily there's no mobs and death is harder to come by than in most titles. So far I've managed to extend my base and not much else other than explore, but it's been fun. The art and sounds of the game are light, airy and could probably lull you to sleep since they're really pastel and comforting. Great work in the art department.
Sadly, this game is as Early Access you can get. With a 6700U and GTX1060 I'm pushing around 40 frames on average at "1080p," but setting the resolution seemingly didn't do anything though I think there's a lot of post-processing to fit the devs aesthetic that it might not matter, things seem really anti-aliased and a tad too blurry. Also, you don't have any options to turn them off. People also seem to have a lot of issues with the game not even loading or lots of crashes. I seem to have lucked out. I have no clue if multiplayer is even in the game yet, because there's nothing on the main menus other than to just load your game or start anew, I assume you have to join via your Friends List? No idea.
So being that the game just came out, has optimization issues all over but a solid base to build a huge game that can only grow into something magnificent, I completely recommend Astroneer. If you can't deal with any of these issues, don't bother and wait for the game to mature. The dev team is small and their project is ambitious, but not too ambitious where we have another No Man's Sky on our hands. Put your trust in the team, I'm sure they're going to knock this out of the park.

Warning: This review contains several spoilers about the game's story. Reader discretion is advised.
Mad Max isn't a bad game per say, but it's a typical example of the Open World formula: the area you can roam is stuffed with sidequests, collectibles, locations and random events which are more or less all the same: get to a location and destroy something, kill someone or find hidden items. Sometimes all three. The problem is, everything feels repetitive, very quickly.
On the plus side there's races which are fun because they offer some more variety and are actually challenging. The main story is pretty good too, with a number of interesting characters.
The world is thematically great: if you enjoy post-apocalyptic wastelands, cars built for utility and not aesthetics, punkish people with attires themed around petrol, gasoline, tire rubber and metal, you'll love Mad Max's world. On the other hand, the scenery is quickly tiring: everything is colored yellow, brown, black or something in between and the few awesome-looking landmarks
lose their appeal after a while.
The characters are fitting this world too: from religious fanatics with cults around cars, fire or people to the semi-sane wastelanders who cling to any shred of hope about how things will improve again everything fits right into the story. The main character fits in almost too well:
I recommend playing it for the theme and the story, if you enjoy postapocalyptic scenarios: these are the game's main selling point. The sidequests, collectibles etc. add very little to the main story and can be skipped for the most part.

In a world where games gradually became easier, duller, dumber and full with useless DLC its hard to find good games out there. Fortunately once in a while a masterpiece comes out. Ori and the Blind Forest is a masterpiece amongst masterpieces. To me this is a game as close to perfection as it comes. Let me sum up why.
1: The game is hard.
Point blank, it will brutally test you if you play it on hard or one life mode. But doing so, it is never unfair. You know you screwed up when you die, it is not because the game is broken, but simply you made a mistake. I haven't finished the one life mode and probably never will.
2: The abilities are great.
Like a true metroidvania game, this one lets you unlock abilities along the way, each time giving you the power to visit certain areas you weren't able to reach before. They built this up wonderfully in the original version, the definitive edition gives you 2 more to make you go even faster through the levels. This game is a speedrunners dream, giving you all the abilities to do this well. For the slower players like me, it gives you room to backtrack, explore and find secrets you never did before.
3: The soundtrack is phenomenal.
Wherever you go, the orchestra surrounds you with every step. The main theme is memorable and amazing to listen to. After finishing the game i could still find myself humming to it, matter of fact i even put the soundtrack on my phone to listen to, its just that great. Every section has its own music and they all fit perfectly. When something big is happening, the tone changes perfectly and supports the epicness of the moments.
4: The level design.
The game feels like you're playing inside a picasso painting. The art style, which is hand crafted feels and looks so friggin beautiful. It made this Indie title look like a AAA-game and probably even better. This is to me the most atmospheric game in that regard i have ever played.
5: Its smart.
It doesn't take you by the hand or shows you where to go. Sure there is a pointer on the map, but if the route is unexplored, you'd have to figure it out yourself. Finding a different route where you need some abilities you don't have can be done sometimes, but you'll find out yourself this is damn hard to do so. But it let's you try if you want to.
6: The story is compelling.
Its a metroidvania in the old style, so don't expect a story where everything is told. Still it does. The narration of the story is done with a dark voice in an unfamiliar language, but it supports this with english artlike letters on the screen. Perfect way to do it, because it stays somewhat mystical this way. The prologue got me the first time, and after ten playthroughs it still does. No spoilers, but it ripped my heart out, and even my former GF who doesn't play games was moved to tears. The story builds up and you will understand what happened and every large piece of cinematic, it will move you in a way i haven't experienced in a game before. Perfection in a platformer.
Verdict:

Prison Architect is a great little simulator in the mould of Theme Hospital/Park, where you have to build and look after your own private institution.
It starts off at 100mph as you uncover the reasons behind a brutal double killing and a prisoner's subsequent execution.
Before long, an intuitive interface and design means you quickly pick up the basics and can run a reasonable establishment.
As you progress, more options of how to deal with your prison population become available.
You'll need them too; that cosy institute of placid inmates diligently counting down the days to their release and reintegration into society will soon morph into a violent cesspit lurching from one crisis to another.
Right under your eyes inmates will be arming themselves and hatching plans to escape - before you know it a huge riot is under way and a gang armed with drills and shanks are making a beeline to the exit, armed with the keys of a guard they gutted in the corridor.
But more often than not you can quickly rectify a problem when it arises by chucking money at it; spam a few guards in the canteen when Dragos and his buddies kick off and the uprising is quashed.
You won't be sort of money either; it's easy to get very generous grants by fulfilling the meagre criteria needed for most of them.
Coupled with a very short campaign (which is really a tutorial), you run out of 'things to do' fairly quickly and you're left with the sandbox mode.
This might be ample for some people, but as someone who likes a challenge, building a prison free of any real pressures or targets is quite boring.
Yes, you can make things more difficult for yourself by doing things like accepting the maximum amount of prisoners on each intake, but it's an artificial goal with no benefits or consequences.
And, of course, you're playing alone.
A multiplayer option putting prisons head to head, for example, would be brilliant, or rival players trying to break out/take over a prison is another opportunity missed.
That said, this is an excellent little game well worth a buy.
- Slick design and interface
- Easy to learn the basics
- Absorbing gameplay
- Brilliant prison escape mode
- Good mod integration
- Sandbox mode
- Very short campaign
- No multiplayer
- Too easy/lack of challenges in sandbox mode
- Can become repetitive

After playing through everything which arkham origins has to offer ( Single-Player, Challenge mode, Multiplayer), I would give my honest review and opinion on this game.
Arkham origins is packed full of content. The single-player campaign has a great story with a suprising twist in the middle and the combat was one of the best aspect of the game as you get to beat up bad guys in a very cool and stylish manner with free flow combat. During Predator encounters, you really feel like the batman as you try to take out bad guys without them seeing you and making them feel fear. The Open world of gotham city is cool to explore around to find collectibles and side missions such as beating up escaped prisoners or solving crimes with detective mode.
The only negative is that there is no manual saving mechanism in this game, there is only autosave. This means you cannot quit the game at anywhere and anytime. You have to quit the game at a specific location or event for autosave to trigger or else you will lose all your progress.
Challenge Mode allows you to complete challenges with either Batman or Deathstroke in a variety of combat and predator maps that were featured in the single player experience. There is a different feel to both character as Batman felt fast and agile while Deathstroke felt slower but more powerful. There is also a highscore features which allows you to compare your score with your friends or the world!
The multiplayer has an interesting concept which has three faction (Bane, Joker or batman and robin) competing with one another in order to win. However, the gameplay itself is boring and repetitive. Basically you capture points (like capture the flag)  and try to kill off the other teams (like team deathmatch). When you level up you unlock weapons, paints and gears. You can also pay real money via microtransaction to unlock those items even faster. There is also barely anyone playing the multiplayer so you have to wait for quite awhile in order to get into a match.
To summarise,
Pros
+Good Story
+Interesting Characters
+Great Combat system
+Great Predator encounters
+Open world
+Huge amount of extra contents such as side missions, challenge mode and multiplayer
Cons
-No manual saving mechanism
-Some minor bugs and glitches
-Boring multiplayer mode
If I have to rate this game, I would give it a 8/10 which means it is a pretty good game.

This game will recieve a nagative review for one singular reason: enemies's attacks are mostly uncounterable because of their randomness; let me explain...
enemies flash Gold when they are about to attack, and flash Red when about to attack 'Low' - ie 'unblockable'. The problem is that that flashing may be 1 second, or 3 - and the same enemy might have a 1, 3 and 5 second animation - and your block has a 2 second animation... meaning you never quite know when to block.
On top of that, red/unblockables are sometimes blockable, if you jump/block... but that takes timing, which is thrown off by the weird timings....
Ontop of that, enemies can cancel their animation/guardblock and do one of their 'unblockables' mid animation of one of their guards (which you need to break with what's basically a QTE)- meaning that you can get destroyed by their most powerful, unblockable attack with no warning, while you are trying to guardbreak them.
These are cheap, unfair, random feeling elements.
Otherwise, the moves look cool, the story feels a bit weird (you feel like the badguy breaking into a temple for no reason) and translated (but a pretty good translation, I think) you can buttonmash moves, you have a block, parry, dodge, jamp attack and a std attack, with more moves unlocked as you play.
Sound is good, keybinds are good, gameplay is smooth and flows well, tutorial is good... everything is good... except that the 'telegraphing' of moves is done terribly. The only issue with this is that it's the basic mechanic that the game hangs itself upon, and it's unreliable. Thus the negative.
After Playing Furi, where enemies are still insanely challenging, but their movesets feel fair.... this game leaves me dissapointed.

Passing Pineview Forest will play with your mind. You can walk, run, use a flashlight, or jump, and that's it. The atmosphere of this game is what makes it scary, along with the game over jumpscare. The graphics are nice, but not extraordinary. Your only objective is to make it to the end of the forest, which seems simple (and in all actuality it is), but ends up leaving you feeling like you need to curl up in a corner and turn all the lights on in your house. When successfully played, the game is only about 20 minutes long, but it will likely take more than a couple of tries to finish it. Possible spoilers below.
This game took me three tries to complete. The first two times, I used a combination of running and walking with my flashlight constantly on and would die right after the statue by the church. The third time, I ran up until the point and walked the rest of the way for the most part, with my flashlight off the entire time. Honestly you need to fail once or twice to get the full experience of this game. Failing gives you a decent jumpscare, which is admittedly pretty poor horror, but it does its job in this title. To be successful, don't use your flashlight, and stop to look around when you hear noises and / or footsteps. You won't see anything, but you also won't get attacked.

During a storm, a leaf from the spirit tree was carried away in the wind. That leaf was a child from the tree, and it changed into Ori, a light creature and the main character, that was found and raised far away by a gentle creature of the dark. Years later, Kuro, a giant creature of the dark in the form of an owl, stole the light from the spirit tree, which killed all of the yet-to-be born light creatures and plunged Nibel - the world of the game - into darkness. Ori, the last light creature, sets out to rekindle the elements of Nibel and bring back the light to the world.
The background of the story is pretty basic, but as it progresses there are some surprising twists. There are also some elements of The Legend of Zelda, as you have to enter a dungeon in different areas to rekindle the elements - like a Water, Earth and Fire temples.
There are no dialogues, only a narrator in some parts, but even so the cutscenes manage to make the player feel the sentiment in it, right from the beggining, when you play during Ori's growth in a son-mother routine.
Both are spectacular. The game is all 2D, with 3D characters and several layers of backgrounds, all very colorful and dinamic - if there's and explosion, everything around shakes according to the shockwave. The animations during cutscenes and gameplay are super smooth and it gives of a Disney/Pixar movie feel.
The music is amazing and instrumental, with chorus in some parts - you'll be searching and listening to the OST of this game on youtube after you beat it, trust me. All of them helps with immersion - whether its a chase scene or a super sentimental one.
Very well made. Ori is super easy to controll, and you can really feel the progress as you gain more abilities. The game works via an old formula: you start of with pretty much nothing, and as you gain new abilities you can access new areas or revisit old ones to collect itens you couldn't reach before.
The difficulty can be high sometimes, for Ori is that kind of platfomer in which you die a lot trying to get pass an area full of environmental hazards. It's not on the level of something like Super Meat Boy, but it can get frustrating during longer hours of straight play.
The greatest problem are the minuscule variety of enemies. There are very few, and most of them are the same old enemies with a different skin and slightly stronger. Also, there are no bosses, and you really feel the lack of them. Kuro is present in the hole game, and I kept waiting for the time I would face her in the end, expecting to be super epic, since she is huge and extremelly aggresive, but it never happened.
Ori follows an old formula of 2D platforming, but it does so extremelly well, with great animations, smooth gameplay, beautiful soundtrack and sentimental cutscenes. The lack of variety of enemies and bosses compromises the experience somewhat, but not to the point of making the game bad. If you like this type of game, go for it.

I'll keep it simple and to the point.
I have played a few hours of this game before at a friend's house prior to buying it and can safely say (not counting later levels, as I'm yet to tackle those) that this is one of the best and most original reinventions of the Beat 'em Up genre available out there.
The combat system is simple but surprisingly intuitive and INCREDIBLY satifying. The game as a dedicated, timing based (but not frustrating) parry button that allows you to easily simulate the kind of 'combo-parry-combo-break enemy's parry' choreography that you usually see in a Kung Fu movie.
It also has a CO-OP campaign and upgrades, and the default difficulty is proper arcade hard, but the game is so satisfying that you'll be coming back to repeat the (short) levels just for fun. This is one of those games that mechanically is super satifying and lends itself to repeated play (just like games like Dark Messiah, Just Cause, F.E.A.R. or Tony Hawk).
It's a shame that, indie game or not, games like these still fall under the radar. I usually play this listening to a music playlist and that works pretty well.

This is an example of one of those games that falls in the Uncanney Valley of gaming, at least for me; it's so close to being really good, but there are smaller issues that hold the game back from being the fantastic product it could be, thus inducing intense feelings of disappointment and frustration.
I dig the more extreme departure from the aethetics of the previous games. Now, for the most part, the enemies AND the environment are quite clean. I'd almost go so far as to say that the enemies are almost cute. The horror in this game doesn't really come from the enemies themselves, even with their weird face-opening gimmick.
Rather than the format of all the previous games where you have to survive for a certain amount of time, you survive nights by accomplishing a linear series of tasks, some of which resemble the traditional FNaF format in some form or another. The difference is that these tasks are actually skill-based, which makes them a lot of fun and rewarding to play.
But the gameplay isn't nearly as front-and-center here as it was in the previous four. In this installment, Scott has decided to cut the crap and make the game all about the story. This is also the first game in the series to feature voice actors other than Scott himself, and the actual quality of it is suprisingly good. The story seems to fill in a lot of the lore gaps left by the previous games, and even presents the possibility of an unexpected, but totally badass, protagonist.
What kills the game for me is the difficulty curve. It's pretty consistent for the first three nights, but the fourth night is brutal to the point of being unreasonable. It was so bad, in fact, that Scott released a patch for the game making it easier. But it's STILL ridiculously difficult. This is especially frustrating, considering that playing through night 5 to get the canon ending is incredibly easy. And when you solve the hidden puzzle in the game to unlock the alternate ending, the alternate ending features the same 12-6 am survival gameplay as the previous titles, complete with brutal difficulty and RNG-based enemy movement.
The bulk of this game's replay value comes from the Custom night, which has the 12-6 am gameplay of the first four games and night 5 of this game, with up to ten different characters to set on yourself at once. It comes with a bunch of presets like the custom night for FNaF 2, as well as difficulty presets. If you complete one of these presets on its hardest difficulty, you are given a cutscene for the final lore clue of the game. After completing all of these presets on their highest difficulty, you are given the final lore clue of the game. But this custom night has the same RNG problems of the previous games. You might as well just look the endings and lore clues up on YouTube.
The biggest appeal of FNaF (for me at least) was the suprisingly dense lore, and the lore clues hidden in the games. Watching people try to put everything together in a coherent universe and story over the past few years has actually been a lot of fun. But you don't exactly need the games to watch people put the lore together, so save your hard-earned cash for something else.

Ótimo jogo, ótimo! Comecei a jogar e quase não consegui parar, zerei super rápido. Sou fã dos filmes de Mad Max, nesse jogo eu consegui me sentir imerso nesse mundo, tem sido uma ótima experiência. Meu único arrependimento é não ter comprado antes =p
Um dos poucos pontos negativos que percebi e, provavelmente, o único relevante a ponto de ser comentando, é que o jogo chega a ficar repetitivo em certos momentos, o que é inevitável nesse sistema de RPG em mundo aberto. Mas isso é facilmente compensando pela experiência imersiva que o jogo passa. Algo que senti falta também no jogo foi uma boa trilha sonora.
Além do que eu já falei, gostei muito também do combate, tanto nos carros, formato que eu nunca tinha jogado antes, quanto corpo-a-corpo, que, apesar de ser uma fórmula antiga já da Warner continua sendo divertido. A mecânica dos veículos é muito legal, a liberdade que o jogo dá de modificar o carro do jeito que você quiser... a direção é muito interessante também, gosto de como fica mais fácil ou mais difícil de dirigir o veícuo dependendo de que tipo ele seja ou de quais são as coisas equipadas nele. Outro ponto positivo é que o mapa, que é bem grandinho até, sempre tem algo pra fazer, apesar do jogo não ter tantas missões, você só consegue se entediar se for o tipo de jogador que precisa platinar e sair caçando todos os colecionáveis do jogo.
A história do jogo é bem legal também, tem momentos inesperados, coisa que não tenho visto com tanta facilidade ultimamente, não foi ela o que mais me prendeu ao jogo mas é realmente interessante.

Great building game, both for casual and hardcore players, although plagued by a few annoying bugs & issues and an atrophied management part.
- The tutorial is a short story mode, nothing extravagant like the game description would make you think it is, but it's still a very nice way to dive into the game theme

- Management part can be almost totally ignored
- Visuals can be a bit hard on eyes are 1st, as the artistic direction lacks a bit of unity

- There's basically no difficulty if you understood the tutorial
- Might be a bit overpriced : $30 instead of $25, I'd say

Ahhh Ori and the blind forest... where to begin?
My life story: Going to my local game store in December 2016 i walked around the Pc section only to see 4 copies of this game on the shelf priced at 19 AUD (Australian Dollars). My first instinct was to scoff at the realatively low price tag but if any game has taught me anything, it can be full of surprises (looks at undertale). Anyway picking it up and inserting the disc into the Pc then activated it through a code, waited for a quick download and the game was ready to play. What hit me next was a journey into the wonderful world of nibel. The menu screen already introduced me into a trance that so little games managed to accomplish, the combination between the sorrowful music and the beautiful background instantly destroyed the essence of my being. The adventure i underwent through next completely took me away from this world.
Gameplay: As most platformers go, Ori and the blind forest brings a few things to the table. The gameplay flows very well, combining quick thinking, timing, interesting puzzles and a decent combat system. The feel of the game is very smooth on my end (you don't really need a good Pc to run it), and i have not encountered a single bug or gamebreaking glitch so far. However do not think this game is simple, it is possibly (especially on one life) one of the most hardest platforming challenges you might face. However with a multitude of abilities that Ori has is able to fight of most of the denizens and dark dwellers within the forest.
//////////// The Story section can contain spoilers READ AT YOUR OWN RISK \\\\\\\\\
Story: As story goes it is relatively simple, an orphan (Ori) is lost to a storm and is picked up by a creature (Naru) who becomes a mother to Ori. A series of unfortunate events (which is revealed later) wracks the forest with death and famine. Ori now Orphaned again now must venture on a journey to restore the forest back to the way it was.
Despite being a very simple story, it is the way it is told that makes it special, full of plot twists, moments of pure joy and moments of utter devastation really plays on your feelings.
\\\\\\\\\\\\\\       End of Spoilers    ///////////

You play as Super Meat Boy, a little red character made of meat, and has an amusing slurpy noise as you jump, hop, and run as fast as you can through the world to save your girl friend "Bandaid girl" from the evil Dr.Fetus. But that's all pretty much explained in the opening cinematic!
The controls of this game are deceptively simple, you can sprint, jump, and run left or right. You also can wall jump and side down walls. The game increases it's difficulty dramatically after the first level.

I think this is a great game... well for the first hour. If you see a review with 0.5 hours or something? Disregard it really, it's not gonna tell you anything about the later game which posesses the issues to make it a not recommended.
Controls:
X is ground attack.
A is air attack.
X+A is a chi attack.
These work well, although X and A don't allow you to do any special combos, the chi attacks make up for it allowing you to buy multiple chi attacks that are activated through stuff like X+A, X then X+A, X+A mid air twice then X on the ground, ect. It's also nice to just mash A and X to go to town on the enemy without thinking too hard about combos.
RT is dodge
B and LT is deflect
One of these is the biggest issue with the game but i'll focus on it later. Dodging is as it sounds, you roll away quickly in the direction you chose then you move about twice as fast for a second afterwards. After this you go back to normal speed. Now to deflect which is a mechanic that allows you to be invincible for a second, and in that second any enemy that attacks you has their attack negatated and is knocked down. There are a few exceptions for how deflect works as some enemies still continue hitting you after you deflect your first attack (with no warning), and some don't even care and will hit through your deflect if they have an ! appear before they attack.
Now to the issues with this otherwise great beat'em up game. This is a review that needs a neutral option as if you look past it's issues, there is a lot of really fun parts to this game that I wish more people could enjoy.
Issues:
Lets start with one mechanic in this game where you hold X against an enemy when prompted too, and then press A to finish it off. This is some sort of guard break on the enemy but the issue i have with it is how long the A prompt is up and how much the X prompt can vary in length. Sometimes the X prompt is almost instant and sometimes it takes a while. If it was a set length, this would work regardless of its very quick-time event feel to it. This is also shoved in your face while you're attacking an enemy too and all you can do is sigh and do this boring mechanic yet again.
If you attack an enemy, other enemies will then attack you during your attack which you cannot cancel, at least to my knowledge. Usually you can get one or two hits off then run but that doesnt' work. So you have to get a few hits off and deflect the enemies, but you can't always do that until later on because of another issue right after this one. Overall this mechanic isn't bad just doesn't work with other issues in this game.
You have to buy the ability to deflect in mid-air and dodge in mid-air which is really ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. This is absolutely nessecary to the game later on and even in earlier levels. So if you do any air attacks, you're wide open until you get either one of these. This issue applies to guard breaks as to finish one off, you press A... an air attack.
Your brief speed-boost after dodging will end without just going to your way too slow normal walking speed, it will automatically make you do a FULL STOP wherever you are for half a second. Why is this a thing? Why don't i just go into normal ground speed, why do i have to go from roll to running to ♥♥♥♥ing stopped without me pressing a button. It's terrible, the only way to avoid this is to keep on rolling and attack an enemy before the stop happens which is annoying and is harder to focus on than you think due to the other issues all hitting you at once.
And now the mother of all issues with this game, deflecting. This son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ doesn't work. It's not that you can't deflect, no you can easily deflect. It's that if 2 enemies attack you, which is very frequent. More often than not, they will attack you so you can only deflect ONE of them while the other will hit you no matter what. This is terrible. The ganking of the enemies ruins this feature so much as if one enemy hits you, usually 2 or 3 more will start to attack. You attack one enemy and then the enemies approach you, deflect to counter them and woopse either 1, the enemy you were hitting suddenly breaks the stun lock you put him in for no ♥♥♥♥ing reason and hits you almost instantly, stun locking you. 2, the enemy attacks in different intervals so you can't deflect them all. Or 3, you get lucky and only 1 or 2 enemies attack you in a way where you can deflect it. Maybe if you're extremely lucky you can just attack the enemy and the RNG doesn't decide to randomly screw you over.
So many issues with this otherwise great game don't just make the side things annoying but effect the main game. I just can't recommend it. It's a blast at first, but it gets boring. Money is too hard to come by to buy new skills and items, the inconsistenties in this game are too extreme at moments, the deflect system that is pressured on you doesn't work enough with the rest of the game, and overall a giant amount of design flaws. You can tell they understand how to make something more fluid in areas like how nice the rolling is. The rolling part feels so nice, you can change direction easily with no worries. The X and A spamming also works very well. I don't know what it is about it but all the combos go how i'd think they'd go. Which makes it easier to use them. The fluidity and challenge that this game possesses isn't fully taken away. What deals the final blow between recommended and not recommended is the pricing, 10 dollars does not match this game's quality and how much content it has fully. Yes it has a lot of effort put into it and I feel bad almost for not recommending this game, but it's true. I'm usually overaly critical on games but on this one, i really think these are really bad design choices. So if it's on sale? Get it. If not, save it as this game's not a short gem. It's a game most people play for 0.5 hours then go "Coll gaem, thums up" and never play it again.

First impressions:
In desperate need of a UX designer and a good artist.
Generic "citizens". No names. No women. Only defining traits are education level and job. No facing the issues of actual social inequality (slaves vs free vs citizens) in the setting.
Generic farms. One of the interesting aspects of Emperor etc is the varying planting and harvest seasons for different crops (which have varying availability in different maps).
No variable speed, though it does at least have playable pause.
No information on what various blessings/curses do, that I spotted.
I've not been sucked in, and I haven't spotted any particularly interesting aspects.
Edit to add more details:
UI/UX/art issues I noticed included the inconsistency of button style and positioning; difficulty guessing which category a particular building would be found in; being forced to place a single house at a time; being unable to draw new roads if they overlapped old roads; and buildings that look about to fall over. I do appreciate that there are overlays, and that the happiness score hover text gives information on what's causing unhappiness.
While I don't expect women to be equal to men (Ancient Rome, after all!), I do expect them to be present in some way, shape, or form; and it is quite disappointing to be able to look at individual workers and not see any personality. Having played many different city builders, I've seen this handled in many ways:
- Glory of the Roman Empire specifies which gender can work at any given job, with some jobs (such as tavern server) being exclusively female and others (such as miners) being exclusively male. This is also the only city builder game that I remember engaging significantly with the fact that Rome also had slavery, with slaves being the primary means of transporting materials around town.
- Cultures assigns women the role of having babies and making the men happy. This amounts to essentially population growth and productivity bonuses.
- Children of the Nile also tracks lineage and family history, with men generally doing work and women generally doing the household shopping.
- Emperor/Pharaoh/Zeus do the least. They don't track individuals at all - but it is notable that the normal employment rate is only around 30% of total population.
Great game, good dev support

I feel like I should like Mad Max less than I do. It doesn't really bring anything new to the table, and has an open world with all of the mandatory scattered collectibles to check off on the menus. Most of the important characters in the story are relatively flat and uninteresting. What kept me coming back, then?
The combat, of course. Whether in vehicle or on foot, Mad Max managed to provide a satisfying experience. On foot, combat plays out in the style of Rocksteady's Batman games: you beat up people while countering or rolling out of the way of those that attack you, occasionally picking up a melee weapon or firing your shotgun. In vehicles it plays out like a demolition derby: you ram into other cars, sideswipe them, use grinders on your wheels, or shoot at them with a shotgun, harpoon gun, or what amounts to an RPG. Of course, as you wipe out enemy camps or such, you'll be able to buy upgrades to make Max better at combat, or make Max's car faster, harder hitting, etc.
Driving feels pretty satisfying generally, with each vehicle handling differently, and adjusting the upgrades on your car impacts how fast it is and how it handles. Light vehicles accelerate quickly and have a high top speed, but generally don't like some of the more uneven roads or quick turns you sometimes have to take. This can be a nuisance when doing some of the races that only offer some of the lighter cars. Granted, they do let you use your own custom car, the Magnum Opus—but only if you have certain combinations of unlockables for it called Archangels, which require paint jobs that can only be found by destroying certain camps.
A number of things hit that sort of feedback loop where you find that doing one thing requires doing another thing, and so forth, leading to a generally small chain of tasks. Still, there are only so many times you can clear camps in a row before it becomes more of a chore than entertainment.
Thankfully, the story missions generally tend to lend some variety in location, whether it's exploring an old subway system or racing around Gastown. The story itself isn't anything to write home about, with some obvious clichés thrown in liberally, but it works. There are at least
interesting characters here, such as Chumbucket, a hunchback "blackfinger" (read: mechanic) who worships the "Angel Combustion", who told him to build the perfect car—the Magnum Opus—and views Max as a Saint delivered to him to help make and drive the perfect car. If only the whole cast was fleshed out like him, but unfortunately, most are more caricature than character.
On a more technical level, Mad Max is quite sound. The graphics are quite good, with nice long draw distances letting you see miles around you. Sure, most of the world is a sea of whites, grays, and browns, but it fits in with the style of the films. The sound design is generally pretty good, and the music sets the mood well, even if it's nothing I'd want to listen to outside of the game. I didn't encounter any major glitches, although I did hit a few minor ones that didn't really impact my time playing.
I do have some minor issues with things regarding the end game, which I will leave in spoiler tags below.
In conclusion, Mad Max is pretty good. I'm not going to rush around and tell everyone that they
, but if you're looking for an open world game with good driving, you could do far worse. It probably would be pretty good for listening to podcasts or music while playing, too, if that's your sort of thing. On the other hand, if you already have a lot of other games on your backlog, this is a game where missing it wouldn't be a terrible thing.

As far as indie games go, I know the awareness of Super Meat Boy is pretty high up there. It was featured in the excellent 2012 documentary Indie Game: The Movie, alongside Fez and Braid. And despite being a relatively popular and seemingly well-liked game, it's also frequently deeply discounted (for like $5 or less) in Steam's many summer and holiday sales. But for those who haven't played or heard of Super Meat Boy, read on. Also if you haven't seen Indie Game: The Movie, stop reading this and go watch it. I'm pretty sure it's on Netflix.
Super Meat Boy is the brainchild of artist Edmund McMillen and programmer Tommy Refenes, who call themselves Team Meat. It's actually the sequel to a 2008 browser based flash game which was just called Meat Boy. Check it out here for free if you're interested in trying it. Just know that the sequel is a massive improvement over the original. Tighter controls, better level design, better artwork, higher music quality, multiple playable characters and a lot more polish overall. Both Meat Boy and its sequel seem to have drawn a lot of inspiration from N, and/or N+ a.k.a. "The way of the Ninja" games, which are also free, flash-based games that I totally loved. The one thing these games all share is that they are infuriatingly difficult, but also excellently designed 2D platformers.
Each level of Super Meat Boy requires you to save Meat Boy's girlfriend, bandage girl, from the evil Dr. Fetus. This is accomplished simply by navigating from a starting point to an ending point on a 2D plane, but there are usually many deadly hazards in between. Once you get into the meat of the game -see what I did there?- you'll probably find this game to be extremely difficult. However, by using a well thought out difficulty curve and smart design decisions, I believe Super Meat Boy handles its difficulty extremely well. First of all, the levels are so short that you don't feel like you lose significant progress when you die. There's rarely a level that takes more than 60 seconds to beat.  It can still be frustrating when you die repeatedly on the same level, but because you respawn instantly at the beginning of the level, it makes you want to go right back at it again. It's the good kind of frustrating. The earlier levels introduce you to the precision platforming, wall jumping and sprinting. Then the later levels add more obstacles that incrementally increase the difficulty. By the end of the game, you're doing things that looked completely impossible when you started. It's still very hard, but it's an extremely satisfying difficulty curve.
Super Meat Boy has some really cool bonus features, unlockables and secrets included as well. There's a built in replay system where you can save and share your times and replays to any of your friends who also have the game. Finishing each level in the game under a certain amount of time will unlock a mirrored "dark world" version of the level which usually includes more obstacles or enemies and is even more difficult. There's also the collectible bandages found in the various levels which are usually either hard to find or hard to difficult to get to. These bandages, presumably dropped by bandage girl, can be used to unlock other playable characters which have different speeds or jump heights which add more flavor to the game. There's even hidden warp zones that lead to even more obnoxiously difficult levels for those who are into ridiculously hard challenges.
Super Meat Boy is probably one of the most difficult games I've ever completed and I'm quite proud to have finished it. It's also probably responsible for the most swearing I've ever done while playing a game. But don't let the difficulty scare you off, Super Meat Boy is a must play if you're a fan of platformers. It's a difficult game, but it's also a rewarding one. It also boasts an excellent soundtrack and some really cool Castle Crashers-like cartoony graphics. There's also lots of very subtle references to Mega Man, Castlevania and Super Mario Bros. in the animations and artwork. It's good stuff. I'm also quite curious to see what Mew-Genics, Team Meat's upcoming game, is going to be like. If it's half as good as Super Meat Boy, I'll probably still love it.

Ahhh Ori and the blind forest... where to begin?
My life story: Going to my local game store in December 2016 i walked around the Pc section only to see 4 copies of this game on the shelf priced at 19 AUD (Australian Dollars). My first instinct was to scoff at the realatively low price tag but if any game has taught me anything, it can be full of surprises (looks at undertale). Anyway picking it up and inserting the disc into the Pc then activated it through a code, waited for a quick download and the game was ready to play. What hit me next was a journey into the wonderful world of nibel. The menu screen already introduced me into a trance that so little games managed to accomplish, the combination between the sorrowful music and the beautiful background instantly destroyed the essence of my being. The adventure i underwent through next completely took me away from this world.
Gameplay: As most platformers go, Ori and the blind forest brings a few things to the table. The gameplay flows very well, combining quick thinking, timing, interesting puzzles and a decent combat system. The feel of the game is very smooth on my end (you don't really need a good Pc to run it), and i have not encountered a single bug or gamebreaking glitch so far. However do not think this game is simple, it is possibly (especially on one life) one of the most hardest platforming challenges you might face. However with a multitude of abilities that Ori has is able to fight of most of the denizens and dark dwellers within the forest.
//////////// The Story section can contain spoilers READ AT YOUR OWN RISK \\\\\\\\\
Story: As story goes it is relatively simple, an orphan (Ori) is lost to a storm and is picked up by a creature (Naru) who becomes a mother to Ori. A series of unfortunate events (which is revealed later) wracks the forest with death and famine. Ori now Orphaned again now must venture on a journey to restore the forest back to the way it was.
Despite being a very simple story, it is the way it is told that makes it special, full of plot twists, moments of pure joy and moments of utter devastation really plays on your feelings.
\\\\\\\\\\\\\\       End of Spoilers    ///////////

I absolutely LOVE this game.
Is it very deep? Not terribly so. Is there a huge amount of content? Eh, not really. Are all levels fun? Definitely not (bomb levels in specific). But, if the stars align, this is one of the most silly fun games i've ever played.
The Swordsman is the absolute pinnacle of my enjoyment. I went from getting absolutely demolished the first 40-50 times, to being able to beat him with no health on the hardest difficulty. You will realize his script. You will know what he is doing, when, and how. And then you will beat him in your sleep. And you would think this is a bad thing, but it really isn't. Because you actually feel skillful when you get to that point. It won't be frustrating. It won't feel cheap.
And the sheer number of moves and combo's that you have are ridiculous. Press X 4 times slowly and you'll get a powerful high damage slam combo. Press x 4 times and hit a twice and you'll get an aerial kick to follow it. Hold x and you will have a huge flurry of punches. Mix and match high's/ lows and you will get some new combos. And once you know all of them, how to do them, and can do them reliably, the game will go from impossible, to you giving the asking hand to the enemies, saying "Bring it".
I look forward to any more content from these developers, and truly want to thank them for this incredibly fun game.
2/21/2017-
I'm a few more hours in at this point (by few I mean more than a few), and I want to reiterate how much fun, how much raw enjoyment I get from this game. I'm more of an ARPG fan, so to get such a fresh new lease on this genre after none of the other major AAA titles did anything for me has really broadened my scope of interest.
When you first play this game, the sheer complexity can be overwhelming. This game doesn't cater to desperation combo's, and those will get you killed fast. You have to make all of your actions deliberate. The enemy AI is calibrated extremely well. So well, that even when you know their script,  it is still difficult. Grunts will rarely try to initiate attacks, but the moment you attack them, others will sieze a chance to strike. You cannot use the same combo or strategy everywhere.
The animations are some of the best quality i've seen in a game, easily comparable to the biggest names.
I've learned to time my attacks so that it's a fluid string of strikes, with very little delay between both. When I spin kick, I wait til my feet touch the ground before I keep going, I've learned to hit block if you've made an attack near a group. I can beat every boss (well, a few still destroy me, namely the final story mission bosses). I have played this for entire days, only to end up playing more the next.
I have a couple of complaints, but they're so small, that the only one worth even mentioning is the lack of online matches. But that's more of a desire than it is a fault.
And do you want to know the best part? The absolute best part of this game? When I think i've learned everything there is to offense, I always end up proving myself wrong with new tricks.
I hope the developers make a sequel, because I would buy it in an instant. Big thanks to you developers.
