Ah, another gem hidden in the indiegame ocean, waiting for being discovered by all of you.
Mute Crimson+ (Plus) is exactly what you see in the store page: another successful attempt into recovering the old gaming spirit with a very complete 2D platformer, difficulty-growing levels and a set of different worlds or zones. This game is actually a huge update of an older Mute Crimson game, which is actually included as well if you want to try it.
The main character doesn't have many different resources and skills but I can tell the dev made some effort to squeeze them, and to feel that every level feels very different. Mastering this game might require some practise since the jump mechanics feels quite odd at first. But once you get the hang of it the experience turns to a much more pleasant session.
Every world features some different levels with a unique background condition (i.e World 2 levels will have wind and you'll have to deal with it the best you can) plus a boss fight at the end, which is your common pattern-learning thing.
PROS:
+ Charming pixel style contrasting black/white with red (being anything red as hostile).
+ This game features Engrish!!! It's totally intended and adds a very original fact that most people have forgotten.
+ Catchy chiptune/8-bit music that gets on well with the rest of the game very properly.
+ A total of 7 worlds and 7 bosses, with about 50 levels in total. I would say that a blind run might take you from 3 to 4 hours.
+ Growing difficulty that ends to be pretty challenging. If you're an experienced platformer player then you'll only find issues from world 5 to beyond, but if you're more of a newcomer get ready for one hell of a run!
+ Many different game modes, including Boss Rush (<3) and Arcade Mode speedrunning (9 lifes for the whole game).
+ Challenging achievements not meant for everybody!
NEUTRAL:
· Getting the collectibles is needed in order to unlock further modes. I'm usually against this but since they add some sort of extra challenge into levels it wasn't that bad.
CONS:
- No diagonal detection for gamepad players. I know oldschool games didn't have it either (joysticks came much later in the end) but that's the kind of thing I would pass since it's a little adapt to the nowadays devices. Several times I died because some frames before grabbing a wall I was pressing my joystick more "up" than "left/right", causing me not to grab it and therefore die.
OVERALL:
Mute Crimson+ is a very enjoyable platforming experience, getting us back to the old days in the best of ways. I can see a lot of feeling put into its developing and despite not being crafted for eveybody, I'm sure all of you will appreciate how good and polished this game is.

I'm going to start off by saying, that I did not grow up with this game like many other people here did. My parents thought it was way too innapropriate for children to be playing. After playing it, I completely agree. It is extremely violent, full of sexual content, drugs, and language. If I had been allowed to play it when it came out, I would have probably called a lot of people the n-word, thinking it was like calling someone "dude" or "bro", which wouldn't be a good thing, living in a place like San Diego, which has a very diverse community.
But, it is an excellent game. Really, one of the best games I have played in a long time. The controls were great (for the most part). It feels really solid, especially after hearing that driving controls are usually terrible on PC games.
And then there's the story. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ I am a ♥♥♥♥♥ for a good story, and man, am I a ♥♥♥♥♥ for this game's story. You have love, betrayal, family, all the key elements to a dramatic story. And the characters are just great to. I am not a gang member, never have, never will, yet I felt like I could relate to these characters on some level.
I only have three complaints with this game:
1) You lose your weapons when you die or are arrested. After a few missions, I just started saving before each mission, and reloading when I died, so I'd have all of my weapons back. I'm a GTA noob, give me a break!
2) I feel like it dragged on a bit too long. I feel like there were too many missions that didn't affect the story. It boiled down to too many missions of "CJ, go do this illegal thing for me!" Do I really need a bunch of missions that are, more or less, the same thing, with no effect on the story?
3) The flying controls are complete♥♥♥♥♥ They are a massive pain in the neck. I'm not sure if they work better on a console, but with a mouse and keyboard, they suck. Hopefully, they will figure them out when GTA5 comes to PC.
All in all, this is a masterful piece of art. I would give it a 9/10. The only reason it doesn't get a full ten, is those three reasons up there. Hell, I'd probably give it full points if the only complaint was reason number 2.

Not sure why some people find this game so offensive. It's quite good! You play as Batman (doi!) and this takes place in the early days. Batman's a little younger, a little stubborn, and yet still has all those magnificent toys.
You're in an area that's roughly twice the size of Arkham City. Though you clearly cover the same area that was eventually blocked off to create Arkham City but before it was all crappy. Plus another section of Gotham. Origins also impliments a much needed fast-travel system.
You'll see some fun Batman enemies like Penguin, Killer Croc, Black Mask, Bane, and a stable of other villians from the Rogue Gallery. Some you've never seen in an Arkham game prior to Origins. I've heard some people complain about the boss battles, but I had a lot of fun with them.
People also complain about glitches. Perhaps this was an issue when the game released, but as of today (1/27/15) it seems to be fine. Only a couple that I noticed, and they were NOT game breaking. Such as a defeated thug clipping through the floor, and some minor animation sync problems. Otherwise I had no issues.
In the end: Fan of Batman? Get it. Fan of Arkham games? Get it. Never played an Arkham game? Start with Arkham Asylum, then Arkham City, then get it. Hate Batman and/or Arkham games? What are you, some kind of joker!?

It is easily one of the best, if not the best, games I have played in the genre of "Military Shooter" in the past fifteen years. After leaving this game for a while when I bought it in the winter sale of 2012, I beat it and thought nothing of it. Then a year later I came back to it and 100% the game (or 106% I guess). When I first picked up the game it didn't seem that unique. I mean, it just seems like a hardcore platformer, right? That's all there is to it? Ok, sure, let's just call it that. Let's also call it the best of it's genre, because it is. Sure, N+ was great, but something about the controls and mechanics made it feel wonky- like you weren't in control of your character at times. I've never had that problem while playing this game. It advertises itself as a platformer, and it pulls it off in the most perfect fashion I've ever seen. The level design is always flawless (save maybe Skyscraper Warp Zone- too twitchy) and character movement is perfect.
The levels never make it impossible to react to something. What do I mean? We, as humans,  can only visibly see a threat (say a sawblade) and react to it in a limited amount of time. Also, they're predictable, making muscle memory a key factor in clearing gsome levels. This isn't a bad thing- I've found myself using certain algorithms developed at previous obstacles to clear ones like it. Sure, there may be a large skill spike between The End and Cotton Alley. However, Cotton Alley is a bonus stage, so it was intentional since you don't have to complete any of those levels to beat the game.
However, I wouldn't recommend this game to everyone. Not just because some people don't like punching their monitors, but also the lack of shortcuts this game has regarding skill. The only possible way for you to improve in this game is by playing it- there are no shortcuts that make you better, like using the SMB Wiki to find info. The Wiki is very useful for finding bandages, character unlocks and warpzones, but it doesn't make you better at the game, mainly because the only strategy to being good at this game is to not die. Binding of Isaac (another popular game by Edmund and his partner Florian) is way more based around research. Basically, if you read the whole wiki you would most likely beat Mom in your first few tries. You just can't do that in a game where you only get better by experience, which is why I love this game.
This game never made me too upset. I mean, The Kid warpzone almost made my cry but that's because I spend almost three hours on it. That's it really. Every time I've died in this game (over 10,000 times) I've always realized that the death was 100% my fault. That kind of death doesn't make me upset. What does make me upset is the element of luck (crits basically) screwing me over because there was no way to plan for it. In short, there is no luck in this game- it's all skillz.
Oh yeah, and Danny B. made a killer soundtrack for this game, which alone would make this game worth the cash.
I highly recommend this game to anyone willing to put a few hours into it

Super Meat Boy is one of the hardest and most unforgiving Plattormer out there. At the same time it somehow manages to never be unfair. The controls are as tight as it gets and dying will always be your fault. If you love 2D Plattformers and a real challenge you will love this game from Edmund McMillen (Designer) and Tommy Refenes.
The Sound design is awesome even if you are stuck on a level it never gets annoying.
The Gameplay feels smooth and fluid.. Controls are tight and there is no long wait time between deaths. Really the weakest part are the boss battles. They range from really good to OK, but one especially feels like playing “Simon Says”.
The retro look suits the game very well and it really starts to shine when colors of levels get “remixed”.
This game offers a lot for you Completionist out there. Finish every level under a record time, collect all the bandages (which are hidden in the levels) and finally finish the dark version of every world. In the end you should have 103% (and many deaths).
If you are not going for 103% you will probably spend about 15 hours in the game. If you choose to go for everything the playtime goes up to about 30-35 hours, but even then there is a lot of potential for speedrunners.
I love it! It’s hard but rewarding. The difficulty curve is perfect. At first it took me an hour or two to beat the first world but going back now I can breeze through it. Every time you enter a world you are greeted by a nice cutscene which is reminiscent of older video games. Another nice touch are Warpzones (hidden in some levels) and “glitch levels” (randomly appear and look like a bluescreen at first glance). If you don’t own it already you really should pick it up, because this is a platformer which can look down on a well known plumber.

1. walking through the bushes for cover.   This is irrelevant to the game

Landmarks:
A. A set of two houses, one on each side, the one on the right has an axe infront of it.  You can't pick it up.
B. Another set of houses

I've played far too much of this game, and let me go ahead and tell you not to make the same mistake I did.
For the sake of new players or those interested without knowing, this game is effectively a PVP only game, everything that results in progression in the game is done through fighting other players of the opposite faction.
The game may see some improvement in the future, but as it stands, this game has so many problems with balance, stability, etc that it simply isnt enjoyable.
For the longest time, I've played this game dealing with what issues it has to enjoy the cornucopia of interesting features and customization that the game has, but all in all it isnt worth it. The servers are laggy constantly, skill level seems to not matter at all as far as player placement is concerned, and many players including myself are stricken with constant jerking and stuttering. Now I can't discredit the game too much for the stuttering, thats probably more on my end, but the game has more then enough problems aside from that for me to wholeheartedly tell you not to play this game.
Notice that matchmaking is in quotes, there is a reason for that. APB doesn't really have much of a matchmaking system to speak of. Players are allowed into and recommended to go to different instances of the games two districts based on their current skill rating, while the player's level is generally not factored into the allowance into a certain instance of a district. This at first seems like a relatively fair system, those who play better would soon be designated 'gold' skill level players that are allowed to play on gold and silver level districts. Gold players are absolutely abundant in this game, and this leads to one of two outcomes for any one given time, Either the gold servers are full, so all of the gold players are in low player skill designated districts,
the gold servers are completely empty, and therefore none of the golds want to go there, so they still go to low skill districts. Now, this basically means that no matter where you are, what level you've achieved, or what skill level you may be, you're going to run into a bunch of golds. And more than likely, they'll destroy you. Now I know what some of you may be thinking "Oh you're just a noob complaining about getting owned by other players, stop whining and get better at the game." And while I will admit I am not the best of players, take this into account: I normally hover around silver skill level, this means that I can access pretty much every level of server, if I feel ballsy enough I can go to a gold district, I can stay in silver (filled mostly with golds) or I can go to bronze with lower skilled players. Being silver and not wanting to fight all of the gold players who all are extremely high ranked and all seem to have a rocket launcher pointed directly at your face, I started to play on the bronze districts. When in a bronze district one of two things happened, I either encountered bronze players and my fellow silvers and had a relatively balanced match, with fair fighting, good play on each side, and everybody had a decent amount of fun, OR I had a team full of bronze players and was matched against a team with 4 out of 5 players being gold. Now, gold players arent generally allowed on bronze servers, but thats the thing, if you purposefully lose enough to get yourself to silver you can go right in, win once or twice and get your gold back, and proceed to stay in the surver murdering everyone.
Now your threat rating generally is supposed to tell other players how skilled you are, its a general measurement of your wins over losses etc, now this could be considered only measuring skill, more often than not however gold players have weapons that were purchased within the games cash shop, which are fully modded, and just monumentally better than anything you could get with in game currency even relatively later in the game. This means that for many players, the only reason they've achieved a gold rating is because of superior equipment. Now don't get me wrong, the game is not entirely pay to win, you have just as much opportunity to destroy people with guns purchased with in game currency, many of the high level guns and modifications are equally effective if not moreso than the guns one can purchase with real money, but the problem is that all of these gold players stepping all over your play space makes it extremely difficult to progress at all. If you're constantly losing to gold players with fancy weaponry then you arent going to progress far enough to get the weapons that supposedly make the game's cash shop "balanced." So basically, 80% of the time or more, any gold you see is only gold because he has a shiny gun he bought for 10 bucks. Some people get there the hard way, but its alot easier when you get great weapons at the get go.
Now, while the cash shop is of course necessary for the game to EXIST due to it being free to play, its also the reason that the game is so damn difficult for anyone who chooses (or simply can't) pay. The problem here is that the game is entirely player vs player. You can't really say that a normal MMORPG that is heavily reliant on player purchases for player success is truly pay to win, because you still have the option of playing the game without conflict in order to reach the goal of power, but in this case, pvp IS the game. You PvP, its what you do. The cash shop gives players the opportunity to buy fancy customization, clothing, cars, gun skins, you name it its there, but it also has straight up weaponry available. If you so choose you can enter the game, and without having done anything, buy a gun who's statistics are on par with a gun that would take hours upon hours upon HOURS of someone who isnt paying for a premium subscription to achieve, and not just because of the cost, but because of the fact that you have to unlock them before purchase. This means that everyone who has bought a gun has an immediate advantage over everyone else, while this may not be very detrimental to a game with more of a PVE focus, this game is ,as I have said far too many times at this point, purely pvp. This means that every person that has bought a gun is not only making the game easier for them to play, but it is hindering the possibility to actually progress through the game for others. If other words, if all I can fight are people with fully modded guns, and I'm say, a level 20 bronze player, then I wont be able to level up very quickly at all, wont be able to get any kills to progress the games statistic based weapon unlock systems for certain guns, and therefore basically can't play the game effectively lest I pay to buy those same guns.
This game has had some of the WORST server performance I have ever seen. With sometimes constant rubberbanding, lag, and general connection issues, it can make the game a downright pain to handle.
To be honest, I used to love this game, even with some of the flaws it had and still has. The guns are fairly interesting, the cars handle uniquely, the customization is one of the game's strong points being one of the BEST customization systems that you can experience in a video game, and even the quirky limitations of the game, such as the lack of head shots or any articulation based hitboxes (everyone has one, uniformly sized hitbox). But to be honest, without paying a metric♥♥♥♥♥ton of money, you are severely limited by the players who do. The community is awful as well, with hack accusations being dropped like raindrops in a storm.
The game just isnt worth it in the long run for the amount of crap you have to go through to get anywhere.
Maybe someday. Maybe someday.

Yes, this game is a retro action platformer, and those aren't exactly rare these days. But this one is worth your time and your money - and come on, $5 USD? That is impulse buy territory, and if you do, you won't regret it!
Why is it worth playing?
The gameplay is tough but fair. There are no "cheats" in the level design, and the controls are tight and responsive, so any mistakes you make are your own. You end the game with all the moves you had at the beginning; there are no power-ups or bonuses, and no random gameplay elements - it's a game of pure skill and experience, both of which you'll need in abundance to meet the game's solid difficulty and complexity curve.
The art design and soundtrack are both very much in the NES vein. The best way to describe the colour scheme is "black and white and red all over" - but although the backgrounds are monochrome, they're also lush and distinctive. The red is reserved for anything that can kill you, and the contrast makes this distinction very effective. The sprite animation is smooth and flows well. The cutscenes are very well done, with a great comic book feel to them, and although the "Engrish" dialogue isn't for everyone, I personally find it hilarious. The music is very solid and catchy, with some great (and varied!) melodies and basslines going on.
In short, there's a lot to like about this game. In addition to the main game mode, the extras add greater replayability to the game. It's clear the developers put a lot of effort into making the game both fun and charming, and they definitely succeeded!

What would you do to save the love of your life? Would you be broken, beaten and scarred by an infinity of fiery pits, vicious rockets, monsters that look like a pile of vomit and, the worst of all, an infinity of saws and edgy materials that will cut you in pieces and splash your blood all over the place just to save your damsel from the evil robotic arms of Dr. Fetus, the malevolent villain of this grotesque world? That's exacly what our protagonist, Meat Boy, does. Bandage Girl, his girlfriend of sorts, is kidnapped by the forementioned Dr. fetus and Meat Boy must go through more than 300 deadly levels in order to save her. She waits at the end of each level, but as soon as our hero touches her she is teleported to the next level, and so on. With a side-scrolling, 2D platformer gameplay, Super Meat Boy is a challenging experience that may stress the calmest player. From the variety and originality of the levels, to the interesting bosses, this is one of the best platformers out there. Along with this, there are also special levels called "Warp Zones", that take players through a 3-level challenge that is graphically inspired by an old retro game. From Mario to the infamous E.T., there are even playable characters, each one with his advantages and disadvantages, that are based in (mostly) retro games, such as The Commander Video from the Bit.Trip Series, but there is also a headcrab from Half-Life and even a Minecraft character. So, this game is also a little tribute to the gaming culture. With achievements that could drive one to insanity (compare them to the XBox version and take conclusions), Super Meat Boy is one of the best indie games of the last few years. Besides some bugs and other small details, it's close to perfection. I give it a 93 out of 100. Buy it and cry.

I got through most of this game without crying, and then the ending cinematic sucker punched me right in the feels.
Ori and the Blind Forest is a tale of love, hope and sometimes, sacrifice. It's on an entirely different level from anything else out there. Even though the few named characters speak very little or not at all, they are filled with personality, bringing to life the gorgeous artwork and letting the amazing music of this game do its job. I haven't gone a day since finishing this game without listening the heartbreaking main theme music. Just getting this game for the OST is worth it.
That said, aside from the story the game mechanics themselves are an emotional journey. Some moments were frustratingly difficult, taking what seemed forever and dozens of deaths to complete successfully. Others were a joy to run through, even though I died several times on them, I learned what killed me and made my way past it much more easily on my next try. Sometimes the game can be confusing, making it a little hard to find out what the objective is at a given point.
A must-buy on sale, and you can put serious thought into buying this game at the full price. Even after I had finished the story, I went back and hunted down all the secrets, just to be able to see more of the beautiful artwork and the care put into making this game.
If you're new to this game, I recommend finding and exploring the Black Root Burrows included with this Definitive Edition as soon as you can. It contains two more trees with new abilities, one of which will make your life much easier in several sections, especially with its supporting skills, and another which will give you access to some secrets as soon as you find them, giving you small boosts which could prove vital.

Heh, I'll start off by saying this: If you're not a fan of games that require precision, And can take hours to pass a single area, I'd recommend avoiding this.
For those of you however, Who enjoy those frustrating Platformer games that are all about timing, This is a pretty fun game. Frustrating, But fun.
It took me about 15 hours to clear the game with an A+ on every level, Not counting Cotton Alley or the Dark World. The game does have it's moments where it feels stupidly hard, But it's really like any Legend of Zelda puzzle. It can be a pain to solve, But once you've figured out the trick it only takes a little bit of effort to manage. The nice thing about this game is there are tons of curveballs that can take a strategy that supposedly works, and disprove it in an instant. And while it may seem like the entire game is the same thing, Running around as a piece of meat trying not to get sashimi'd by a spikewheel, Or eviscerated by a pit of spikes, There's a bunch of nice Variations on levels that can keep things interesting.
Then there's the Retro levels, Man some of those are just evil. To this day I still haven't been able to pass the first level of the Skyscraper. But that's just it, The constant amount of failures is what's keeping me entertained. Just knowing if I'm able to avoid that mistake I'll be one step closer to passing. (If only we had more than three lives :( )
Also the achievements, I managed to get all the "Take No Damage On This Floor" achievements on The Binding of Isaac, That seems like nothing compared to this. Even the first one for taking no damage in The Forest, It's requires much more skill and patience to unlock.
Overall I have enjoyed this game, And at some point am going to try those twisted Dark World levels. I'd recommend this to people who fit the criteria at the beginning on my review.

First Call of Duty to feature nonlinear gameplay and last good one.
Campaign: 8.5/10

The single player in this game has one of the most riveting stories due to the fact that your choices impact the outcome and fate of certain events and characters. Alex Mason and Frank Woods return along with some new characters. The story is spread out between flashback sequences set in 1986-1989 and the main game which takes place during a distopian 2025 where a lone antagonist has raged war against the wars superpowers to get revenge for the loss of a loved one. The premise is simple and full of tropes however the intricate details aren't just a facade for a generic shooter; it was one of the more innovative shooters. Possibly the most engaging campaign and one to replay to see all the different endings. The Strike-Force missions are interesting but are relatively poorly executed; fortunately, you can skip them, but bypassing them eliminates certain endings. Overall, the campaign was a highly enjoyable experience.
Zombies: 7/10; DLC: 10/10
Tranzit is the included zombies mode with Black Ops II and it was a fun but frustrating experience. I felt that it was too complicated for new players and the atmosphere was comical at best and cringy at worst. The better zombies maps were included with the DLC map packs, my personal favorite being Mob of the Dead. Origins was also very well done and so was Buried. Overall, zombies was decent without DLC but the DLC maps add many more hours of enjoyment and make the mode feel more polished and complete
Multiplayer: 8.5/10
Multiplayer in Black Ops II has to be the most balanced multiplayer in any Call of Duty game. Sure the AN-94 and Skorpion EVO were annoying, but there always exists a way to outplay the users of these two guns. The "pick ten" system allowed for a vast amount of customization and allowed people to remove items they rarely used or would otherwise not want. Unfortunately, the PC user base has diminished greatly; only about 1000-2000 people are playing at any given time, though it averages around 1100.
Overall, this game has many flaws, but most are minor and not game breaking.  Truthfully, the $59.99 price tag is quite outrageous for a game from 2012, but if it is on sale for $29.99 or less, it was definitely worth picking up. As for zombies, the DLC is essential for the complete experience.

The true sequel to Blood Money is here. The maps are huge and there is a lot to explore within them. If you loved Blood Money for the sandbox gameplay, the target experimentation, and the exploration then you cannot go wrong with purchasing this game. HITMAN™ is like a much larger modern version of Blood Money.
I do have a few issues with HITMAN™ though such as the inability to choose a difficulty setting (some may argue the difficulty is adjustable in the gameplay menu), the unlimited saves, and the all too frequent human storage bins. The unlimited saves and the nonexistent difficulty mode problems only pertain to the campaign itself. There are challenges you can take where your save feature is removed and the security is beefed up; I would have liked this game even more if this increased difficulty was an optional setting in the campaign.
Fortunately, these problems don't affect the overall positive experience I've had with HITMAN™. I will definitely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Blood Money, especially now since the first season of HITMAN™ is over and all of the locations have been released.
Note: I completed this game on a console not a PC.

Batman Arkham Origins is the 3rd action-adventure gamein the Arkham series where you play as Batman in Gotham. Arkham Asylum, the first, was great. Arkham City, the second, was even better, even though the story did get convoluted at times just to fit in all the content. Arkham Origins just feels like it's something to tide us over until Arkham Knight is finally released.
The story is both better and worse than City. It definitely has more focus than City, which started off simple but had an incredibly convoluted build-up to the end.
The gameplay is definitely worse, in both small things and bigger things. There are glitches where Batman can get stuck or enemies suddenly stop registering as enemies and just stand there looking goofy, ground takedowns seem to work only when they feel like it, and sometimes necessary encounters simply don't happen until you leave an area and come back. Mind you, this is with all the patches and fixes that are likely to ever be applied this is as good as it gets. It never gets so bad that it makes Origins unplayable, but it's just not as polished as City.
Multiplayer had so much potential, it was awesomely paced, had an easy to understand objective, well balanced set of teams and skill ceilings. Servers wouldn't save data for the opening week though and no one played it again. Sucks to see such squandered potential.
Pros:
+ Another installment into the Batman franchise
+ Good Plot
+ Improved and interesting boss fights
+ Great voice acting
+ Incredible amount of side quests and other things to do, albeit it was poorly paced
+ Incredibly fun multiplayer if you can get a group of friends to play with you
Cons:
- Basically just Arkham City rebooted; Same combat and gadget system as Arkham City
- Bigger map but somehow more boring to explore
- Multiplayer that dropped the ball on launch
- Plethora of bugs and glitches scattered around the game
TL;DR
7/10
Fun game if you like the Batman story, gameplay-wise and innovation-wise you're better off playing Batman Arkham City or Knight. I definitely got my money's worth but it wasn't as fun as the previous.

I found it impossible the first time through. After about a dozen tries, I started a new game and changed how my abilities were laid out... putting everything into armor. I'm not saying it's a bad game. That is for people who play a LOT more than me to decide. I am saying that I didn't have much fun during my time with it, and I do not think it was worth buying. Just my two cents.

Chinese Dark Souls.
The game gets pretty damn difficult in the later levels, but sadly not only because of overlapping mechanics (the good type of difficulty), but because the AI breaks the rules firmly established earlier in the game (the bad type of difficulty). As you start out, the game teaches you how your Chi-attacks (or whatever the red glowing attacks are called) break enemies' Chi-attacks, for example- the further you play, the less true that becomes. Sure, they are the only attacks that
break enemies' Chi-attacks, but that does not mean that they necessarily
, if the hitbox decides otherwise.
There is, for instance, a fight where when you attack the AI, they dodge your attack and counter-attack with a Chi-attack, but it's very hard to block (pretty sure it's the most timing-crucial thing in the game I have encountered) and if you try to counter their Chi-attack with your own, it will hit them, then drop them out of it (if you did WW kicks), and then they will punish you with another Chi-attack for half your health, You are punished for countering their counter. Did I mention you fight two of them at the same time?
In essence, I would only recommend this game to masochists, as it simply isn't a fair game. I still have a blast with it, but it also gets super frustrating. If you don't mind that kind of unfair design, this is a very fine & addictive game with DMC-style combo mechanics and the only other tangible flaw I could find was the camera, which can be somewhere between inconvenient and outright terrible to the extent of flying off in a wrong direction because of it.
6.5/10, would buy again in a sale.
P.S.: Very playable on arcade sticks, which is always a plus in my book!

This is a good game for those who like a casual missile defense game but are tired of all the flash Missile Command clones. This game differs from Missile Command in two major ways...
#1 being that it's in 3D of course. and you get to set the locations of your units before each match.
#2 It isn't all about defense. You have to take out your enemy to win.
Think of it sorta like the classic board game Battleship. You are the total missile commander flicking between defense and offense as easily as you press the space bar. The controls are simple enough, using your mouse to aim the recticle and fire your SAMs as well as plot targets on the map for your offensive missiles which depending on the map can come in 6 different flavors (3 standard 3 special)
Now there is multiplayer over LAN and IP but I haven't actually tried that yet but for $4.99 it makes for a good singleplayer skirmisher, casual but still fun.
A pleasant little game, reminiscent of an augmented form of battleship, which is quite fun to play with a buddy.

Bamham: Origins from Liberty City is a game that revolves around figuring out why everything seems to be capped at 30 FPS. Superman, feeling unloved and uncared for, plants a nuclear bomb within the walls of Gotham City/Town/Hamlet. With a small-yet-humorous altercation between the two, revolving over an argument as to who is the "biggest guy", the game kicks off with a roaring start. As Bamham, you're expected to just press X to attack your enemies. Hit X enough, and they die. You also hit Y sometimes. That's fun.
With a deep combo system, revolving around proper placement of sliverware at a royal dinner party and engaging guests in a minigame where you force yourself through robotic, meaningless conversation, Bamham will eventually gain access to his gadgets. He has a hook, another hook, a boomerang, another boomerang, a different boomerang, a different type of hook altogether, and a sonic screwdriver that does anything the plot demands it to do.
Sometimes you look at crime scenes. There are many secrets to be found here. Can you find out who stole the cookies from the cookie jar? I bet you can't!
Run, jump, and fight your way through one really large city that was pretty much lifted directly from the last game. Really, it's kind of sad.
Batman: Arkham Origins. Buying this is like putting money in Josef Goebbels' pocket, in that you probably shouldn't do it because it supports bad business practices and anti-semitism.

Ori is well worth your time if you enjoy games like Super Mario Maker and Super Metroid. Don't be fooled by its cute anime looks, because at the core Ori is a very technical and demanding platformer that derives much of its appeal from a 'Dark Souls'-like journey of failure, learning and ultimately mastery (at least that's how it feels on 'hard' difficulty, which I highly recommend). Thanks to the game's excellent pacing and teaching of new mechanics you never feel overwhelmed by those challenges and the awesome save point system helps to keep the frustration of repeated failure at bay.
You will die a lot in Ori, but not all deaths will make you a better player next try: one of the game's strengths is also one of its weaknesses, and that is the context-sensitive control scheme, which is both highly efficient and intuitive, but you will experience many situations in which a move won't come out due to the game not recognizing your input (or your analog controller being inaccurate) and that is frustrating. Plus enemies can hit you even if you fought them a hundred times and environmental hazards in uncharted areas are often unavoidable death the first time you encounter them, which will make those aspects of the game feel unfair to some and maybe even tedious to others who don't have the patience to respect the game's world all the time.
Nevertheless, Ori is an outstanding game with great music, a very cute protagonist and a solid story. Growing on and overcoming its challenges is extremely satisfying and after the 13 or so hours it took me to beat the game I was wishing for a level editor. Go buy it, have fun.

Well I guess after over fifty hours of this game, I'm qualified to write a review.
[Spoiler for french readers : Ca tue, les contrôles sont au poil, la durée de vie dantesque et les combats plus épiques les uns que les autres, en bref : mangez-en !]
It's a very original mix between two genres which can seem very weird but in the end it works very well. The gameplay may need a few hours to be fully able to play with all the abilities to control perfectly your character. The game is very progressive in the beginning to let you accustom yourself to the dash/slow-time/barrier making but to truly use them all and switching at the right time between each to get the best of the different cooldowns you'll need a bit more time !
It's a easy to play/hard to master gameplay and it'll allow you to keep improving yourself and elaborate new techniques even after lots of hours.
That's the gameplay but how is the game ?
Boss fight, boss fight, boss fight !
18 bosses, 3 difficulties and even 3 challenges to boost your score when you've mastered a boss.
You can fight bosses you've beaten a long time before but in a harder difficulty or add one or two challenges to change your mind from a boss you can't beat.
Each boss is very unique and you'll have to thoroughly analyze its patterns to find the best way to counterattack by using your powers. At this time, there are still one or two patterns that I can't really understand and where I'm almost always hit.
If you like platformer gameplay, hard but highly rewarding games, fights for survival or playing until you get the top score, this is perfect for you !

to be attacked every time, but beyond the jump scare that ends the game and send you to the main menu, there really isn't much to be scared of.

Really. that's all. I don't know if this game is supposed to "read your fear" like the full version, but it certainly doesn't seem to do anything along those lines. The game tells you to keep calm or the forest will get you. I honestly couldn't have been calmer. I walked straight, didn't stray or jerk the mouse around at all and I was still attacked around the same point. The reviews saying things like "[The game] scared me very much and left me shaking," are obviously opinions and everyone will feel differently, but I just don't see it being that extreme. I'm a fan of horror so maybe I'm not as easily frightened as others, but I just don't see the huge scare here. Try it if you want, but don't get too hyped from all the ridiculously positive reviews here.
EDIT: People keep telling me I shouldn't complain because this game is free. That's just not the case. This is a "prequel" for 'Pineview Drive', a game which costs $19.99 currently. This "free game" is what people will base their choice on when they look at 'Pineview Drive'. I'm not saying it's a terrible game, but I am trying to give an alternate opinion that is different than all the other extremely positive reviews. Maybe the game is better since I played it, maybe I just missed something the game has to it, but there was nothing in it that seemed to "react to my fear" as advertised. That's all I'm saying. Again, play the game yourself and decide. Along with that, stop telling me to not complain about a free game. A price tag doesn't change the actual quality of a game or my opinion on it.
I enjoy this game, and looking back on it, they put a lot of effort into it. But it's really not worth $60.

HITMAN™ is like a much larger modern version of Blood Money.
I do have a few issues with HITMAN™ though such as the inability to choose a difficulty setting (some may argue the difficulty is adjustable in the gameplay menu), the unlimited saves, and the all too frequent human storage bins. The unlimited saves and the nonexistent difficulty mode problems only pertain to the campaign itself. There are challenges you can take where your save feature is removed and the security is beefed up; I would have liked this game even more if this increased difficulty was an optional setting in the campaign.
Fortunately, these problems don't affect the overall positive experience I've had with HITMAN™. I will definitely recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Blood Money, especially now since the first season of HITMAN™ is over and all of the locations have been released.
Note: I completed this game on a console not a PC.

When you get past the initial reaction the beautiful stylization and high energy beat-em-up the first few levels have to offer, it rapidly becomes clear that Kung Fu Strike is a game made of quality component parts that simply don't fit together in any sort of intelligble way.
The mechanics of the game shine early on, where you're facing a handful of tough enemies and mobs of weaker ones, but as the game progresses and throws more and more boss-type enemies at you simultaneously, players may begin to get the impression that player character Loh was made for an entirely different game than the one he stars in. Guard breaking takes a random but always too-long amount of time, making it impossible when facing multiple enemies and of questionable use when you do manage to pull it off, as it puts vulnerable enemies outside of Loh's prohibitively short range. Physics-based encounters involving explosives demand more mobility than Loh, possessing only a cumbersome roll and no dedicated jump button to speak of, actually has. KFS's touted "jaw dropping combos" are nearly impossible to execute by mid game due to sheer enemy quantity, most of whom possess the ability to interrupt them on a whim. It doesn't take long for Loh's meaty arsenal to be reduced to special attacks and parries as his only valid tools, making what should be a fast-paced and energetic beat-em-up an almost purely defensive game of blocking and waiting for meters to fill. KFS describes itself as a hard game, when in fact it's merely a long one, demanding far too much time for much too little pay out when better, fairer, and indeed, more difficult games exist in the form of Godhand, Dark Souls, or even One Finger Death Punch.

I am quite big on graphics, and I have to admit this isn't so bad. The trucks/cars both look great and so does the interior of the trucks. Sound doesn't seem to be much of a problem, it has realistic car, weather, truck and engine noises.
Having to deliver more and more in order to gain more money, does take a lot of time. But this leads to the game being more addictive and actually worth it. However, if driving back and forth for a while isn't really your thing, this can become a problem, though I ensure it wont be when you actually try it out, and even better, unlock more places.
One thing that has annoyed me while driving around on here is how stupid the other drivers are. They either go the wrong way, beep at me when I am not doing anything wrong, and/or randomly brake when there was no need to which leads me into hitting them, which leads to me having to pay for hitting them. Adding pedestrians or animals would also be something which would make the game better (no I do not want to run them over)
Another thing is how the cities are extremely small, and only have up to 5-6 roads, which is bad for when you want to explore other places other than the highway. The sound is good, but not so great. It sounds like I'm driving ontop of the truck rather than inside (might be because the windows are always open for some reason) and the radio does not sound like it's actually coming out of a radio in the truck.
Honestly, I love this game even though it has some flaws which I have to live with, however those are probably fixed in ETS2. I recommend this game if you either have a older computer, have a Mac and cannot buy the second one (which is my case) or have a few cash left or is low on cash to spend it on this. An overall 6/10 from me.

If you love arcade games, the kind that's all about boss fight, like Alien Soldier (megadrive/genesis), Sin and Punishement SotS (wii), or Hard Corps : Uprising (XBLA, PSN), then Isbarah is a great title to add to your collection.
Gameplay-wise, it's a perfect 10, and the presentation is nice too.

On a list of things I didn't know I wanted, Isbarah would no doubt be at the top. I love bullet hell games that require you to focus and memorize patterns, and this takes that idea and completely reimagines it. Everything about the game feels polished, and all of the visuals look crisp, clean, and sharp. In the spirit of bullet hell games it keeps you constantly in the action, with only brief periods of downtime between fights for a comicbook-styled storyline. As far as the flow of the game, it feels very much like Touhou. Most of your game time is spent in a fight, and in the event of a game over it only takes a few seconds to be right back into it.
The game has really tight and responsive controls. I've yet to have an issue with them, or a single instance of the controls being the cause of a death. On top of the normal dodging mechanics you'd expect from a game like this you are also given three abilities. The ability dash, which quickly sends you in a a straight line for a short distance. The ability to create a platform, which halts incoming bullets for its duration and can also be stood on. Lastly, the ability to slow time, which slows yourself and all bullets, which is useful for dashing through really tight spots, or placing a platform in the perfect position. Even with these at your disposal each fight still presents an impressive, yet fair, challenge.
The only thing that has been a downside to me with this game is that the railguns sometimes have a habit of floating away from you into nigh impossible to follow places. Not always a problem, and even when it is it usually just requires patience, but can be a little annoying when you have one left to activate and it just seems to flee to the most inconvenient spot it can. Again though, even when that happens it's still a matter of just playing it right and knowing where to go. Beating a stage is very satisfying, and clearing a spell without taking a hit even moreso. I very much recommend the game to anyone looking for something out of the ordinary, as well as anyone looking for a good challenge that doesn't feel cheap or unfair.

I wish this game was more widely known. I'm currently having an absolute blast playing through this and I love the challenge it provides. The mechanics are precise and feel amazing to play.
Usually I don't really care much about artstyle, but this one seems to hit a sweet spot where it definitely deserves to be mentioned for being absolutely gorgeous

Name: Isbarah
Gameplay Style: Platformer, Danmaku
Personal Score: Infuriatingly Fun
Isbarah is one of those many games where the term danmaku shooter or bullethell shooter should apply in which player dodge hellish amount of bullets and return fire with their own bullets as swarms of enemies, bosses and special bosses line up for a shot [at the player].
However, Isbarah removed the countless mooks, the player shooting and instead of top down shooter we get a platformer instead which should means devastation upon the game but what they have put in place is enough to make up for it and i argue even differentiate it from the others in the saturated market. But does it play as well as it should? Read on.
Remove the shooting, the buildup before the bosses and the mocks, what do you end up with? A brilliant little game where the aim is no longer about how many power-ups you collect nor how many mooks you kill but instead you ended up with a clean fuss free game where the boss is your one and only enemy [save for some unkillable backup that shoots bullet occasionally] locked into an arena. Each boss has a set of 3 railgun that the player must dash towards to activate before remaining within in its area of influence to charge it up before it knocks off 1 shield bar from a total of 3.
Once all 3 railgun are activated and the shields are gone, the boss power up and now the player must stay alive within a small part of the arena as a magic circle is being slowly charge. Once completed the boss are weaken and player have a limited window of time to dash towards the boss to receive a hefty point bonus and a restore a lost life or should their life be full they will receive an unstackable shield instead. Failure to do so will trigger the auto attack and no bonuses are awarded.
Easy enough to say but much harder to perform these feats requires to defeat the bosses as they will quite literally spew out rains of bullets towards you requiring you to dodge them should you lost one of your 3 lifes.
Good news is the controls are smooth and tight, this coupled with the 3 powers you are given makes the boss manageable rather than impossible with each defeat[s] serve to hone your skill in preparation for the next battle.
The powers are slow, platform and dash. Dash is the most important as it allows you to escape bullet filled situation and is what allows you to attack the boss after the final spell and activate the railgun needed to bring them down to the final spell stage. Slow basically slowing down time allowing more time to aim the dash or to simply perform tight maneuver  in between the bullets. Platform is basically that, allows you to place to place a platform to reach high grounds or its more important function, to be use as a shield blocking bullets from everything. All of these powers have a cooldown time with Dash being the fastest to recharge, platform the second and slow the slowest but it does has the highest reserve.
Each boss you fight often has a gimmick to each of them which affects their bullet pattern somehow, teleporting sudden bullets, fiery bullets and such.
And lastly the game has 3 bosses in one chapter with increasing difficulty as you go further before finally facing the final boss who is very hard compare to the first. Next chapter 1st act, the first boss is as hard as the 3rd final boss before that.
Also your hitbox is a tiny little circle, so long as nothing hits it you're safe.
Nothing much to say here other than the guitar rift really gets the blood pumping, Especially during the boss power up sequence it switch to a more dramatic version of their songs.
Although you wont be able to appreciate the song much being barrage by bullets and all.
Like all danmaku games graphics should be good but not intrusive and Isbarah nails it down very well, bosses and environmental items uses bright colours while background and non essential are relegated to muted colours.
However while everything sprite is pretty the bosses seems to lack some animation frames which results in stilted movement akin to wooden puppets, but it doesnt really affects the game so oh well.
Isbarah, very difficult and very frustrating but at the end of the road is the satisfaction of earning lots of points from pounding out that boss is really satisfying. Do beware the difficulty ramps up quickly though as Danmaku shooter should.

DO NOT GET HIT.
DO NOT GET COCKY AND CHOOSE THE 7TH HEAVEN DIFFICULTY.

Do use normal mode if its too hard.

The last game I ever played with danmaku tier mechanics that isn't actually a danmaku is probably one of the Touhou spinoff games, Touhou Suimusou (Immaterial and Missing Power). To have the concept as a 2D platformer but more heavily focused on the dodging and survival aspect is an absolutely brilliant concept.
Controls are tight, fluid and responsive. There are no wasted moves, you get three specials and they are all you need to carry you through the game. Survival and wins are heavily dependant on proper use of these skills. You will die, make no mistake... you will die, die again, and again, and then you will die yet again, and with each death you will never feel a boss was unfair. If you die, you know YOU screwed up, which has the effect of making you try harder the next time.
The game is extremely challenging. You'll pick it up within minutes, and then it gets harder... much... much... harder. But no matter how hard it gets, it never feels UNFAIR, which is important.

Wow.  For a ninja themed platforming game with simply controls and straightforward levels, this is one serious little game!  The levels are well laid out and the idea is simple, anything red all over will definitely kill you.  There are coins that you can collect, at your peril I dare say, that unlock certain game cheats or bonuses that only serve to make the game harder to be quite honest like, no continues for example.  The music and sound effects are top notch in this game as well and lend a hand in creating the familiar NES feel of eight bit gaming.  As I said earlier, the controls are super easy to use.  Only two buttons are used in game with the d-pad/control stick and that too gives the game an NES feel since the NES only had two buttons on their gamepads anyway.  All of this familiarity doesn't just stick out in the graphics/art/sound and controls either.  The levels are no nonsense and straight to the point kind of like Ninja Gaiden or Castlevania.  The bosses at the end of each level are also pretty well designed and definitely have been programmed like bosses from the great old days of NES too!  The challenges of the game are pretty damn good and will have veterans of the platforming genre memorizing their layout and timing.  All in all a great game and well worth the price of admission!  Get this game if you like platforming a la Mega Man, Ninja Gaiden and others of the platforming genre!  A must have for the low, low price!

You might be tempted to think "Aw geez, not another retro platformer." STOP RIGHT THERE!
There are a lot of reasons this retro platformer is worth your time:
It's a dramatically improved update of a quirky Xbox Live Indie game (which comes packed with this game as an unlockable, btw)
It's a love letter to the retro platformers of days gone by, well-served with tight controls, tough challenges, and a tongue-in-cheek story to string it all together.
It oozes with a silky-smooth, visual style that actually has function! Anything bright red is certain to kill you, and enemies delightfully explode blood everywhere like action tomatoes as you slay them.
It's cheaper than lunch at a fast-food joint.
The game can be difficult but there are no cheap deaths. Everything depends on your skill, and though you might die (a lot) the game doesn't waste your time. It wants you to learn how to beat whatever it throws at you and feel proud in doing so.
Congrats if you are still reading this, but seriously. Go buy this game.

Context: I played this game in single player mode.
PRO: Art style, and from what little story text presented, there's some humor. Music is OK. Seems to not have technical glitch.
CON: Need for repetitive trial and error, plus some luck.
1. Enemies and/or level design often have "special trait" that requires a "correct" method to fight. The problem is that making "wrong" move usually result player getting killed rather quickly.
2. More significantly, even with right strategy in mind, the number and mix of enemies rushing the player in a given level tend to result in multiple attack types (blockable+unblockable, ranged+melee...) happening simultaneously or near-simultaneously. The need for precise blocking / dodging timing often means that at least some of the attacks get through. This also tend to end fights quickly, necessitating level restart.
IMHO #2 (quantity instead of quality of enemies) is by far the greatest source of difficulty. This gives me the impression that the game was designed and tested for local co-op. Even in single player mode, when backup AI characters are available fights get noticeably better.

My childhood mostly consisted of drawing, stuffing my face with sweets and of course, the PS2. At that time, I was given two games, both in the same series, being GTA: Vice City and of course, GTA: San Andreas which was pretty new for it's time. I instantly fell in love with both games, what with both of the game's poop-crazy storylines, well developed and memorable characters and of last but not least, the multiple crimes that will rack up those classic wanted stars!

Sadly, I had lost this game a while back, due to moving and such and I was absolutely devastated. Looking for an alternative, I stumbled across Steam, with it's little miracle of putting the entire GTA series bundle on sale for an unbelieveably cheap price.	 I immediately smashed £20 into my steam wallet and hastefully slammed that purchase button and I've never looked back. This game astonished me, what with it's massive and immense game world it has. The chunk of data on that one compact disc still amazes me to this day.
Going back to the hood, as Carl 'CJ' Johnson a young representant of the Grove Street Families, an African-American street gang and one of the oldest street gangs in Los Santos, San Andreas. ''After five years on the east coast, it was time to go home.'' was the exact words from CJ's mouth, as he arrived to pick up his luggage at the L.S Airport. His motive remaining clear, after he received a call before the planned flight from his older brother, detailing that their mother had been murdered by a mysterious hustler. Giving a warm welcome by his grieving older brother and sister, along with his two Grove Street comrades, Big Smoke and Ryder, you soon find yourself spraying graffiti, drive-by shooting, exploring the far and wide sprawling sun-drenched state of San Andreas, popping some caps in the asses of the corrupt ''bustas'', and of course putting other sworn rival gangs in their place.
The gameplay on foot is top-notch. Interactivity with NPC's and overworld objects are very simple and the character animations are clear and very personified. Though the driving in this game is what I found a little problematic, what with the controls being a little messed up, but it's hardly noticeable over the irresistable charm the game has at it's repetoire.
I definitely recommend a controller for this game. Since, it's argueable to say that again, I found the controls somewhat 'sloppyish' and a little finicky, with just using a mouse and keyboard.  All the while it does feel just right when using a PS3 controller, if you can wire that up to your PC's controller port. Truly adds to the nostalgic flare, since the reminiscence of both the Dualshock 2 and 3 controller.
The only problem I've recently discovered is that a notorious patch has bestowed upon this classic game, thanks to Rockstar and now I believe that this game is now unmoddable and a handful of songs have been removed due to legal copyright reasons, which kinda sucks now.
Now looking back, I still do recommend this game, but not so much for Steam now. Definitely either get it on the Playstation Store or the Xbox Live Marketplace.

The gameplay of this game is very good. An open world truck driving simulator that's also fun to keep playing, and doesn't get boring after an hour or so. There are some issues with people going from one lane to the other, but I can see through that with the great stuff the game has to offer.

I really like the game and am definitely recommending it to everyone who likes to have a truck driving experience without actually getting a truck's driving license and buying a truck in real life.

* A very important aspect of Isbarah is the difficulty. It's tough. Tough that there are achievements that mock you for dying multiple times in a row to the same boss. The difficulty is a lot like Dark Souls where you may need to face a boss multiple times to learn its move sets before beating it, so you will die a lot. But it's a very enjoyable difficulty, you will want to keep trying until you win!
* The core mechanics in this game are really neat. You have the ability to slow time which will allow you to dodge projectiles more easy, you can dash to maneuver around the stages and you can create platforms or walls to stand on and or block most projectiles with. You will need manage your resources for each of these tools well to be able to beat a stage.
* The games graphic style is really nice to look at. Between each stage the story is told in a comic strip style, and the backgrounds to all of the stages are well animated and detailed.
* The story is fairly decent, though a few parts of the dialogue in the game caused me to cringe because it was so corny, and the pacing sometimes felt a little odd as well; Such as teleporting to a new area in one frame because 'something' happened.
* The music in the game is very good. It really fits the style of the game and makes you feel like you are in an epic battle.
Overall this game is extremely fun, and I seriously recommend it to anyone who loves the Bullet Hell / Shoot 'Em Up genre. Plus the price is very resonable for the amount of detail and work that was put into this game.

Once upon a time games where challenging...
Once upon a time games required skill to complete...
Once upon a time you could feel proud of your accomplishments in games...
That time has long passed... we live in the era of copy/paste shooters, re-skinned sequels, DLC, the era of movies trying to be games. We don't care about new mechanics and originality, about the challenge of a brand new obstacle... we care about how many pixels does it have, how shinny is it and how many lady parts can be seen.
Isbarah stands proudly in defiance of this bitter-sad trend. Why you ask ? Let's get into it.
What we have here is a unique blend of platformer with bullet hell and a smudge of shoot 'em up. Every single level is a old-school style boss fight, these fights will test your reflexes, speed, coordination and problem solving skills. You do not have checkpoints, what you do have is the right to mess-up once, once that "continue" is used you better not fail or you will have to start the level from scratch! The game does not forgive you and it does not hold your hand. You get all the info you need on how to play the game at the first level and from there on outward you are on your own!
Feel free to select what difficulty you feel good with but my suggestion would be to start on normal until you get a feel for the game, after that push yourself and see what you can achieve!
Graphics ? The game just screams old school but with the advantages of modern technology. Sure... it is not everybody's cup of tea, for me they are a pleasant reminder of how games used to be. Overall the art style is just amazing but then again art is a subjective matter, so take a look at the screenshots and decide if you like what you see.
Sound ? Strong rhythms that flow perfectly with the pace of the game, it does not break the feeling and it does not stab you in the face screaming "HEY LISTEN TO ME!!!". It blends perfectly into the overall feeling and it keeps your heart pumping.
Now, i know a lot of you might be thinking "why no controller support?" well... there is a good reason for that. The way the mechanics are thought-out it would be impossible to do such precise and quick movements with a analog stick, thus enters a superior input device to do the job, the mouse! The mouse is used to trace platforms/barriers and to dash. Depending on the situation these must be done very quickly and at very precise angles and lengths.
I can go on and on about Isbarah and why it represents the true spirit of gaming, but i rambled on enough.
If you consider yourself a real gamer then you must face Isbarah and conquer it! Don't want a challenge ? Just want a leisure pace platformer you can unwind to and relax ? You are not going to find it here.
From me this is a wholehearted recommendation!

Black Ops II is an amazing game, so I will break apart what makes this game good and bad.
Campaign- The campaign is scattered and truly awful. There are multiple outcomes that are very interesting and makes replaying the game enticing though it is not worth it, since the endings are just a few minutes and are different in variety. The campaign adds onto the original black ops I campaign by taking place in the future and you walk in Mason's sons perspective, though it did not do the original story justice and felt boring and not creative by any means. Also there are hidden political agendas in the role which should have no place in a campaign based game. The only thing about the campaign that is exciting are the voice actors, environment, and weapons. 1/5 stars
Multiplayer: multiplayer is fantastic, but some added maps are poor and just remastered versions of previous maps which were not favorites, but were said to be so. Guns are great, but are forgetful since they are from a different era that is not yet come, and scorestreaks are amazing, but overpowered in some respect. Great multiplayer and very enjoyable! 3.5/5 stars
Zombies: Story kicks off with a new perspective as you fight in the shoes of a new group. Story is interesting and the maps are more light hearted and less greyscale in nature which takes away from that iconic zombie feeling. Maps in the map packs were fantastic, but transit was truly awful to play. Map felt unfinished, rushed, and virtually unplayable at times. If zombies is to continue, maps need to be centered around the basics- grey scale tones, sounds native to area which bring fear, horrific zombies with more apparant groaning, more maps at night versus day time, and finally a map which is centered around WW2 premise versus the new maps which are more futuristic and less likely to be accurate. They need to take on futuristic ideas, but add WW2 tones to the maps, weapons, and areas. Also new maps, such as BO2 and BO3 need to have weapons on walls native to that timeline, instead of futuristic weapons not native. 2.5/5 stars

Pros:
+ A return to the "good ol' days" of Hitman, trying its best to take lessons from Blood Money yet keep up with the features Absolution brought forth. Gameplay is far more balanced around doing things professionally, and going around killing indescriminately, while possible, is far more difficult.
+ Visually impressive, with a majority of the levels open enough to really explore different options. Not linear in pathing as Absolution was.
+ Elusive Targets, escalations, an expansive point system with unlockables, and custom contracts ensure that you'll be spending quite a bit of your time in the game, potentially expanding your playtime far beyond the first run.
+ Game has a solid story that is interesting, but is not particularly detailed yet outside of cutscenes.
+ Season system allows Hitman to be supported for many years using the same system, with levels being added as they are completed.
+ Took out the obnoxious in-game pointing system that Absolution introduced, kept instinct mode but made it far less powerful.
Cons:
- Massive crashing problems at first that inexplicably fixed themselves, and I'm lucky to have that happen. Optimization is a huge problem for the game at this time that needs to be worked on.
- Always-Online 'DRM' that feels largely unnecessary and invasive in a singleplayer game, not to mention a simple wifi disconnection can cut you off from your online playthrough.
- There are a lot of weapons that you really don't get a serious chance to use with how quickly Agent 47 dies. This is great for the normal gameplay, but it feels even more harsh than Blood Money. It would be interesting to play an alternate difficulty mode or gameplay mode where I can test out all of these weapons.
- That being said, the overall stealth portion and saving system can feel very easy compared to how harsh the systems were in the past (limited saving, not knowing immediately who could see through your disguise (or everyone could see through it)). Some of the UI is toggleable, but not all of it. A more crushing difficulty option might satisfy people who want a harder challenge.
Overall:

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often times made the review too long to submit, I've decided to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: As far as the controls go, Super Meat Boy is as simple as it gets. You've got four buttons in total: move left and right, jump, and run. From that, the handling mechanics of Meat Boy become increasingly deeper and deeper, all without telling you explicitly what it is that you should do. In fact, the level design does an excellent job overall of teaching you how to do these sometimes incredibly tricky manoeuvres without saying a single word. The idea with the levels in Super Meat Boy is that they rarely exceed 20-30 seconds in length, and in keeping such a length, the levels are allowed to tax your platforming abilities to their fullest. Another result of the short level design ethos is that you can make A LOT of levels. This game certainly has a lot of levels; 310 to be precise. Overall, I'd say about 90% of these levels are very good (and I am including Cotton Alley in this count). The other 10% is comprised of either really boring and uninteresting levels to levels that are honestly pretty terribly designed. These tend to come around more in the end of the game, specifically in the Rapture and Cotton Alley (which is optional, so meh), but the other 90% more than make up for the occasional stumble.
This game does have boss fights, although calling most of these fights is a bit of a misnomer. I'd say there's really only one actual fight in the game (Larries Lament) and it ends up being the worst of the bunch, so it's not all that bad. Otherwise, the stages are usually some form of autoscroller usually containing an environmental pressure from the boss itself. I would've liked to have seen Dark World variants of the bosses in which the stages become much more difficult, but it's hard to really complain about that when there's so many levels in the game. Hidden in three of the light world stages and one of the dark world stages in each area are warp zones, which either take you to an 8-Bit, 4-Bit or Gameboy graphical style level or a warp zone that allows you to unlock characters. These characters are, for the most part, not too useful. Pretty much the most useful character apart from Meat Boy that you can unlock is the one in World 3. There is a better character than this in World 5, but by that point, it's too little too late.
You also unlock characters by obtaining bandages throughout the game. There's 20 in each of the five major worlds, and they're usually a pretty challenging task to get. Some of the placement of the bandages isn't the greatest, and in fact one particularly notorious one requires you to play through a Warp Zone stage twice in order to get. One of the things that I found kinda disappointing is that you can't get every bandage as Meat Boy. Considering that a selling point of this game is that you can beat every level as every character, that feels a bit cheap. Apart from that, they're completely optional and not necessary to complete the game.
As for the other warp zones, they're done in a  "retro" style, meaning that you've got three lives to clear each of the three levels in that warp zone (every warp zone has three levels, save for the Glitch level), and the live counter resets after you beat a level. Get a game over, and you've gotta replay all of the stages. You get infinite lives for the character warp, though. The introduction of lives can make for some very frustrating sections of the game in which you pretty much have to be a masochist in order to enjoy playing these levels. To be honest, it just seems like a waste of time to have to restart the levels each and every time you game over.
Overall, though, I had a lot of fun with the game. Sure, some of the levels here and there were honestly pretty bad, but for the most part, Edmund and Tommy did a fantastic job with this game. This is actually my third time playing through the game; once when I borrowed the boxed copy from a friend, once on the 360, and this time. It's still enjoyable, even though the game's only been out for four or so years. 10/10.
Story: You can pretty much sum it up in a paragraph. The game makes a point to not really care about the story, so why should I?
Graphics: After playing Isaac so much and seeing this game on a relatively big monitor as opposed to my tiny TV I used to play the game on the 360, I can see why Edmund wasn't too happy with Isaac's style. This game certainly does look a whole lot better than Isaac. One of the things that some people have issues with in this game is lag, which can make you teleport through walls and ruin playthroughs. With my i5-3470, I never once had a lag spike, so your mileage may vary. Anyways, as for the art style, all of the levels and worlds look great. The levels have a great deal of detail that you can sometimes appreciate whenever you're not trying to barrel through the stages in the journey for an A+ time. If you're into that kind of thing, you can spend a good while appreciating the architecture of the levels. 5/5.
Sound: Pretty much just music to talk about here. Again, much like the levels, there's about 90% really good music and 10% music I wasn't too hot on. The main culprits of me turning off the game sound and opting for external music was the chiptune remixes of the songs. I dunno; I don't usually mind chiptunes, but they just ended up making me want the songs they're based on with their glorious, glorious layering. Since you don't run into those songs too often, it'd be silly of me to dock a full point, especially when the rest of the soundtrack is so good. What I will do, though, is dock half a point. 4.5/5.
Overall scores are: 10/0/5/4.5; cumulative score of 9.8/10. Definitely worth your purchase at $15 and ESPECIALLY worth the purchase at the $2.50 or so it goes on sale for (which it goes on sale quite often).

Black Ops II is an amazing game, so I will break apart what makes this game good and bad.
Campaign- The campaign is scattered and truly awful. There are multiple outcomes that are very interesting and makes replaying the game enticing though it is not worth it, since the endings are just a few minutes and are different in variety. The campaign adds onto the original black ops I campaign by taking place in the future and you walk in Mason's sons perspective, though it did not do the original story justice and felt boring and not creative by any means. Also there are hidden political agendas in the role which should have no place in a campaign based game. The only thing about the campaign that is exciting are the voice actors, environment, and weapons. 1/5 stars
Multiplayer: multiplayer is fantastic, but some added maps are poor and just remastered versions of previous maps which were not favorites, but were said to be so. Guns are great, but are forgetful since they are from a different era that is not yet come, and scorestreaks are amazing, but overpowered in some respect. Great multiplayer and very enjoyable! 3.5/5 stars
Zombies: Story kicks off with a new perspective as you fight in the shoes of a new group. Story is interesting and the maps are more light hearted and less greyscale in nature which takes away from that iconic zombie feeling. Maps in the map packs were fantastic, but transit was truly awful to play. Map felt unfinished, rushed, and virtually unplayable at times. If zombies is to continue, maps need to be centered around the basics- grey scale tones, sounds native to area which bring fear, horrific zombies with more apparant groaning, more maps at night versus day time, and finally a map which is centered around WW2 premise versus the new maps which are more futuristic and less likely to be accurate. They need to take on futuristic ideas, but add WW2 tones to the maps, weapons, and areas. Also new maps, such as BO2 and BO3 need to have weapons on walls native to that timeline, instead of futuristic weapons not native. 2.5/5 stars
