A game with much controversy surrounding its release due to both the stylistic change and the developer's confrontational and punk-like attitude.
The result, while not being the pinnacle of hack and slash/spectacle fighters that one of its predecessors was (DMC3), still comes off as very enjoyable and even addictive at times.
Starting with the bad, the fighitng system has been simplified from past releases. Gone are the variety of styles and in their place two new types of weapons are available by holding down each of the triggers. Each weapon type has in turn two sub weapons that behave differently.
This doesn't mean that this is a Fisher-Price, nursing school fighter. The game still requires skillful and deliberate actions in order to be able to deliver a standing ovation worthy, class A demon spanking. It's just that, in what i guess was, an attempt to trim some of the franchise's fat the devs cut off some of the meat as well and this in turn hurt both the gameplay factor and the overall longevity of the title.
Another drawback is that there is no visual indicator for the targeting system so focusing on different opponents and prioritizing your targets feels more clunky.
Finally the point system feels off as it awards more points the more enemies you hit in one blow or the more hits you deliver in a short ammount of time rather than handsomely rewarding precise actions like countering hits.  This in turn makes combat feel more spammy and offense-based rather than the "taunting", bursty type of combat in previous DMCs.
From the above you'd guess that i don't like DmC?
Well you couldn't be more wrong.
First of all the level design in this and level variety in particular is one of the best of the series so far, with levels like Lilith's Club, and the News Network stealing the show.
I really liked the punk/pop/street culture based style of the visuals as well.
The fighting while simplified as mentioned above is still very satisfying and fun to play and the angel/demon based mechanics, aside from a cool nod to Dante's duality as a character, are well implemented allowing you to pull off every move imaginable on the fly.
Opting for including platforming rather than puzzles that slow down the pacing was a solid decision on the dev's part imo. It just keeps the game flowing better.
The game's story bears strong similarities to J.Carpenter's "They Live". Personally i found it enjoyable yet nothing groundbreaking given that it's a concept that i was already familiar with through said film.
Character performances are solid as well with Mundus's standing out for me.
The only sour note in that department was that Dante's one liners come off as forced and "wooden" at times.
I also liked the soundtrack as well but i realize that given the niche of the genre (Electro/Industrial) it won't be for everybody.
On the technical side of things QLOC have done a terrific job making this game look spectacular while mainting very high fps and motion fluidity on max settings, resulting in this being one of the best uses of UE3 to date imo.
Overall, a very fun to play H&S title, excellent for newcomers to the genre as well as those that want to rekindle their interest in spectacle fighters.
Recommended.

In reviewing this game, there are a few primary things to consider.
The first being that this game is free. That certainly does not imply that one loses all entitlement to negative opinions when criticising such a game, but it does suggest that in courtesy, reviews should be considered upon fair standards.
The second being that the game was developed by a smaller studio, the members of which consist of people whose first language is presumably not English.
The third consideration is simply that the game itself was by design intended to be a short experience.
Moving on.
Suffice it to say, that in terms of graphical quality, the game put my gpu under considerable strain, as I was playing it on a budget laptop of a $400 price point with specs reflecting slightly dated hardware. Nevertheless, I found my computer up to the task of playing the game with smooth frame rate on medium settings in spite of running an AMD R5 series graphics chip. Techincal business aside, the imagery was certainly NOT cutting edge, but more than adequate in providing a convincing horror simulation. Trees looked and behaved like trees, the moon held a glossy white glow high above the clouds, which were also nicely detailed. However, it would require no keen eye to spot repeated objects, and template building design, which regrettably showed little variety. Though the horror experience was admittedly engulfing, the scenery did quickly become dull.
The truest highlight of this game was its use of 'negative space'. I mean this figuratively to represent an overwhelming and paranoia inducing ambience which was created by the game's expert use of high quality audio. The music, which behaved in very misleading manner, served as a jarring magician, conjuring up imaginary fears to play with your mind. What it demonstrated was the underrated element of horror which is as people say "less is more".
Regrettably, in the shortness of this game, its greatest quality was simply a kife sharp ability to create suspense and a feeling of unrelenting dread. Though this is a wonderful quality, and meritable enough to recommend this game, I will express a small disappointment in the nature of its ending, which left something to be desired.

Hmmm...this is a very curious item indeed. Having just recently bought and played Pineview Drive, and seeing that this is both free and standalone, I can only surmise that this is meant to be a "teaser" of sorts to help sell the main game.
The question, then, is does it do a good job of this? Again...hmmm.
I had slightly mixed, but mostly rather positive, feelings towards Pineview Drive, and I will say that one thing which both this "demo" and the main game itself have in common is a need for PATIENCE.  Having said that, the patience required by the main game was that of the long distance runner, while this one...is more like a short sprint in which you HAVE TO MOVE REALLY SLOWLY AND STOP FREQUENTLY OR YOU WILL DIE.
That's pretty much what this is, in a nutshell, and in that regard it really only represents the gameplay of the final (read: THIRTIETH!) "day"/chapter of Pineview Drive...'cause prior to that, you're really not in that much danger and would take perhaps HUNDREDS OF HOURS to complete the ♥♥♥♥ing thing if you moved as slowly as you're required to here.
So is it an accurate "preview" of what you'll get if you purchase the parent game?  Hmmm...not really.  Apart from possessing a similar atmosphere - something which both "games" positively drip with - we're really only talking a companion piece which, well, hopefully "compliments" the main product, while not really giving a terribly accurate indication of what to expect from it.

But was this even the intention of the developers in producing this mini-game? Buggered if I know, considering that it has a substantially different title, and no link to it on Parkview Drive's store page. It certainly stands well enough on its own, though it does unfortunately feed one of my pet hates, which is games where you can play for twenty solid minutes, die, then have to start from the beginning again 'cause they're AIN'T NO FRIGGIN' SAVE POINTS.
I know this was intentional on the designers' behalves, but I really do seem to lack the patience and/or stubbornness to endure this kind of treatment from a mere video game. I mean, come on, these things are supposed to be FUN!  Amnesia: The Dark Descent pulled similar♥♥♥♥♥♥on me with its "Justine" side-game, and I threw the towel in on THAT one, too.  And since I've already given nearly ten hours of my life to playing Pineview Drive Senior, I'm not sure I feel the need to humour this one any more for now. Oh well.
But given that this is FREE, and probably less than thirty minutes long if you manage to get through it the first time, why not give it a go anyway? It's spooky, atmospheric as hell, and genuinely tense (if only because you don't want to have to repeat the first twenty minutes all over again if you die two minutes from the end). In other words, it's all the things a good horror game probably "should" be. In theory, anyway.
I seriously look forward to what these devs can achieve in the future, once they're done with dangling all those yummy carrots in our faces for minutes on end before finally giving us a taste.

Hitman is an easy contender for one of the games of 2016, and an example of how to do episodic gaming correctly. There may have been the odd technical hiccup along the way, but the end result is excellent.

HITMAN is a fantastic addition to the series, going back to its roots while obtaining some features from HITMAN: Absolution. Each level has its own unique and diverse way to tackle them and the unlocks just adds more ways to assassinate your targets.
While the DRM may be a turn off for most people. For PC, this is only for challenges and leaderboards. In mission, it will not prevent you from playing the base game. On top of that, the servers seem to be reliable unless your connection is not.
Below, you'll find what i personally think are the biggest pros and cons to the game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Fantastic visuals
- Diverse and multiple ways to assassinate targets
- Neat unlocks after completing challenges
- Simple controls, allowing even the most casual player to handle it well
- NPCs spot you and become suspicious easily, adding more difficulty
- Unique levels, never assassinating the same target in the same way as the last
- Interesting dialogue between NPC characters
- Hundreds of different challenges per level
- On top of challenges, escalations and elusive targets adds more play time
- Longevity
- Great score
- Fantastic sound design
- Frequently updated
- DRM can cause problems if you wish to complete challenges, meaning if the severs go down or if your connection drops, you cannot complete them
- Many gameplay elements from previous games seem to be missing, such as keyholes, breifcase etc.
- Poor optimisation, even on high end systems such as mine, playing on high or max means you will experience often drops
- Overall price is not currently worth it, as a season 2 is on its way. may be worth buying from a different cheaper site, or waiting for sales
- AI can be a bit dumb sometimes, but often than not can be very unforgiving, accusing you for being suspicious for absolutely no reason
Overall, the game is amazing. You can go ahead and ignore the previous reviews about the DRM, as you can play the game without it. And if you have a decent connection that doesnt drop all the time, you shouldn't have any worries about it dropping off every two seconds.

So, this review starts as most reviews do... with a Steam Sale.
Being a Hitman fan myself I tried to avoid this game for quite a while, given the reviews it has.
However Sales got the best of me and I ended up buying the whole First Season, and I do not regret it.
The way this game works is that you have the Story Missions, and what I'll call the "Free Missions".
What most reviewers so innocently leave out is that the Story Missions can be saved, you can disconnect or whatever and continue where you left them, this alone is a game changer for me.
It's the "Free Missions", custom created by users or special events made by SE, such as the Christmas one, that you can't save and pretty much have to complete in one go.
A theme that stands regardless of the mode you tackle is a usual for Hitman games, theres a ton of ways to tackle a target, some are suggested on the "opportunity" system, which is updated by conversations you overhear, things you read and so on, others less "cinematic", you improvise, same you always have.
The Story is obviously short, its Season 1, but for what it is, damn good, we start getting a LITTLE background on Agent 47, character interaction is good and overall I enjoy it.
The Free Missions, all I have to say is that they give replay value, because you can play new missions on the maps, and since the sandboxes are HUGE, you do get to discover a lot of stuff that you didn't see on the Story.
And most importantly, the overall tone of the game is as good as any before it, you find weird crap going on in the world, you can find awesome costumes to blend yourself with, all that good stuff.
On that topic there is this mission where I was going about random places, I forced open a door and found an explosive golf ball on a mundane "lab" in the kitchen, right above the oven, with all the lab tubes and all, and yes, it explodes when you throw it.
I also found a Plague Doctor costume, completely useless to blend anywhere other than on that specific room, but awesome nontheless.
TL;DR If you are a Hitman fan get it, but only during a sale, the thing is not worth $60 yet, even if it is as good as Hitman has always been, replay value is very high, especially if you have played old hitman missions enough that you want to master new maps.

This is an excellent RPG which incidentally is also the prequel to Whisper of the Rose. I have played both these games to completion and had a very enjoyable time.
I enjoy the combat mechanics, especially the point-base system. You have to hunt for points (which appear as gold coins) which motivate you to explore every small little corner of the game map. There is also an achievement for getting all the points. Furthermore, the points can be used to buy furniture which you can display in your house and they will give you combat bonuses. Furthermore points can also be use to buy dresses (armor) and weapons for Lily too.
Monsters will drop crafting materials when they are vanquished, and these crafting materials can be used for making Spells, Potions and Furnitures.  I love this system.
Scattered on the ground are small green circles which will heal you when you step on them. However, there is a difficult achievement which will only trigger if you activate less than 20 healing circles in the entire game. So, this turn the game mechanics in a whole new direction --- as you are now trying to AVOID stepping on healing circles whenever you do exploration. However, this is not always possible, as some healing circles are on critical paths and there is no way to get through a dungeon without stepping on certain healing circles.
The story itself is well thought out. The starting scene is misleadingly simple and looks like an RPG for kids. However, this is not the case as there are a lot of depth and the story gets darker as you proceed. However, I love the major themes of the RPG which is actually love, mutual caring and cooperation. I get a warm feeling at the end of the story, which is excellent.
I would strongly recommend this game to any old school RPG gamers out there who like a good story with interesting game mechanics.

This game is a lot of fun. If you like Grand Theft Auto but want a straight PvP experience, this is for you. There are NPCs who give you missions, but the missions are all PvP. It's still fun to play alone when I have some time to kill, but it's a far better experience if you can partner up with at least one other person to help coordinate against your opposition.
A wide variety of mission objectives keeps things very interesting. It's rarely a situation of "kill all the cops before they kill you." Jacking cars, tagging walls, hacking satellite dishes, stealing people's organs for sale on the black market, bounties on high threat players, bombing buildings, mugging people, stealing and destroying evidence before it can get into a court, street racing, raiding electronics and jewelry stores, fencing the stolen goods, laundering money...it's crazy how much trouble you can cause!
Customization is awesome. You can apply custom graphics all over your car, your clothes, your body. People who don't like the in-game clothing options will often tattoo their own clothing designs right onto their characters' bodies. It makes for a really deep customization experience, and you'll regularly be turning your head to get a closer look at what cool customization someone else has come up with. It is amazing.
I have one complaint. This game is most definitely "pay-to-win." $40 of G1C (cash shop currency) gets you an amazing gun with amazing mods that eats through all other players easily. So if you usually spend $40 on a game you'll play for a couple hundred hours, go for that since you otherwise don't need to spend any money to play this game. People who spend money will often beat you no matter how skilled you become.
The cash shop has cheaper pay-to-win guns, but they expire after X number of days. The guns you buy with in-game money all expire after 10 days. Fortunately there's not much else to do with all the in-game money you accumulate so it doesn't really hurt.
Tons of guns, tons of funs.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often times made the review too long to submit, I've decided to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: As far as the controls go, Super Meat Boy is as simple as it gets. You've got four buttons in total: move left and right, jump, and run. From that, the handling mechanics of Meat Boy become increasingly deeper and deeper, all without telling you explicitly what it is that you should do. In fact, the level design does an excellent job overall of teaching you how to do these sometimes incredibly tricky manoeuvres without saying a single word. The idea with the levels in Super Meat Boy is that they rarely exceed 20-30 seconds in length, and in keeping such a length, the levels are allowed to tax your platforming abilities to their fullest. Another result of the short level design ethos is that you can make A LOT of levels. This game certainly has a lot of levels; 310 to be precise. Overall, I'd say about 90% of these levels are very good (and I am including Cotton Alley in this count). The other 10% is comprised of either really boring and uninteresting levels to levels that are honestly pretty terribly designed. These tend to come around more in the end of the game, specifically in the Rapture and Cotton Alley (which is optional, so meh), but the other 90% more than make up for the occasional stumble.
This game does have boss fights, although calling most of these fights is a bit of a misnomer. I'd say there's really only one actual fight in the game (Larries Lament) and it ends up being the worst of the bunch, so it's not all that bad. Otherwise, the stages are usually some form of autoscroller usually containing an environmental pressure from the boss itself. I would've liked to have seen Dark World variants of the bosses in which the stages become much more difficult, but it's hard to really complain about that when there's so many levels in the game. Hidden in three of the light world stages and one of the dark world stages in each area are warp zones, which either take you to an 8-Bit, 4-Bit or Gameboy graphical style level or a warp zone that allows you to unlock characters. These characters are, for the most part, not too useful. Pretty much the most useful character apart from Meat Boy that you can unlock is the one in World 3. There is a better character than this in World 5, but by that point, it's too little too late.
You also unlock characters by obtaining bandages throughout the game. There's 20 in each of the five major worlds, and they're usually a pretty challenging task to get. Some of the placement of the bandages isn't the greatest, and in fact one particularly notorious one requires you to play through a Warp Zone stage twice in order to get. One of the things that I found kinda disappointing is that you can't get every bandage as Meat Boy. Considering that a selling point of this game is that you can beat every level as every character, that feels a bit cheap. Apart from that, they're completely optional and not necessary to complete the game.
As for the other warp zones, they're done in a  "retro" style, meaning that you've got three lives to clear each of the three levels in that warp zone (every warp zone has three levels, save for the Glitch level), and the live counter resets after you beat a level. Get a game over, and you've gotta replay all of the stages. You get infinite lives for the character warp, though. The introduction of lives can make for some very frustrating sections of the game in which you pretty much have to be a masochist in order to enjoy playing these levels. To be honest, it just seems like a waste of time to have to restart the levels each and every time you game over.
Overall, though, I had a lot of fun with the game. Sure, some of the levels here and there were honestly pretty bad, but for the most part, Edmund and Tommy did a fantastic job with this game. This is actually my third time playing through the game; once when I borrowed the boxed copy from a friend, once on the 360, and this time. It's still enjoyable, even though the game's only been out for four or so years. 10/10.
Story: You can pretty much sum it up in a paragraph. The game makes a point to not really care about the story, so why should I?
Graphics: After playing Isaac so much and seeing this game on a relatively big monitor as opposed to my tiny TV I used to play the game on the 360, I can see why Edmund wasn't too happy with Isaac's style. This game certainly does look a whole lot better than Isaac. One of the things that some people have issues with in this game is lag, which can make you teleport through walls and ruin playthroughs. With my i5-3470, I never once had a lag spike, so your mileage may vary. Anyways, as for the art style, all of the levels and worlds look great. The levels have a great deal of detail that you can sometimes appreciate whenever you're not trying to barrel through the stages in the journey for an A+ time. If you're into that kind of thing, you can spend a good while appreciating the architecture of the levels. 5/5.
Sound: Pretty much just music to talk about here. Again, much like the levels, there's about 90% really good music and 10% music I wasn't too hot on. The main culprits of me turning off the game sound and opting for external music was the chiptune remixes of the songs. I dunno; I don't usually mind chiptunes, but they just ended up making me want the songs they're based on with their glorious, glorious layering. Since you don't run into those songs too often, it'd be silly of me to dock a full point, especially when the rest of the soundtrack is so good. What I will do, though, is dock half a point. 4.5/5.
Overall scores are: 10/0/5/4.5; cumulative score of 9.8/10. Definitely worth your purchase at $15 and ESPECIALLY worth the purchase at the $2.50 or so it goes on sale for (which it goes on sale quite often).

Bought in a bundle, this is worth the buck or two spent especially if you have an older PC to play it on.  ETS1 was a great idea and has been improved with the release of ETS2.  Pros and cons of this game...
Pros: Graphics not bad for its day and you can play a short run in 10-15 mins.  While getting in accidents, speeding, and running red lights gets you penalized, you can also play the jerk driver cutting other drivers off and hogging two lanes (which is almost a necessity if driving via keyboard).  Hint for new players--get your hazardous cargo cert ASAP so you can make more money faster.
Cons: A careful study of the road map shows this game was unfinished.  Back roads all over Poland, a few in Germany, and none anywhere else.  When driving around, you see several overpasses that were likely intended to be used for backroads, but were left unconnected to anything.  There are also loads of no-go zones in the cities, where AI vehicles can drive, but you cannot.  Another minor complaint; the physics of the truck in a cloverleaf turn allow for too much drift and jackknifing the truck is easy to do, even at low speeds.  I have learned to go real slow through these.
I am looking forward to playing ETS2, but if you have an older PC and/or a light wallet, you should give this game a whirl.

That is all still true. But upon going back and replaying Origins, I found myself appreciating it and enjoying it a lot more. (Note that I have not played Arkham Knight, so this change of opinion is not inspired by any disappointment with that title).
So what changed? I love the “young, angry Bruce” angle of the story. Even if Roger Craig Smith tries too hard at times to sound like Christian Bale, fury and anger were never a more appropriate halo for the caped crusader. Given how violent this version of Batman is, it's easy to see why criminals fear him. Alfred is more than just a voice over the radio; I liked being able to traverse the Batcave (even if there isn't much to do there besides challenge maps).
But the features that most improved my opinion of Arkham Origins are the boss battles. Previously I knocked the story for having bosses turn up seemingly at random; that is still true. But I found myself loving the heck out of the bosses. Rather than just have Batman spam a single attack and spend the rest of the time dodging (like the bosses in Asylum and City), Origins really attempted to throw you into the middle of the action. Deathstroke, Bane (twice!), Shiva and Deadshot all stand out as unique encounters. Button-mash, and you'll die quickly. Counter, use gadgets and takedowns. The bosses elevate the game from a boring, marginally negative experience to a positive one (though the Riddler is frankly a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥.
The missions themselves don't feel particularly new, though the Predator encounters have some new features and layouts. Crime-solving is fun, if a little laborious. The setting has some great backdrops, and like Arkham City, snow blankets the landscape (though it is more copious here). If you have a beefy gaming rig, you can crank the settings for some great screenshots (though strangely, fire still looks low-res). Rather cool that many structures are “cleaned up” versions of Arkham City architecture; Wonder Tower, for instance, is here (though you can't go up to the top, only into the lobby), as are many other landmarks.
Still not on the same level as Arkham Asylum or Arkham City, and a middling recommendation overall. But those boss battles....
On bugs:
Aside from the gliding animation routinely messing up (making Batman flap his cape like wings, good for lols) and the occasional crash (try repairing the PhysX installation), Arkham Origins ran smoothly for me.
On DLC:
Cold Cold Heart is a great piece of DLC, containing an all-new campaign (that re-uses a part of the main campaign's map) that introduces some new mechanics, new gadgets, and another great boss battle. A great addition to Arkham Origins. Heartily recommended.
For the rest, it's skins, challenge maps, and “Online Supply Drops” for the (now-dead) multi-player. If skins and challenge maps are your thing, get the Season Pass (which includes Cold Cold Heart, skins, and challenge maps) and the Black Mask Challenge Pack (strangely not included in the Season Pass) and you'll have all the DLC worth owning.

Considering this is my first game in the DMC series, I guess I don't really have much to go by, but without a doubt, this was one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time.  Qualms about Dante's character aside (though I actually found Dante quite likeable as his character developed), the visual style and art direction are fantastic.  The world of Limbo crawls alive around Dante, often begging you to stop and look out into the distance.  Yet before you earn this respite to enjoy the view, you'll often find yourself engrossed in combat with the various monsters that'll be thrown at you.  By far the strongest and most important aspect of the game (besides the divvying up of angel and demon monsters), DMC's combat feels tight, fluid, and (though apparently simpler than previous games) feels very much streamlined.  Though there are no huge combo strings to learn (thank god) attacks flow seamlessly into each other, each weapon with its own rhythm and set of attacks.  DMC combat appears simple, but still feels incredibly satisfying when self-made combos can be pulled off.
Vergil's Downfall (which I also ended up buying after I beat the main game) is satisfying in its own right.  Though it lacks the fantastical environments of the main game, playing as Vergil and seeing an "end" to his story has its own unique yet highly enjoyable feel.
Recommended for those trigger happy fingers who are out chanking out combo on their controller.

I wasn't positive if this was non-beta game or not. That said, creative endeavours like this are always appreciated—it reminded me of simple, experiential games like "The Plan" or "The Stanley Parable", both of which I find incredibly charming.
This game is as deceptively simple as its title suggests. You literally pass through Pineview Forest, for a while, along a delineated path.  Having replayed it a couple of times now, there *is* room for variation—I've yet to work out exactly what kind of choices do what (do I walk? run? ignore sounds, or stop each time? is x or y sound on a timer or is it based on your location or a mix/variant of both? does acknowledging what you hear change anything? etc; each of these concerns seems to have some bearing on the outcome). So there is a suprising amount of depth and variability to such an unassumingly-simple game.
This game is played with your ears and only barely your hands & eyes. That said, it's telling that this game was designed with Oculus Rift in mind, as that would be a much more intense bodily experience—it's unfortunate that the vast majority of us may never get to experience the game that way, turning 180° in an instant to see who or what is "behind" us. I can only imagine it is doubly stressful and frightening.
There are some very minor quibbles though, and they are over the "gamiest" of issues—looping sounds, invisibly-obstructed travel zones (hopping over a flight of stairs nearly gave me a heart attack because of the noise that I was afraid I was about to make) and the like. Overall, this is a game that is a part of the vangaurd of the new direction that indie developers are helping to steer us toward, and it's nice to see that they are experimenting and playing with the possibilities of the core mechanics of games whilst doing so in such a ruthlessly simple yet effective manner.

- Should I buy this? (aka the Short Review)
This game is made in RPG maker, so you need to like that style of gameplay (Ib, Corpse Party, Mihao... without the horror), with final-fantasy-turn-based kind of battles. There are card drops, but to get all the achievements you need to complete the game twice. Playtime to complete the game once was 17 hours for me, which is very good. The story is well told and the mechanics are enjoyable. It's not a horror game, but it has 2 or 3 scary/dark moments.
You play as Lily, accompanied by a party of 3 as you travel to several dream worlds, each inspired by a different real life book. I loved the various references, such as the Kingdom Hearts intro, and the end lets open the possibilities for a sequel.
NOTE: I played this, abandoned it, and picked it up much later. I learned that the game gets MUCH more enjoable after the first world (aka once your party is formed and you start travelling trough dream worlds). Keep an open mind.
- The art is awesome. Not necessarily what you would expect from an AA game, but considering the RPG maker kit this is truly wonderful. The developer mentioned that they tried to stay away from the kit as much as they could, and it really shows. It's unique, nice to look at, and makes you see that they really put thought into it.
- The story is also really nice. At some point I started believing they were "telegraphing" the ending twist, but that did not happen (not that I would have minded). It does a good job of making you feel involved and care for the characters. After the end, a little scene shows a cliffhanger, but it doesn't ruin the story.
- Gameplay is fun. I usually dislike turn based battles, but in this game I had lots of fun all round. There is a little bit of crafting, and some customizing (Lily can wear one of four outfits), which I think are a nice touch. There are puzzles, so be prepared to scratch your head a bit!
This is why I took out 2 points for my review:
- You HAVE TO complete the game twice, to get all the achievements. This is a big no-no for me. I am NOT going to enjoy being forced through the entire game.
- Missable achievement: you need to collect all the game coins to get this one. There are one or two places that become unavailable as you go along, and again you will need to replay the entire game to achieve it.
Overall I RECOMMEND the game based on its great playability, nice story and pretty art style.
I would not recommend it to completionists, unless they are prepared to go trough it twice and consume a lot of time.

Hitman is an easy contender for one of the games of 2016, and an example of how to do episodic gaming correctly. There may have been the odd technical hiccup along the way, but the end result is excellent.

HITMAN is a fantastic addition to the series, going back to its roots while obtaining some features from HITMAN: Absolution. Each level has its own unique and diverse way to tackle them and the unlocks just adds more ways to assassinate your targets.
While the DRM may be a turn off for most people. For PC, this is only for challenges and leaderboards. In mission, it will not prevent you from playing the base game. On top of that, the servers seem to be reliable unless your connection is not.
Below, you'll find what i personally think are the biggest pros and cons to the game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Fantastic visuals
- Diverse and multiple ways to assassinate targets
- Neat unlocks after completing challenges
- Simple controls, allowing even the most casual player to handle it well
- NPCs spot you and become suspicious easily, adding more difficulty
- Unique levels, never assassinating the same target in the same way as the last
- Interesting dialogue between NPC characters
- Hundreds of different challenges per level
- On top of challenges, escalations and elusive targets adds more play time
- Longevity
- Great score
- Fantastic sound design
- Frequently updated
- DRM can cause problems if you wish to complete challenges, meaning if the severs go down or if your connection drops, you cannot complete them
- Many gameplay elements from previous games seem to be missing, such as keyholes, breifcase etc.
- Poor optimisation, even on high end systems such as mine, playing on high or max means you will experience often drops
- Overall price is not currently worth it, as a season 2 is on its way. may be worth buying from a different cheaper site, or waiting for sales
- AI can be a bit dumb sometimes, but often than not can be very unforgiving, accusing you for being suspicious for absolutely no reason
Overall, the game is amazing. You can go ahead and ignore the previous reviews about the DRM, as you can play the game without it. And if you have a decent connection that doesnt drop all the time, you shouldn't have any worries about it dropping off every two seconds.

So, this review starts as most reviews do... with a Steam Sale.
Being a Hitman fan myself I tried to avoid this game for quite a while, given the reviews it has.
However Sales got the best of me and I ended up buying the whole First Season, and I do not regret it.
The way this game works is that you have the Story Missions, and what I'll call the "Free Missions".
What most reviewers so innocently leave out is that the Story Missions can be saved, you can disconnect or whatever and continue where you left them, this alone is a game changer for me.
It's the "Free Missions", custom created by users or special events made by SE, such as the Christmas one, that you can't save and pretty much have to complete in one go.
A theme that stands regardless of the mode you tackle is a usual for Hitman games, theres a ton of ways to tackle a target, some are suggested on the "opportunity" system, which is updated by conversations you overhear, things you read and so on, others less "cinematic", you improvise, same you always have.
The Story is obviously short, its Season 1, but for what it is, damn good, we start getting a LITTLE background on Agent 47, character interaction is good and overall I enjoy it.
The Free Missions, all I have to say is that they give replay value, because you can play new missions on the maps, and since the sandboxes are HUGE, you do get to discover a lot of stuff that you didn't see on the Story.
And most importantly, the overall tone of the game is as good as any before it, you find weird crap going on in the world, you can find awesome costumes to blend yourself with, all that good stuff.
On that topic there is this mission where I was going about random places, I forced open a door and found an explosive golf ball on a mundane "lab" in the kitchen, right above the oven, with all the lab tubes and all, and yes, it explodes when you throw it.
I also found a Plague Doctor costume, completely useless to blend anywhere other than on that specific room, but awesome nontheless.
TL;DR If you are a Hitman fan get it, but only during a sale, the thing is not worth $60 yet, even if it is as good as Hitman has always been, replay value is very high, especially if you have played old hitman missions enough that you want to master new maps.

I'd use my starting character to tunnel out (staying in medium security while doing so), and using tougher prisoners to do all my dirty work, like bringing tunneling materials to my cell. However, I recruit someone with the surname "Redman". He's a skinny guy, red hair, bumped up to maximum security.
I then decided to try and use Redman to fight guards. At this point, Redman has been upgraded pretty highly. He can one-shot people, shrug off being tazed, and start riots. Redman breaks into the psychologist's office. He steals a lighter. Redman begins to burn the Common room to the ground. He kills every guard. The common room is burning to the ground, the fire has spread to other rooms. Half the prison is on fire, Redman has started a riot. Redman is unstoppable. Redman is carrying the team on his shoulders while Cliefe sits doing nothing in medium security. Redman has seen hell, and he doesn't want to stay. Redman stands while the prison burns to the ground - he's burning to death. But if he dies, he dies a maytr, a figurehead of a greater cause that is escaping prison. He sprints. The walls have burnt down. Redman is an unstoppable wild beast. The snipers have their sights trained on him, but Redman is too fast - he escapes. The prison that I worked hard on, spent hours on, poured huge amounts of effort into running has been totally destroyed, alongside nearly all the guards, prisoners, and staff that worked there.

This game is an absolute wonder and I am honored to be able to play it. It's like an interactive work of art that perfectly melds an AMAZING soundtrack with beautiful visuals, intuitive and responsive controls, and an increasingly challenging experience that pushes your capabilities.

It always sounds good, it never falters or seems misplaced, and the transitions from song to song in-game are flawless. I downloaded a bundle of Braid, Fez, and of course Super Meat Boy after watching Indie Game the movie.  I was really inspired by the movie.  My favorite part was when Team Meat guy said he made more money in just one day than he had during his past 6 years!
Anywho, back to the game, Super Meat Boy is a hardcore over the top platformer.  Let me tell you, you will die a lot.  I mean A LOT.  However this game is what I call "Addictively Difficult" that you come for more everytime you die.  Kinda similar to Flappy Bird in that way.  The reason why you come back for more after dying dozens of times is probably because you can feel that you get better (worse in some cases though) every time you try, and the sattisfaction you get after clearing a stage is priceless.  There were times I got really frustrated because I died by falling into a pool of blood.  Why do you die by falling into a pool of blood?  Anyhow other than that, the game's great.  I would recommend to anyone who's looking for a good platformer.
Oh last thing, I don't think this game's for anyone who has anger issue or has no patience.  It will only make your blood pressure soar.  Cheers!

The writing and references in Borderlands 2 are awful and takes priority over creating an enjoyable apocalyptic world with a large variety of weapons. The loot system can make or break your experience with this game, and chances are you will be on the receiving end of the unfair random number generator. Borderlands 2's practice of releasing downloading content and the way they handled the season pass is also unacceptable while Gearbox's actions since 2012 have only escalated. I cannot recommend this game, or its prequel, at least TellTale's adventure game does this series a service.

Borderlands 2 is not everyone's cup of tea, but it's definitley mine. The story is engaging and hilarious, managing to establish meaningful and emotional characters who are also immensely funny. The story itself is interesting and of the perfect length, making multiple playthroughs with the four diverse classes satisfying. The RPG elements and gunplay blend flawlessly, with interesting active abilities based on what class you're playing. But the real stars of the show are the guns: burst fire snipers that spit electricity, SMG's that explode when reloaded, and heat seeking cluster grenades are just a few of the thousands of insane, hilarious, and downright fun weapons available to all classes. And the desire to loot more powerful ones is insatiable! Side-quests and customization are very fun, and the level cap is well-thought out. The base game itself is very fun, but in my opinion the DLC is a necessity to get the most time and enjoyment from the game. I bought the DLC bundle on sale, and it was the best steam purchase I have ever made. The first and last DLC are simply aamazing, but the middle two are short and  just adequate. However, multiplayer makes this game even better and more long lasting. In conclusion, the hilarious fun of borderlands 2's RPG FPS crossover is perfect for those seeking a less competitive, more gameplay and comedy-oriented shooter. It's a welcome break from Battlefield, CoD, and Halo, yet can suck up just as many hours with it's funny and engaging gameplay and story.

Very fun:
There aren't too many fighting games left that allow you freedom of movement that extends beyond Left and Right (that I've seen, at least). Once you start whaling on someone, it's very much like DBZ... with better sound effects.
Despite that, it's more like Onimusha with your fists; without all the *expletive* that comes with a terrible port (though the Options menu is severely lacking by PC standards).
The story isn't to do with daemons, though; you are General Loh. You have been tasked with requisitioning a Dojo for your battle against The Rebels.
Though a master of Kung Fu, Loh is dismissive of the tenets pertaining to; at least the potential for slight chuckles.
Loh is nowhere near as (readily) nimble as Onimusha; no doubt, with practice, Loh can float and glide around the arenas just as well as Oni', but the default dodge is a pitiful roll (invest in Air Dodge ASAP).
Terrible camera:
At times - if the fight is in a corner, but spills momentarily out of it - the camera tries to adjust accordingly, making for a nauseating in-out-in-out or disorient(at)ing revolutions.
I got through Chapter 1 - final fight is on a roof against Swordsman; he is prone to jump so that half his body is cut off  the top of the screen. That, actually, might be because of the resolution that the game has been forced into(?) (didn't see an option for it) or maybe even just the bosses' health bars.
I'm now fighting the Master of the Dojo, though, and the camera is still... wonky.
This causes one to be prone to not connect because of perspective.
Again, I can only emphasize Air Dodge. It's the most effective tactic I've found thus far (...and, in my opinion - still learning the ropes - that's not saying much).
I don't understand blocking:
Loh moves in a way that throws me off - game prompts "Tap B [at the correct time]," but, with that motion, I don't know when's the time.
Haven't found a Practice mode and it seems that every enemy, with their unique attacks, requires a different approach to it.
Seems like it's necessary to allow for a split-second before the enemy actually attacks; he moves his hands in a sweeping manner. It isn't a standard block - it leads me to believe it's as if he catches the enemies' attacks... gotta give it more time.
Nothing but arena after arena; not even a linear path to run down
(yet, at least - there are checkpoints apparently).
Contrary to how it may look, the game is not (necessarily) a button-masher. Neutralize the enemies when you have the chance, but always be on your toes.
The two worst things in the game: Camera -- Combat seems unbalanced.
This next bit may be attributed to my inability to "git gud":
Enemies are able to damn-near spam their Heavy Attacks, whereas you must wait considerably longer for your Chi to charge. They can interrupt your attacks with blocks or attacks of their own; I think the rule is "If their feet are firmly planted, beware."
'S'far's I know, you can't cancel any of your actions.
Air Dodge. It's not necessarily a button-masher.
The graphics are stylized, to the point I'm not sure when they'll be considered outdated. The one exception is Master Mo... his head... looks like he belongs in a budget PS2 game, while the rest of the models look (almost(?)) cell-shaded.
"Cutscenes" are presented in series of four illustrations with subtitles, a la comic book.
There is a shop to buy new Attacks and (")Equipment(") and also a "My Army"; certain enemies will drop scrolls that you can use to call Allies (provided you pay for them too).
That Equipment and your Allies must be bought before you enter the level; they are one-use items.
I recommend this game, for all the frustration it may cause.
It satisfies the need I have had since I found a copy of Fighting Force a few years back (and subsequently cried into my pillow for the loss of the glory days). Though I do believe that Onimusha is the closest comparison I can make, I treat it as a fast-paced Fighting Force; that camera, the inability to cancel actions, etc.
For the rest of y'all, the more appropriate comparison to Onimusha should be enough to convince.

From my point of view game has not been balanced very well and in some stages (or some bonus challenges) it leads to the frustrating sensation that you have to repeat the same stage several times, before winning for pure luck or because AI says so.
This is the biggest flaw for which I don't feel to recommend this game and it's a pity because it is great for everything else:
- game is very enjoyable to play before enemies become overpowered
- graphic is beautiful, coloured and clean
- there are different levels to play, each with its own style
- local co-op

- xbox controller is supported

Very good game, but very hard on normal or hard mode.
Pros
-2 player Co-Op if you have a friend or a brother.
-Perfect defense system that encourage you to stay on your toes at all time.
-Perfect offensive  system that encourage you to hit the weakpoint of your enemies with 2 different buttons on 2
different occasion. Or, as your enemy turns red to use a strong attack, you can counter-attack with one of your abilties to deal massive damage with a cool sound effect along with that.
-Very fast paced game
-Very good progression system: You must pay to increase your health and your gauge, you must unlock new abilities and combos, you must find new allies to use as decoys to complete your objectives.
-The AI is impressive. They all attack you at once, often and fast, but because the defense system is perfect, that's not really a problem. You can still defend yourself perfectly agaisnt all of them.
-The game is challenging and fun overall.
-There's multiple fun extra stages.
-You can go back every on stages to grind for more money to use to unlock your skills.
-Very good replayability. I'm having fun fighting the same bosses or redoing the same stages that i already did over and over again.
Cons:
-Bad camera angle: sometime, the camera can be too far away or it can will go wild on you as something else or an event appear. That will mess you up. Other times, the camera will be set in an angle that will completely foreshadow your character so you cannot see since the objects that covers your character completely will not become transparent like in most games.
-There's a very hard part in the game where your character become poisoned for a couple of stages. It's doable, but frustrating. You will need to perfectly plan your strategy to complete these few stages.
-Very luck based game on drop rates. Sometime, enemies and the objects you break will drop food for health, other time, they don't at all and the lack of food can be the reason you lose.
-Decoy cost money and you need money to unlock new move sets. Because of that, if you keep on losing, you eventually end up losing more money if you keep using decoys.
-The last boss of the game with no DLC is way way way too hard on normal or hard mode.
-At the end, you have to grind to unlock everything to stand a chance agaisnt the last boss(That is optional, but recommanded).

Prison Archietct is a fantastic in-depth management game that had me hooked for hours the day I got it.
In this game, your aim is to build and manage a prison. You must take into account costs, resources, and most importantly, your prisoners, who can range from peaceful and law-abiding to fearless and aggressive.
Though it is fun to torture your prisoner in a cruel institute of hell, it's important to pacify your prisoners' need s for food, family, education and more- otherwise, they riot and unleash chaos in your prison. The action can be fast-paced- prisoners can tunnel out of your prison, forcing you to quickly take action- and if you're not careful, your marvellous creation can quickly go horribly wrong.
Personally, I enjoyed every moment of it. At first, I was building cells as large as dining halls, without taking into account my prisoners' hygiene or other needs. This quickly lead to financial issues, and frequent incidents of prisoners stepping out of line, butit was all part of the experience. The thing about this game is that you learn new skills every step of the way.
As for th escape mode of the game, it's nowhere near as fleshed out as it needs to be to compete with that of The Escapists. However, this in no way ruins the fun of the whole game.
All in all, this is one of the most fun, if not THE most fun management game I have ever played, and one of my favourite steam games ever.

Batman Arkham Origins. This is definitely not like previous Rocksteady-produced Arkham games. The previous Arkham games seemed like well-thought out and planned games. This instalment doesnt seem so.
Dont get me wrong, this game is still a good Batman game but it pales in comparison to the other two. Firstly, the controls. When combatting and aiming for free flow bonus, I feel lucky when I get to hit the final thug. In the previous games, while the thug is rolling on the ground, you can do a ground pound to end the combo. In Origins, you will be lucky to get that last punch because 90% of the time, the attack whiffs and your combo is broken.
Second, the challenges. The riddler challenges were easy compared to the previous games. Then there are the other miscellaneous challenges that were not thought out. I am referring to the Shadow Vigilante, Gotham Protector and the Worst Nightmare challenges. These are best completed during the story when certain areas of the map are accessible. You cannot complete these challenges in free roam after you have completed the story. Which is stupid. It cannot be completed in the challenge maps. Which is stupid. They said they will patch the game to allow it to be completed in the challenge maps but it has been one year. I played it more than a year after it released and it still hasnt been patched.
Other than that, I just see a rehashed version of the previous Arkham games. You have an equivalent electrical gadget in Origins, similar to the previous games. You have a similar item to create flotation devices and choke pipes with, like in previous games. You have a gadget that creates a zipline, similar to previous games.
I'm glad I got this at a discounted price. All that being said, this should help your batman fix til Arkham Knight comes out. Recommended at a discounted price. :)

Ori and the Blind Forest is an imaginative and atmospheric world in which you play a fox/bunny hybrid spirit that attempts to save the forest with challenging platforming, inventive puzzles and abilities, and a fantastic soundtrack to follow your journey.
The forest is filled to the brim with countless strokes of beautiful textures whilst the expansive backgrounds create this atmosphere of three-dimensional space in a two-dimensional platformer. The forest feels alive and in someplaces, even eerily dead, but that adds to the atmosphere the visuals create. The music in Ori is reminiscent of games such as The Legend of Zelda, Shadow of the Colossus and Ico; the vocals and instrumentation breathe character into an already very immersive expanse. Many people have cited Ori's soundtrack to be one of the main reasons as to why they picked up the game, to me though, it's one of the many reasons as to why I couldnt drop it. Needless to say, Ori is a beautiful game. It's well worth your money if you decide to also pick up the soundtrack add-on for the game.
The story is quite simplistic in nature and drives the player to explore more of the forest on their own incentive rather than being forced to, which is also a point that can be supported for good mechanics and game design, but I digress; although the tale of Ori is simplistic in nature, the characters convey themselves very clearly despite their vocal limitations. Kuro, The Black Owl, who is the implied antagonist of the game is visually pleasing and at times commands a very imposing status on the screen. In size comparison, Kuro is vastly larger than Ori which allows the player to know that Ori is threatened by the existence of this creature. Many have cited that the game attempts to tug at your emotional heartstrings, and I must verify that it does so with success. Although the game's story is very good, I felt that the universe could have been expanded a tad more; perhaps explanations as to how the Spirit Tree works and why the light is so damaging to some species.
The real meat of the game is in it's tight controls and entertaining (almost addictive) platforming. The game and level design leaves nothing to be desired, allowing you to revisit past areas with new abilities to then access previously unobtainable items is key to a good exploration game and Ori succeeds in delivering a full-fledged adventure with many things to keep you busy with, but enough to not distract you from the main route. Ori has several fast-paced sequences that challenge not only your platforming skills but also on how well you use your ability kit. There are many abilities to unlock and all of them are constantly being tested, so one must be able to know it's full capabilities to be able to proceed in the game. The game has no handholding and although it's not insanely difficult, it has a very good balance on difficulty, although I do recommend playing the game on the 'Hard' difficulty to fully understand how well the level design has been thought out. This area is not a full 5/5 due to my personal gripe with the lack of boss battles, as there were only a handful of them and the few that existed were excellent; there were many opportunities to insert three or five more but they were pretty sparse in the latter half of the game.
Ori and the Blind Forest has impressed me to no end. With a beautiful soundtrack and immersive world, smart level design, and a touching narrative, it was able to seduce someone that had no previous concrete platformer experience and able to keep him playing right into the end of the game. This game is well worth full price for 12+ hours of gameplay and a steal on a discount. Again, I'm not a very big platforming fan but this game sealed the deal into the genre. I am looking forward to Moon Studio's next IP.

Honsetly, this should've been the original sequel to FNaF.  I don't even know where to start with this game. For the story, it's actually given to you, instead of it being in the form of secrets deep in the game. The story itslef is pretty easy to understand. But for a person that will first enter the game, nothing story related will make sense to them in this game. You pretty much need to be a fan already to understand what's going on. But for people that are already interested in the story, your mind will be destroyed! You could pretty much say a big chunck of the lore was solved in this game, which is a huge relief. The gameplay is way different than it was in the past four games (which again is a huge relief). Each "Night" in the game will have you doing something different, which will keep people's interest in the game consistant. But, sometimes the save points in the game can be tedious. For example, in "Night 2" when you face Funtime Freddy in the Breaker Room, if you die on that part of the "Night" you will have to go through Ballora Galllery agian which is tedious in itself cause of the constant stopping and going. Same with "Night 3", If you die in the Parts and Service Room when facing Bon-Bon, you'll have to go through Funtime Foxy in Funtime Auditorium all over again, which to takes a bit to understand. Don't even get me started on "Night 4"! Look, I realise that parts of a game have to be hard, there would no challenge to the either way. But why do you have to make the fourth "Night" that f&^king hard? So, many had a problem with that "Night" in particular that they just stopped playing the game altogether. Which is extremely unfair to the people that don't have alot of patience to begin with or don't have alot of time to chill, relax, and play the game for an hour or two. I don't really have to mention "Night" 1 and 5, they're pretty easy and I have nothing to really pick about them. Except, there's and option on "Night 5" to not follow Baby's instructions and enter this "Private Room". To get actually get to this private room, you have to beat this "Death Minigame" that's pretty tedious and unfair at some points, I don't really need to explain it, it's pretty self explanitory. But after you beat that, you can enter the "Private Room". The "Private Room" is pretty much a homage to FNaF 1 in the way to controls with mechanics, of course it's tied into the story. It's a pretty hard area to beat, but you won't have too many problems with it hopefully, just look for a guide if you need help on it. Okay enought blabering about gameplay, let's talk about characters. Their are actually characters in the game this time, so that's a plus! They also have full-on voice acting, which was amazing btw! The character development worked for what the game was laid out as, no complaints here.Finally, let's talk about the "Custom Night". This addition to the game was a very good decision that Scott could've made. Making extra content for a game that was pretty good by itself, made the game even better in my opinion. The game mechanics work, theirs nothing too tedious with the obviously impossible challenges. All-in-all, pretty good extra content. Espeacially with the inclusion of little peices of lore after each "Very Hard" challenges. Do I recommend this game, yes. For people who are like me and are interested in the story or if you're looking for a good scare, I recommend this game all the way!

You know that game that you always come back to. That one that, no matter what, draws you back again. The one you say you'll quit, but you know that, in the end, you'll just be taking a brief break. For such a long time, Borderlands 2 was that game for me.
I first tried Borderlands 2 after a good friend recommended it to me during a free weekend. I played it for hours, but after that free weekend ended, I uninstalled it and forgot about it until it caught my eye in a steam sale. I bought Borderlands 2 Game of the Year edition without a second thought, grabbed the UVHM 2 DLC on a whim, installed it, and threw myself into the game I still consider to be one of my all time favorites. Since then, I've cleared it more times than I can count, 100%'d it on a couple of save files, and yet I kept coming back.
Borderlands 2, like its predecessor, is a first person shooter, with a humor filled story that again throws the player into the crazy world of Pandora. The story is easy enough to understand without having played the previous installment, but, while the story is quite strong, the two things that got me hooked was the Diablo-style loot system, which offers the player thousands of variations of guns. The main, and to an extent the subsequent True Vault Hunter Mode, can both be completed with minimal knowledge of how it all works. The humor of Borderlands 2 was the other thing that drew me in. Prison Architect is a Management, Simulation game inspired by Dwarf Fortress where you're given the role of Prison Warden and are tasked with building and managing your own prison. There's a Campaign which effectively is the tutorial for sandbox mode. To aid you in the management, you will be required to learn how best to utilise your given tool set which is extremely easier even if you haven't done the Campaign. You must hire staff, set up daily routines, understand how certain rooms work and overcome random events if you desire to run an effective prison.
+ Very in-depth prison management with easy pick up and play mechanics.
+ The Campaign is fun, while nothing to write home about. It essentially acts as the game's tutorial.
+ Building and expanding your prison is extremely easy. This is your prison and you can build it anyway you like.
+ For the most part all of the game's mechanics is well explained though some aspects still need some explanation.
+ The Program Scheduler is a godsend allowing you to allocate which program takes centre stage at which time of your preference.
+ When it comes to your prison nothing happens without a reason. Why are prisoners angry, maybe you're over working them, why are your prisoners rioting maybe because you haven't fed them in a while.
+ When your prison is well managed it runs smoothly and when it's not, well, it goes off the rocks very quickly.
+ There's a sense of joy when figuring out why something doesn't work i.e. Take the mail room for instance, all it needs is a table, sorting desk and 5x5 space. When your prison grows a single sorting will not work so you'll need to up the sorting table quantity as well for it to function.
+ Not only do you build a prison but you can also try to escape from it when you're bored of building.
- While the micromanagement is serviceable, it needs to be improved to incorporate a lot more aspects thus allowing for better (mis)management of your prison.
- There's no way to manage what is classified as "Min/Med/Max Sec crimes" for prison intake. The majority of the time you get Max Sec prisoners with what seems to be a minor crime like Gross Indecency. There should be some way of stipulating what crimes are designated for which Prison Section at intake for better sorting.
- There are too few random events. The current ones happen way too frequently that which gets repetitive after a while of play. For instance the Meal Quantity one should not happen as frequently as it currently does.
- The Sick Prisoner event seems tedious and somewhat broken. Rather than attempting to quarantine prisoners your Doctors will just mill about while the sickness spreads.
- You can't hire more than 1 Foreman who's in charge workshop training. So if you have 2 workshops, 1 for Min/Med and the other for Max/Super Max you have to stagger their work times.
- The Deployment menu is not explained (unless I missed it in the campaign) and is a bit obtuse to figure out.
- The Workmen A.I. is utterly stupid at times during construction jobs and sometimes abandons jobs for no reason. Rather than stockpiling a central stack of items needed for a particular construction job, each workman brings his own stack of items and when it runs out they run back to the main stockpile for more items. This essentially makes construction longer than it needs to be.
- A.I. pathing needs some work. Workmen would rather go around the automated security checks sometimes taking what is the longer path just because there are fewer automated/jail/remote/guard assisted doors. The same can be said of visitors' A.I. where visiting families and every external body tends to take shortcut routes into staff only designations rather than the secure path because of all the security checks in place like secured prison gates.
- Sometimes there's simply too little information about making objects/rooms work. For instance, the visitor's booth never states that it needs to be between 2 walls or that there must be a secure door on the prisoner's end.
- There's no prisoner check event with penalties which kind of undermines the entire point of managing a prison. Oftentimes when prisoners are acting up to the point of riot/attack staff, I sentence them to the dungeon which is a solitary building encased with double walls and cells are locked behind more walls when filled. From here they are starved to death or beaten until they're unconscious and left for dead with no medical attention before they starve of bleed to death.
+/- Most times your Workman will wait for a Prison Guard to open a cell gate when deconstruction rooms when there are no surrounding wall. This just seems too stupid.
+/- For some reason there is no rectangular selection tool for object removal. When building walls, you're given the option of constructing in a rectangular selection, the same goes for destruction. However when placing objects, you must do it individually. I don't mind the individuality when adding objects but why is there no rectangular selection for removing objects. There's a "Clear Indoor Section" tool but that dumps all items in the range.
+/- The UI bar should have the option to be sorted alphabetically to allow for better clarity when looking for certain items. Certain menu categories have a search box where you can search for the item rather than perusing the list with your eyes.
+/- Certain menu categories have a search box when you open or focus on the category but it doesn't automatically focus when the item is opened.
Prison Architect delivers in what it sets out to be, an entertaining prison management simulation. Even though it has some issues and can get boring after the first 20 hours, the fun I had overshadows everything that could bring it down. The main draw oftentimes is overcoming the random events the game tends to throw at you or determining what to do when things go wrong. I often found myself saying "I'll just play for 1-2 hours" then it's 4 hours later and that's the mark of a good game.

Sweet Lily Dreams is an older fashioned RPG Maker game that uses various Folk Stories and childrens books from different countries and creates an intricate game play story. The knowledge and background research for these various stories helps to make the game flow smoothly between worlds and stories. The various dreams brought up are common among almost every young child and adults fears or insecureties. Whether it is facing a blood sucking Dracula in Transalvania, to chasing witches in Russia, or even running with the headless horseman, the story will keep your heart racing. The game has maybe one or two scary moments, but it really not a scary game to most.
Sweet Lily Dreams is like every game and has some minor flaws to it that can detere some people from the game. I had some  problems myself, but to be honest most of them were cused by me. Many areas are maze like maps that have to be navigated through while dealing with respawning enemies. This actually helped me stay a few levels ahead of the bosses and made the game easier. However, it gets annoying trying to traverse some areas and not knowing how to get through them (again, most of them were my fault). Patience is a must with this game and requires you to think outside the box. Some of the side quest puzzles can also be hard if you are not very good with certain types of puzzles, but are rewarding when you do solve them.
All in all Sweet Lilly Dreams is a decent game for hard core RPG Maker Fans who are looking for a different take on the RPG genera. The game is not super long, taking anywhere from 20-40 hours, depending on how much of the game you decide to explore (puzzles and sidequests) I would greatly recommend this to anyone who is willing to try the game out and is a fan of older RPGs. With some patience and understanding of the mechanics even new fans can be made with this decent take on Folk Lore and childrens books.

There are also some characters from other games like Commander Video, the Headcrab, Mr.Minecraft, etc.. all  of which who are unique in some way. I haven't unlocked a lot of them, but so far, my favorites are Commander Video and Jill. There are two ways of unlocking new characters. One is going to specific Warp Zones, and the other is collecting enough bandaids (collectibles in this game that are in some levels).
I don't recommend this game to people who like easy platformers. You WILL die a whole lot. Cheap and nasty graphics, ear bleeding music and non-existant story I could live with, but the controls make the game artificially difficult. I don't care how many levels the game has if it's impossible to play.
Yes, I know that's it's supposed to harken back to the olden days of games being incredibly difficult, as if this is somehow supposed to be a beacon of hope in the modern age. No. Games in the olden days were hard because they wanted you to keep feeding quarters in as quickly as possible. But once we got home computers, that gradually faded away. It didn't die completely, as anybody who has played "I Wanna Be The Guy" can attest.
But given that this game's sole selling point seems to be it's artificially hard difficulty makes me sad. It could have been so much more. Maybe the developer found that even though it has hundreds of levels the game could be beaten in one afternoon, so in a last ditch attempt for credibility he deliberately sabotaged the controls, forcing players to attempt the same levels dozens of times over before either beating it or hurling their keyboard out of the window in frustration. WHY does the character have so much inertia? WHY is there always a fraction of a second before he responds to any button presses?
There are plenty of decent modern 2D platformers out there. VVVVVV, Escape Goat, Fez, Thomas Was Alone and LIMBO, just to name a few. Only buy this if you're a masochist.

Classic Hitman. A return to form.
What I don't like about the game:
* The graphics look good, but require a strong GPU. I have a 780ti and a 2560x1600 monitor. At my native resolution, I have to turn all the settings to low/off, and the fps still dips into the 40s. I turned the game resoultion down to 1920x1200, and I still couldn't max out the other settings without some frame drops.
* A lack of diversity among voice actors, and mismatched accents. You will hear white, American or British voices coming out of Asian and African mouths, and you will hear the same voices repeatedly. When 47 is pretending to be someone else and he talks to people, he doesn't even try to match their accent and nobody notices.
* The keyboard controls are convoluted. There are 6 different actions in particular that could have been lumped together as the Use key.
* There are things about the game that get a little repetitive. On every single map, you can find the exact same ematic rat poison, and then poison someone's drink and follow them to the bathroom where you can drown them in the toilet. A little too often, a target has conveniently scheduled a meeting with someone they haven't met yet, and that person just hangs around doing nothing so that you can knock them out and take their clothes. On every single map, there's a security room where you can destroy the video surveilence. Too often will you throw a coin around a corner, wait for a person (wearing the disguise you need) to walk over, and then knock them out.
* The always online requirement is dumb, but honestly, I haven't had any problems or disconnects.
* This is more of a suggestion to IOI, but: The game would be even more fun and creative if we could engineer more elaborate accident kills. Right now, doing an accident kill is something like: create a gas leak, and then wait for the person to make a spark that blows up; or release a lever that drops an object on their head. Pretty simple stuff. It would be awesome if we could plan out a whole chain of events and then watch it unfold.
Having said all that, everything else about the game is top-notch. Big levels, lots of things to do, many disguises, many challenges for replayability. Anyone who enjoyed Blood Money will enjoy this one too. You *will* get sucked in and sink a few dozen hours.

Sweet Lilly Dreams is a game made in the same vein as the JRPGs of the 90's, except it didn't quite manage to get the same charm as those games.
It starts off reasonably well, the premise for the game is cute and interesting, so it made me want to play more to see if it also has a good story and gameplay to back that up. Sadly, it does not.
The story fizzles out soon, as it is let down by bad dialogue writing and worse still it instantly derails you to a less interesting story plot.
Not to mention the fact that I thoroughly dislike the art style. The environments are passable, however the characters and the character portraits look absolutely horrible. It simply constantly makes you think that you are playing a game made in a school project.
The combat itself is a very generic turn based combat that you see in pretty much every game made with RPGMaker. It would've been OK if only you had received more abilities at the start. As it stands now with 2 of your characters all you do is press attack and with the other 2 you have one reasonable ability to choose from. You can create scrolls to get more abilities but even then you don't get much choice as you can only get a good selection of abilities later on in the game. SCS Software specialised in making truck simulations from its humble beginnings back in 1997 with Hard Truck. From then on in, it concentrated on the American theater with its successful 18 Wheels of Steel series. This game, Euro Truck Simulator is the first of its kind hauling cargo throughout Europe and whilst it has the same feel as its cousin 18 Wheels of Steel, the simulation experience is not quite there as it does feel a little arcade. And if it wasn't for the career objectives, I probably enter this game into an early retirement.
The gameplay length is pretty much unlimited as there is no official ‘end’. You can literally go on forever however even the most dedicated truckie sim fan will eventually want to give up. However the game cleverly designed career progression chart, where you need to complete certain tasks to raise the ranks from being a novice to the master trucker. Five ranks in all and designed in a way to get the maximum usage for this game however it does take some considerable time to become the master. And because there are many feats (achievements) to earn, it provides you more reasons to play it so if it wasn't for those I'd probably give it a flick a lot sooner.
