(please note, this does NOT take Custom Night itno consideration. from what i've seen it's just regular old FNAF, so there's not much i like or dislike about it.)
the thing i enjoyed about this game is that it's basically Five Nights at Freddy's for those who don't like Five Nights at Freddy's, because while still being first person and clicking and such, there's a much more involved in game story that makes every night actually feel like there's a point, all i felt the old games were is just five versions of the same resource managing that got a little bit harder every time, four games in a row- that's just... boring to me, and it didn't even feel like a real game at that point. this on the other hand, drops the micromanagement entirely and is much more close to (story-wise) the likes of Portal 2, which is something i have a really big soft spot for, so i can't give any criticism for that. (excuse my bias :P)
gameplay, however, is a bit different. every night is very different in the way it's played (except for the second and last night)
and even when the gameplay getting to the location is similar, what you have to do there is usually different. (third and last night is the only exception i can think of)
i really like this, honestly. it makes the game feel new every night, but reuses things when it needs to so that it doesn't feel like the fun parts of the game only happen once.
on the difficulty side, though... it's a bit of a rollercoaster. first night is just a tutorial, second night is a little tricky, third night i remember actually being pretty annoying, especially because once you fail the bonnie minigame, you gotta go all the way back to the last room and do it again. fourth night... jesus, it's the only time i can think of (besides the second night and custom night to an extent) that the game gets heavy on the micromanaging. it's basically about 2 minutes of spam clicking on certain points on the screen AND making sure that some puppet dudes don't get you. even if he nerfed it, it's still the worst part of the game and a very annoying segment that isn't very fun. last night is pretty much story but can be a little tricky if you're stupid.
so we go like this -> just a long cutscene -> medium -> hard -> very hard -> easy
so pretty much only a little over half of the game offers real challenge, which kinda sucks... but still, the game is a very fun experience if i do say so myself. it has a nice story to keep me interested, and some really good humor here and there. price tag is a little high for only an 1 1/2 hour experience, but overall it's a fine game.

The game is an average shooter at the first sight. First hour it is indeed. But there are some tracks of what seems to be a good narrative. But as the game drives on, and so do you and your character, it turns out to be the best worst shooter. Mainly to its atmospheric sounds and plotline.
I got many good impressions from it, because I expected nothing. Not to my surprise, all my friends who expected this game to be something great in terms of plotline thought this game is "meh" nonetheless, so surprise factor is very necessary.
Game is loosely based on "Heart Of Darkness" by Joseph Conrad, which has a film adaptation by Coppola called "Apocalypse Now". Game follows a typical squad on a typical mission, game progresses as a typical modern warfare shooter. The game puts a question mark on all these typical twists and actions that affect world by player following narrative. Some scenes in the game are very postmodernistic and quite often break 4th wall, asking some very obvious but interesting question, like "Do you even remember why you came here?".
Gameplay - it is an average "Gears Of War"-like shooter. Nothing special.
Sound - it is awesome, it adds alot to devastated world of Dubai. Ambient music suits well. Radio chatter is quite ok, voices are done great and radioman turns on some really good Vietnam-era music during your adventure. Not to mention, he often mocks you.
Graphics - they are pretty ok. Aren't the best even for its time, but the game does make some great scenery.
Controls - on gamepad, as my friend told, it is ok, though I didn't play like this and I don't recommend it. On keyboard it's uncomfortable for first two hours, but you get used to it.
To conclude, I recommend this game to be played by everyone just to have an opinion on it. I can't say definitly will you like it or not. But what have I noticed is that people who expect something from this game ofter are dissapointed in it, and those who don't are amazed. So if you want to play it - remember, it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ shooter you downloaded just to kill some time! Funny as hell, it was the reason I played it and it turned out to be my favorite narrative shooter easily overtaking bioshock.

(please note, this does NOT take Custom Night itno consideration. from what i've seen it's just regular old FNAF, so there's not much i like or dislike about it.)
the thing i enjoyed about this game is that it's basically Five Nights at Freddy's for those who don't like Five Nights at Freddy's, because while still being first person and clicking and such, there's a much more involved in game story that makes every night actually feel like there's a point, all i felt the old games were is just five versions of the same resource managing that got a little bit harder every time, four games in a row- that's just... boring to me, and it didn't even feel like a real game at that point. this on the other hand, drops the micromanagement entirely and is much more close to (story-wise) the likes of Portal 2, which is something i have a really big soft spot for, so i can't give any criticism for that. (excuse my bias :P)
gameplay, however, is a bit different. every night is very different in the way it's played (except for the second and last night)
and even when the gameplay getting to the location is similar, what you have to do there is usually different. (third and last night is the only exception i can think of)
i really like this, honestly. it makes the game feel new every night, but reuses things when it needs to so that it doesn't feel like the fun parts of the game only happen once.
on the difficulty side, though... it's a bit of a rollercoaster. first night is just a tutorial, second night is a little tricky, third night i remember actually being pretty annoying, especially because once you fail the bonnie minigame, you gotta go all the way back to the last room and do it again. fourth night... jesus, it's the only time i can think of (besides the second night and custom night to an extent) that the game gets heavy on the micromanaging. it's basically about 2 minutes of spam clicking on certain points on the screen AND making sure that some puppet dudes don't get you. even if he nerfed it, it's still the worst part of the game and a very annoying segment that isn't very fun. last night is pretty much story but can be a little tricky if you're stupid.
so we go like this -> just a long cutscene -> medium -> hard -> very hard -> easy
so pretty much only a little over half of the game offers real challenge, which kinda sucks... but still, the game is a very fun experience if i do say so myself. it has a nice story to keep me interested, and some really good humor here and there. price tag is a little high for only an 1 1/2 hour experience, but overall it's a fine game.

Terraria: A Minecaft like world awaits
You load up Terraria; a vast colourful 2d world sprawls out in both directions. Peaceful chip tune music plays in the back ground while cute bunnies hop next to you. Night falls and the music turns a little bit more threatening. Then zombies and flying eyes come and eat your face. Welcome to Terraria.
Comparisons to Minecraft are inevitable when it comes to Terraria, if anything the most jaded of reviewer might even say that it is Minecraft wearing the skin of 2d pixel art. I do not entirely disagree with this statement as you do have to build a house before nightfall and it is strongly advised by the game to not go outside at night but rather dig downwards to get better resources and explore. However Terraria does have original elements such as NPCs who, after moving into your home can act as vendors or healers, there is a continual threat of corruption taking over the land which you and your friends have to manage and there are boss fights you can do. Provided you are ready for them of course.
The game does not have a story so I cannot give a summery, the NPCs do mutter some vague statements that could be considered as world building but it is a bit of a stretch, this can be an issue if you plan to play single player if you are the type of person who needs some sort of story to keep you going. I normally play these types of games multiplayer as I can find myself burning out on non story single player experiences. If you are able to play the game for hours just based on the building and crafting then more power to you. Playing multiplayer can have the added benefit of being able to chat with friends or make new ones due to the mostly relaxed nature of the game.
Game play is mostly inventory management and building, you use A and D to move in both directions and space to jump, the mouse is used to interact with the world as well as for combat. The combat is not the most advanced thing in the world but it gets the job done and is fun. You get a wide verity of interesting weapons ranging from guns to swords to magic wands and staffs. They all feel good to use as well as fun to see monsters get blown up in very silly ways. I have not tried the PvP as of yet but I would be interested to see how it handles. As per usual with these types of games the Wiki is going to be your best friend as the game does not really explain much in terms of crafting, it is a little bit of oversight when it comes to crafting games as certain items need to be crafted in order to progress, but the game never tells you how to make anything. It can be a little annoying but not a deal breaker.
The graphics and soundtrack are some of the best things about the game, the game looks crisp and colourful and the cartoonish background art style mixed with the foreground pixel art creates something that is not only beautiful but somewhat unique look and feel. It also adds a sense of whimsy even after the evil starts to spread. The music also adds to the sense of wonder as you discover new bio domes, each bio dome has its own sound track as well as the time of day or night. The game has a really nice atmosphere as a result of this.
Terraria is a fun relaxing adventure, if you wanted a 2d Minecraft you cannot really go wrong here, grab some friends (or don’t) and enjoy exploring a world.

Well there are some goods and a lot of bads. I'll start with the goods and end with an in-depth overview.
Goods:
-EXTREMELY vast customization options (though limited by lack of Premuim)
-Fantastic Social/'chill out' District
-Very easy to use and grasp
-Decent backstory
-Simplistic
-Potentially great teamwork
Bads:
-Hello hacker city
-Pay to win
-Customization limited by Premium/P2W
-Godawful driving (the action-reaction delay is horrific)
-Very awkward controls
-It's on PC instead of console
-Too many kids to count
-VERY CPU instensive
Overview:
Basically, APB is a simplistic, visually stunning, F2P MMO very much alike Saints Row. The variety of weapons and vehicles is nice, the customization is second to none and actually tops Saints Row and any other MMO and the gameplay is addictive, racey and smooth. Though the game does have a tendency for lag spikes.
Sadly, I feel the bads outweigh the goods. The ratio of hackers/cheaters to legit players is 50/50 or MORE on the hacker side unless you play with newbies. The P2W and Premium feautures of the game are disgraceful. You will be MILES above the rest if you purchase with real money - and a LOT of it. This also sadly limits the lovely customization. The benefits and potentially essentials you get from  Premuim are completely unfair and a rip-off for what they charge.
The community for the game is frankly disgusting, too. Primarily due to it's fanbase being kids, low-esteemed 'girlgamers' and social-networking rejects. Expect to be called a noob and whined at in a moments notice and don't be suprised if the chat seems like it's been taken over by an army of 14yr old scene kids and CoDfans. The marketplace is lacking within this too. I would say that "Gold Threat" players are far worse than any whiney tryhard in a CoD hacker lobby. Avoid them at all costs.
Verdict:

Some will call this the worst Arkham game or a failure compared to its predecessors, but Origins actually has a lot to offer, including the best story of the series thus far. The writing GREATLY surpasses the wacky twists and laughable dialogue of City or the by-the-numbers plot in Asylum. Origins actually gets into the deeper psychology behind Batman and the Joker, and any comic fan will appreciate the stuff they've dug up from The Killing Joke, The Man Who Laughs, Batman: Year One, etc. The game also complements its plot with very good voice acting. Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill are absent, yes, but their fill-ins do an excellent job and Batman actually sounds like he's got some real emotion in his delivery this time. Not hating on Kevin Conroy, but I think his voice acting skills are at their best when he's in a booth with other actors, a la Batman: The Animated Series. When he's just reciting solo for a video game he can come across as sounding really flat at times (go back and listen to some of Batman's lines in Asylum and City and you'll see what I mean).
As far as the gameplay goes, it's similar to City with many of the same gadgets, map locations and freeflow techniques, but the boss battles are FAR superior - every single one from Killer Croc to Bane (this game presents the best version of him to be seen outside the comics thus far) is memorable. The fight with Deathstroke is a particular standout, forcing the player to quickly get used to the counter technique and really making you feel like you're up against someone who's Batman's equal. Then there's the fight against Firefly on the flaming bridge, which is much more cinematic than anything in the other two games.
The game's biggest flaw is that it's more of an incremental update to the Arkham series than a transformative one (which City was). Give it a go - by now most of the bugs that plagued its launch have been fixed and its certainly worth at least 15 hours or so of your time.

SUMMARY
The combat is far more in-depth than one once assumed, the game cheats to ensure you remain challenged, and the game always has a new mechanic/trick/challenge up its sleeve that keeps fighting interesting. Lightly strategic, and amazingly visceral combat to boot. As of this writing on 10/3/14, it's $0.99, how could it hurt to buy this?
STORY TIME
Well, what an unusual situation I am in with this game: I had the 'misfortune' to play the demo on another platform (probably the 360) a long time ago, and the demo only included the first 2 acts in stage 1. I played it, deemed it a mashy beat em up with no depth, and disregarded it entirely. Come 4 or so days ago, I notice it on sale for $0.99. I decided to buy it, not entirely remembering what it was that i disliked about it.
I finish the first 3 acts of stage 1, and felt the same way. Then I played the 4th act, The Swordsman. Suddenly, the game wears its true colors, and mashes me into a fine paste. Of course I get mad, decide the game was cheating, as it was indeed breaking a lot of rules it had already established. After a dozen or so tries, I win, and that should have been the end of it. But I keep playing either way.
Act 2 is already off to a good start, wailing on me mercilessly, but despite the game going out of the way to break rules, it slowly dawns on me that it probably wouldn't stand a chance if it didn't. An hour of arduous play later, I beat the 2nd Stage. Now I'm hooked.
VERDICT
This game is really really FUN. The demo I played so long ago did an excellent job of selling itself short. The light content the game gave me convinced me the combat was overly simplistic; not the case. The BASIC COMBOS are very unique, in that both directional inputs, timing, and the speed at which they are pressed changes your attacks. This allows for a very fluid, natural feeling attack sequence that is wildly variable based on user input, as well as highly adaptable to the enemy. The sounds they chose for some of these strikes are so viscerally satisfying, you're likely to react quite strongly at the earth shattering, bone crunching, lighting-esque chi strikes you'll be landing on the enemy.
The COUNTERS/GUARD BREAKS are a neat mechanic too, it's a little cumbersome at first, because the Hold X commands are not easily understood at first, but how it works, is if the enemy is trying to do light parries, the hold X command is a rapid flurry that aims to overwhelm them and break their guard. At any time, if they can't, or wont, let their guard break, they'll go into a full guard, the jumping attack (A), is used to break their guard in this case. Depending on the enemy, you can get anywhere from a few hits to a full blown series on them. This system, I realize, is meant to punish mashing. Yes, I said it, mashing is bad in this game. Mashing some situations is damn fun, but the game demands carefully chosen attacks. A layer of, dare i say, STRATEGY. That or PATIENCE.
The enemy can use your PARRY and CHI STRIKES as well. The white glow is their parry, and the red glow is the wind up of their strongest attacks. You can bait their parries with carefully placed strikes, and CRUSH their powerful attacks with your own, giving huge damage, stunning everyone in the fight, and giving that oh so wonderful thunderous crashing sound that I crave so very very much.
What surprises me is this game, despite pulling so many stops on me already, still finds ways to make each new fight even more interesting than the last, new enemies, new challenges, new mechanics to learn. On top of that, every act is a small, self contained fight that is short, but exciting to play, and easy to jump into and attempt.
ISSUES
I daresay my BIGGEST QUALMS with this game so far are the lack of integrated settings (you have to go outside of the game to adjust your video settings), the lack of the ability to remove the letterbox that forces 16:9 ratios, even on 4:3 ratios, the lack of a quick restart option in the pause menu (Really frustrating Stage 2 boss, I'm looking at you), having to sit and wait for your body to settle before you can continue (2nd stage boss again), and unusually high costs of items. I suppose the latter most is resolved by playing on all difficulty levels, but I'm still practicing here, give me a break.

Just looing at how many hours I have put into this should show that I truly adore this game. Sure the game has a lot of problems and the always online requirement for unlocks is truly horrible, but despite that this is clearly the best Hitman game ever made.
I've heard the argument that it is half a game since it has fewer locations than the rest of the series but this is all about quality rather than quantity anyway. Hitman 2 and especially Absolution (♥♥♥♥ that game) have over 20 missions but they're not nearly as replayable as ones found in Contracts, Blood Money or Hitman 2016. Contracts has fewer missions but some of them are duds (like most of Hong Kong) and even the truly great missions in Contracts aren't as replayable as most of Blood Money's content. And this of course is the case if you compare Blood Money to Hitman 2016. The few locations here are far more replayable than what we ever saw in the series even if you just look at their story missions, but thrown on top of that is the escalataion challenges, the contracts mode, elusive targets (shame they're temporary) and the bonus missions we saw in the Summer Bonus episodes. People like to complain about the dumb things missions here force us to do like destroy a virus or kill a single target in Bangkok who does nothing but walk a very scripted and short path, but dumb requirements are nothing new when you think about how Dance With The Devil and Amendment XXV also forced us to complete annoying and out of place kills.
Every map here is incredible and a highlight of the series, even the ones that I didn't like immediately on my first run. Paris and Hokkaido are without a doubt the two stand out missions here with no wasted space. Sapienza and Marrakesh do have plenty of empty space but they make up for it with their bonus episodes that actually combined make full use of everything. Bangkok has an incredibly amazing target to kill and at the same time it has the worst one in the game so I'm split on how I feel. Finally Colorado took a lot of getting used to but I actually do like it, just wish the ending wasn't so scripted, let us use the other exits like we can in contracts, also it is by far the most Hitman-esque looking level. The rest are too bright and/or James Bondish which I don't have a problem with exactly, I just wish they followed the style of Colorado's visuals.
I love the new music but I'll be crucified if I say that so pretend I didn't.
The new gameplay here is top notch. It has its quirks but what game doesn't? It's still amazing to play if my playtime didn't already give you that impression. Finally the game is just a fantastic return to form. We all expected IO and Square Enix to make an Absolution 2 and I'm really glad they didn't. This feels more like Blood Money than any past game and that's just great. I am looking forward to the Landslide mission and most importantly season 2. I expect to have many more hours with this gem, it's not only my GOTY for 2016, but it's by far my favourite game in many years.

FULL REVIEW:
The textbook example of a corporate cash grab. This game is a copy-paste of Arkham City except without any understanding of what made Arkham City amazing.
The first 2 games were developed by Rocksteady (who is being brought back for the 4th installment thankfully!) and published by WB Montreal. They are NOT a developer.
This game was "made" by WB Montreal. I say that very loosely. They literally copy-pasted Arkham City with some trivial new components and virtually EVERY new component is not properly bug tested nor developed. They ditched Rocksteady knowing players would buy this game on name alone....and it REALLY shows.
Specific list of issues I experienced (I did not bother finishing the game as I couldn't tolerate playing it, but for clarity I have nearly 100%'d both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City (on my own account and my cousins account; thats 4x playthroughs):
-Grapnel issues:
Arkham City navigating (grapnel) was a breeze, had long range, and worked on almost every ledge. Perfect.
Arkham Origins is the opposite. The VAST majority of ledges cannot be grapnelled to; EVEN LEDGES THAT COULD BE IN ARKHAM CITY CANNOT BE IN ARKHAM ORIGINS DESPITE THE COPY-PASTE OF THE MAP!
**This results in an extremely aggravating time navigating the city and was one of the leading reasons I quit playing the game. The closest comparison to this is Catwoman's navigation in Arkham City, but I think even that was just slightly better....
-Certain game elements can only be accomplished at a specific point in the plot. If you miss it, you have to play the entire plot to that point again to do it.
--This kind of thing existed back in the early days of game development because nobody knew better. WB Montreal makes this type of mistake because they don't know how to develop and IT SHOWS.
---For example: one of the predator dark knight achievements can only be done on a couple of late-campaign missions which have areas presenting all the necessary take-down components. If you miss it, you literally have to replay the entire campaign toward the end parts to get the chance to do it again. Of course, you won't know you missed it until you are in the post-game and turn to the internet for help....(yes, I missed it)
-Upgrade menus .....
Arkham City you could upgrade (mostly) in any order you liked allowing you to advance the character in your preferred playstyle. Good.
Arkham Origins makes sure to take a step backwards by forcing a certain upgrade order on the gear. And then to top it off, some upgrades aren't available until later into the campaign so you just get stuck in an upgrade tree unless you advance the campaign first.
--To make ti even worse, there are a large number of meaningless upgrades, but they are required to get the higher level ones.....
---Still worse, there are too many upgrades overall that make combat not only easy but repetitive (and this game is focused on combat MUCH more than predator).
-Combat is EXACTLY the same. I mean EXACTLY. Copy-paste is not an exaggeration here.
NOTE: I've heard some people say the "martial artist" enemy is a new type, but they are similar to Ra's Al Ghul's assassins so I don't know if I consider them entirely new
-Equipment is almost exactly the same but has different names.
There is one new item: the line launcher (2 point grapple). The "Freeze Cluster Grenade" is now called the "Concussion detonator" but the mechanics are the same (just graphics change). The disruptor has a new graphic, but they didn't even bother to change its name. The rest is essentially copy-paste...
-There is a new crime-solving detective mode. It is "pretty" but requires quite a suspension of reality. Oh really, you just created a 3d video of the entire crime based on a 3 drops of blood and some broken glass?
--This game takes place BEFORE Arkham City yet Batman has the same or better gear (ex: grapnel boost was 'experimental' in Arkham City, but you start wtih it in Arkham Origins) [I can let this one slide since it is a mechanical improvement in gameplay but if they took the time to rename other gear, why not this one?]
-Did I mention the bugs? They seem to have fixed most of the gamebreaking ones (ex: at launch, the vent in one of the towers was bugged and your char would get stuck requiring you to restart the entire game due to autosave in that room; thankfully those are fixed now but tons of little aesthetic or non-game breaking bugs.)
--Most annoying one: the animation for "counter" when you miss (he just kinda throws his elbow into the air). SO many times I am right clicking for other reasons that in Arkham City would have certainly worked but results in that stupid animation, a loss of my combo counter, and a delay during which i almost certainly get hit (most commonly a slightly distanced ground knockout). Extremely aggravating esp since this didn't happen in Arkham City and the combat seems to be a direct copy-paste....but its somehow sloppier.
For everyone's sake, don't support this game not even on sale. It might be worth playing for $5, but don't support the cash grab on principal if nothing else.

I loved this game, as I loved the previous two. Everyone seems to complain about bugs and glitches but I completed the game without encountering more than 2. The two which did come up cleared by itself within 10 seconds. The story in my opinion is the best out of the series because unlike the previous ones which seemed to almost be like a montage of Batman Adventures, this one shows Batman going through some growth. It feels more like a movie because the main character does not stay static like the previous ones. I love the new voice actors and it's a great re assurance that we will still have Batman and Joker in the future since Konroy and Hamill seem to be retiring soon. The boss fights are quite good, I really don't get what everyone is saying. Although the mechanics are pretty much the same as City's it feels just as satisying to clear a room as it always had. If it ain't broke don't fix it. The cutscenes are amazing and the soundtrack complements them better than City did. Graphics of course have been improved and the added part of Gotham is great to see since it contrasts the Old Gotham so much.
TL;DR, Judge this game for yourself and not join the circle jerk of "omg so many bugs" because there really aren't that many.

To be honest I was a bit hesitant on playing this game, and put it off for quite a while because of all the negative reviews and comments being made. A few of which being that it is a carbon copy of Arkham City's environment and little was made to "improve" on the previous game in this now trilogy. Gladly I did not feel this to be true in my opinion and had a fantastic time pummelling bad guys to a pulp, searching and uncovering the Riddler's hidden data and experience what I felt was a well written and enjoyable story arc. I was even a fan of the quick time events which in most games are either hard to detect or simply don't apply. I was always engaged in my seat and had my finger on the trigger, rather then placing the controller down and waiting for the cut scene to finish.
Although the game was fun and I enjoyed it throughout, there were a few noticeable bugs. One being the mobs would occasional get clipped into walls or objects and were unable to interact with rendering you unable to proceed any further. Or on one particular occasion the enemies stopped moving altogether along with some being clipped into walls. Hopefully it was only a minor feature that few had experienced.
I would recommend this game can't wait for arkham knight.

Terraria. Just finished my 5th playthrough and thought I should write a review.
Visuals:
Terraria is a 2D sidescroller with pixel art graphics, nice lighting and pretty particles. Whoa
Gameplay:
Terraria is based around combat and exploration. You get gear, fight a boss, get better gear, fight a harder boss and repeat. Lots of grinding, fun boss fights and hours of combat. Currently there are over 20 bosses in the game, not including modded, which brings us to a whole different level. If you don't like fast paced combat and grinding, don't play.
Sounds:
Probably has one of the best soundtracks I've heard. Needs more boss fight songs though, 8/10
Conclusion:
100% Recommend if you like pixel art games or difficult boss fights. This game is less of a rip-off of minecraft and more of a side-grade. Also try the space version of Terraria, Starbound.

I stayed up till 2am for nights in a row till I had 14 hours in this game, but having spent all that time I don't feel like I acomplished anything.
Similar building games like Sim City 4 or Cities Skylines also manage to suck up so much time but whenever I stop playing SC4 I lookback on the city that I've expanded and feel proud of however many new citizens I have or how slightly closer I may be to one day getting skyscrapers; but in Prison Architect I just do not ever get that feeling.
And I think that's caused by a number of reasons: first and formost is the ugly pixel graphics or poorly implimented menu UI, this is just not a pretty game to look at, so I can never really enjoy looking back on what I've just built. All of the joys of building come from your imagination of what you want a prison to look like.
This needs a bit of explaining: I don't just mean that the way you design the prison looks prettier in your head because the graphics look bad, though that is certainly true. The problem comes that way you arrange ammenities is almost completely arbitrary; while other building games require some logical design in where you place objects prison arcitects ammenities act as a checklist. You could give an office a desk with a chair behind it and a filing cabinet in close range, or you can push the desk innaccesably up against a wall, block the door with the chair, and put the filing cabinet in the center of the room and the game will say thats just as good. To keep up with how many prisoners the game was giving me at one point I simply made a set of large rooms with 50 bunk beds and a few toilets and the prison was functioning just as well as it ever had.
The second big reason that this game lacks the satisfaction that building sims need is that the inflow of prisoners always specific and timed. In a city building game the joy comes from having successfully pulled in more citizens by building more blocks or bigger buildings. In prison architect you know that in 24 hours you are going to get X number of prisoners, and so you build to fit more, not to bring in more. This is just stressful, real prisons don't constantly build new wings, that would be absurd, but this game expects a constant and ever increasing prison and forces you to do this or else.
Every part of the design in this game works to successfully suck hours out of you; and if all you are looking for is something to make you forget what time it is and ignore the depressing realities of life then fine, it does its job well enough. But if you want something a little more then that, where you can feel like those hours were well spent then look elsewhere.

So, I beat the game pretty quickly and this is the first Hitman game I've ever played.  I don't really have anything to compare it to because I've never played anything quite like it.  Some games I've played have some stealth mechanics, but none come close to this sort of thing.
All in all, I found it very charming.  The setting feels very populated with conversations you can overhear ranging from opportunities to help you hit your target to just commentary on the situation at hand and that sort of attention to detail is something I, personally, really like.
So, why don't I recommend this game?
To put it as simply as possible, it's just too expensive.
Requiring players to be online is something that benefits the company at the expense of player experience and, as you can see from other reviews, this has caused some problems.  This feature aught to lower the overall cost of the game from $60 (and it is a $60 game, even if you chop it up into smaller parts).
Aside from that, there's just not a lot of content there right now.  Elusive targets and other extra missions in the same settings creates some definite replayability, but in the end, you're running through the same settings again and again.  To be clear, this game does have replay value, I'm not denying that, but that seems to have been a crutch in it's development.  Less content now for the promise of content later, content they don't have to work as hard to produce.  This aught to lower the price as well.
It's just not up to the caliber of other $60 games.  I got it during the holiday sale for 50% off and, for a $30 game, I think it was worth it.  Not the full $60, though.

A good Arkham game. Not the best sure... But still overwhelmingly good!
The backlash at this game is surely reasonable, seeing that it's done by a new developer and as such is not a Rocksteady game. But, the backlash is unjustifiable. This game is really good and a solid addition to the Arkham series. It may not be Rocksteady, and may not be too innovative. But it does innovate and does the Batman: Arkham formula right!
The game's story is set on Christmas Eve when Black Mask decides to put a bounty on a very young Batman, who's still in his second year of crime fighting, which attracts the world's 8 deadliest assassins to track him down. The story is easily the best part about the game and is a very good Batman story. It does what other Arkham games dind't do, which is explore the dynamic between Batman and his allies, mainly Alfred, Barbara (AKA Batgirl) and Comissioner Gordon. The story is set 5 years before Asylum, but quite honestly, it should be 10. The characters are way, WAY younger than their Asylum counterparts and really, since Asylum depicts Tim Drake as being the current Robin, while Origins depicts Batman working alone. It just doesn't fit well... but that's a nitpick.
The gameplay mechanics are pretty much the same as City. Free flow combat. Stealth gameplay. Crime scene investigations. Open world gliding and grappling. Riddler trophies. It's really similar to City, but still has some twists of its own. Some new gadgets such as the Reverse Claw and the Concussion Detonator offer some cool dynamic gameplay mechanics to both Stealth and Combat. New enemy types such as the Martial Artist are also a very welcome addition that really make combat much more interesting and less repetitive.
It's easily noticeable that this isn't a Rocksteady game since the way the grappling works and the enemy AI are, really feel different... I feel like this is a nitpick, but it's just something I felt having played both other Batman games. Still, glitches and bugs were a rare occasion for me personally, yet I felt they were more than City or Asylum ever had.
Multiplayer is interesting, offering a 3v3v2 scenario. Playing as a goon in Joker and Bane's gangs is acceptable. It's a very standard 3rd person shooter. Still, the feeling of having Batman or Robin on your tail really helps you understand how the goons you beat up in singleplayer feel like. Batman and Robin themselves are the same as usual, but knowing that the goons you take out are players really change the feeling of pulling off a sucessful takedown. The assymetric aspect of the multiplayer however is its downfall. Having Batman, Robin, Joker, Bane and goons all play different is not only confusing, but also frustrating since you never seem to catch a break and play with who you want.
This is a Batman game however and what matters is the singleplayer. Thankfully Arkham Origins delivers a good Batman experience with some minor tweaks but innovations nonetheless. An amazing story and the solid gameplay from past Arkham games make it a very cool game. Just don't expect a Rocksteady game. Still, WB Montreal's first game is an amazing one for a first game.
Buy it if you want some more Batman action before Arkham Knight. It's really good but if City was just the ammount of Batman you were craving, you can skip it without missing out on too much. But, if you haven't played the others, by all means, buy this game. It's really good!
Highly recommend it.

Now while the formula hasn't changed too much will mean that users of previous games will come accustomed to this game pretty quickly. I dabbled in the online mode (which annoyingly seperates your control scheme from your single player game) but got owned pretty quick as I didn't know what I was doing :)
This game has plently of info on the characters and some *nudge nudge wink wink* moments where it references things gone before in the previous games (even though this takes place before both of them). I may not have played on the maximum graphics settings but Gotham looks gorgeous with the texturing being top notch!! Let down a little by the faciail animations which I feel were better done in previous games.
Sure there are a couple of bugs I noticed, like sometimes when starting to glide Batman will flap up and down erractically and not get anywhere fast, rectified by gliding again.
Now while I enjoyed the plot lines and the activities in this game, in some ways it tried to fight too many characters into the game and they seem to be spread thin. One particular character seen in previous games was still stunningly represented, even if the voice was a little "off".
Now where Arkham Origins seems to fall down is in it's constant hand holding of the player. Now I appreciate those that haven't played before would appreciate this but for playing on normal level I felt at times I was a passenger and the game was telling me how to do everything without me working it out on my own. The "riddles" seemed a lot less complex than previously. "Go here, press this button, get a treat". The differences between the cutscenes and the live action seem more than before and stick out "like a sore thumb". In many ways the fad of quicktime events takes some of the enjoyment out of the experience. Many times with certain segments of the game Batman: AO can't seem to figure out what kind of game it wants to be with a camera swinging around the player making controlling a bit of a pain.
If you are a Batman fan and you can ignore a couple of faults then you will enjoy this.
If you have played the previous games then this might be a bit mediorce in comparison.
In just over 33 hours I had completed the main campaign and all the side quests, still have bits to do on the many challenge maps! I am hoping their next game isn't just more of the same, I want them to take the Dark Knight to some more interesting places.

Loot Box Quest is a fun little clicker that has an actual ending, and the premise of the game is, you guessed it, loot boxes... Not sure what else you expected from this game really...
So, what can you expect from Loot Box Quest that isn't already shown in the trailer? Well really that is all that the game has to offer, and that's by no means a bad thing. Considering that the game is basically a parody of Loot boxes (*cough* probably something to do with EA's Starwars Battlefront 2 loot box system *cough*) it portrays what it wants to in the time that you put into the game, and considering that there is actually an end to the game there is a goal to reach to make you keep playing.
For a clicker game it's adds a slight bit of complexity more near the end game, but obviously things start off slow like in most clicker games. As you progress the game makes you upgrade your gear, making automation possible to help get money faster, pretty standard for most clicker games. As you progress you will start creating your own games to make money, and will slowly start adding micro-transactions to your games. This is where the complexity starts to go up a bit, you have to pay devs to make your game analysts to improve the next game you create. You'll have to manage how many you hire, the more you hire the higher their cost will be but the faster they will create games/improve upon your next game. It makes for some interesting game play, being slightly strategic about how many you hire, although not at all that difficult.
Eventually you'll get to the point where you will build your own company and have to manage your budget, what percentage of the budget goes into what category, and the assets which is what you need to upgrade further. A small nitpick I had was when this new mechanic was introduced nothing was really explained, only took a few minutes to figure out what everything did, but I would've liked a small explanation on what each budget percentage did.  Eventually you ill get to the end, maybe in like 3 - 4 hours and if you're feeling very adventurous then you could complete it in one sitting, but I would recommend coming back to it every now and then throughout a day or two.
Clicker games seemed to be divided into two different categories, those that are humorous but simplistic art style, or those with decent graphics and even though this one has simplistic graphics it's humour defiantly makes up for it. The layout of everything looks very clean, nothing too fancy but at the same time is still easy to look at and doesn't overload you with numbers of information about the game.
Generally the in-game music is a bit annoying in my opinion after playing it for a while, but there's always an option to turn it off, and even better you can listen to the music you have on steam to play in-game so that's pretty neat. Don't really see a lot of games do that nowadays
+ Great parody game about loot boxes
+ Great complexity that goes slightly beyond normal clicker games
+ The game has a great humour throughout
+ Simplistic graphics
+ Custom Steam music that you own can be played in-game
- Nearer the end, the game doesn't really help you all that much with how key performance indicators work, although after a few minutes of analysing what each indicator percentage
Loot Box Quest is a great little clicker game that is funny, has simplistic graphics and can be completed in a day or so. For the price it's asking for, I think it's defiantly worth it, but hey even if you don't like it the developer tells you after playing the game for 90ish minutes that you can refund it if your not enjoying it. A gem of a game, highly recommended, even if it's for sh*ts and giggles.
One of the funniest idle games I've played with clever jokes and observations about the games industry. An excellent choice among the dollar tier games.

Great, well written, incremental with surprisingly deep structure, great pacing, and an enjoyable meta-commentary on the state of gaming.
Especially given the low price of the game the unfolding mechanics are deeper and have more layers than I would have expected. The ending is rewarding enough and evokes a bit of a Paperclips-but-loot-boxes feel.
Like most incrementals it's not a 'hard' game and not progressing, while technically possible, is easily avoided. The pacing makes it a fun experience with shifting paradigms every 15 to 45 minutes. It goes through more than five distinct stages of gameplay and each is thought out and well designed. Most incrementals have the draw of doing something else and coming back to the game every once in a while. Loot Box Quest will keep you actively clicking and managing for the first hour or so and then let you wait more towards the end.
In total, the game takes around 3 hours to complete and the only real replay value is finishing off some achievements that can be missed along the way.
Having played shorter, more story focused, incrementals like "A Dark Room", "Paperclips" or "Spaceplan" and more long-running mechanicals ones like "Kittens", "Trimps", "Factory/ReactorIdle", "Realm Grinder" and "Sharks" this one definitely falls towards the side of a tightly paced, finish-in-one-sitting experience but has a comparable level of polish to the early versions of those games.
It's a new entry for my short list of incrementals to recommend to people that might not be too familiar with the genre and a wholehearted recommendation.

This game is a very challenging game, the diffiulty may push players away, but it is also a very fun game once you get the hang of it. This game is not for those who like having "the victory" given to them.
Here's some quick gameplay notes:
Each enemy has something unique that requires a different approach.
Levels have unique setups enemy setups and conditions, so the game never feels stale.
Animations are well done. The staff wielding enemies are a prime example.
Attacking an enemy is very satisfying because of the way they react to it.
There are various power ups, attacks, abilities, and items that can be unlocked. One ability that you should focus on getting is Air Guard.
The game supports local co-op (the entire campaign) via gamepad and KB. Both Xinput and Direct Input gamepads are supported (you'll have to configure Direct Input gamepads through the buggy config.exe. Xinput works by default). The game is difficult enough for you to "take turns" with 2 or more friends around.
The combat is not broken as some say and the game does not break its own rules; the only attacks that are unblockable are ones with exclamation marks, it does not depend on the enemy using chi attacks (I do not recall the game ever saying that chi attacks are unblockable) there can be a combination of chi attacks and unblockable attacks which are indicated by an exclamation point.
You have to use common sense when fighting some enemies. You can generally tell if an attack will cause you to stagger should you attempt to guard against it. Some enemies will try to land successive hits. Your first block requires less precision; subsequent blocks require greater precision. You can dodge/block mid-combo.
The game's graphics remind me of the newer Street Fighter games and another game called Power Stone 2 (I'd love to see that on Steam some day).
All in all the game is fun if you like a challenge, you'll have fun retrying over and over again by yourself or with a friend, if you know how to laugh at yourself.

Kung Fu Strike is a deceptive game, that at first seems to just meet the quality you would expect from a game with a price tag that is the equivelant of a cheep subway sandwich. However, looking past the inabilty to change the resolution and it's sometimes frustrating levels, it shows excellent design in it's combat system and difficulty curve.
Much like classic critical darlings such as Megaman, the game teaches you new gameplay-elements in relatively safe/easy to overcome environments, such as teaching you to kick bombs to dispatch a few groups of smaller enemies, only to end in a bossfight with a giant statue who can also prime bombs, cause chain-reactions with bombs etc.
The level of frustration fluctuates. Fun levels wherein you face pole-wielding monks are offset by gauntlets in which you face 20 enemies that can either shoot you, attack you, or do an unblockable pound with an AoE that is just slightly too big for how far your dodge-move goes.
It's other main issue is that it doesn't teach you two essential gameplay elements, which are critical strikes(wherein you use a (chi-)move on an enemy in the apex of it's attack), and the fact that pushing a direction twice will make you run for a short distance(which is done automatically after a dodgeroll).
The actual fighting is fantastic. Taking qeues from both beat 'em ups and modern fighting games, the game involves basic attacks which you can string into launchers, parries that can be performed in-between attacks(much like Metal Gear Rising), counter-attacks which can triple your damage on hard-hitting attacks, and even wallbounces which makes positioning in the very small arenas a key element.
This is complemented by an exceptional amount of enemy variety, decently artsy graphics, and a decent if generic soundtrack that changes tunes at just the right moments during enemy and boss encounters.
Kung Fu Strike is an excellent beat 'em up that does itself a disservice by calling itself oldschool. It's frustration comes from unfair levels, but the fighting mechanics are rock solid, and it doesn't put the game down enough to make it not worth your time.

So, I beat the game pretty quickly and this is the first Hitman game I've ever played.  I don't really have anything to compare it to because I've never played anything quite like it.  Some games I've played have some stealth mechanics, but none come close to this sort of thing.
All in all, I found it very charming.  The setting feels very populated with conversations you can overhear ranging from opportunities to help you hit your target to just commentary on the situation at hand and that sort of attention to detail is something I, personally, really like.
So, why don't I recommend this game?
To put it as simply as possible, it's just too expensive.
Requiring players to be online is something that benefits the company at the expense of player experience and, as you can see from other reviews, this has caused some problems.  This feature aught to lower the overall cost of the game from $60 (and it is a $60 game, even if you chop it up into smaller parts).
Aside from that, there's just not a lot of content there right now.  Elusive targets and other extra missions in the same settings creates some definite replayability, but in the end, you're running through the same settings again and again.  To be clear, this game does have replay value, I'm not denying that, but that seems to have been a crutch in it's development.  Less content now for the promise of content later, content they don't have to work as hard to produce.  This aught to lower the price as well.
It's just not up to the caliber of other $60 games.  I got it during the holiday sale for 50% off and, for a $30 game, I think it was worth it.  Not the full $60, though.

Batman Arkham Origins is the third in the Batman video game series and is a prequel to both Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. While the returns dwindle a bit in this game, it's still worth your time and a worthy entrant into the series. If you've played the previous Batman games, this will fit you like a glove. The free flow combat, gadgets, puzzles and even vent crawling all return. That may be the problem with Batman AO. It's a bit too much of the same and the cool events were few and far between. The part where you reconstruct a crime scene was fascinating but you do it only once. The boss fights were kinda meh, except for the third (yes third) and last fight with Bane was very tense and very cool. Doing inverted takedowns and clearing a room full of bad guys without them seeing you also never got old. The voice acting is stellar as usual. There are some irritating bugs of which the most EGREGIOUS is the last fight with the Joker which required me to lower the resolution all the way to the lowest setting so I could see the QTE prompts (props to the Steam Community for the help in solving this). That said, this is still a fun game. I'd rank it behind Arkham City and Arkham Asylum but on a sale at around $10 with base game and the season pass you're definitely getting your money's worth. I've heard great things about the Cold Cold Heart DLC and I'll check that out in due time. Arkham Origins still gets an easy 8\10 from me.

Spec Ops: The line is a bit of an odd beast. It starts as a very average 3rd person cover shooter. You get to hear the usual gung-ho callouts, and slaughter the usual terrorists. Then, somewhere an hour in or so, the story starts to pick up speed.
And what a story it is. Unlike the vast majority of shooters this isn't a story about heros slaughtering evil goons to save the world. This is a story about actions and their consequences, about atrocities commited in the name of a greater good.
This is not a game for 18 year old kids who still think war is a fun adventure. Or maybe it is. Maybe it will make them stop and think for a few moments. Maybe it will make them read heart of darkness.
For the adults, if you can look past the average game mecanics, it's well worth playing.

Suicide Mission was chosen for my first run, and Fubar second time.
No spoilers in this review, after all, there is no fun if you know any story of it before enjoying it.
Compared with other shooting games, Spec Ops: The Line is not unique at all or even much more tedious about its gameplay. What players have to do is shoot targets, take cover from gunfire and  move on to a next point, continuously.
is a bit clumsy, sometimes it may get you killed and repeating under some critical situations couple times. For instance, Sprinting to sandbags for cover, taking cover and vaulting through it, all of the movements do not seem to flow smoothly. Mere conditions that some spots look available to interact with, like beside a low closet of a bar table,  actually not for cover,  are annoying.
is not that appealing even in 2012 , but it is still fine and acceptable. Personally, I like how the developer created the feel while a desert storm is striking. When headshots happen, there is a moment of slow motion effect. With some high-caliber rounded weapons, there is also a gore effect.
is great, and some classic old rock songs are introduced as well.
The essence of this game is about its
. I guess that is something worth playing, especially for players who have played lots of shooting games, shooting games especially like CODs. Spec Ops: The Line will definitely blow your mind and thought on shooting games.
If you are an enthusiastic shoot'em up gamer and want something different, this game is absolutely for you.
Strongly advised, do not read any articles related to its story before finishing the whole game.

Despite the complaints I’ve read, I find the battle system beautiful. It looks and feels like a kung-fu movie of old. The game incorporates enough basic battle moves and concepts to allow the design of true fighting strategies:  chain combo attacks, evasions, blocks, block-breakers, critical hits, critical hit breakers and henchmen summoning. All bosses obey the system, and the side that can best exploit it will be the victor.
The game’s only flaw is the combination of a lack of targeting with a dynamic camera, which causes missed attacks and rage-fueled baldness.

A lot of reviews here complain about the community. A lot of reviews complain about the "current state" of the game. The fact of the matter is, even if its been this way for a while, the game is in Early Access. There are almost always weekly patches that add new content, revert unwanted content, and sometimes drastically alter the core gameplay. This is both the best and worst part about Rust. Being excited to try something new every couple weeks keeps players from getting too bored, and even when they do, they'll generally revisit. Salty players tend to leave bad reviews because they are dissatisfied with the game "today" and don't give it a fair enough assessment, considering all of its high points. This game is absolutely not for everyone and if you don't enjoy a challenge or can't accept loss and defeat then move on. This is a survival game and surviving isn't handed to you on a platter at all.
The game is rough around the edges but slowly coming into its own. It has been the most fun game I've ever played, the most awful game I've ever played, and the most frightening game I've ever played. Nothing is as heart-pounding as spending a week gathering loot and fortifying your base to have some guys all-geared-up knocking on your front door with rocket launchers in-hand. Making a run to a monument, finding a rifle for the first time and trying to survive the run home. Filling your inventory with wood to build a giant base just to get wrecked by a homicidal helicopter and losing it all. The feeling of persisting through all of the terrible things that can happen to you in Rust, shooting down and raiding your enemies, and coming out on top is one of the most gratifying feelings a video game can give to you... especially since this is online and hundreds of others are playing alongside or against you. You can revel in your accomplishments and know that if you run outside, get into a firefight with a group of dudes and die, you can re-spawn back at home and brush it off with plenty more gear to keep trucking. Not to mention the insatiable gratification that comes from revenge after destroying what your enemies worked for... just like what they did to you days ago.
You will like this game. Not immediately, maybe not even after a week... but its worth the learning curve.

Arkham Origins is what I would call a not-so-great game in an awesome series. The absurd success of the previous Arkham games makes it very difficult to dislike Origins. However, it doesn't by far reach the awesomeness of Asylum and City. The graphics are great, however the characters may look a little cartoonish in a close-up (just like in AC). The story is amazing, and gives you that "I know what's going to happen in the future" feeling. The voice acting is, of course, flawless, and the game mechanics are pretty much like Arkham City's. The biggest problem with Origins, in my opinion, the motion capture. When not in a cutscene, you can see the mouth movement is extremely bad and breaks the barrier of realism completely. The mocap in cutscenes is great, but the image quality goes down to near 480p, which really made me angry. The missions are easy and somewhat boring, and I
missed the large ammount of stealth predator encounters of the previous games. I am well aware that this game was made in a hurry, so I'll have to wait for Arkham Night to pass a veredict on the Arkham series. I am recommending the game, but I can't say it is great. Sorry, Splash Damage, you are never going to be as awesome as Rocksteady.

So I've been a bit harsh about Arkham Origins (still a terrible, lazy title though).
It's glitchy, which none of the previous Arkham games were, and it doesn't really do anything new, which both the previous Arkham games did, but it's still built on a base of probably the best action-adventure series of the last ten years.
The boss fights are actually better, to be fair. They're actual fights that suit the villain in question, where you use the skills you've learned in combination, rather than Legend of Zelda-esque "Use the last item you found to expose the weak point, punch the weak point 3 times, dead boss". Bane in particular is much more like the comics version than any previous iteration.
All in all, it's more like an old-fashioned expansion pack for City, rather than a full sequel and I guess it's pretty good judged on those terms.

Overall: This game had me screaming "hot ninja hot ninja hot ninja" over and over as I desperately smashed buttons to survive.This isn't a terrible game, I had some fun and there are things to like about it. BUT, the difficulty is too hard, even at the easiest level (also suffers from bad camera angles), to be accessible to someone just looking to pick it up and have a bit of over the top kung fu fun!
Do you like grueling levels that will stomp your a** into the ground? Well even if you do you won't like this game. The novelty of being a bad a** kung fu master wares off after you start to get into the later levels and consistently get beat to a pulp by mobs of enemies.  I love a challenge but this game does it all wrong. Low attacks that are unblockable, having special attacks interrupted when you're hit from behind and soul crushingly bad camera angles when dodging that seem to come at the worst time. Even on the easiest level you will find yourself getting abused, but it's not in the same vain as Dark Souls where you feel the urge to come back for more and over come by thinking of a new strategy. I just found myself not really having fun and even over coming tough bosses didn't feel that satisfying, but more like a waste of time. They could of implemented some strategy to it but when you're being over run by swarms of enemies and they can hit you  with unblockable moves in the middle of your move it leaves little room for enjoying your move sets and what could of been a fairly fun counter system. The juice isn't worth the squeeze on this one. You're better off investing your precious time into a game where the challenge matches the reward.
PROS:
Old school kung fu style
cool looking moves
local co-op
CONS:
really bad camera angles
unnecessarily difficult
no online co-op

If you are a die-hard fan, you will have bought, played and judged this anyway, so you can stop reading. If you're not a die-hard fan, make sure you've played Arkham Asylum and Arkham City before this, and if you are then still hungry for more Batman and can't wait for Arkham Knight, consider getting this only on a good sale.
Arkham Asylum was great.
Arkham City was even better, even though the story did get convoluted at times just to fit in all the content.
Arkham Origins... is just something to tide us over until Arkham Knight is finally released.
If, like me, you are a massive fan of the Arkham series, it's likely that you've already bought and played Origins, so I don't need to review it for you. If you are someone who merely liked Arkham City rather than playing it to death, and who's wondering if you should pick up Origins: probably not. You've already seen (almost) all the gameplay there is in Arkham City, and done better at that. Yes, Origins has a bigger map -- but it doesn't manage to fill that map with sufficiently interesting stuff, so that, paradoxically, it somehow feels
than Arkham City. Yes, Origins adds a story that qualifies as a prequel (even though, in spite of the title, there is very little there that could be called an origin of anything), but it's ultimately inconsequential.
The story is both better and worse than City. It definitely has more focus than City, which started off simple but had an incredibly convoluted build-up to the end, certainly compared to Asylum. By contrast, Origins simply has Batman targeted by a bunch of assassins because Black Mask put a price on his head, and most of the story is just Batman taking them all down in order. There's one thing that could be called a twist, but it happens pretty early on, and actually (and unfortunately) makes the story less interesting since we trade a new villain for an old one. But with the increase in focus also comes a loss of depth, and there's nothing in Origins that compares to the daring ending of City. True, Origins hardly has room for something like that given that it's a prequel, but more could have been done with the premise. As it is, most of the characters you encounter in Origins undergo no development -- Batman included.
The gameplay is definitely worse, in both small things and bigger things. There are glitches where Batman can get stuck or enemies suddenly stop registering as enemies and just stand there looking goofy, ground takedowns seem to work only when they feel like it, and sometimes necessary encounters simply don't happen until you leave an area and come back. Mind you, this is with all the patches and fixes that are likely to ever be applied -- this is as good as it gets. It never gets so bad that it makes Origins unplayable, but it's just not as polished as City.
Upgrades are now partially tied to achievements in the form of the Dark Knight system, and this manages to do little more than unbalance things. The fatal flaw of this system is that it requires you to do certain things in order, so unless you're carefully keeping track of what exactly you're supposed to do next, you may find yourself short of an upgrade you want with no easy way of getting it, or doing something silly you've already done dozens of times in the game which only now counts as an achievement. I spent the majority of the game without the "disarm & destroy" move because you can only get this if you complete a side mission that's extremely easy to miss until you've already finished the story (and in fact it doesn't unlock until a good way in). And if you haven't completed the Predator track by the time the story finishes, well, it sucks to be you because most achievements can't be completed for lack of appropriate Predator encounters. This is all the more galling given the fact that Arkham City actually had respawning Predator encounters, even though you almost certainly didn't need it.
The Shock Gloves are an upgrade that's
tied to achievements but part of the story, and they deserve to be singled out as a bad idea. When you have this, after enough punches, you unlock the use of this "super gadget" that allow you to punch enemies that normally couldn't be punched, and counter things that normally couldn't be countered. Rather than making fights more exciting, however, it just makes them less interesting because you don't have to think about how to take on enemies as much anymore. Activating them is optional, but also very easy to do unintentionally. I would have given good money if I could have traded the Shock Gloves for the disarm & destroy combo... but that's not an option.
The side missions are uninspired. Detective investigations are back in the form of case files, which is a neat idea but they're far too simplistic to hold the attention for long -- visit crime scene, rewind things back and forth until you've scanned the things that obviously need scanning, then go somewhere else to apprehend the perpetrator. The data packs you collect this time (replacing the Riddler trophies) aren't half as interestingly protected as the trophies. It makes some sense since, after all, the Riddler isn't even calling himself the Riddler yet, but if that's what they were going for they should have just reduced the number of them and saved you the tedium. There are no surprise encounters that lead to interesting diversions like in City; you'll pretty much hit all the spots during the story and what's left is collectibles and endless "crimes in progress", which are just repeated brawls. There's too much copy and paste like this and not enough memorable stuff.
If it sounds like I'm doing nothing but comparing this game to Arkham City: that's because Origins all but invites the comparison, since in both premise and execution it's just like Arkham City. If Origins could be judged on its own merits, perhaps in a universe were Asylum existed but not City, it would come out much more favorable -- but since City does exist, the game can't be seen as anything more than what it is -- a repeat exercise. It's a good repeat exercise, mind you, and it does actually try new things even if those don't always work out for the better. The developers should be appreciated for their efforts, but the spark of genius is missing. Origins ticks all the boxes, it includes all the stuff that City did and adds some more besides, and yet somehow it manages to do less with it.
Oh, and there's multiplayer. That is definitely new, but it's also the one thing I can't say anything about, as I haven't tried it. This is not a shortcoming of Origins, by the way, I'm just a solo player. And we are talking about Batman, after all, who does his best work alone. If you need to know if the multiplayer is worth it, you'll have to look for another review.
Do I recommend Origins? Yes, as long as you get it on a good sale. It would be unfair to say Origins adds
to the Arkham experience, and as much as I've criticized it, I can't call it a bad game. Not revamped, not rejigged, not redesigned. Reloaded. APB’s new suffix is apt, as this free-to-play reincarnation of 2010’s deflated cops and robbers MMO is a retread of the same ground. The same drab city, the same hollow combat, the same lopsided results.
The original city of San Paro has been left standing, a monument to badly judged level design and the colour grey. The first game’s devs, Realtime Worlds, intended the place to live and breathe. Instead, it spluttered a few times before its life support failed. Its resurrection is a miserable one.
Reloaded’s missions usually pit two small squads of human-controlled criminals and enforcers against each other, asking them to perform a multi-stage series of mini-jobs. One team has to drive to a place, collect a thing, and deliver it somewhere else. The other team has to stop them. Occasionally this leads to the kind of scenes that flicker through the minds of non-players when you describe APB to them: high-speed chases through busy streets, lastsecond jumps into getaway cars.
Most of APB’s problems remain in Reloaded. It even inherited a few new ones, as it is currently seeded with cheaters. The original game was arguably killed too soon, so the switch to free-to-play means interested parties should at least take a weekend city break back to San Paro. But this is no revitalisation – APB Reloaded is rehash, replication, and repetition.

I really, really want to love APB (All Points Bulletin): Reloaded more than I do. Yes, the original APB was riddled with enough cracks and flaws to take it from diamond-in-the-rough to half-eaten-Ring-Pop-that's-shaped-like-a-diamond, but some of its more ambitious ideas were very nearly brilliant. And hey, Reloaded – for the most part – smartly tweaks APB's little problems while leaving its cops-and-robbers core undisturbed. On paper, it sounds like every wannabe grand automobile thief's dream come true. So then, what exactly went wrong?
Above: If only he'd just worn his safety belt
The short answer: A lot of things. First, though, it's essential to point out what went right, because – without a doubt – APB: Reloaded is a more enjoyable experience than its short-lived predecessor. APB's DNA – once a criss-crossing-crashing amalgam of MMO persistence and barely functional riffs on GTA's best ideas – has been straightened into a much finer point. Weapons now do more damage, resulting in faster, more satisfying firefights. Cars, meanwhile, actually possess unique driving models. In other words, no more sports cars that drive like minivans. There's also a teensy bit of weapon-usage-based stat progression to give you something to do beyond amassing a gun collection that'd make even John Woo's bullet-loving doves flee in terror. And then there's a real-money-based in-game store that... well, more on that in a bit.
In a lot of ways, APB fights desperately to be the antidote to modern MMO drudgery – sometimes to a fault. Beyond rudimentary side objectives (things like raiding stores if you're a criminal or returning stolen cars for enforcers), the game is essentially PVE-free. Missions auto-plop you into a group of fellow ne'er-do-wells (or loose cannon cops who don't play by the rules) and assign you objectives – for instance, investigate a vehicle or commit some nice, wholesome arson. The twist, however, is that your enemies aren't trash mob NPCs - they're flesh-and-blood members of the opposing faction. So missions unfold more like objective-based shooter matches, but in a completely open, vehicle-packed urban playground.  When APBR works, it really, really works. There's nothing quite like racing neck-and-neck against a sports car full of gangbangers – guns-a-blazing the whole time – toward an objective, crashing and twisting through the air like you've been punted by Godzilla, and then emerging from the wreckage into a hail of gunfire and, er, regular fire. Other MMOs, meanwhile, ask you to collect 20 boar gizzards because, f*** you, don't question it, chore peasant. Better still, similar chaos unfolds all around you, thanks to other groups on similar – though separate – missions. Bullets fly. Cars careen through the streets. Magic happens.
Before long, though, you can't help but see behind the curtain of explosions and car shrapnel, because that's pretty much all there is to it. Mission types are incredibly limited, generally breaking down into “find and deliver a thing,” “stop the other team from finding and delivering a thing,” and “hold a point for a really long time.” New self-contained “Fight Club” districts attempt to spice up the rather vanilla proceedings with large-scale team deathmatch and king of the hill battles, but the two currently available maps lend themselves more to haphazard lone wolfery and camping than interesting team tactics.
APBR's city, meanwhile, is utterly lacking in the loving attention to detail of, say, a GTA or the zany outlandishness of a Saints Row. It's just a sprawling sea of gray spotted with shamefully tiny islands of intrigue. So, by and large, APBR devolves into a very simple shooter with very simple modes in a very simple environment. On top of that, the story's basically non-existent. Occasionally, your contracted mission-givers will send you emails, but there's no sense of escalation or progression. It's just an unending tug-of-war between cops and robbers that never actually goes anywhere – a dynamic justifiable only if APBR is secretly set in Purgatory.    That general lack of personality becomes all the more disappointing when you start really digging into APBR's absurdly robust character customization suite. Once you've filled out your wardrobe and unlocked a few decal templates, anything's possible. So, of course, we created something that could best be described as the unholy offspring of Batman Beyond and the mopiest, most blue-haired JRPG character you can imagine. At one point, we actually encountered an incredibly authentic Harley Quinn – jester cap and all – and it was love at first sight. Then she shot us in the face. Long story short, APBR's players supply nearly all of its personality. And while that's an interesting idea on paper, it fails to thaw a frozen, unchanging world whose bag of tricks is about as deep as a drought-devoured puddle.
But what about all that free-to-play razzle-dazzle that APB savior GamersFirst can't stop clamoring about? Business models, after all, can make or break MMOs. And while APBR's “Armas Marketplace” certainly isn't broken, there are some very worrisome cracks in its armor. For one, the game constantly pestered us about biting a $10 bullet and signing up for a month of Premium access, and it's not hard to see why. Among other things, our piggy bank's valiant sacrifice more than doubled our end-of-mission cash rewards, hugely boosted our faction gains with mission givers, reduced cooldowns, and gave us a 20% discount on all marketplace items. Basically, Premium's the way APBR was meant to be played. Free, by comparison, feels downright sluggish. Then there's the extremely sticky issue of buyable weaponry. Armaments that cost you an arm and a leg aren't necessarily better or worse than those earned by the sweat of your tattooed brow; they're merely different variations on similar ideas. So, ultimately, a kitted out character and someone who upped their arsenal the old fashioned way will be on a roughly even playing field after many hours of play. However, we were able to roll a completely fresh character and immediately buy a fully modded gun that many experienced players swore by. Suddenly, getting matched against fellow low rank players didn't seem so fair. APBR's early goings, then, can be a figurative trial by fire and bees. Because the fire wasn't bad enough.
APBR is a game that suffers from a serious identity crisis. It tries to be both an emergent, skill-based shooter and a full-blown free-to-play MMO, but only succeeds at falling into the abyssal middle ground between the two. Thanks to a number of tiny tweaks and larger additions, Reloaded is definitely a step up from the practically DOA APB that crashed and burned a couple years ago, but the two are still incredibly similar. Fundamental mission structure and variety flaws, unfortunately, stuck around for the ride, and its (improved) simplistic shooting and driving aren't enough to right those wrongs.
It's honestly heartbreaking, because many of the game's ideas teeter on the cusp of being revolutionary. As is, however, All Points Bulletin: Reloaded fires far too many blanks. Free is a tough price to turn down, but the city of San Paro is – at best – a vacation spot. We simply can't recommend an extended stay.
