I've flirted with the franchise before, playing Silent Assassin, Blood Money and Absolution. I'd seen some negative reviews about this game when it came out - each mostly citing a lack of content. It's hard to want to pay full price for a game that isn't full content, right? I picked it up on the winter sale, because I loved Blood Money, and played through Absolution (a little grudgingly). What I found was the most pure Hitman game I've yet encountered.
Usually in the series, there are 4-5 paths to take out a target. The paths are usually relatively separate, and it becomes fairly clear the sequence of actions you have to do to (for instance) strangle the target or poison them. In this game, however, I can't even name all the paths for a single mission. To say that the maps are huge is doing injustice to the word "huge". Every map is filled with criscrossing paths, patrols of NPCs, scripted interactions that you're highly likely to miss (but which provide ideal openings for an assassination), and dozens (plural) of ways to approach the mission. And best of all, the different ways to complete missions are far from mutually exclusive. Even something relatively straightforward like poisoning a target might have a few different poison locations, disguises needed to pull it off, and points at which the poisoning could happen. A good amount of missions have multiple targets, so you can combine the many ways of assassinating them.
And every mission is like this. With the exception of the tutorial mission, they're all packed to the brim with content. I'm sure that there's a handful of "perfect" ways to complete each mission, and that there's a certain "max" you can achieve. But unlike previous games, that "perfect" execution isn't probably even 10% of all the possible ways to do it. And in past games saying something like that would be code for "oh, you can just go in guns blazing, that counts, right?", but in this game, all those possible paths to completion are pretty stealthy, not usually involving extra casualties.
Look, I could go on. But I think the point is made - this game has a ton of choice and content. It's the best Hitman yet, as far as I can see. If you're an old acquaintence of the series like me, pick it up. If you're new and want to see what all these greybeards are on about, pick it up.

Kung Fu Strike is a needlessly difficult game in which the rules are defined and immediately broken. The combat system is initially exciting but soon becomes tired and clumsy when met with a particular group of enemies or a very unrelenting boss battle. You can not lock onto enemies, instead the game will automatically choose who you're fighting at any given time. There will be times when the game will wait for you to initiate an attack only to have your character unintentionally go soaring over the head of your opponent.
The arenas in which you brawl are often claustrophobic and allow little room for error. The size of the stage will at times be so small and swarmed with such a large amount of enemies that you will lose focus of your character and not be able to clearly see who you should attack and when you should counter.
Speaking of, the counter system is confusing. In the beginning you are told to counter against enemies by following their attack animation and that enemies who suddenly glow red can not be countered. In a later level you will face an opponent who can be countered when glowing red, destroying whatever rules the game had just set. You can not counter low attacks, even when the enemy isn't glowing red. Sometimes countering an attack will not break an opponent's combo as they continue landing attacks, even though it's possible for them to break your combo. If you immediately begin to counter an enemy whose attack animation has just begun your counter animation will sometimes end before they land their attack, often causing you to take significant damage if caught in a combo. Sometimes you may be swarmed with enemies who will all attack at once or immediately one after the other, forcing you to forever counter their attacks or risk taking damage as you focus on a small group of enemies whilst the other group pummels away at you.
The character is always at a disadvantage. You are required to fight, earn money, and then purchase unlockable items in order to stand a chance in future fights. Unfortunately you never really know which items are most appropriate until after you've failed the next battle, there is a lot of trial-and-error involved here and that form of repetitious mechanic isn't very appealing.

If you had any doubts at all about this game because of everyone complaining about how Dante looks or how ridiculous his lines sound or how it's a world apart from the original Capcom DMC lore, forget them.
By itself, this is a GREAT ACTION GAME with great gameplay and great presentation. Ninja Theory did an excellent job, aesthetics wise, and with the cinematic and in-game storytelling (as opposed to the storyline, which you could argue can be somewhat silly. Though I don't mind it at all. The whole plot is coherently an amusing play on who Dante is: a rebel, a son, a brother, a person of two extreme opposing halves, a spiritual entity who can see the world split by truth and lies... all that stuff) .
Most importantly, the gameplay is excellent. It's slick, satisfying and the combat system is flexible enough that it allows you to execute combos and strings of moves as crazy as you want to be.
Set next to DMC4, this is a huge jump in terms of storytelling, game direction and gameplay. Compared to this DmC, the older games felt a lot like just random things happening to Dante/Nero while they run around random worlds. In contrast, DmC is put together really well.
And Ninja Theory took the best elements from the Devil May Cry games (a bit of platforming, a bit of exploration and finding secret stuff, a lot of combos and monster-to-attack-type strategies, cheezy one-liners), then took out a lot of the fat. In my book, this makes DmC a great Devil May Cry sequel.. or prequel... or reboot... or spinoff... or whatever it actually is.
That said, it's true that the bosses tend to be a lot easier compared to the older Devil May Cry games, but it's partly because the control system and aiming in this game is much more accurate/less frustrating than the old ones where you always tended to be out of weapon range. If you're a fan of the old games and want a challenge, play on Nephilim difficulty.
But the DLC... not that great. I encountered a few bugs while playing it, it's also really rough around the edges in terms of game design (color choices, skill balance, skill behavior, level design, etc). I also think the music is tormenting, which fits the theme of what Vergil's Downfall is about... but it does become something you have to bear with while playing the game, instead of something you could listen to.

I've flirted with the franchise before, playing Silent Assassin, Blood Money and Absolution. I'd seen some negative reviews about this game when it came out - each mostly citing a lack of content. It's hard to want to pay full price for a game that isn't full content, right? I picked it up on the winter sale, because I loved Blood Money, and played through Absolution (a little grudgingly). What I found was the most pure Hitman game I've yet encountered.
Usually in the series, there are 4-5 paths to take out a target. The paths are usually relatively separate, and it becomes fairly clear the sequence of actions you have to do to (for instance) strangle the target or poison them. In this game, however, I can't even name all the paths for a single mission. To say that the maps are huge is doing injustice to the word "huge". Every map is filled with criscrossing paths, patrols of NPCs, scripted interactions that you're highly likely to miss (but which provide ideal openings for an assassination), and dozens (plural) of ways to approach the mission. And best of all, the different ways to complete missions are far from mutually exclusive. Even something relatively straightforward like poisoning a target might have a few different poison locations, disguises needed to pull it off, and points at which the poisoning could happen. A good amount of missions have multiple targets, so you can combine the many ways of assassinating them.
And every mission is like this. With the exception of the tutorial mission, they're all packed to the brim with content. I'm sure that there's a handful of "perfect" ways to complete each mission, and that there's a certain "max" you can achieve. But unlike previous games, that "perfect" execution isn't probably even 10% of all the possible ways to do it. And in past games saying something like that would be code for "oh, you can just go in guns blazing, that counts, right?", but in this game, all those possible paths to completion are pretty stealthy, not usually involving extra casualties.
Look, I could go on. But I think the point is made - this game has a ton of choice and content. It's the best Hitman yet, as far as I can see. If you're an old acquaintence of the series like me, pick it up. If you're new and want to see what all these greybeards are on about, pick it up.

Graphics in this game are breathtaking, whether it be witnessing a beautiful sand covered city to the gunfire and grit in those streets. The only slight complaint i'd have would be the gore, as it felt a bit needless at some moments, yet lacking in others.

"One of the greatest games ever made."
That's what I said about Vice City and that's also what I think about San Andreas.
The game is set in the nineties in a fictional state called San Andreas. You play the role of Carl Johnson (CJ), who has been living in Liberty City. But then he got a phone call. His mom was killed by a drive-by. He rushes home to Los Santos to do honour to his mother. Back at home he has to put in work for his hood. A cycle of violence begins: drugs, gang wars, corrupt police... Welcome to Los Santos!
What GTA San Andreas delivers is classical GTA gameplay with many improvments:
- the huge world with 3 different cities, smaller towns and varying environments like desert, farmland, forests, hills
- an amazing shooting and movment system compared to Vice City
You can duck, swim, dive, climb on rooftops etc. Which gives you a new feeling of freedom
- there is even a bigger variety of vehicles: bikes, bicycles, sport cars, SUVs, pick-ups, boats, helicopters and planes!
- customisation: tattoos, clothes, hairstyle, tuning cars
- RPG elements: you have to eat, you can level up skills
- many details and mini-games: robbery, basketball, video games, billard etc.
- amazing music: especially rap music (nwa, 2pac, ice cube, eazy-e), but probably not as good as Vice City's music
The story of GTA SA is okay, but sometimes confusing and hard to follow. I also think that parts of it are a bit over the top. However Rockstar Games did a good job connecting the story of Vice City, San Andreas and GTA 3. They also did a good job with the characters.
Some of the missions are a bit annoying, but overall the missions are very good. I really like the addition of stealth in some of the missions.
Rockstar added a lot of details and mini-games, which often made me wonder: "Wtf? You can really break into a house and steal TVs? This game is amazing!" I love such moments.
What I also really liked was the hood part of the game. Getting green shirt, rag and shoes, spray a car in green, call your homies to join you, drive through other gang areas, provoke a gang war... even if the KI is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and could have been improved. Of course it's a matter of taste and actually not the whole game is about the hood life.
Conclusion:
GTA San Andreas offers so much content, that everyone will get countless hours of fun out of it.
If you haven't played it yet, go get it now or you'll miss a part of video game history!

I have mixed feelings about this game. One on hand, I had a blast, on the otherhand, I stopped playing the game due to a few fatal and poor gameplay decisions by Rockstar. The car handling and mechanics are fine, although depending on the car they can become very crappy especially in nicer cars which spin out anytime you try to turn them. The flying controls are attrocious, almost undoable with a keyboard, the worst flying controls I've ever seen in a video game. Worst, you are FORCED to do the flying school missions, and worst, the game lacks controller support so it's impossible to play the game with a controller which could help flying siginficantly. This game is a pretty poor port all around, locked at 30fps (unlocking it screws with the physics) the draw distance is incredibly low, cars spawn a block away from you. The keyboard controls suck and require rebinding to get them playable. The default mouse settings are unplayable, you need to set the "fly with mouse" and "drive with mouse" and "invert mouse" all to off, otherwise the mouse wont work at all.
The story is fine, the missions (for the most part) are fun and engaging, but the game's controls lack polish and Rockstar's instance on forcing you to do everything (flying, racing, swimming, ect) gets in the way of having fun as some of what Rockstar has in the game isn't very fun, and will make you want to rage quit.
Can I reccomend this game? No, sadly. I've enjoyed my 40 hours in San Andreas, but I will forever look back on the game with a sour taste due to the incompitence and ignorance of Rockstar.

Don't let my 12 hours of gameplay fool you. In addition to the campaign, I've spent 25 hours im multiplayer, and over 95 hours in zombies mode.
I've loved most COD games, especially the Modern Warfare series and World At War - BO2 triology. BO2 is the only futuristic CoD game that has a very positive rating on steam, and there are several good reasons behind that.
After playing the campaign twice, although the setting is different, the feel of the first Black Ops has been kept. New and efficient guns, plus the fan favourites from the first game like the AK47, Galil and RPD. New military technology plays a part in the game; rather than being just a couple of non-playable first-person cutscenes showing off gloves or wings, the player can sometimes take control of Armoured Ground Robots and Drones just to name a few, which changes the experience of the campaign without changing the feel. There is nothing more satisfying than making an enemy take a face full of energy from your trusty Galvaknuckles.
You can see how much effort has been put into the campaign alone, from the branching storylines, to the introduction of strike force missions that change the way us gamers complete objectives. We also get a more rounded conclusion of the characters' stories from the first Black Ops. The old missions sandwiched between the new missions give us vital storytelling details, while serving as a contrast that the characters from the first game like Mason and Hudson are in a time long gone, and a new generation (literally, Mason's son) must take over and fight. Most importantly, the game reflects a future that is becoming more and more real to this day. Drones, and the economic war over Rare Earth Elements.
I have to praise a specific mission where you play as the antagonist himself. Rather than serving as a mere rage-only charge and fight, it shows us what the antagonist's motivations are, and nudges us a little in the way of empathising with him.
Multiplayer plays out fast-paced and gives players a variety of experiences. Players have many options to customise their own class with their unlocks and this also varies their playing style. I haven't met the best players online, but if you get tired, there's always bots and custom games. Playing 1v1 on a party games custom playlist has been one of my best times yet. Nuketown 2025 returns as a bonus map and this is the one map along with Hijacked that have rapidly become the automatic choice for players, earning its own 'Nukejacked' playlist.
Zombies mode is perhaps the mode that is most praiseworthy. It may be useful to state that I have bought both the Nuketown Zombies map and the Season Pass, which offers me four main maps, Die Rise, Mob Of The Dead, Buried and Origins. I have never seen a game universe or story more defined than Black Ops' Zombies mode, and almost four years on from the game's release, we are still discovering new things about the Zombies universe. The shipped in-game map Tranzit may have been unpopular among the community, with its tedious and seemingly useless mechanisms, lava, disgusting colour scheme, but the broken-up Tranzit map, split into three mini-maps of the Bus Station, Farm and Town still offer players some varied gameplay. Trust me, Treyarch learnt fast from their mistakes and the remaining 4 maps that came with the DLC's or Season Pass really made from a good time. Die Rise takes us to high-rise and overturned skyscrapers in China, Mob Of The Dead brings us 4 prisoners in Alcatraz who formulate a plan to escape, although things turn out different from expected, Buried takes us to an underground mining town in Angola, and Origins, which many regard as the best map from World At War to Black Ops 2, takes us to a diselpunk recreation of World War 1.
Zombies is a unique gamemode and no other game feels like it. When starting out, you will die on low rounds, but when you get the gist of it, you will get much better. There's a learning curve to this mode, as well as individual strategies on each maps, along with a slight tinge of luck involved, but practice makes perfect.
At the moment, the Season Pass gives you 4 DLC packs for little over the price of 3. Coupled with the unique gameplay of each 4 DLC maps and how they all offer new and chilling experiences, it might be worth it if you're going to be spending a lot of time in Zombies mode (the DLC packs come with 4 multiplayer maps each, and the maps are pretty good, but I can't find DLC playlists in multiplayer servers). Nuketown Zombies is sold separately, and well, it's a tediously hard map, definitely not for beginning players, but it will help you get better at Zombies in general.

TL;DR I'm pretty biased for 2-d games that are either fighters or platformers. That said, this game is great. I really like games where every death is entirel your fault. You can see what's ahead of you. There's no surprises. The game also has a great way of rubbing your face in all your mistakes in that, every death is played back in series when you do finally complete the level. There are definitely better platformers in my opinion, but this game is among the top 5% easily. 9/10 game.
There's something to be said about making a platformer. The idea isn't terribly difficult. You get a buncha sprites and give them properties on their ability to interact with the player whether that be by being a temporary platform or a spinny killy thing. This game defintely delivers both. It's a platformer in like the most pure sense of the genre. There are no powerups for you to use, instead, everything is laid right in front of you. It's just you vs the level you're on. No surprises, no gimmicks, no ability to fly over the level with a cape, no shooty thing to kill enemies, just pure jump and run.
I mean, sure, there's totally wall jumping too, but that's about it. Controls are pretty simple. Hold a button to run, press directional buttons to move, press a button to jump. That's it. Something about the controls being so simple is pretty appealing considering there's so many levels where they force you to do unique things with so few inputs.
The music is pretty ok. It's certainly atmospheric, but it's not something I'd listen to all the time. The game sounds are pretty good though. The squish from running as a juicy meat boy is pretty interesting.
I kind of have trouble explaining why platformers are good because there's just this inherent bias in me toward platformers. I mean, I can tell you which platformers are bad, but I haven't actually played bad ones. Well, actually, I Wanna Be The Guy is bad, but the fact that it's bad is considered a novelty so people generally think it's good or something. This platformer isn't bad. It's really simple and has just enough difficulty to be engaging. That's the only way I can really sum it up. I like difficulty.

Ori and the Blind Forest: Definitive Edition is basically the same as the original:
It has gorgeous visuals, fluid control, heart-warming story and perhaps one of my favourite OST in a game. I rarely play any game twice, but Ori strongly earns replay value. It was that of a masterpiece.
BUT I need to warn a couple of points for interested / new Ori gamers
1. New areas for only Definitive Edition is easily accessible after obtaining first skill, however the difficulty level is quite high at that time and should be explored after finishing Ginzo Tree. Do not access new areas too soon. Basically if you stumbled across any area and find it too difficult, come back with stronger Ori.
2. The first chase. That part is either make or break for players, and possibly what half of negative reviews pointed out. If you’re interested what it’s all about, there is a section where players must run and perform rapid & perfect set of skills with almost no room for error. That particular part, is the reason many reviewers voted the rating down with “rapid difficulty curve”. If developers took that particular section out, then really there’s no rapid difficulty.
I loved that chase. On the original game I tried a hundred times, anger in frustration & swearing at myself. Then eventually after completing it I put my controller down and gasped for air. To me it was the most challenging and memorable part of Ori and the Blind Forest.
I understand it will put some population off, holding me off to say I recommend this game to EVERYONE. If you are casual gamer, or hating to die hundreds of time then this game may not be for you. Otherwise for Definitive Edition you can play/change difficulty level to easy and add a checkpoint in the middle of escape.
As far as rating goes, the original edition is 9/10, losing a point due to lack of quick teleportation, no difficulty settings and unable to backtrack certain areas. In Definitive Edition they have addressed all three, earning a full 10/10. Well done, Moon Studios.

(TL;DR) Exelent game for plataform players. Great for anyone and even more attractive for indie fans.
Before I start I need to tell that most of my playtime is on offline on all my games (I mean, all that can be played on offline), so I have probably more than 50 hours into this and due to some problems I got not all the achievments, despite had completed the game a dozen times with all the conditions to get.
Ori and the Blind Forest : Definitive Edition set up my hype to the sky aroud two or three years ago, when shown on Gamescon 2014, and unlike most indie games that look amazing but lack a clear meta or deep gameplay (looking at you Owlboy).
This game instantly present you with a interesting grow curve and a skill tree that you will only understand in depth when you finish the game and try a speedrun or no death run. As the kid you are on the game you know nothing that is about to come and a big part of the game is based on discovery and exploration, but you don't need that if you want to just rush the whole game.The puzzles are simple but require a certain amount of photografic memory or just a nice knowledge of the mechanics.
The history can be pretty simple but deep in meaning and feelings. Mostly of the history is shown by the scenario, and it plays a huge part on atmosphere. One of the golden shots this game should present is how the music, the audio efects and the scenario are so well bound together that you really fell the diference between a dark swamp and a deep valley, even if the main cliches of these areas are quite similar ( lack of heat, low light, gross enemies, water, etc).
The background and the real ground are really well bound, so you don't feel like you're playing Grand Chase, where you see a plataform and the background don't even explain why this♥♥♥♥♥♥floats. Again, the music plays nicely and if not entirely orchestral, at least a nice part of it is. The lack of music in some parts is not a mistake, is a class of ambient creation and resources management. The cracks on the ice make you fell cold, as well as the little grass sound show you the mood of the place.
The combat system is extremely simple and this just contribute tho the type of game. Hardcore outplay possibilites in combat are not what Ori would do or aim to. Even so, the whide range of skills you adquire ( even more on Definitive Edition ) are quite unique and can be used in sync to maximize the power of the forest hope(you). The game don't tell you that the area is hard, because it's aways on your level  ( one exeption if you are a explorer as I am ). The game guide you
beautifully through the areas and when you come back to get hidden points you can seen how you've grown up as a player and in power. This piece of art reward you for beeing creative and let some really nice extrategically well placed rocks so you can "Cheese" some jumps or enemies.
I've finished the game 100% and am abble to tell you about every area and enemy, how to solve the puzzles and what powers can do what in synergy. The game is memorable and, on Definitive Editon even more, pretty deep in a lot of moments. Also, DE took away some problems and the game should be Bug free to anyone ( unless you search for it to speedrun or something like that).
This is a must buy if you like plataform gaming like Super Meat Boy, who let's you find some amazing ways to aproach the same situation. Is a must buy if you like gorgeous artwork and atention to the players. If you have any problems with the run of the game you can be sure the game makers will help you,as they did to me. Is probably the best "New Classic" game of the last 10 years,side by side with other great indie games, who try to delivery you amazing experiences by the game inself, not by hats or extreme violence/boobs/pointless maps or anything like that. I will aways love these guys for this huge game they gave me and all the other players. If they release another game, I will buy, and will play,and will be pretty happy to say the game is another masterpiece. If it sucks, I will tell as well. Because even someone who don't know anything about gaming design like me can have some ideas that might be wrong, but might as well help the big guys out there to plain some things better.

Let's be honest here.
This isn't DMC5. But that game would never have been made anyway.
What it is is an easier, more accessible DMC game. Some parts of it are dumb, some parts of it are bad, and some parts of it are great, and ingenious.
If you have the rocks to give it a chance, and stop comparing it to what could have been, you might just be suprised by quite a few of the tricks DmC has. At the very least, the environments are something everyone should see at least once, and the combat, while much more basic then that of the previous entries, is still interesting enough that it'll keep you going to the end.
And if you are one of those unlucky people who could never get in to the old DMC games, someone who picked up DMC3 and got rocked by Cerberus, someone who couldn't even beat Dante in DMC4, and couldn't understand what others saw in DMC1, well, you'll probably enjoy this game quite a bit. It's more complex then most action games these days are, and has enough interesting ideas to make it worth it.
I originally refused to give this game the time of day. A friend convinced me otherwise, and I'm glad he did. This isn't the DMC5 I wanted, but it's a good step in the right direction from a studio who just started dabbling in the franchise. Even though I doubt it'll ever happen, I'm anxious to see what they could do going forward, if they manage to understand the mistakes they made.

Feral Interactive has done a fantastic job porting Mad Max over to Linux, and the addition of Vulkan only enhances what was already a great port.
As Linux is such a diverse network of distributions, I feel I need to mention what I'm running so fellow Linux users can better understand where my experiences are based. Throughout I have used Arch Linux as my distro. Hardware wise I started off with an Intel CPU with a Nvidia 1080 using Nvidia's proprietary drivers. I eventually I joined team Red, and I'm now using a Ryzen 7 1700 with a Radeon RX Vega 64 using open source drivers.
I will not go into spoilers but instead, focus on the port quality as I feel for Linux gamers the quality of the port is as important as the gameplay.
The port is very well optimized, and I found the experience to be very similar to what Windows gamers have shown in their benchmarks. Optimization of this level is a rare occurrence among Linux gaming community. It's hard not to notice the high frame rates and almost complete lack of spikes/stutters in the gameplay.
The world is your standard fare open-world game, full of minigames to keep you busy as you progress through the story. The thing is Mad Max would go unnoticed in the Windows market as open-world role-playing games are rather abundant. However, the Linux market is somewhat starved when it comes to open-world role-playing games let alone good ones.
If you're a Linux gamer, who likes open-world role-playing games and wants something that is less fantasy and more gasser head madness broken up with Batman Arkham style combat. Then Mad Max might be just what your brain is looking for when it comes to shutting down, enjoying the explosions and guzzoline.

While I have not progressed terribly far in this game, I cannot in good conscience recommend it. I did not go into this expecting much, and the mechanics, animations, and sound design are really good and solid (with minor exceptions). However, there were frequent times I found myself wrestling with a spazzy, undecisive camera that would swing around wildly or get obstructed by foreground objects. Most enemies have very boring ways of defending themselves that come with bright button prompts telling you how to break their guard, and many large enemies have attacks that are unblockable and very troublesome to evade (although the parry and super-counter systems are well-implemented and very satisfying).
I would have still given this a pass, but what broke me was a level where you must fight off stone soldiers while bombs are being dropped regularly into an arena. This would be fine except that the smaller bombs always drop next to you and always explode before you have time to react. It legitimately shocks me that this level went through concept, design, builds, testing, and at any point, somebody -anybody- said "Yes. This level is a good idea to have in our game."
The game is surprisingly high-quality otherwise, and if these issues don't dissuade you, feel free to spend your money. But folks, if you need a great new beat-em-up, just go buy Aces Wild or Double Dragon Neon.

"One of the greatest games ever made."
That's what I said about Vice City and that's also what I think about San Andreas.
The game is set in the nineties in a fictional state called San Andreas. You play the role of Carl Johnson (CJ), who has been living in Liberty City. But then he got a phone call. His mom was killed by a drive-by. He rushes home to Los Santos to do honour to his mother. Back at home he has to put in work for his hood. A cycle of violence begins: drugs, gang wars, corrupt police... Welcome to Los Santos!
What GTA San Andreas delivers is classical GTA gameplay with many improvments:
- the huge world with 3 different cities, smaller towns and varying environments like desert, farmland, forests, hills
- an amazing shooting and movment system compared to Vice City
You can duck, swim, dive, climb on rooftops etc. Which gives you a new feeling of freedom
- there is even a bigger variety of vehicles: bikes, bicycles, sport cars, SUVs, pick-ups, boats, helicopters and planes!
- customisation: tattoos, clothes, hairstyle, tuning cars
- RPG elements: you have to eat, you can level up skills
- many details and mini-games: robbery, basketball, video games, billard etc.
- amazing music: especially rap music (nwa, 2pac, ice cube, eazy-e), but probably not as good as Vice City's music
The story of GTA SA is okay, but sometimes confusing and hard to follow. I also think that parts of it are a bit over the top. However Rockstar Games did a good job connecting the story of Vice City, San Andreas and GTA 3. They also did a good job with the characters.
Some of the missions are a bit annoying, but overall the missions are very good. I really like the addition of stealth in some of the missions.
Rockstar added a lot of details and mini-games, which often made me wonder: "Wtf? You can really break into a house and steal TVs? This game is amazing!" I love such moments.
What I also really liked was the hood part of the game. Getting green shirt, rag and shoes, spray a car in green, call your homies to join you, drive through other gang areas, provoke a gang war... even if the KI is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and could have been improved. Of course it's a matter of taste and actually not the whole game is about the hood life.
Conclusion:
GTA San Andreas offers so much content, that everyone will get countless hours of fun out of it.
If you haven't played it yet, go get it now or you'll miss a part of video game history!

I have mixed feelings about this game. One on hand, I had a blast, on the otherhand, I stopped playing the game due to a few fatal and poor gameplay decisions by Rockstar. The car handling and mechanics are fine, although depending on the car they can become very crappy especially in nicer cars which spin out anytime you try to turn them. The flying controls are attrocious, almost undoable with a keyboard, the worst flying controls I've ever seen in a video game. Worst, you are FORCED to do the flying school missions, and worst, the game lacks controller support so it's impossible to play the game with a controller which could help flying siginficantly. This game is a pretty poor port all around, locked at 30fps (unlocking it screws with the physics) the draw distance is incredibly low, cars spawn a block away from you. The keyboard controls suck and require rebinding to get them playable. The default mouse settings are unplayable, you need to set the "fly with mouse" and "drive with mouse" and "invert mouse" all to off, otherwise the mouse wont work at all.
The story is fine, the missions (for the most part) are fun and engaging, but the game's controls lack polish and Rockstar's instance on forcing you to do everything (flying, racing, swimming, ect) gets in the way of having fun as some of what Rockstar has in the game isn't very fun, and will make you want to rage quit.
Can I reccomend this game? No, sadly. I've enjoyed my 40 hours in San Andreas, but I will forever look back on the game with a sour taste due to the incompitence and ignorance of Rockstar.

tl;dr : Not bad but not as good as it could have been. Choices don't have the impact they should have and are advertised to have.
I will start with a few thoughts to explain what I mean when I say the choices don't make you feel bad as they should (and as it has been advertised) :
- If someone attacks you and you "choose" to defend yourself, and later you realise they attacked you by mistake, you have no reason to feel bad about your choice, since THEY still attacked YOU, so defending yourself was still the right (and logical) thing to do.
- If you have no information and still have to make a choice, you don't feel bad about it because you just couldn't know, you had to pick an option randomly.
- If you can't choose what you actually want to (and what would realistically be possible in real life, but just isn't an option in the game), you don't feel bad about the choice because it was forced onto you.
- When it's obvious that there is no "good" choice, you don't feel bad because you know for a fact that the other alternatives were as bad or worse.
Maybe I'm being too rational about it, but I can't feel bad about a choice I made if I feel like I did nothing wrong. To me the decisions should have involved having enough information to make an educated choice, but not enough to predict every possible outcome, and also a good reason for options to be unavailable (because it's very frustrating to wonder "Why on earth can I not do that ? It just makes no sense !").
You're supposed to be put in "unspeakable situations", but you're not. You just have to choose "do I kill that guy or not ?", "do I strike that area or not ?" and that's basically it. No sick twisted horrible psychopathic situation you would expect when you're told about "unspeakable situations".
You're supposed to make important choices, and feel bad about them, but you dont.
There are not so many story-changing choices, and in some cases there are obvious alternatives that you cannot choose (you just have to go with one of the two possibilities the game forces on you).
Most of the time they don't really make you feel bad or hesitant since you "don't really have a choice" : there are a lot of choices where you have no information whatsoever about the situation, so you don't make a decision, you just pick randomly, and other situations where it's obvious from the start that both possibilities will have the same kind of bad consequences so it doesn't really matter what you chose. There are very few nuanced situations where you have information to make your choice but you can't predict the consequences, either you just pick whatever because you have no info or you just pick whatever because it won't make a difference. And when you realise the consequences you're like "Meh, whatever...".
Only a few choices are actually made (with information to help you make your decision) and have unpredictable consequences. And some of them are cases where the game just wouldn't let you choose an obvious alternative.
The game is not bad. But it's just a generic warfare shooter. Not worth the price (maybe get it on sale), and certainly not worth the hype.

Just to start this review off : I have payed 1$ for 3pack of games including this one (Got a discount by voting in Golden Joystick Awards 2016)
Spec Ops : The Line is a interesting mix of serious war story and dynamic action, all perfectly mixed. Game puts us in a boots of Martin Walker, a Delta Force Operator with 2 companions by his side, Lugo - A highly trained sniper and Adams - M249 wielding support guy equipped with grenades.
One of the most important mechanics of the game is commanding the said two. There are 3 types of commands :
-Stun (Orders to throw a flashbang into crowd of enemies)
-Attack (Orders squad to attack selected target, usually also suppresses enemies close to the target, effective but forces your allies to be more exposed to enemy fire which can end in them being injured)
-Heal (Availabe only if ethier Lugo or Adams happens to get shot too much, then you order the other one to heal the downed one, if both are down you need to come close to revive your allies, its quick tho)
Its not a spoiler, your squad wont be at your disposal all the time, there are a some parts when you are ethier separated or need to cover them, but you can rely on them for most part.
We are being sent to Dubai to investigate a lost 33rd Infantry Division sent there to evac the city after the giant sandstorm which cut the city off and totally ruined it by burying it under tons of sand. Thats all i have to say in department of explaining storyline, cant say more without spoilering, and please dont play this game if you already watched playthrough of it, its not worth it just due knowing more than you should.

Okay, I've honestly never really loved a game quite as much as I've loved this. I've certainly never really wanted to recommend one. If you're looking for something that is somehow based in logic puzzles, existentialism, philosophy, challenge of authority, nostalgia, and deep rooted emotions, look no further. Play Able Black. Somehow, within minutes of play time, I was hooked -- not just hooked, but keenly aware of my own feelings.
The game is on the dark side. It is not a game that makes you feel comfortable while playing. It intentionally unnerves. Still, I think it's very much worth the play.

Able Black is a pretty cool puzzle-story game, where you play as Able Black, an android whose main purpose is passing his Citizenship Exam in order to become designated to help humanity from potential disaster. This is the updated Steam version of the original mobile version of the game.
The way the game is presented is by two parts - the Story part, and the Puzzle-solving part:
- The Story part consists of mainly text. You'll be presented with the story of Able Black and the overall circumstances that lead him to take the Citizenship Exam.
- Then there's the Puzzle part, which consists of stories, imagery and options that you shall pick depending on the question or objective that's being asked for you to do. After solving the Puzzles, the cycle starts over with another Story part and so on.
The Story is, without fail, pretty good. If you're into science fiction stories, where you're given enough space to form your own conjectures until the story proves you what the truth is, then you sure are going to enjoy this. Though it's mostly only text and very few visuals appear, I found myself highly interested in it, wanting more. The few turns and twists that were slowly presented to me, were enough to make me continue all the way to the end. On the other hand, there's the Puzzles.
The Puzzles the game includes are not particularly hard, but they sure are meant to be given a focused line of thinking. You will be given all the information you need, so there's no need to worry about obtuse puzzles. In any case, you will be given hints for each puzzle, so don't be afraid to use them if you get stuck.
Something I need to remark, without trying to give any kind of spoilers: if you do NOT like psychological tests or the feeling of being psychoanalized by the choices you make, then I'm afraid to say this isn't the game for you. The game will present you with moral dilemmas and choices related to the Story and the game will present you with a result/conclusion based on what you choose. If you feel not interested or annoyed by this kind of gameplay, be wary if you still decide to try this game.
I really enjoyed this game, it was a good experience and I highly recommend it. The overall design and presentation the game gives on both the Story and the Puzzles is very cool; even though "simplistic/minimalistic" looking, it works in favor of the game, making it enjoyable and giving it a more polished look, a detail that seems to be overlooked by several indie games.
Though the main story is a bit short (around 1.5 hrs, puzzles included) you still are presented with secrets that you can feel free to explore in the game if you so desire.
This is a very cool little game, and I'm really glad I was able to enjoy as one of the last games of the year. Hopefully it will get more attention!

Kung Fu Stike was a very unexpected blast to play. But be warned it is a very difficult game that wants you to lose. I would not suggest it to gamers that get easily frustrated. So you may be wondering what is this game about? Well it is a weird mix of a beat'em up and a fighting game with a rather cool option to call in reinforcements if you don't mind paying some much needed gold. The story is well....I have no idea what is going on to be honest, but you can safely ignore it without missing much of anything due to its paper thin plot.
The visuals are pretty nice and remind me of Street Fighter 4. The music is nothing memorable but it gets the job done. Pretty much everything is just average in Kung Fu Strike, but where it really shines is in its fast paced, combo centered gameplay. Controls feel nice and responsive, be it in a 3d brawler areana or a 2d boss section. And I love how the crowds of enemies don't just sit around and wait for you to punch them like in the Batman or Dynasty Warriors games. They will attack you from all sides at once rapidly draining your health unless you block or dodge out of the way. This is not a game where you are a overpowered god like character, you are simply a General trying to put down a rebellion and may occasionally need to rely on the help of your comrades if you are not skilled enough at the game.
Still your character is no push over. Deal or take enough damage and you could pull off some special moves that deal serious damage and have a generous area of effect arc to take out the lowly grunts or just get some breathing room when a boss is in the middle of a combo. You can also equip up to three items, from a herb that brings you back from the dead to taking less damage from explosives and thrown weapons. You regain life by picking up rice balls that fly out of a defeated enemy and they may also drop a item that you need to be able to call in for backup.
The game is not perfect though. By far the biggest problem I have with it is that the camera is just bad. Too the point of costing you more than a couple of fights due to it freaking out and spinning all over the place or some object being in front of the camera blocking your view. Another problem is that you cant change the resolution in the option menu but have to go into the game files and set it through a "Config" file. And the last problem worth noting is that alot of the time you require alot of luck. What I mean by that is you can sometimes go a match with the enemies dropping nothing but coins and no other useful items. Makes it quite frustrating when this game is very stingy with its checkpoint system and the overall difficulty.
Overall I would suggest you try the demo before you buy to get a feel for what this title offers. If you enjoy it and dont mind knowing it will get very difficult later on, it will have you addicted and wanting yet another go at that seemingly impossible boss fight. The sweet taste of victory when you finally bring down his health and dive quick him 20 feet through the air is more than enough to warrant the full price of $10 :p

I'm enjoying the Hell out of DmC (pun intended).  It's got some of the most inventive level design I've ever seen coupled with some truly unique art design.  Beyond the aesthetics it's got a great fighting system that can be a bit challenging to come to grips with at first, but allows to pull off some amazing looking combos without resorting to quick time events.  What pulls it all together are some genuinely impressive character  performances.  You're in the middle of an over-the-top comic book style story, yet the high quality facial animation and voice acting result in sincere performances that lend the story more gravitas than you'd think it would have.
All-in-all a simply fantastic character action game and so far the best game I've played in 2013.

Believe it or not, DmC manages to do more for the franchise than DMC1-4 ever did. A much more streamlined but intriguing storyline, intense but more accessible combat, and dynamic level design that make the previous games levels look like boring corridors and arenas make this exactly what the Devil May Cry franchise needed. The storyline, voice acting, and motion capture should also be praised, and while it doesn't have the over-the-top stunts, it humanizes the characters and makes them much more believable, and the script is well-done, especially compared to the Resident Evil-quality of previous installments. My only complaint would be the music. While certainly more varied than the industrial butt-rock of previous games, it just doesn't work for me.
Overall, a solid action game with dozens of hours of content, and plenty of replay value. Great entry point for new fans, and with depth for the older fans. It might not be perfect yet, but this is a good start for redefining Devil May Cry as one of the perennial action franchises.

The PS3 demo is a clunky mess, and a horrible representation of new Dante, and of this game. Do yourself a favor, and get the PC version, which runs at the standard 60 FPS, and allows the game to look as visually stunning as it should. Don't cheat yourself by playing the console version with this one.
Dante (or Dante In Name Only, if you prefer) is a simply obnoxious character, for the first hour or so of the game. However, this quickly changes over the course of the story, which yes, this game has. Is it a great story? Maybe, maybe not, but much like Assassin's Creed 2, the main protagonist starts off as an obnoxious, overgrown teenager, and slowly matures over the course of the game, and while I submit that this game doesn't pull it off as well for me as AC2 or DMC3 did, I didn't find myself wanting to strangle the main character for 40+ hours. Can the gameplay carry itself well for that long? For the average, "beating-the-game-on-DMD-is-good-enough" crowd, yes. TrueStyle Tournament levels of depth? Not really, but fancy enough to be fun. Completely braindead easy? Only if you allow it to be.
Love it or hate it, don't dismiss it. It's something to be checked out. Give it a chance if you love the Devil May Cry series. If the series hasn't appealed to you yet, perhaps consider giving this one a shot.

I'm going to base this review mostly on Zombies because that is what I have played the most and enjoy the most about this Call of Duty. There are spoilers in this review. The campaign is really good. It has intense moments, its emotional moments and its action crazy moments. It’s fun because the action changes and does not repeat over and over. The story sometimes talks about what happened in the past which was not explained in Black Ops 1, some games chapters revert to the past so you are playing in the past. This helps fill the gaps in Black Ops 1 and helps explain some new things in the current campaign. Multiplayer is also really fun. The guns seem to have a nice level of damage so the guns do seem fair. A lot of the maps are great and momentum changes based upon the map you are playing so again it does not repeat. NOTE: there are a few lobbies online that are modded. ZOMBIES!!! Even though I don’t particularly like one or two maps, they are all amazing. Each map has its own atmosphere that suits the map and its lighting. There are some great weapons and some new awesome perks to help you fend off the undead. Some of the buildables in the game are fun to use and helpful in surviving. Each map just as it did in Black Ops 1 features its own unique Easter Egg which continues the story from World at War. It’s fun figuring out the steps towards completion and finding out what happens next. But in doing so makes more questions and anticipation for the next map. In my opinion, Zombies is the best Call of Duty mode created so far and its intricate story like makes it that much better.

+Fantastic presentation, the art is amazing but I'm particularly in love with the music. +Sound design is some of the best I've heard in a 2D platformer and has this deep rumble that gives it a theater-like effect.
+Challenging gameplay and fluid controls, platforming is legitimately tricky sometimes but never unfair.
+The medroidvania-like power collecting makes the game get more and more fun as you play.
+-Decent sense of exploration, though not nearly the largest or most open metroidvania I've played. Length is middle ground, not too short, not too long.

Want to explore the morality of the prison industrial system? If so, this game is for you! Don't want to get into the issues of for-profit-prisons? That's fine too! Design your prison to be efficent with the goal of rehabilitating criminals... or just go all out cruelty with "tough on crime" tactics! The choice is yours! Fortunately, the premise of Prison Architect is matched up with well designed strategy mechanics which challenge you to expand your prison as your budget grows. Reinvest those profits to make even more profit! Or just go all out with sandbox mode where you have unlimited funds. One thing of note, you might want to watch some basic tuitorals in order to figure out how some of the UI works. Simple things like building foundation instead of walls to make an "indoors" area might not be obvious when you first start playing. Other than that, Prison Architect is fantastic!

Almost feels likes it should be in early access there's so much polishing needed to be done. Nonetheless, a satisfying game with a story that expresses the two competing models of crinimal justice, the retribution/deterence and the medical model, mostly competently.
Something almost laughable if it wasn't so tragically accurate was that there was no regulation whatsoever on the placement of family cells and nurseries in female prisons. Whatever your view on criminal justic, you cannot be putting completely innocent, vulnerable children so close and at farily easy access to dangerous convicts. C'mon world.
Buy it, go on. This game delivers everything it promises, and then gives you more. Pack a lunch, say goodbye to your loved ones, and get playing. See you in a week or so...

As a newcomer to the series (and I'm stressing "newcomer"), I found it a very enjoyable game, from start to finish. First of all what impressed me was the fluidity of the combat, and as I progressed and unlocked more abilities it only got better. The weapons are designed with symmetry in mind and they work together in ways that are not only devastating to the enemies, but is beautiful to watch.
The landscapes are truly works of art, psychedelic colors mixing together to form a world that gives you a thrill as you traverse though it. The Demon and Angel pulls are tools which help you navigate the broken, demon populated world (Limbo), and the freedom you enjoy as you zip through the air is a large fun factor too.
I've yet to master some longer combos, but by playing with the training mode I've managed to come up with some that I've found useful - normally I'd try to bring them up in the air or try to bunch them up - and with all the freedom it's fun to come up with new stuff on the fly. Abilities that can be unlocked (there are quite a lot of them too!) give you yet more freedom as you progress as well. Dante spinning with Angel blades like a hurricane/ballerina is simply sexy, hell yeah.
The bosses are very modern looking, as well as really trippy. The soundtrack is amazing as well; the track featured in the trailer - Tommy's Theme by Noisia - is now one of my favorite songs. Combined together some areas simply left me breathless.
Whether it's a title that fits well into the Devil May Cry series I really don't have the right to say, but as a game, it's addictive and I found myself replaying many times just to get that perfect score. Also the Devil Trigger is somewhat overpowered, but so far I've seldom used it.
One bit I don't like about it is how sometimes the dialogue is just weird and without any depth - but it's actually not that bad compared with many other games. The learning curve was great for a newcomer like me, but after the first boss the new enemy types quickly bring more challenge as well as unlocking all the basic weapons.
*Personally this game is one of my top purchases, as a newcomer, but it's extremely true that the difficulty may leave a lot to be desired for older players of the series.

tl;dr : Not bad but not as good as it could have been. Choices don't have the impact they should have and are advertised to have.
I will start with a few thoughts to explain what I mean when I say the choices don't make you feel bad as they should (and as it has been advertised) :
- If someone attacks you and you "choose" to defend yourself, and later you realise they attacked you by mistake, you have no reason to feel bad about your choice, since THEY still attacked YOU, so defending yourself was still the right (and logical) thing to do.
- If you have no information and still have to make a choice, you don't feel bad about it because you just couldn't know, you had to pick an option randomly.
- If you can't choose what you actually want to (and what would realistically be possible in real life, but just isn't an option in the game), you don't feel bad about the choice because it was forced onto you.
- When it's obvious that there is no "good" choice, you don't feel bad because you know for a fact that the other alternatives were as bad or worse.
Maybe I'm being too rational about it, but I can't feel bad about a choice I made if I feel like I did nothing wrong. To me the decisions should have involved having enough information to make an educated choice, but not enough to predict every possible outcome, and also a good reason for options to be unavailable (because it's very frustrating to wonder "Why on earth can I not do that ? It just makes no sense !").
You're supposed to be put in "unspeakable situations", but you're not. You just have to choose "do I kill that guy or not ?", "do I strike that area or not ?" and that's basically it. No sick twisted horrible psychopathic situation you would expect when you're told about "unspeakable situations".
You're supposed to make important choices, and feel bad about them, but you dont.
There are not so many story-changing choices, and in some cases there are obvious alternatives that you cannot choose (you just have to go with one of the two possibilities the game forces on you).
Most of the time they don't really make you feel bad or hesitant since you "don't really have a choice" : there are a lot of choices where you have no information whatsoever about the situation, so you don't make a decision, you just pick randomly, and other situations where it's obvious from the start that both possibilities will have the same kind of bad consequences so it doesn't really matter what you chose. There are very few nuanced situations where you have information to make your choice but you can't predict the consequences, either you just pick whatever because you have no info or you just pick whatever because it won't make a difference. And when you realise the consequences you're like "Meh, whatever...".
Only a few choices are actually made (with information to help you make your decision) and have unpredictable consequences. And some of them are cases where the game just wouldn't let you choose an obvious alternative.
The game is not bad. But it's just a generic warfare shooter. Not worth the price (maybe get it on sale), and certainly not worth the hype.

Just to start this review off : I have payed 1$ for 3pack of games including this one (Got a discount by voting in Golden Joystick Awards 2016)
Spec Ops : The Line is a interesting mix of serious war story and dynamic action, all perfectly mixed. Game puts us in a boots of Martin Walker, a Delta Force Operator with 2 companions by his side, Lugo - A highly trained sniper and Adams - M249 wielding support guy equipped with grenades.
One of the most important mechanics of the game is commanding the said two. There are 3 types of commands :
-Stun (Orders to throw a flashbang into crowd of enemies)
-Attack (Orders squad to attack selected target, usually also suppresses enemies close to the target, effective but forces your allies to be more exposed to enemy fire which can end in them being injured)
-Heal (Availabe only if ethier Lugo or Adams happens to get shot too much, then you order the other one to heal the downed one, if both are down you need to come close to revive your allies, its quick tho)
Its not a spoiler, your squad wont be at your disposal all the time, there are a some parts when you are ethier separated or need to cover them, but you can rely on them for most part.
We are being sent to Dubai to investigate a lost 33rd Infantry Division sent there to evac the city after the giant sandstorm which cut the city off and totally ruined it by burying it under tons of sand. Thats all i have to say in department of explaining storyline, cant say more without spoilering, and please dont play this game if you already watched playthrough of it, its not worth it just due knowing more than you should.
Game is in 3rd person view, very similar to GoW in many aspects, not in a bad way! Movement mechanics are very similar to said Gears Of War, you need to rely on taking cover by pressing space by obstacles and you have an option to vault over them, it may seem awkward to PC gamers, but trust me it really suits the game. Only flaw with this system is sometimes not taking cover right after leaving a cover by "Slip Out" option (Sprinting out of cover) You need to stop before trying to take another cover because otherwise it is likely to dont do anything. Thats just flaw of the whole system, that issue was even in GoW :P
Game offers us a wide array of guns Pistols, Assault rilfes, SMG's, LMG, Shotguns, Snipers, Damn even Rocket Launchers and Drum Grenade Launchers. Most of the guns have additional feature activated by pressing C by default it can be a underbarrel GL, Silencer, Scope, Fire mode etc... Gunplay feels really fun and smooth, Ammo is Scarce in this game because most of the time you end up trading you weapon out because enemies use a diffrent weapon and you are out of ammo, one sure way to get ammo for any gun from any enemy are Executions, just walk to a bleeding out enemy and press melee button , animation will play and you will get some ammo, regardless if its RPG or a pistol. Other way is of course an ocassional ammo box.
Game has 4 difficulty levels, i personally played on 2nd lvl its like normal in most games, yet it was fairly difficult, enemies  dealt significant dmg and took a bit of dmg themselves, especially later on ingame. I did not seen any major flaws with it, they reacted fast, flanked, used nades and did their best to bring you down, If you like challenge play on 3rd one, that one is really hectic :P
This game delivers one of the best single player experiences in shooter genere at least if we are speaking about modern times semi-realistic war setting. Cautiously recommended.
The puzzles are good and get quite tricky, and the graphics are charming.
The mechanics are interesting, and introduced without any hand-holding.
The mix of real-time and puzzle may not to be everyone's taste but I like it.
But it feels quite unpolished in many of the finer details of how things interact:
I've had blocks get stuck in mid-air (after being pushed off my head by a moving platform)
Sometimes fireballs don't kill you
There's no way to viusally distinguish between holding a block over your head and having it balanced on your head
I fell through the world once (level 13, after climbing over the exit in case there was a secret there)
A cat-slime on top of a block seems to weigh a different amount to a block on top of a cat slime for purposes of triggering switches
Animation of blocks controlled by switches sometimes jumps around instead of being smooth.
Finally, I wouldn't recommend it if you have low tolerance for re-doing things - a lot of the time a single mistake near the end of a level will require you to restart the whole level. (Exacerbated by the fact you cannot manually scroll the screen, and there's no way to tell what switches do without triggering them so there's no way to plan out the whole level ahead of time)

Playing this game again after so many years reminded me of why I loved the GTA series in the first place; but it also made me realize what's missing from games today.
I was hyped when GTA IV was first announced, but when I finally had the chance to play it I quickly got bored after a few hours. Sure, getting drunk was interesting; but where was the fun? Everywhere I look I see the defenders talking about graphics. Really, graphics? That's what makes a game great? Sorry, but I don't play games because they look nice. I play them because they are fun. And when you take out the fun-factor, I lose all interest. There are some pretty sharp-looking video games out there. But if their only purpose was to look good, I would rather go to an art museum. There's nothing wrong with good graphics, mind you, but I want something I can sink my claws into.
GTA: San Andreas was, in my opinion, the last worthy installment in the GTA franchise. The new ones don't even come close. It's a perfect example of how a game can both look amazing and play great. It's also a sad reminder of what used to be a cool genre and why we all loved playing it; and why the new games just pale in comparison. The scope of San Andreas is so vast and has so much to do that completing it 100% is akin to resolving an epic life journey. Finding the Holy Grail would be easier, but you wouldn't have this much fun doing it.
There's so many things you can do in this game that I cannot list them all without accidentally leaving something out. I'll give it a try nonetheless. There are the usual vehicle missions that became a staple in GTA; including police car, taxi cab, ambulance and firetruck missions. In addition to these, there are truck driver, pizza boy, and home burlary missions. There's also arcade games, marathons, auto races, gang wars, drive-bys, gambling, billiards, character and car customization, girlfriends, swimming, weight-lifting, exercising, skydiving, and flying.
An extremely long story campaign takes the player to three sprawling districts that were fashioned after major American cities. These are seperated between vast areas of highway, desert and wilderness. All of this provides unlimited exploration for the hundreds of collectables that are hidden on the rooftops, back alleys, or under the waters of the game world. Countless drivable vehicles are also scattered throughout the streets and parking lots. There's so many things that you can pilot or drive that I haven't found them all. The world of San Andreas is so impressive that it even has its own set of urban legends. Witnesses and myth debunkers often argue about the sightings of Bigfoot and UFOs.
When I first played this game many many years ago I became very fond of the bicycle. I would spend long nights just riding my bike around San Andreas and practicing stunts in the Los Santos skateboard park. If I got bored of that I would drive cross country in a stolen car listening to the golden oldies and laughing at the crude humor of the DJs. This is all I would do for hours upon hours. Eventually I would get around to completing the main storyline and the endless side missions, but I will never forget how much fun I had just cruising around in a car or on a bike. Can I say this much about any other game? No I cannot; and sadly, I doubt to be able to again. The fact that this game is still being played and replayed after all these years is a true testament to its longevity and why modern developers should take a flippin' hint on what makes a game fun.

As a person who has been a flight simulator addict for going on three decades now...  ( I cut my teeth on a green screen IBM bootleg copy of Pilot trainer circa 1988 )  I have often been skeptical of the 'ground runners.'  Trains, racing cars and boats all have the same singular fundementle flaw on the virtual stage.  Primarily that no matter how much you REALLY want it to be true, you are NOT going to get a realistic perspective view of ... well ... ANYTHING.  Land and city scapes will always be a generic  reflection of what you just saw and are about to see again.  SO; having established my rational for skepticesm, what am I doing here?  To put it plainly.  I'm cheap and my entertainment budget can be bought.  In short for $20 I got the whole euro-truken-paint joben collection.  You should too, hopefully here is why....
Pro # 1.
It's Europe and there isn't a freken war going on.  Well okay...  Actually about 2 thirds of Europe.  Sans the Balkans half of Italy and 1/3 of Iberia.  If you like Scandanavia.  You are officially S.O.L.  Rather Ironic in fact, considering that no less than half of the riggs you use in this series are models made in either Sweden or Norway.  Back to the point.  See something of the great old country without having to shoot it, dog fight over it or deal with Hitler or Napoleon.
# 2.
Beautifully simple.  Elegantly addictive.  I honestly went into this game with little if any knowledge of truck driving and after 6 hours that passed by like 30 minutes, I not only know something about the actual life style, I can also add that it was fun doing something curiously different than trying to beat a bunch of crazies to a finish line.
The one and only con I can come up with, is that the technology of it's day DOES let it down somewhat.  However; as I mentioned before I got the collection so I expect the second edition to be a bit more advanced.  Not only graphic wise but the over all control experience.  This first one is the best to learn on.  If you can get comfy with this one then you can graduate to more complicated challenges.

Call of Duty: Black Ops II is a first-person shooter developed by Treyarch and published by Activision. It is a sequel to the previous game Call of Duty: Black Ops in terms of storyline.
Call of Duty: Black Ops II gameplay are quite interesting, compared with Modern Warfare series, this one does have improvements over the first Call of Duty: World at War and Call of Duty: Black Ops. The single player campaign are not so linear, the story goes on depends on how or what you do. For example you could decide if you want Alex Mason, the series character, dead or alive in the end. There is also new Strike Force mode in the campaign, which the success or failure of these mode will affect the story. Strike Force mode let's you control a squad, a robot and many assets to complete the mission, but if the player dies, then it recorded as loss and will affect how the story campaign goes. The Zombie mode are back also, with more feature and more weapons to use, and more zombies too.
Call of Duty: Black Ops II graphics are still not as advanced as Battlefield, but it'll do. After all, Call of Duty is not about graphics I think. But it's not that bad. The performances are also great, very smooth and making Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 performances like ♥♥♥♥.
Call of Duty: Black Ops is a good sequel, has real improvements to the Call of Duty series, it's worth it. I recommend this.

Despite having a less than par fanbase and a reputation for releasing the same game every year, Black Ops 2 brings several unique things to the table. For example, the ability to have the campaign play differently each time, and the ability to tame the language and violence you're exposed to during the campaign are both qualities that I believe make BO2 one of the superior installments in the frachise. The multiplayer is also more balanced compared to games made before and after this one, giving newer players an easier time learning the fundamentals (besides point and shoot, of course).
I do recommend taking a look, but I also highly recommend either buying it on sale or buying it on PS/Xbox/Wii U as it is too expensive for a four year old game. For $20 during the summer sale, though, it was a good purchase.

This game is highly recommended from me.
I would describe this game as a throughly enjoyable drive across Europe if you're into driving simulators like this one. You get opportunities to create & own your own trucking company by having your own garage or by owning multiple garages if you're seriously that ambitious business wise, buying a large fleet of trucks, hiring your own drivers as employees & by getting paid an evergrowing serious amount of money (not real of course) from other contracting companies by completing deliveries on time to various delivery spots around Europe.
You're given a chance to do this by taking out a bank loan, which is optional by the way, which is dependable on the amount  of money in your bank balance from your completed deliveries from A to B. Or you can save up your own money to buy stuff for your business instead but that is if you want decision yourself. You can base your company garage from one of a multitude of countries around Europe that are available in the game from the beginning. You can add DLCs to the game to add more countries in it if you wish.
Once you carry out deliveries; you start off doing small contract work to give a stepping stone in building up your reputation as a law-abiding & compentent truck driver. You do have to obey road traffic laws & speed limits in roads of each country you visit in the game otherwise you will be subject to speeding fines & fines for being involved in road accidents along your journey.
While you're driving your truck; you can do things like adjust seats, mirrors, lighting on the outside of the truck. You can also listen to music from your mp3s stored on your computer or by listening to live streamed internet radio stations just by pressing R on your computer keyboard.
The other good thing about this game is that keeps itself contantly updated all the time every time you play it on Steam. You can also add updates from the games official website to update to the latest version but that is entirely up to yourself.
Once you set up your company; make sure you set up an online World of Trucks account for yourself to help gain achievements in that account. You can link both ETS2 & American Truck Simulator in the same account.
I will also say that sadly the game is not saved on the steam cloud. You would have to back up your files on another external cloud service or from an external hard drive or solid state drive to save your progress.
If you're into trucks & into driving games; have a go at this game if you feel you can be successful at it. Happy trucking.

Here lies one serious gem of a game.
It shouldn’t work, it’s a ‘licenced title’ based on a movie franchise which is decades old, however, just as the most recent film managed to capture the imagination of its audience, this game is also very well crafted to deliver a unique experience.
Pros:
- Size of the world
- Sound and visuals (Seriously, the sand storm fronts coming through make for an epic ‘well, let’s see how this goes’ moment)
- Variability of upgrades and other cars to acquire
- Theming throughout the game
- Multiple approaches to take down enemies and their bases mix up gameplay quite well.
Cons:
- Sometimes repetitive tasks (though this isn’t as aggressions as other similar sandbox titles)
- No Multiplayer (though this really fits in with the Plot of the game, I’d have loved the option to wander the wastes with another player)
- I’d have loved a ‘hardcore mode’ where fuel is far more scarce, and scavenging is somewhat more necessary.
The bottom line:
If you like sandbox games, enjoyed any aspects of any of the Mad Max films, and are looking to wander the wastes continuing Max’s legendary tale, this is a game you need to play.

I bought Kung Fu Strike for like $2.49 which is what the game is worth in my eyes. The basic premise is: "Lets make Martial Arts easy." Kung Fu Strike doesn't bother with fancy moves that require the reaction time of a rabid Monkey on Speed but rather hands you the button: "Kick stuff until it dies" and "Punch stuff until it dies" and leaves you off to chain those moves together into one sweet devastating chain of destruction. Now you might think that being able to juggle three enemies midair with your fists and feet of fury makes things to easy but the game takes your desires for challenge into consideration and becomes exponentially more difficult to pull off. That rabid Monkey we left from the combat has gotten cozy with our Parry ability that sometimes is incredibly hard to time right.
All in all: Kung Fu Strike will neither break your keyboard nor your bank and will certainly make you feel like Neo meets Jackie Chan.

Coffin of Ashes reminds me of survival horror in days past, and I'm talkin' old...like Clock Tower or Alone in the Dark. Back in the day when you had to aimlessly wander a scary house while some mysterious psycho stalks your every move; without the game holding your hand and guiding you through every step of the way. Coffin of Ashes can seem unforgiving at times, even cruel in its old school ways. But you will feel a true sense of accomplishment as you gather your wits and use them to the utmost to survive.
The puzzles will really put your brain into cognitive overdrive, sometimes requiring the use of notes (which I'm not complaining about, I love it when games require you to think outside the computer and put pencil to paper to figure them out). I also respect the way the game repurposes common items/sprites/backgrounds in RPGMaker and utilizes them in new and interesting ways. The original art was great as well, adding flavor to cutscenes and helping us to have a more personal connection to the characters. The music and sound effects also help to set the mood perfectly. The protag is adorably deadpan, and it's fun to watch her interact with certain other inhabitants.
There's a twist in it, which I certainly won't spoil, but it adds a different dimension to your perception of the game and how its played. All in all, it was a difficult but very satisfying overall experience. Can't wait to see what comes next from the dev!
