As a latecomer to HITMAN Season 1, I can’t speak to the merits of the episodic format which this game has taken, but when taken in its entirety, HITMAN is an excellent game. Though this season is approaching its end, it’s not too late to enjoy this game, as more online content will continue to be released for a while longer until Season 2 comes out.
A few observations:
HITMAN fulfills your need to eliminate your targets in disguises and methods you never knew you wanted. Have you ever wanted to assassinate someone while disguised as a masseur or a yoga instructor? Ever wanted to drown someone in a toilet or knock someone out with a coconut? HITMAN has you covered.
The great thing about the Story mode is the background storyline that develops while Agent 47 is on mission.  In it, a more threatening plot unfolds, in which he and Burnwood are unwitting pawns in a deadly conspiracy. It feels like a grand spy thriller in the making, and its continuation is something I look forward to in Season 2.
In voice acting, David Bateson reprises his deathly portrayal of Agent 47, while Jane Perry brings a witty Bond-esque English flair to Diana Burnwood.  On the other hand, I found the American and British accents among the minor NPC’s a bit too commonplace, given the variety of locales.  It does break immersion at times, but overall it is not a deal-breaker.
My favorite mode is the Elusive Target, a time-sensitive contract that pops up every couple of weeks, and permanently disappears when the contract expires or when the mission ends in success or failure, with no do-overs.  As a latecomer, I’ve only played one Elusive Target mission so far, and I was immediately hooked.  It’s disappointing that I won’t be able to play previous Elusive Target missions (especially the Gary Busey one), but future updates to HITMAN Season 1 are planned in the new year, at least until Season 2 comes out.
Overall, my experience with HITMAN Season 1 has been extremely positive, and has made me a likely early adopter for Season 2.  Here’s hoping that IO Interactive can keep this momentum going.

I have now played the entire game through once as well as most of the challenges and side-missions.  I am now about half way through playing the game for a second time as well as having since purchased several of the add-on head-hunter missions and ultimate vault hunters upgrade 2.
If I had to make any criticisms they would be the lack of a basic guide to how the backpack works, how level-ups and badass ranks are worked etc.  I think I reached level 7 or something before I figured out how to use them, as for customizations, about a quarter of the way through my second game(but since it is mostly first person whats the point), I also did not understand a few other things but perhaps I am just slow. The gameplay is still quite similar to the last 4, but this time you have an array of different things to do in different rooms and only one of the rooms is survival related. To any fans who wantted the classic gameplay, there is the custom night, which is unlocked by beating the unfairly difficult fake ending and by completing the tedious minigame. The custom night is like the classic FNAF formula, but each character has their own (completely different) behaviour, which does add to the replayability. The custom night also adds on some lore to the game. Despite all this, the game still has strange problems like you not actually being able to edit the animatronics in the custom night and a lack of an options menu. If you are a fan of FNAF, you'll enjoy this game, if you hate FNAF, you won't, if you want to try out a horror game, give this a go, this is clearly the best one since the first and it's clear that Scott Cawthon is starting to head back in the right direction.

Open-World Action-/Racing-Game developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games on the 26th October 2004 for Sony Playstation 2,and on the 7th June 2005 for Microsoft Windows and XBOX.
The Story is set in the State of San Andreas,which is based on Areas of California and Nevada,with the three major cities
(Los Angeles),
(San Francisco) and
(Las Vegas).
The Main Character,the African-American Carl '
' Johnson,returns to his old hometown Los Santos after five years of living in the fictional city Liberty City(A city that also appears in several other parts of Grand Theft Auto,such as GTA 3,GTA Vice City,where it only gets mentioned by the main character Tommy Vercetti, and GTA 4). After an Introduction Sequence CJ gets to meet several old contacts such as his older brother Sean "Sweet" Johnson,his sister Kendl Johnson,and his old gang mates Ryder and Big Smoke. Several plot twists bring CJ to the cities San Fierro and Las Venturas,where he does Missions for several old and new contacts.
The player starts with getting dropped off in a district of Los Santos.In the beginning the Player has to do a few Missions first to unlock all the World's content such as clothing shops,hairdresser's,tattoo and gun stores,restaurants and tuning garages. After unlocking the whole content the player is able to find the mentioned features all around the map.
With playing the Story missions,the player starts to unlock more of the map,such as the countryside around the cities as well as the cities San Fierro and Las Venturas themselve.
The player can travel through the world of San Andreas by using cars,bikes,motorbikes,boats and later even helicopters and planes.
For fighting,the game offers a big amount of guns and other weapons that can be found all over the map or bought at one of the several gun stores.
The game also includes several minigames such as races,lowrider competitions and dance contests.
The Game's World attracts the player with a realistic,plausible setting and map.
Eleven Radio Stations can be heard while riding a vehicle,also players can do their own radio by dragging mp3-files into the user files.
- Funny and addicting gameplay
- Huge,beautiful and interesting map
- Cool characters
- Interesting story about betrayal, family and the Drug War between Gangs
- Huge amount of weapons
- Sometimes weird and unplausible moments in story
- Car and motorbike stearing got much worse than in the prequels
- Irritating Minigames
Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is a funny,addicting Game which has a huge amount of content and is absolutely worth buying. Although it sometimes has it weak moments,most of the time it is awesome to play!
Rating: 90/100
The stearing of cars,motorbikes,etc. gets better the longer you drive em'(driving skills improve with time spent riding the different types of vehicles),but without cheats it takes a while to get 'pro' on driving a car!

"He who fights monsters must remember not to become one"
That quote can summerize Fresh Body, a unique concept not in the genre that it is itself, but how it executes it
Fresh Body is a rouge lite game thats very similar to Nuclear Throne, precisely the post apocalyptic feel, needing to find portals to the next room, and being a mutant. But not in a convention  sense, it's map structure and special rooms are very similar to Isaac
Where the game differentiates however is that it takes a Kirby element to a more creative, albiet slightly more morbid, approach
As you kill mutants and other ghouls or monsters, aside from dropping items, they will also literally at times drop body parts, these are unlocked once you picked them up (they are then added to a monster encyclopedia) and each body part of different monsters literally alters how you not only look, but how you play (body parts can be switched with ease)
You get a bag (which serves as a body part focused inventory, an actual inventory for other non body part items is seperate) and a combination of parts can affect every aspect of you, from special abilities such as a rotating severed monster head that can regenrate health when touching foes, to shooting eyeball bullets from your stomach, to causing mini explosions where you are facing as a mini bomb attack, to more simple things like jumping in particular manners (hoppinh, leaping etc) or just a speed boost with movement, these body actions recharge over time
The idea of quite literally becoming the monster you fight is an interesting concept, espcially because  a reason to replay old worlds/bosses is to get their different body parts
You also have a hub world that implements half of the rouge lite elements. That half focuses on you using materials and money you find during runs, some of the upgrades include the following
A converyor belt that allows you to start runs with some freebie usable items, the more upgrades, the better quality
A body part inventory expansion-self explanatory
A repair bench (as you use body parts, they eventually "rot' after so much use, and you can throw them away to get a secondary currency, which will be mentioned later in the review)
A freezer, to preserve body parts until you need them or want to use them
These are just some of the examples of the games hub upgrades
The other half of rouge lite elements comes in the form of secondary currency, that currency being serums, which are then used to buy permanent character upgrades, they are bought from a cop you can find during runs, and as you upgrade yourself, as expected things get more expensive but have better benefits, these can range from simple max health expansions to increasing percentages of critical hits or elemental attributes being added to some attacks (as some examples)
You can also use money and serums for other things like put them in an atm (at the hub or during runs) because if you die, you lose everything you had on you except body parts you were holding and "wearing" but if you keep things in the atm, you can save up serum or coins for another run and buy something expensive, as long as you dont die, or save up money and serum for a hub upgrade
Other things include trading serums to unlock body parts (which are located in demon rooms, similar to Isaac) paying money to gamble at a wheel of items style game, with benefits and drawbacks, or go to the shop room to buy items, you can even pay a woman to kiss you and heal you, or sometimes she can hurt you, and a nurse can be paid to throw potions your way (or sometimes a carrot, potions are better than food, but those girls are examples of gambling)
Despite the game being weird in the concept of doing things like talking to a cop to upgrade your character, girls to heal or hurt you, and that the developer's may not know english that well (mistranlations) and maybe a weird/confusing vibe you might get from the game at first, don't let those fool you or discourage you
With great controls, an innovative concept, and solid gameplay and a somewhat confusing, but still understandable and interesting story, Fresh Body was a risk I took, but a great one, and I hope the game gets more attention

This game is amazing!  I was talking massive amounts of♥♥♥♥♥♥about this game from every little bit that was being revealed up until the actual release, but I decided to pick it up because the original creator of the first DMC game was vouching to give Ninja Theory's attempt at the series a shot.  Another thing that pushed me was that a certain someone was threatening that they were just going to buy the game for me if I didn't pick it up myself, and I really hate it when people waste money on me, so.......
As of right now, I've only played about two hours, and would be playing more if it wasn't 4 AM my time!  I thought the dubstep would really detract me from enjoying the game, but you don't really notice the music most of the time while you're trying to dodge/parry/strike at enemies.  The weapons that I have are really fun to use, as they are all extremely varied.  Sometimes it gets a little confusing, as I'm not used to having so many options to dispatch enemies in a game!  It's only going to get worse as I upgrade my weapons to maximize my combos.  I've been playing on the normal difficulty, as I figured easy would be too easy, and hard might be a bit much considering I have never been 'great' at action games like the DMC series.  I haven't died yet, although I've come extremely close during boss fights!
I personally don't like the look of new Dante, but I think my game came with a preordered bonus skin to make Dante look like his old self, and I'm really happy they included that with the game!  He still reverts to his old self during cutscenes, but it doesn't really matter that much as I don't really care about the story (since it seems really dumb).  The combat is really the highlight for me, and I'm really surprised at how well-made this game is considering it's out for console systems as well.  One of my IRL friends told me that they actually designed the game for PC (as the framerate is actually capped on the console version), and I would believe them considering how smoothly the game is running on my 2-3 year old machine!  I'm running everything at max with vsync@120hz and have only noticed tearing during some cutscenes, although that's incredibly minor (since the game runs pretty flawlessly during actual gameplay).  The environment is absolutely stunning from what I've come across thus far, and I'm excited to explore more of the game later!  I haven't even unlocked every available weapon yet, so I'm extremely excited to experiment with what combos I can create using all the techniques and weapons are available.
I think this game is going to be really great just from judging what I've played so far, and I'm really happy I was wrong about how horrible I thought this game was going to be after following its development for so long.
As someone who has never completed a Devil May Cry game before, I'm happy to say that I'm having a blast playing through this one, and fully plan to beat this (eventually)!  Pick this up if you're looking to have fun with an action game!
Also I'm playing this with a 360 controller, so I have no idea how different it would be on keyboard/mouse!!  IF YOU PLAY GAMES LIKE THESE ON PC, YOU SHOULD REALLY INVEST IN A WIRED 360 CONTROLLER (if you don't have one by now).

Ori and the Blind Forest may not have been completely in line with my personal tastes, but there's too much it has done right not to give it massive amounts of credit.
The game is virtually as polished and well put together as a 2d can. I'd go so far as to say that Ori sets a new standard for what a 2d Metroid-esque platformer should be like. At first, the art and gameplay feels a lot like Dust: An Elysian Tale from a few years back, but Ori takes advantage of its available resources to go the extra mile, combining a gorgeous art style, fluid animation, and an excellent sound track to bring the forest to life.
Then there's the controls. As with a lot of games with a ton of powerups, it can sometimes get hard to keep track of which button does what once they all come together, but fortunately Ori does have nice, responsive controls to keep the player feeling like they're the ones in charge, even if there's perhaps a few too many buttons once the game really gets rolling.
Level design is succinct and to the point: puzzles aren't so easy that they don't take a few tries (especially reflex-centric puzzles), but neither are so difficult that one would feel compelled to look up a guide - all the objects to solve a puzzle are always in the same room as you, save for the occasional bonus power up which may require an item you don't have yet (or may simply be cleverly hidden).
The difficulty is adjustable. I started on Hard and felt like I had a solid challenge; Ori lets you save nearly as much as you like ('saving' actually drains energy, an in-game resource), so if you do wish to make it even more difficult on yourself, you do have the option of simply using less save points, though be warned as Hard really is Hard. For the hardcore, there's even a one-life mode, but given the game's emphasis on exploration and penchant for the occasional bottomless pit, it's recommended you know what you're getting into.
Last is the storytelling. Though personally the content wasn't my cup of tea (again, that's personal taste), the way it is told in is hard to fault. A pleasant intro, a few cutscenes right where they need to be, and a near-silent storytelling style which is almost completely unintrusive make Ori a joy to listen and watch.
Overall, highly recommended, even if you're like me and don't much like 2D platformers. Make the exception: Ori is worth it.

A good, but not great, open world game that went above my expectations for a Mad Max game, but still with its shortcomings. I can recommend this game to both fans of the movie series as well as fans of the open world genre.
PROS:
+ Large open world for players to explore
+ Lots of activities for players to take part in, with great diversification amongst them. You won’t find yourself doing the same thing twice in a row, unless you choose to.
+ All activities are rather fun, and there is something for everybody. Races, outposts of different varieties, and difficult “top dog” camps that will challenge even the best players.
+ Unlike a lot of open world games (I’m looking at you, Ubisoft) many of the side activities feel like they have meaning in the world, and all offer useful benefits. Similar to, but not perfected like the Witcher 3, you feel like you are getting something out of doing the side missions other than resources or XP.
+ Combat system is essentially identical to the one found in the Batman Arkham games. If you’ve ever played one, you’d know that that’s a great thing. Combat is easy to get used to, but still requires some strategy even in latter portions of the game.
+ Lots of upgrade options for Max. You can upgrade Max’s physical abilities, his gear, as well as his car extensively. Moderate replay value to be had here alone.
+ All gear and upgrades are implemented well into the game. You will not likely find yourself crafting something that sounds appealing, only to later have it be useless.
+ Good/Okay story. There are a few plot points that slightly confused me (maybe I wasn’t paying close enough attention, but hey I can follow Kojima’s insane stories in MGS.) Overall the story is engaging, but not surprising in any way. For such an open world game, the story follows a linear path with no surprises throughout.
+ Story missions themselves are all fun and diverse. I didn’t really find myself doing the same thing or same few things at all in this game. This was very welcome by me.
+ Side missions (not activities in this case) are unique and all offer different goals, as well as each having their own little “story” for you to follow.
+ True sense of survival as ammo is scarce and must be utilized at opportune times.
+ The game is VERY well optimized for PC’s of any caliber. Running a 6700k and GTX 1080Ti, I did not go under 155 FPS at 1440p at max settings throughout the entire game. A very pleasant experience indeed.
NEUTRAL:
+- I doubt this is at fault of the game, however this is the one and only game in which I have had my video card driver stop working unexpectedly, and force me to close my game. This happened twice during my time with the game.
CONS:
- Despite being pushed to players as something that is important, the driving in this game is both bad and annoying. I was often finding myself frustrated with the lack of control I felt I had over my vehicle, despite upgrading the traction and handling almost all the way.
- On the subject of driving, there are several missions where you are forced to use your car, or an enemy’s, to travel great distances, or win a race. This became extremely frustrating as I kept failing my objective not due to my skill as a player, but due to poor game mechanics I was forced to use.
- There are several side missions that require night to start them, but there is absolutely no way for you to pass time by quickly. Even when you save and exit the game, it will almost always be sunny when you resume. Therefore, you just must find other things to do until it becomes night.
- There are 2 instances in the game where you are forced to buy specific upgrades for your vehicle to create what is essentially an archetype for a specific type of vehicle. However, these upgrades in both instances were worse than what I already had equipped for my car, so I was forced to buy worse components for my car than I had at the time.
OVERALL SCORE: 8/10

I'm going to go through the more technical issues I had with this game, rather than the ones involving the story, since the story has a clear message about it, and I don't want to tread on that.
First off, I rather enjoyed the watercolored art that Freshman Year had, and for some strange reason, very much enjoyed the simple faces on the characters. However, the groping scene, in which is the best I can call it, seemed a bit messy, in which I didn't understand what was going on until the next scene with her being groped by the bouncer. Also, there seems to be no real build up between leaving the bar and the scene itself. Again, it could be a way of showing that these things happen when you least expect them to, but in each scene themselves, you couldn't tell what was happening until after it was all said and done.
Also, one personal pet peeve that most of these games fail to place in, is the feeling of choice. For this story, you have to enter the shoes of the main character so to understand better the feeling of danger that women can face on a daily basis. However, you're strung along, unable to make a choice on what YOU would do in this same situation, taking out the immerson of being a game itself.
Overall, if this was the first game the creators have made, then I believe they have a good jump start in making the dangers to women a more widespread acknowlaged situation. However, in order to do that, a little more work is needed. For a free game, you have nothing to lose when trying it out.
It's short and to the point, but it really sits with you once all is said and done. Don't want to go into detail but with the short play time, I would recommend everyone to experience it.

First of all, i'd only recommend this if you dont mind steep learning curve. I'm gonna start off with the bad stuff and the glaringly obvious first problem is that the game gives you very very little direction. Although i kinda like being left to my own devices, it feels like a lot of basic things you need are pretty hard to find, mining traditionally just simply isn't worth it, as the stuff you really need isn't easy to find just by mining tiles, your best bet is smashing diposits you find in caves, which is kinda tedious to go around and find them. The second huge problem this game suffers from is the UI is terrible, it looks nice, i like all the bags and how they sort themselves depending on what kinda bag they are, but the items are so small that it's hard to find what you're looking for.
Now i'll go on to the good parts, the biggest thing i love about this game might be weird, but i love how great this game controls, all the movement and animations are really smooth and just feel great. And to go along with this game having a steep learning curve, it has tons of stuff in it, loads of stuff to craft and read, but of course this also means that the amount of stuff is kinda overwehlming, there's a lot of stuff with no direction.
Overall, this game plays great and has a lot of content, although you can go through the content rather fast and the dev team seems to be rather slow with how fast they make content for the game. Fighting is pretty basic in this game but it's far from clunky, i feel like melee weapons are just way stronger than ranged, i understand that this is for balance, but running up and hitting them with your sword is way less hastle than crafting tons of ammo and slowely chipping away at enemies, as ranged weapons seem to do less than half the damage of melee.
As for if i'd recommend this, if you love crafting games, i would recommend this, it's a good time sink for just running around fighting, building and mining, the crafting can be a bit tedious with certain recipies needing a lot of small and rather trivial items which seems kinda unneccessary but overall i'd say it's a good game.

Ok, so I picked this up for $7, which is cheap enough in my book that even if it was a let-down, it wouldn't anger me.  I was pleasantly surprised by how well done this game is!  It is a repetitive open-world style with combat similar to Shadow of Mordor.  I approached the game in an organic fashion, focusing only on story missions & distractions that caught my attention at the moment, and I must say that this will be the most enjoyable way to play, unless you are a completionist.
Art design is amazing, especially at maxxed graphic settings.  Captures the visual presentation of Fury Road perfectly, and I lost count of the amount of times I was blown away by post-apocayptic vistas (i.e. driving across a vast expanse of dried ocean-floor, replete with rusted ships half-buried by the sands).
Sound design was executed briliiantly, which is admirable considering you will be listening to your machine's engine for hours.  I never got tired of the sublime roar of the Magum Opus' V6, or the throaty bellow of the V8 as the story progresses.  Music is okay, but I ended up turning it down to increase immersion.  Combat sounds are satisfying with wet bone-crunching strikes, and screams of tortured metal.
Gameplay is solid although a little dated by now, with some strange choices in keymapping.  However, I got used to it by hour 3 and began merrily stomping war boys into dust.  Close-combat is Arkham-style with an array of extra skills that can be purchased to keep it from getting stale.  Car-combat is simply a blast, and truly unique, as we haven't really had anything like this since Twisted Metal.  Car upgrading is rewarding.
Story and characters are classic Mad Max universe tropes, with deranged over-the-top personages with hilariously vulgar names like Lord Scrotus, Rim Jobber, and Stank Gum.  Pacing was good, with a couple twists and turns at the end which kept it from becoming a cookie-cutter plot.
Overall, I'd give it a solid 8/10, and would actually recommend it at its $20 price, considering my first playthrough was 30 hours (focusing mostly on story missions).  It also gets kudos for being a game without microtransactions/lootboxes, and I am a little bummed there is no DLC or hope for a sequel (but you never know).

Terraria is the first steam game that I played and since then, despite having so many more games to play I always find time to start it up and play with a friend every now and then. Terraria is a sandbox game, so you get all the joys of building to your heart's desire, making complex machines that could beat the entire game for you (if you hve the skill and time to build such a thing, some have) and while there is no creative mode like say minecraft you can always hope onto a "hacked" sever and cheat in all the items you could ever want (I recommend maxing health and mana, get a nice set of armor and building accesories, getting the drill containment unit, and all the blocks you want) and if you don't know what you need there is a well-done wiki that can be found simply by googling "terraria wiki".
Now I personally love some aspects of sandbox games but I tend to lack the attention span to play them for very long, the reson this is my most played game on steam though is that there is plently of combat, mining and other things to do with a clear progession as you start killing the first bosses then they get harder, you need better gear so you gather and craft that gear, then you go fight harder and harder bosses, you go to hardmode which adds a bunch of new things to the world once you defeat the wall of flesh boss and so on until you kill Cthulhu or the moon lord as they call him. If that isn't enough for you they have three character difficulties: one where you lose half money on death, one where you lose everything on you on death, and one where it deletes your character on death but does allow you to fly around the world as a ghost before being deleted.
Another great reason to play this game is how easy it is to play with friends on your own private or public server. There isn't some compete obscure bit of coding or a program to install. Simply go to multiplayer, click host game, then invite your friends to the server through steam. It's that simple and it is really fun to grab a friend or two, go voice chat on discord and just play for a dozen hours at a time.

Interesting game. There's really no direction what so ever as far as plot and objectives go, but they're pretty easy to figure out (hint: the plot seems non-existent).
What makes this game fun is the intriguing way that equipment works. You pick up body parts from felled enemies and then mix and match them in a sort of DNA/genetic splicing screen. You have a limited number of inventory slots available (I believe around 15-20), but the only loot drops in the game are attachable limbs so you never really notice the lack of space. For me, that's a nice deviation from the standard loot-hoarding simulator that most ARPGs tend to be.
The game doesn't use the mouse at all for combat. You're stuck purely with keyboard for movement, aiming and attacking. It sounds a little primitive, and in some respects it is, but there's beauty in this game's simplicity. You can create some very interesting builds despite the fact that you've only got 4 active skill slots, and this is made possible because every limb you pick up will have it's own unique statistics and/or accompanying ability.
As far as actual immersion and enjoyment go, I'm definitely having fun so far. The price tag is more than fair; the devs are consistent and in constant communication with their players :) Besides, if you're a fan of roguelight randomgen dungeon crawlers, you'll have a ton of fun here, regardless of the game's amazing community/devs.

The strongest mechanically and yet the weakest story-wise of the Batman: Arkham series, this game is both a thing of beauty and a shame. Combat has been tightened up mechanically, there are a variety wide variety of bosses, and the game is very beautiful...
...and yet, at the same time, feels somewhat hollow. The predator sequences, where you sneak around taking out goons from the shadows, feel shallow compared to previous installments - not because they're worse, but because they are, fundamentally, the same as ever. You have done this before, and there is no real difference between what you've done and what you are doing.
Likewise, the formula with the villians has worn thin as well - you fight the Joker yet again in this game, despite having already killed him in the previous one. They went out of their way to make this a prequel just so that you can fight the Joker yet again for no good reason. And indeed, the story in the game is disappointing - you are facing down eight assassins, but you never fight more than one of them at the same time, unlike in the trailer, and a number of them are just fairly anticlimactic fights with a super-goon surrounded by a bunch of goons. The story doesn't feel as coherent as either of the previous games, and while the riddler trophies were better than they were in the second game, they're still inferior to the Riddler's mechanics in the original Batman: Arkham Asylum.
All in all, it is still a good game, but it isn't great like the first game was. Had no one ever played any of these games before, it might have been better, but as this is the third installment which uses the same game mechanics and same villain, it just isn't as fresh.

Alright, so we have here Signs of Life. Same genre as Terraria and Starbound, but with similar elements trying to spin it off in different ways. The manipulator tool requires gem fragments to use better and better, which is a nice element. The background story is relatively decent enough, and it has been a fun game. Getting suprised by a giant robot chicken is always interesting, and it put up quite a fight. (The mech though..huh.) As long as this game has been around though, I normally would expect way more to keep me going.
Its a tough call to recommend or not, but i'd honestly wait until more is added at this point, because the "whys" drop off tremendously after a time. There is basically no real reason to use a lot of things.
-Why build bigger tiers of things?
-Aside from the mech...why build better armor? Decent enough weapons..hell, Steel is basically the cutoff point.
-There is no real endgame as far as i've been able to see. Terraria had all kinds of bosses and regular progression. Starbound had other worlds, and Crea had alternate universes and gateways. While Signs of Life has some nice POLISH to it, the substance is incredibly lacking. Not enough to demand a refund over, because ultimately it DOES play well, but its like going to a fine dining establishment and all they have to serve you is rolls. They look nice, smell nice, and taste great..but you didn't come for JUST the rolls.
And that for me is what really kills it. It looks great, plays well, and the little tinker things are decent enough, but it doesn't ultimately deliver. It needs more content. It needs a reason to keep pushing. The devs need to play their game from the perspective of a player and ask themselves what makes this fun. Base defenses? Okay, but why would I take the time to really make them? What is there to defend from? (Nothing) New weapons? Um, okay..but is a new damage rating really all there is to fun? Granted I can keep killing things and that's nice. I can move deeper down, but even getting the Steel stuff..there is some hefty imbalance there and the difficulty to acquire the needed substance ramps up a bit much and a bit too deep. Objective..move on. Objective..move on. Ultimately, what I care about is...is the game fun? Past a certain point..it stops being fun. Its just a grind that drops off. Learn from other games in the genre, and add to this game. Give us a real challenge, not a time-enducing headache to get the next tier to dig deeper..to get the next tier.
The game has been out a long while now. This kind of stuff aint gonna fly. Take notes on other games of the genre, again, as a player, and see what fun you can bring to the table to keep your players engaged. Fix that, and i'll be happy to change my review because I really would love to promote this game. I just can't especially given the time table to promote something that leaves a lot to be desired.

Ok, so I picked this up for $7, which is cheap enough in my book that even if it was a let-down, it wouldn't anger me.  I was pleasantly surprised by how well done this game is!  It is a repetitive open-world style with combat similar to Shadow of Mordor.  I approached the game in an organic fashion, focusing only on story missions & distractions that caught my attention at the moment, and I must say that this will be the most enjoyable way to play, unless you are a completionist.
Art design is amazing, especially at maxxed graphic settings.  Captures the visual presentation of Fury Road perfectly, and I lost count of the amount of times I was blown away by post-apocayptic vistas (i.e. driving across a vast expanse of dried ocean-floor, replete with rusted ships half-buried by the sands).
Sound design was executed briliiantly, which is admirable considering you will be listening to your machine's engine for hours.  I never got tired of the sublime roar of the Magum Opus' V6, or the throaty bellow of the V8 as the story progresses.  Music is okay, but I ended up turning it down to increase immersion.  Combat sounds are satisfying with wet bone-crunching strikes, and screams of tortured metal.
Gameplay is solid although a little dated by now, with some strange choices in keymapping.  However, I got used to it by hour 3 and began merrily stomping war boys into dust.  Close-combat is Arkham-style with an array of extra skills that can be purchased to keep it from getting stale.  Car-combat is simply a blast, and truly unique, as we haven't really had anything like this since Twisted Metal.  Car upgrading is rewarding.
Story and characters are classic Mad Max universe tropes, with deranged over-the-top personages with hilariously vulgar names like Lord Scrotus, Rim Jobber, and Stank Gum.  Pacing was good, with a couple twists and turns at the end which kept it from becoming a cookie-cutter plot.
Overall, I'd give it a solid 8/10, and would actually recommend it at its $20 price, considering my first playthrough was 30 hours (focusing mostly on story missions).  It also gets kudos for being a game without microtransactions/lootboxes, and I am a little bummed there is no DLC or hope for a sequel (but you never know).

Character design is classic but the facial features are a tad worn out.

Night 1 is fairly easy because you have nothing to really do.
Night 2 escalates a heap, taking a little while to get around.
Night 3 escalates a lot further and again, it takes a couple of tries to complete.
Night 4 takes difficulty to the max, being maybe the hardest night in the game.
Night 5 is hard too but not as hard as night 4 (in my opinion.)
I recommend the game for those who love instructive games or to those who have been following this franchise.

Prison Architect is a great management strategy/sim game. The concepts of building and running a prison are simulated as well as could be expected from a game. It also fulfills the "game" part much better than many sim games, which often fall into the trap of being too realistic to be fun. There are a variety of mechanics present in the game, mostly based off the needs of your prisoners, which provide a considerable number of gameplay opportunities. The design of your prison can be literally whatever you want, as long as the prisoners can't escape and don't destroy it. There are many possibilities for different designs and playstyles.
The developers of this game have done a great job with how they manage it (from what I have experienced at least). They initially released an alpha game years ago, then improved it hugely over time and finally released it in full last year. Even though the game is now in full release, the developers continue to add interesting features and mechanics to keep players on their toes. They have fully embraced modding, so there are a large number of player-made mods on the Steam Workshop which are simple to activate and use.
One of the few things this game is missing is the ability to build multi-floor buildings. It also can become very laggy with large numbers of prisoners. There are also some issues with two mechanics: heat and tunneling. The heaters in the game do not have real thermostats, so they will sometimes make certain rooms too hot, and there are NO AIR CONDITIONERS or even vents to lower temperature in summer. Tunneling is also a problem: prisoners will tunnel under their toilets and out of the prison, and the only way to detect this (the Dog Handler) is very unreliable. However, even with these issues, it is still a great game.

Action rogue-like game. Move around an area, killing zombie-ish things. Each zombie has a chance to drop it's head, torso, or legs for you to wear. Then you go through the portal to the next area. After 3-4 areas, you reach a boss monster. You'll occasionally meet people who stay back at your base and do things for you, like repairing "freshness" (Durability), cold storage for parts, or allowing you to combine body parts to increase stats.
The head, torso, and legs act as equipment, providing increases in attack, defense, health, and/or dodge. Each part also provides you with it's own usable skill. The torso also changes your basic attack, which can range from basic punches to whipping with red tendrils to launching redish balls of something from your chest.
If you die, you lose everything you were carrying.
On top of that, you have passive ability/skills that you can buy/increase with green vials that zombies sometimes drop. Basic stat increases mainly, along with some oddities mixed in - a sword falling from the sky that increases your attack speed in the area or occasionally adding electric damage to your next few melee attacks, etc. These are permanent and not lost on dying.
The coins can be used if you find a nurse to buy healing items, or the blonde girl for a randomized buff (or even a debuff if you're unlucky.)
It's definitely worth getting. I look forward to seeing what kind of weirdness they have planned.

Post-traumatic Stress Disorder can occur following a life-threatening event like military combat, natural disasters, terrorist incidents, serious accidents, or violent personal assaults like♥♥♥♥♥♥ Most survivors of trauma return to normal given a little time. However, some people have stress reactions that don't go away on their own, or may even get worse over time. These individuals may develop PTSD.
People who suffer from PTSD often suffer from nightmares, flashbacks, difficulty sleeping, and feeling emotionally numb. These symptoms can significantly impair a person's daily life.
PTSD is marked by clear physical and psychological symptoms. It often has symptoms like depression, substance abuse, problems of memory and cognition, and other physical and mental health problems. The disorder is also associated with difficulties in social or family life, including occupational instability, marital problems, family discord, and difficulties in parenting.
If you are suffering from PTSD, or know someone who is, the following list of resources and information will help you find help in dealing with PTSD and related conditions.
Each VA medical center has PTSD specialists who provide treatment for Veterans with PTSD. Plus, the VA provides nearly 200 specialized PTSD treatment programs. A referral is usually needed to access the specialty programs. You can use this VA PTSD Program Locator to see if there is a specialized program near you.
NOTE: If you are in crisis dial 911 or 800-273-TALK (1-800-273-8255).

The arrange of this review may seems a little confusing. But the game is "little confusing". It's like the movie "The Usual Suspects", you can't play the game with the same experience, twice. The players who completed the game knows that. That's why I want to make a spoiler free review.
The Spec Ops: The Line is the 10th game of the Spec Ops series. A not very memorable and commercially successful series. That's why the publisher bets on the successful formula of the "generic third person console shooter" with exrtas-multiplayer; co-op, achievements. And they received by the developer a "generic third person shooter"..... or sort of...
The multi-player: There is a multi-player and co-op but it's deserted. No one plays it. The good thing is that there aren't achievements attached to it.
The achievements: Like I said, you will not be forced to play the multi-player just to get all of the achievements. There are only single-player ones. But It's hard to get them, not because the single-player is difficult.
The single-player: Like I said, the game is a generic third person console shooter like "Gears of war". You command a team of two NPCs, you shoot people and you go from one area to another. Technically the game is good: no bugs or glitches. The control and respond of the NPCs may feels awkward only on the highest difficulty- they can die much more faster and thanks to this it's difficult to them to complete the given orders. But the "main problem" is that the developer took this generic formula and put one of, the best military story ever, in it. Not a "Michael Bay, Top Gun, Call Of Duty" kind of story. More like "The Deer Hunter, Platoon, Full Metal Jacket" anti-military kind of story. Some people are seeing this game as the newest modern multimedian adaptation of "Heart of Darkness", after the film "Apocalypse Now". Everything inside the game is design to support the grim story. The design of the enemies- Travis Bickle will try to stab you. The soundtrack resembles many anti-"Vietnam war" songs- lots of psychedelic distortion rock. Even the loading screens will start to give you "useful" information. The game will try to drown you into madness.I can even add that the use of the "generic" gameplay formula is adding much more darker (I think unintentional) ironic line into  the satirical part of the story. The story of game is asking questions about the violence in the same generic type of  video games. After finishing this game I doubt that you will have the will to replay it. (I said that, the achievements are hard to get;)
This game is "underground hit". It's a very mature story, some will not understand it. This is a "You must to have it!" game. The value of this game rises with every year, with every review. This is the end and probably, we will never see another game from the Spec Ops series. Or not as good, as this one. Maybe this game is not a commercially successful but it's definitely a cult classic.

I've played this game extensively before it came to Steam.  If you're looking for a F2P version of GTA, this isn't it.  Move along, nothing to see here.
It's not a bad game but it shouldn't be taken seriously.  It's rife with hackers, griefers and players who will "ghost" you during missions.  You won't be able to kill them and they can follow you around, distract you, block your objectives, ram your vehicle and tell their allies exactly where you are.
The cash shop in this game is ridiculous.  It's like Korean MMO-worthy.  One gun can cost you $60 and that's just for a single gun.  The monetization doesn't stop there...not on your life and it's incredibly Pay2Win as well.
Now, I know I was just complaining about how the game is full of griefers but to be honest that's really the most fun aspect of the game...doing stuff like taking 4 dumptrucks and blocking off a major highway or parking outside a car garage, leaving a little open space for cars to get through...and when they try to get through...moving in their way as they angrily yell at your immovable dumptruck, causing them to spend more money to re-spawn their vehicle elsewhere.
If you play the game with that kind of attitude, just messing around and having fun...it's not bad.  But if you try to play the game seriously, you'll get punked out everytime by either hackers (which run rampant and unchecked) or people who have spent hundreds in the cash shop...or both.

If you are a HITMAN fan, and don't buy this game, you are missing out. Period.
Yes there are only 6 episodes, but this game is different from other HITMAN games in that each level is meant to be played multiple times before moving on, unlocking equipment that you can use in future missions. If you just play straight through, it's pretty short, yes, but you are really scamming yourself out of a rich and diverse game experience. The variety of challenges keeps things pretty fresh and you may find yourself trying some of them for a long time and still scratching your head.

The new Hitman is very close to a 007 license game, or a James Bond Simulator, you play as a badass emotionless psychopath that are good at everything, attending parties, infiltrate military base, going on vacations in different countries to achieve your objective, which is assassinate or steal/destroy stuff.
The most fun part of Hitman is you beat a level, unlock new cool equipments, starting disguise, starting area etc, and replay the level in a different ways, then repeat. The progression system encourage you to replay the same missions.
The voice acting in this game are very basic, there is a Bangkok hotel missions that every staff speaks like an American. NPC dialogue are cringe worthy, sometimes they just spit random words that dosen't make any sense, its could be immersion breaker but i found it hilarious.
Unfortunately this game get held back by online DRM, not recommended if you have bad or unstable internet connection. Because if you can't connect to their server, the progression system is disabled, the game lost some of it's fun and replayability. You technically paid same price for inferior version of the product.
I cant recommend such a short storyline for the price. Not as good as the older Hitman series. Not to say this is a bad game, but the main missions are short.

Good day, and happy new year,
Today, I will explain why Terraria is an amazing game.
Starting with the items.
There are so many choices for a 10 item loadout. There is a sword made out of NYAN CAT power. Believe me, I've done 1.2, but I'm still in easy mode for this version. And there are enough blocks to make LANDMARKS stand out, like Polished Granite, Snow Bricks and DUNGEON BRICKS.
Second, the bosses.
You've got an EYE, a SKELETON HEAD with arms, a MUTANT FLOWER, and a fusion of a pig, fish and dragon. All of the bosses aren't too easy without the requirements. Take the Moon Lord for example. It's the final boss, unless you use mods like crazy. You need the best armor for the job.
Third, the community content.
There are amazing, well thought mods for this game, like the Tremor and Calamity mods, adding a new feel to Terraria. The bosses and weapons in the mods are balanced and all have a litte gimmick. The prefixes mod is cool, just for laughs. Imagine seeing a tiny hornet, that sends you flying into the air!
TL;DR, worth the money.

This was my all time favorite shooter game on console, and it still is my favorite on PC. Spec Ops: The Line is a game that eveyrone should at least play. You may learn something.

The saving grace of this game is the subtle split-second time-slow when getting a headshot. Outside that it's kinda a generic third person shooter, besides the story. The story is entertaining and the gameplay was good enough that I'll probably get a second play-through out of it, just for those nice headshots.

Spec Ops: The Line really wants to be the gaming industry's Apocalypse Now or Heart of Darkness. The developers want to give the player an unflinching look at the horrors and murky, moral grayness of modern warfare.  It's a subject that few developers want to tackle.  It's not fun or empowering, but it's honest and thought-provoking.  Few games have brought the subject fully to the player's attention while film has examined the futility of warfare several times over.  Spec-Ops wants to bring that same message, spoken through a game, in a genre that is overrun with games that want to make you feel like Rambo in First Blood or Dutch in Predator.  And while Spec-Ops's story certainly invokes a lot of emotion, it feels like one of those games that would rather be a movie.
The gameplay is boiled down to moving from Point A to Point B while killing wave after wave of blank-faced enemies.  There are one of two deviations from this formula, but player agency is reduced to walking down linear hallways, hiding behind cover, and killing anyone that isn't in your squad.  That's all you'll ever be doing in a story that, although provocative, lacks in-depth characters and a plot worth following.  Everything else, from the out-dated graphics to the clunky controls, is disappointingly sub-par.  Spec-Ops: The Line rests alongside the Gears of War series and Uncharted series as games with little to no merit, better watched than played.

I've recommended Rust to friends since I started playing some time ago. I've invested some 925 hours or so to date. Back when Rust was Legacy it was a great game, but was largely pointless. Grind, build a base, grind, raid other bases, grind, and defend your base until the server wiped. The game has since progressed, and has new challenges and gameplay. The new version of Rust is still a decent game, but isn't without its flaws.
This game has always favored the raiders. Legitimate defenses have always been too resource intensive to actually build/implement while playing solo and often result in a diminished experience. Bottom line is that every time you start this game up, you need to have hours devoted to it in order to find an ideal location, gather resources, and build something that will stand up to raiders early in the game. Although, nothing will stop large clans/groups, except maybe other large clans/groups. These groups get more and more powerful as they take down helicopters and raid smaller bases, making it impossible to ever level the playing field. With the twigs update (being able to build twig structures within areas protected by a cupboard), this has become even more difficult to combat.
Bottom line, be prepared to lose everything and start over again. This is the reality of the game. You will, at one point, log into the server and find all of your stuff gone, your base destroyed, or you'll just wake up on the other side of the island wondering what happened. Exploits in the game have also proved a problem, although less noticeable now.
All in all, this game is infuriating, and has a toxic community that will always KOS, but is still fun to play when you've got enough time/energy to devote to it and occassionally you'll find good people on the servers. The devs are working on it, and make mistakes with features (as we've seen recently), but they really do listen to their community and make changes based on feedback provided by the players. Definately worth a go, even more so if it's on sale.

Solid game, but plays exactly like a mash of Tomb Raider's gameplay with Far Cry 3's open world with a progression system influenced by both in equal parts. What I mean is, if you liked any of those games and would like to play a Fury Road equivalent, you will like Mad Max.
Besides the somewhat repetitive missions and gameplay, most NPCs were designed with the intent to be distinct and with a unique personality but they end up feeling kind of distant and do not manage to make me care about them at all, they're quest hubs and exposition dumbs, nothing more. This is coming from somebody who thoroughly enjoys depth of character in NPCs and has a general distaste for upright, animating ragdolls who do nothing more than send you from one fetch quest to the next.
If this doesn't bother you then there's plenty of content to enjoy in Mad Max. From customizing your car to upgrading Max's skills to getting baked with a certain person -not gonna spoil- to wandering the vast open world chasing convoys or simply going from one landmark to the other, you will get totally absorbed and immersed.
Graphics are top notch, capturing superbly the feeling of the movie especially during long convoy pursuits or roaming the wastes during a dust storm.
Overall, I am still enjoying the game and will continue to do so. Grab it on sale while you can.

1)  It's a real nice change of mechanics. Instead of each night getting progressively more difficult, you have new objectives to do each night, each varying in difficulty, making this game way different from the others.

In my opinion there is 1 con to this game and that is night 4 in general (if you have played the game, you'd know what I mean). Anyway, I really recommend this game to anyone. Even someone who hasn't played any of the games (if you haven't, what are you doing? Go buy all the FNAF games now). I hope this review was helpful

In terms of the way that this game is designed, this game is wonderful. Behind Five Nights at Freddys 4, Sister Location is one of the best in the franchise, but only in terms of gameplay. It still has its shortcomings:
-The biggest disputation that I have with this game is the way that it complicates the franchises story even more than it already is. I have heard that Scott wanted to make this game part of a completely different storyline along with the books, but how does that explain the FNaF 4 eastereggs in the secret ending, unless those magically arent canon either? If that is the case, then why add them in the first place?
-The characters in this game were boring. You never actually get to see anything fascinating or enthralling in this game in terms of the way the characters are portrayed or interact. There is no development with the animatronics or the humans you so rarely "hear" in this game. Circus Baby is never seen until the end of Night 5, and Ballora and Funtime Foxy are only ever seen twice and you have to run through their showrooms just to see them. Funtime Freddy and Ennard, especially, are the only interesting characters in this game. But then again, Ennard is only seen once at the end of the Night 5 and in Night 6, a night in which isnt even canon to the main plot of the story.
-The main game has very little difficulty, unlike the previous 4 games, which was something I found oddly charming about this series. Scott Cawthon released a patch to make the Night 4 section of the game (in the Springlock suit with the Minireenas, is what Im referring to) easier. I played it before the patch, and it was difficult, but now newer players wont be able to experience that because it was removed.
-Despite what I said previously, the "Fake Ending", I believe it was, was TOO difficult. It took me a few hours at the minumum just to finish the ending with Ennard and it wasnt worth it because the ending wasnt canon and didnt show a surprising or interesting cutscene.
Here are the positives:
-The gameplay is much different from prior games. Instead of sitting in an office where strangled toddlers possessing heartattack-inducing robotic furries try to kill you, this game seems to have more of an objective. The player is not sitting for the entire game, flicking a flashlight or playing sounds, you actually move around the facility. As stated before, along with FNaF 4, this game might be more interesting in terms of gameplay.
-The soundtrack and ambiance is outstanding. I loved the menu/ending music and the music that plays in the background of the fake ending and custom nights.
-The graphics are really nice, but this game does not have the 1980s-1990s vibe the first game had or even the creepy, anxiety-inducing atmosphere the fourth game had.
If you are interested in the story of Five Nights at Freddys, I do not recommend this game at all. It will only confuse you even more than you likely already are. If you interested in the gameplay, I would recommend, as it has some of the best gameplay, though I personally believe FNaF 4 is the most enjoyable of the series. But it does not have the difficulty of the precious games, that is if you enjoyed the difficulty of the precious games like I did. It all depends on what you want out of this game. And as for me, who wanted both, it was not worth the play.
I just want to say that this is one of the best Five Nights At Freddy's games in the franchise, it does change the formula of FNaF, I like to give this game a 9/10.

Spec Ops: The Line really wants to be the gaming industry's Apocalypse Now or Heart of Darkness. The developers want to give the player an unflinching look at the horrors and murky, moral grayness of modern warfare.  It's a subject that few developers want to tackle.  It's not fun or empowering, but it's honest and thought-provoking.  Few games have brought the subject fully to the player's attention while film has examined the futility of warfare several times over.  Spec-Ops wants to bring that same message, spoken through a game, in a genre that is overrun with games that want to make you feel like Rambo in First Blood or Dutch in Predator.  And while Spec-Ops's story certainly invokes a lot of emotion, it feels like one of those games that would rather be a movie.
The gameplay is boiled down to moving from Point A to Point B while killing wave after wave of blank-faced enemies.  There are one of two deviations from this formula, but player agency is reduced to walking down linear hallways, hiding behind cover, and killing anyone that isn't in your squad.  That's all you'll ever be doing in a story that, although provocative, lacks in-depth characters and a plot worth following.  Everything else, from the out-dated graphics to the clunky controls, is disappointingly sub-par.  Spec-Ops: The Line rests alongside the Gears of War series and Uncharted series as games with little to no merit, better watched than played.

To be brutally honest, Spec Ops' agonizing, barebones, and repetitive gameplay would prevent it from being an enjoyable experience even if the story was as fantastic as everyone claims it to be. Spec Ops has nothing more than the most basic mechanics present in every single shooting game, and yet it still manages to muck those up tremendously. Movement is horrendously clunky, sprinting is unresponsive, the cover system is buggy, and the control scheme is without a doubt the worst I've ever encountered. Sometimes I would stand up and get myself killed by accident because melee and vault over cover are mapped to the same button for whatever brilliant reason. Also, going into cover, as well as leaving it, requires you to sprint, which often times sent me bolting forward when I really just wanted to stand up. Would it be so hard to create a designated cover button like nearly every other cover based third person shooter?
The story, the only thing anybody ever praises this game for, is completely linear; player decision plays a nonexistant part in the narrative. It's main method of eliciting an emotional response from the player is by forcing you to commit senseless, atrocious warcrimes and then showing you how awful you are. The game misses so many opportunities to set up two choices and force you to choose the lesser of two evils, opting to force you to carry out whatever the uninspired, B movie tough guy of a protagonist decides to do instead. It desperately wanted me to feel bad for what I had done, but failed to do so because I cant feel bad for doing something that I had literally no choice but to do. Realistically, the only other choice I ever had was to close the game and forget about it, which I sincerely regret not doing sooner.

I like great storytelling in games.  I like moral choice systems in games.  I like well polished shooty action.  Spec Ops: The Line has one of these.  Just one.  But it does it so incredibly well while giving the illusion of having 2 and the third is good enough to pull through.  So I'll go a bit more in depth on these 3 elements.
Spec Ops has absolutely great storytelling.  This isn't a war game where you go to another country and shoot foreigners from behind chest high walls with the most advanced technology on offer.  This is a war game where you go to another country and shoot rogue American soldiers from behind chest high walls with adequate technology.  Rogue American soldiers have much more room for excellent storytelling because it gives the impression that you're killing men that don't deserve death and are only fighting for survival and the right thing, just like you are.  Everyone, including your character Captain Walker, is rogue and ♥♥♥♥ed in the head, just trying to do something right in the wrong place at the wrong time.  You see things through his eyes, but seeing things through the eyes of a man with a fractured mind is different from what reality would be.  You make choices you think would reflect your personal decisions at the time, but after they are made, they're an outcome you hate.  It tells the story that in war, there is no good outcome, only death and horror and misery.  And that is a good story about the evils of war, the terrible things man does to fellow man.
I'll stop you right now if you haven't played the game and don't want a simple spoiler at all, because what I'm about to say could be considered a spoiler.  So go forward to the next paragraph if you don't want to know about it.  You gone?  Good.  The moral choice system is fake.  It's meant to be fake.  It's designed to give you the illusion of choices that affect the story but all outcomes are the same, this is a linear story with all choices being the same outcome.  But this is fine in this situation because it adds to the storytelling.  This isn't a moral choice system that you feel is empty and faulty, this is one that gives depth to the story because you realize it's a core part of Captain Walker's insanity and disconnection to reality.  It is an illusion, but the best kind of illusion that is welcome in the mind of a crazy man just trying to do some good in a world that is 110% ♥♥♥♥ed.  So despite not having an actual moral choice system, I give this game a pass on it for adding it in to enhance the story and give more meaning where they could have just left it out.
Finally, the shooting.  I play a lot of shooters.  Destiny is currently my absolute favorite for the best shooting mechanics, guns are responsive and feel powerful, bullets go where you aim, ranges, damage drop off, aim assist, and weapon stability all feel well done and polished and necessary.  Spec Ops does not have the best shooting mechanics.  Simple as that.  However, that doesn't make it bad.  You pick up a gun, you fire bullets into enemies, they die.  It gets the job done.  Some guns are incredibly inaccurate and you tend to use those only as a last resort.  Since weapon ammo is actually quite scarce, the game pushes you into these kinds of situations, forcing you to be challenged.  This game has balls, it doesn't hand you everything you could want or need and then hold your hand through the level afterwards, this system is in place to make you feel helpless and alone.  Sometimes you find a fully loaded (insert weapon of choice here) lying on a box somewhere and you feel rewarded and safer, but you can count on that ammo type to be incredibly scarce as you move through the level and you're left with the choice of leaving your favorite gun behind in favor of having enough ammo to get through the next section, or winging it with one weapon that you don't like but can count on enough ammo lying around if you don't get ♥♥♥♥ed.  I found meaning in this system, another choice you get to make to try to ensure survival.  The bullets don't always go where you want them to go, but it feels well done enough to get through the game and also add to the atmosphere of helplessness and difficulty in surviving in a land that actively wants you dead.
I recommend this game very highly, it leaves you feeling fulfilled but sad.  This is more of a horror game, meant to scare you and confront a darkened heart from the horrors of war.  It will not scare you in a way that traditional horror games and movies would do, but in a way where you have to confront your own opinions of war, which could be that you want to see more war or less war, it doesn't matter, but either way it teaches you that war is not something to take lightly, it is absolutely destructive to men and women who have to fight it and who simply just get caught up in it unwillingly.  And for that, I give this game high marks for being decently functional and telling a story that gives us something important to discuss that otherwise would just get ignored.

Solid game, but plays exactly like a mash of Tomb Raider's gameplay with Far Cry 3's open world with a progression system influenced by both in equal parts. What I mean is, if you liked any of those games and would like to play a Fury Road equivalent, you will like Mad Max.
Besides the somewhat repetitive missions and gameplay, most NPCs were designed with the intent to be distinct and with a unique personality but they end up feeling kind of distant and do not manage to make me care about them at all, they're quest hubs and exposition dumbs, nothing more. This is coming from somebody who thoroughly enjoys depth of character in NPCs and has a general distaste for upright, animating ragdolls who do nothing more than send you from one fetch quest to the next.
If this doesn't bother you then there's plenty of content to enjoy in Mad Max. From customizing your car to upgrading Max's skills to getting baked with a certain person -not gonna spoil- to wandering the vast open world chasing convoys or simply going from one landmark to the other, you will get totally absorbed and immersed.
Graphics are top notch, capturing superbly the feeling of the movie especially during long convoy pursuits or roaming the wastes during a dust storm.
Overall, I am still enjoying the game and will continue to do so. Grab it on sale while you can.

Short Version : Good Batman game if you haven't played the previous two Arkham installments. If you have then you are better off with Arkham City.
Things I didn't like about Arkham Origins :
1. Combat is broken. Its very slow even at advanced levels compared to Arkham City from which it borrows.
2. Many people say open world is good but like the masses I still found it an empty shallow experience after playing it.
3. Graphics feel slightly degraded from Arkham City.
4. Story is a mess. Though Batman always goes after the bad guys it never feels like there's a $50 million bounty on batman's head.
5. Boss battles are too easy and predictable.
Things I did like about Arkham Origins :
1. Gadgets are fun to use. Though some of them like the shock gloves make the combat pretty easy.
2. Enighma challenges are actually doable. But they won't make you think hard/ smart like riddler challenges.
Overall wouldn't recommend purchasing this. You are better off with Arkham City.

Good game for fans of the other two games, or of course diehard Batman fans. If you can get it on sale then it may prove to be a worth while distraction while you wait for Knight to come out. The plot is well executed, despite it being very obviously/predictable for what is going to happen. However if you purchase a game called Origins, then you probably expect a bit of the above in a well known franchise. More or less from what I could tell the plot isn't a reboot or anything but sets out exactly how Arkham became the hell hole we know it as from Asylum and City. Shows the rise of the Joker/seeds of other masked villians, and the fall of the classic crime syndacites due the events Batman arguably set in motion himself by donning the mask and cape. Of course were not talking acadamy awards stuff here or anything, but it is a good service to the game series, its versions of the characters and settings so far.
Summary:
The good:
-Classic Batman story/gameplay
-Great graphics as expected from the series.
-Has all the hits from the past games, so for a good price its a fair bit of gameplay to take on.
The bad:
-NOT FOR PEOPLE WHO FOUND THE OTHER GAMES EVENTUALLY BORING, OR AREN'T THE BIGGEST BATMAN FANS. Save your money for Arkham Knight!
-It has ALL of the hits from the other games. It literally plays like a greatest hits collection at points, but if your a fan of the games then that is not a bad thing, and in an odd way makes it a good game for someone to get into the Arkham franchise as well. Where as the first game, may not be the best point due to its...arguable technical flaws comapred to City.
-Frusterating difficulty curve at times, stick with it however and you'll figure it out/luck out on one particular boss fight it seems. Once you get through all the BS though, the cutscenes always reward with some classic, badass "I'm Batman" moments.

If you liked Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, you'll like this one. For sure.
The Good Stuff:
1) You dive into some interesting, lesser-known villains (Firefly)
2) Gotham is pretty cool when you visit sites that were in Arkham City and compare them to what they looked like in Arkham City
3) The voice acting is great
4) The dialogue is much cooler than it was in Asylum and City. I found myself cringing at a lot of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t Batman and the villains said in the first two games. Every character (expecially Batman) frightened me a bit during their dialogue-heavy scenes in Origins, however. Batman scowls and seems to carry legitimate hatred with him through some of this game.
5) Combat system is the same
6) This game is definitely prettier than Asylum and City. I attribute it to more highly detailed assets, rather than other tricks like fancy lighting and blur.
8) Some really, really cool action-y things happen
9) Electrocutioner
The Bad Stuff
1) That ending. Seriously? Where's the rest of the game?
2) Not all 7 assassins are serious parts of the game. Two of them, in particular, are just optional mini-games. And one of those two is just a normal brawl.
3) One character, Shiva, is positioned as the most dangerous person on the planet. Yet, in the story, her character is entirely underwhelming, posing little more threat than an average gang of thugs. Copperhead, on the other hand, is scary as holy grandpa♥♥♥♥♥♥ Yet, she has almost no buildup and zero aftermath.
4) We get it. Turning places into funhouses is Joker's version of terraforming. This was cool in Asylum. Now, it's like that friend who repeats that one funny joke he said that one time, hoping it will still make you laugh.
5) The bosses are just brawls. Every time you see a super criminal, you just put your fist in him as many times as it takes to make the birdies come out. Asylum and City were way better at boss battle variation.
6) Joker over the loudspeaker has absolutely zero effect, anymore
To sum it up, this game is equal parts "Hell yes, that was awesome" and "Ugh, Jesus, this stuff again?"

I love me some grand theft auto, but this steam version of this is pretty bad faults with it. The game is great from a story/gameplay standpoint, but many bugs have caused me to dislike my experience so far.
First thing I noticed was the controller support in the options, which originally I thought was great, but failed to work properly from the start. You can do few things with a 360 pad and the setup is so asinine, it feels nothing like how it originally played on playstation. You can't move the camera for starters, unless you have a 3rd arm so you can also use the mouse, you'll have problems as well.
Secondly, the resolutions that are put in there are all outdated, It cannot display 1080p+ unless mods are used to "unpatch" the game. This is what I find really silly, in the 1.1 and 1.0 version of the game, 1080p and several other resolutions that were available are now removed in the 3.X version of the game. It would be understandable since it is an old game after all, but they were there originally, why remove them?
Finally the framerate. With the framelimiter put in place, the maximum FPS you can get is 24 which is god awful to look at. You can remove the limiter with the simple toggle of an option, BUT when you do, the physics of the game start going ape♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cars bounce all over the place and just try swimming in water. Again, there's probably some mods out there that can fix this issue, but I shouldn't have to do that. I shouldn't have to spend hours of my time researching, downloading and installing mods into my game to make it run well.
With all that said, if you can stomach playing GTAsa at 720p, 24fps, and no gamepad, this game should work fine.
Final score
10/10 for the story/gameplay
4/10 for the amount of fixing that needs to be done to the game.
Maybe a 8/10 with the inclusion of mods.

Disclaimer: The stats... 20 hours... completed most bosses and unlocked all the cool car stuff.
If I were describe this game in a few words it would be " not enough".
The good:
I loved every second playing Mad Max, the scrap grind people complain about really became easy once you unlock a few upgrades, however it does follow the feedback loop of "collect scrap to get something that makes it easier to collect more scrap". What makes this loop bareable is the Fury road world. The amazing desert and sandstorms, you honestly feel apart of the mad max world. Linking back to my first sentence, there is just not enough of the world... I want endless amounts of desert I want a world the size of skyrim... Maybe thats abit ambitious.
The car combat: Alot of people  complain about the way the driving handles, I think it is great. You are driving in the desert with a piece of old carbage... do people really expect this to handle like GT?
Hand combat is just your standard Batman model, however there are some brutal slow motion kills to break up the combat. Kind of a wierd mix between Assains creed and Batman.
The bad: There is just not enough content :(. Im not talking about all the silly scrap hunting missions you can do... I mean  quality storyline. The story is over before you know it and its left leaving you with so many more questions than answers. The story although short is good.
Overall- This game made me go rewatch all the movies multiply times, I became immersed in the experience and was left wanting more... There was no more :(

Get it, if you're a hard core Mad Max fan. Its got Batman Arkham Asylum's fighting combat mechanics, its got wild and crazy weaponized 'Death' races, and a beautiful landscape to stare at (plus the crazy cool upgrades to the car and to Max himself). What more can you ask?

Mad Max from Avalanche Studios has a brilliant open worrld design. It also has a large upgrade-system for the protagonists vehicle, skills, gear and tools. The resource-management is well balanced. Battle with enemys has a deep structure of physics and variations. All is done very well.
Driving and fighting goes very fluid. Mad Max - the exploring of the Wasteland - is like a raw jewel, that must be dragged with progression. The atmosphere of Fury Road is jaw-dropping transformed into this game.
I don't like car- or hand to hand-combat but I love this game. - It's simply good made.
Addendum: There are mixed feelings, especially from Videogame critics, and if you got any concerns about this game, watch "I will now talk about negative Mad Max reviews [...]" from Cynical Brit...
If you like roaming and upgrading in a realistic scenario, Mad Max should have your attention. I'm really impressed with the game art from this title like landscapes, structures and vehicles etc. - The further you go, the more you will be rewarded. The only thing, that should be different, should be some textures, these are not up to date.
If you build up your strongholds, resource-management will be a piece of cake.
