Another great entry to a great series. Batman: Arkham Origins deserves none of the hate it gets from fans of the Batman games. I'll tell you one thing, though, WB did not innovate too much on the gameplay from the previous Arkham games. But, I ask you a question: is this really a bad thing? WB was wise to do this instead of taking the risk to change the game in a series that doesn't belong to them. So, what we get is another Batman game that lets us explore Gotham City once again and relive the beginning of the Dark Knight. The story, by the way, is a great excuse to throw in some SICK boss battles. The boss battles are each so different and challenging, I'll tell ya. And while I hear this game has major bugs at launch, all seem to be entirely fixed at this point in time, more than a year after launch. Speaking of fixes, this PC port is AMAZING! It runs beautifully, all settings maxed out, getting 40 fps (which is good enough for me for a 3rd person game) on my GT755M, a laptop graphics card, mind you. And with all of the nvidia-specific features, you'll be happy you're a PC gamer. And going back to the game content itself, Batman: Arkham Origins has the usual massive amount of side quests and things to do outside of story missions. Now, I've, for the most part, only played the story missions, but I plan on going back soon enough to do more side quests. One string of side quests I saw a bit of on youtube has you finding the Most Wanted Criminals of Gotham, letting you fight more boss battles, and ultimately squeezing as much as you can out of this worthy entry. While Origins doesn't add too much to the gameplay aspect (which is already simply perfect), there is no reason you shouldn't pass up the chance to enjoy it again in addition to a surpringly good story.
9/10--Origins is a game which follows the rule: "If it ain't broke, don't fix it".... and I appreciate that.

I like this game: I think it's pretty good, but it's definitely my least favourite of the Arkham series. The gameplay is still well done, but I think some of the new gadgets make it a bit too easy (e.g. the shock gloves, the remote claw). The story for me was kinda disappointing, mainly because of the fact that (spoiler alert, although it's all on the posters) the game relies on the Joker AGAIN, despite having a great premise; 8 assassins that are after Batman for a bounty put on him by Black Mask. Once the Joker is in, all the assassins are completely forgetten about, and it just turns into another 'Batman vs Joker' story, which works, but is something we've seen loads of times already, expecially in the Arkham series. I also felt the story lacked focus. The game looks great, but I came across a lot of bugs and glitches. I mean the first two weren't exactly completely glitch free, but it wasn't very common, whereas in this one, I come across lots every time I play. This isn't a nitpick: while it doesn't really ruin the experience, it can be really annoying sometimes. I heard there's a common bug (I haven't got it, so I guess I was lucky) that actually prevents you from completing one of the Enigma side missions- now that's not good. Another thing is while this game is packed with loads of great content, a lot of it feels too similar to what we saw in Arkham City. I'd say that there are two areas where this game improves over its predeccesors; one being its boss fights, and the other being the crime scene investigations. Overall, I'd say if you're new to the series, definitely play the others first. If you're a fan of the series, like me, and you just want more of the excellent combat and predator takedown stages, then this is  worth checking out. Just be aware of the glitches, as they can be a serious problem sometimes, but I still think you'll have a good time with this. 7/10

Thus I didn't really know what to expect gameplay-wise. I was frankly appalled at first by the simplistic platformer style the game offered me, but that eventually came to drift away. The music and the art hit me like a brick. Stunned by the beauty I wanted to play more and more, even though the gameplay maybe wasn't that interesting.
The more you played it though, you fell in love with the gameplay. Every action feels fluent and graceful, and even though you're maybe not the best gamer out there you can still feel like a boss when you maneuver through the hostile and beautiful environment the game presents.
One thing that really surpised me is that there's no levels or loading screens, but a complete open platformer world. This was not only satisfying gameplay-wise but also aesthetically. The world (or forest) that you're in is a place of magic, every little tunnel beautiful in it's own way. The art really pops with the main characters pure white, giving you joy everytime you take a little leap or climb a wall.
And don't get me started on the story. It's a wonderful story, set in a wonderful world. When you've started playing you don't want to stop until you're finished. It all ties together with one of the best music tracks and sound effects I've encountered in a game.
It can be a difficult game, depending on your standards. Sometimes it can even be frustrating as there are segments that are quite long. Speaking of which, the save method in this game is very lovely and player-friendly, nevertheless this game might be a challenge for all us noobs out there, but an enjoyable one.
9/10

Hi guys. This is my very first review and don't know what to say that hasn't already been said. This game is a pure gem that will never ever get old. There are many spot-on reviews I've read here that get in depth as to the game mechanics so I'll skip all of that bit.
I actually found Terraria by accident. I was a hard-core Minecraft addict and heard through the grapevine that this was a 2-D clone. While that couldn't be further from the truth, I'm thrilled that I was enticed to it this way or I may have never given it a chance. There are similarities, though nothing more than Pac-Man and Maze Craze both being maze games. This is a survival game that has a TON of items to find. You have multiple types of crafting tables each serving their own purpose. You can easily build a run-down shed for a house, though as you delve deeper into the game you'll likely find yourself wanting to build a beautiful mansion. You'll be building many many houses for NPC players that will move to your abode, each with unique traits / items.
I've played this game faithfully for almost a year now and am still finding new things all the time. Each time I play it's tempting to begin a new world as they are randomly generated. I don't think I could ever enjoy a game again that isn't randomly generated lol. The replay value gets a 10/10. No two people will ever play the same game the same way. The world of Terraria is absolutely massive and I generally play in a medium sized world. I cannot wait to delve into a large world starting afresh, but am saving that time for after I finally beat this awesome game. Expert mode is a wonderful addition that offers unique and better loot.
In a nutshell, I joined Steam solely for this gem and cannot commend the devs enough for making me feel like a child again. When I'm not playing Terraria I'm watching playthroughs on utube. Watching others play is a wonderful learning experience as well as adapting new strategies. When I'm sleeping I'm dreaming like a true Terrarian. I honestly wonder how many people have lost their jobs over this addiction.
Being a gamer from quarter arcades in the 80's, so much here is new and unfamiliar to me. I cannot comment on multi-player as I've yet to venture that direction. I can honestly say that this the best $8.99 I've ever spent. It feels too much like a steal and I want to support the devs as much as I possibly can. Please know that a year ago, I laughed at anyone that dared to tell me I would find a game that I would enjoy more than Minecraft. From the time I first started this fantastic game, I haven't even been back. Do yourself a favor and buy this game. Only in Terraria can you ride through the desert on a unicorn while shooting a rainbow gun and wearing a wedding dress.  Thank you for reading and hope this helps. Again, there are many wonderful reviews here that sum the game itself up much better. I plan on buying this for everyone I know at some point. There really are no words other than, "Thank you for this magical in depth world that I never wish to leave".

Mediocre grinding game which delivers GTA 5's multiplayer experience in singleplayer mode. I gave this game two attempts to show me it is worth playing. After one hour playing the game, I had to remove in-game advertisement for Rockstar energy drink by restarting the story. After that I played another three and a half hours and it kept failing over and over to fascinate me. Here is my impression of Mad Max:
Graphics are actually not that bad although they consist of the recent blurry soft-drawn outlines drowning in motion blur. Maxing all graphics option will even make the world look somewhat lively, as far as this is possible in a wide desert. I did not explore the whole map, but it seems to be designed decently for the most part. Designated roads allow faster driving and there is a fast travel system which additionally allows you to highlight POI.
Sound and music are there, but nothing that sticks out. Engine sounds seem to be a little bit emphasized, which fits as cars are important in this game.
The story is potentially intriguing, however after only a few hours of playing I will not judge it further.
Controls are sluggish par exellence and mark this game actually as a poor console port. This sluggishness heavily influences combat which is about half of the game. Perhaps developers were aware of this as slight auto-aiming which cannot be disabled is present. Controller input is a chore and I did not even bother trying mouse & keyboard. There are two button mapping presets for controller input which are only different by exchanging LB and B on Xbox controller. Apparently the game happily cycles those two layouts without noticing you, making controls even more unbearable. In addition, control layout for driving mode cannot be set up separately from normal controls, you either use default layout or alternative layout for both.
Driving sort of works, simultaneously shooting is made easy by weak spot highlighting and slow motion.
On combat system: There are guns and close combat, the latter one being important at least in the game's beginning. Gun handling actually seems to be okay, although I was not able to use it properly since said cycling of button mapping made me fire my shotgun instead of dodging and vice versa. Scarcity of ammunition and a limited supply to carry around prevent you from becoming a mindless gunslinger which is nice.
Close combat consists primarily of pressing and holding one button to execute attacks. Occasionally parrying and dodging with two other buttons are required. Targets are locked on by moving in the desired direction, collateral damage will hit surrounding opponents. Unfortunately your striking animations cannot be interrupted which leaves you vulnerable to attacks. Especially in the beginning of fights, you are very likely to take several hits due to this.
As usual these days, Mad Max features autosaving and does it a terrible job on this. Not only that you have to replay stretching parts of story missions, you will also restart at the last base you visited if you die outside of a mission. This means
travels unless you have unlocked one of the few fast travel points. This is a major letdown.
Gameplay consists mostly of driving around, collecting scrap to buy upgrades, beat up a base of baddies and repeating this. I cannot tell if this will become repetetive (some other reviews mentioned this), but it probably will. What I can tell is that collecting scrap is the most annoying task since you either have to find a small camp with loot boxes or you have to fight enemies and enemy cars and hope they will drop some. Car fights are no rarity but as soon as your opponent's health has almost emptied, they will flee. Congratulations, you just wasted three minutes driving in circles without getting a reward.
This leads me to mentioning GTA 5's multiplayer mode: While driving around the map you will either have the feeling you are the last one on earth or you will be spammed with attacks. The latter one will have you make a stop to repair your vehicle which will leave you inevitably vulnerable. At some point you will be forced to exit it and desperately fight hordes of enemy cars on foot. Instead of a desirable loop of "win fights, gather loot, upgrade, and repeat" another one is established which consists of "barely survive a fight, evenutally find loot, get run over, and reload last checkpoint".
The only thing positive about gameplay is that there is no automatic health regeneration. Instead you rely on finding food and water which are rather scarce. Perhaps designed to keep suspense, this keeps up frustration as low health is a rather common state.
All in all Mad Max is a disappointing and boring experience. Glad I bought it on a sale and not for full price, still it bothers me that I bought it at all. The only thing positive about it is its native Linux support. As mad as I am about this game, I do not recommend it.
###
Additional notes after finishing the game:
First, "mediocre" in the beginning of this review was not supposed to be any reference to scenes from the Mad Max movies. It is merely the attribute that describes this game, although I was tempted to replace it with "average" and even give it thumbs up. Here is why I did not chose to do so:
More than once I had to deal with lagging controller input during close combat. This intensified in later parts of the game where difficulty is raised by spamming more and more enemies which require you hit the right button even more precisely than in the beginning of the game. Switching to mouse & keyboard did not help either.
Car combat was not affected as heavily but still was a chore due to issues with the camera. Both with manual aiming and Chumbucket's auto aiming the camera turning back follows the most awkward way to return to its usual position after successfully engaging an opponent. For example: After looking 90° to the left instead of rotating these 90° back the camera would often decide to go 270° in the opposite direction, presenting your car from all directions. Meanwhile slow motion ends and the road takes a sharp turn. Imagine the rest.
Boss encounters are following the same schematic over and over. Only three stood out, although two of them needed the same tacticts applied. The only one notably different was Scrotus who had to be made smash some barrels. The final boss fight was actually fun but way too short.
Collision detection and protection during cutscenes are two additional weaknesses of this game: In sniper mode there are many single pixels that will bravely protect your target. Ramming your car into other ones, houses or stones will deliver a small amount of damage an make you drift slightly, but beware of gravel that will wreck your car and throw you half a mile away from where you stood. Seeking shelter from storms is often advised but I was hit by debris several times while standing inside a camp or hideout or while I was in a coversation. In addition to this, I was hit by a randomly spawned shortly after I entered the last of the three encounters prior to the final mission, which instantly killed the mood.
On sounds: I mentioned emphasis on engine sounds. I was wrong. I had hopes that as soon as the V8 was unlocked some sort of this sweet chugging which turns into roaring would be audible. Nope. Just a compressor which becomes louder.
After all this ranting: Why did I play Mad Max anyway? Because of the story! I admit that it is pretty shallow and takes some time to kick off but still it caught me in a strange way.
Nevertheless, it does not compensate for all those terrible mistakes in this game and I stay with my opinion of not recommending this game.

tl;dr
A very grindy game (191 locations to scavange, many with one or two things to pick up) with not great driving mechanics (even fully upgraded the car constantly loses control) and a super disappointing and unsatisfying ending (no spoilers, I get it's a Mad Max game but come on!)
Really torn about whether or not to recommend this game. It's a Batman Arkham style game, drive into a region, unlock and collect everything, repeat 3 more times, and I mean repeat, exact same things to collect and location types to visit. But if thats your thing then this is the game for you.
+ Very true to Mad Max cannon. Dark, apocalyptic environments filled with sad and or terrible people.
+ Tons of side quests and missions, lots of challenges to do (almost 50 hours and I'm no where near completing the driving challenges).
+ Decent graphics for a 2 year old game.
- Driving is just not fun. Hard to tell where the road is sometimes and hitting an object may send you completely out of control (you can plow through rusted out car skeletons but a relatively small rock will send you flying). Even after extensive upgrades the Magnum Opus just doesn't feel great or powerful.
- Achievements are very grindy, 191 locations to scavenge is a lot. Probably 40+ hours was spent running around collecting and clearing locations.

A strong, albeit lesser known, title in the Terraria genre.  Polished combat mechanics and solid character progression raise this above many of the others in it's class.  The game offers a good bit of exploration as the player tries to solve for all the unknowns on this alien planet.  The story isn't fully finished (as of this review) but what is in kept me intrigued.  While the game starts you out with little more than the clothes on your back, progression is still made fairly quickly.  The inventory system is a bit of a throwback to the days of Ultima Online but gives strong enough inventory filtering to make it easily manageable through early to late game.  At such a reasonable price I'd say it's a must buy for any fans of this genre.

1st off coming back I had forgotten everything about it (my first 100 hours of game play). So I'll talk about my last 20 hours of gameplay.
The game needs a tutorial or better explanation as to how things work, Here's why:
The first 15 hours I spent fighting with the action/toolbar. There are two. One is predetermind what goes in it and the other you can put into it whatever you want. You can only see one at a time. So on the first actionbar #1 is you Meg tool (main digging tool), #2 is your fists. Etc. When I got my first pick, I assigned it to #2 on the second and an then the frustration would start, When I switched to the 1st, the pick would be there replacing the Meg tool, I did see little up and down arrows but couldn't figure out how to use them. I had hit every key and nothing had happened. Only after misclicking did I notice that the middle mouse button controlled these. After that the game became easier and funner.
After 18 hours into the game I finally figured out how the map works. You press the M key to bring up the map. All you see is 4 dots on it. One of them being you. How does that do anything for you? Well, I misclicked again. The purple Meg tool sends out sonar when you hold down the mouse button and updates your map with cave walls. I have as of yet to figure out how I got the map to stay on.
Took me over 10 hours of experimentation to figure out I didn't have to chop down trees to get wood, only cut of branches, that eventually grew back.
Crafting is well done. Everytime you pick up something new, for instance iron ore, your crafting icom sort of blinks and you're presented with your new options in yellow. All your craftables are organized into various categories.
Picking up items a year ago was a pain, you had to hold down the C key. Per the Dev, you can turn on auto pickup in the settings menu. I for one would have never thought of looking in there for that.....ever.
There are bugs still present. Initially coming back my game crashed a few times creating charaters. Sometimes when taking out back blocks and if there are items on the ground, your tool will stop working for a bit.
Base building is obsolete in this game, you come with two prebuilt metal bases. So there is absolutely no need to ever build a third.
I also didn't like that you get almost a full set of iron armor and a copper pick from both bases, thereby making all armors below iron obsolete as well.
I was a bit disappointed that in sandbox mode you can select the size of your world but not in single player mode. I have not tried multiplayer yet.
Otherwise the game has good graphics. There is more content to play with. I haven't run into any game breaking bugs yet, so that's also a plus.

Note: There is no end goal at the time of writing this review of the game.
Interesting game at first. But I find that the game is very uninviting very soon after you've explored the topside of the planet and gain access to some of the buildings.
What you'll soon find out is that (at this time of writing) the majority of the game has you digging underground.
So much to the point that they should have called this "Signs of Digging". It's very repetitive and a chore at times. Unlike say terraria where there are many surprises both above ground and below ground. Signs of Life turns into a sci-fi mining simulator for material to craft items which is actually the other interesting content in the game(at this time) but even this has it's own problems.
Now I've played the game way back before and I got to say. The UI was terrible because everything was just text in the crafting menu.
But after coming back it to see if anything changed. I liked how the UI for the crafting has pictures/icons instead of text. If only it would have extended into the items you could be crafting and also giving highlights to items that are craftable. Instead of just text.
I'll say this, at least the game this time took up a good couple of hours of me finding material to craft items. But after finding out that there's no end goal and that the game is still in early access. I stopped playing and will return much much later to see if there is anything new to actually do.
Long story short do I recommend it?
Honesty no I don't, the reason I have so many hours in the game is because I have patience and having to put up with the frustrating and boring aspects fo the game.
Also another thing is that at points I needed to look up a guide to progress in the current state of the game. Which I immediately put a strike on the game for driving me to look up what to do next.
But hopefully the developers will improve the game and make it better. I mean they actually responded to my review so at least I got their attention about the game.

This, like many MMOs, is hard to boil down to a thumbs up or a thumbs down.  This is my favorite MMO of all time.  I've spent even more hours in game then steam shows do to the stand-alone client. They add progression systems, content types, access levels and often lose overall player base. This means, especially for new players or even returning players, things can seem overly complicated and obtuse.  It can also be harder to find people to teach or to enjoy content with.
If you're willing to drop a few dollars on a daybreak all access subscription I certainly recommend trying this game out.  While you’re at it try out all the daybreak titles you gain membership to.  Hopefully you'll find something to love in it or one of their many other titles as I once did.  However, I must admit that this game, and the rest of their titles, have passed me by.  I feel daunted and lost the moment I log in and have a hard time recognizing the game I once loved.

In 2004 the game was ahead of its time. In 2009 it was behind the times. But in 2017, EQ2 stands out as a game emblematic of '00 gaming. The graphics are deceptive charming, the combat rhythmic, and the music nostalgic. The crafting is immersive if not tedious. Character progression, like crafting, suffers the same fate. But once these elements of the game are understood, they provide yet another layer of depth to this rich MMO.
Of course one could argue that the lore of EQ seems like a direct (DIRECT) ripoff of DND, that somehow adds to its unique character, and haunts us with questions of, "What if *this* was the MMO that had taken off?"
As an avid MMO fan, I solidly recommend the game.

Spec Ops: The Line is a game rife with contrast. In the sandstorm-wracked city of Dubai, refugees huddle in crude shanties erected in the opulent atriums of luxury hotels, and soldiers construct rough outposts in swanky rooftop clubs. On these makeshift battlefields, most of your time is spent casually gunning down hundreds of enemy combatants, but your squadmates still argue passionately over the value of one anonymous virtual life. Mechanically, Spec Ops is an utterly commonplace third-person shooter, but narratively, it strives to raise philosophical questions and put you outside of your comfort zone. These contrasts create some intriguing moments, but they are too often muddled by mediocre execution.
The environmental design is one of the highlights. A fierce sandstorm has left Dubai with an entirely new geography, one defined by sliding dunes and sandy canyons. Trapped by the swirling debris, the citizens are forced to create makeshift shelters amid the towering skyscrapers, carving out settlements in the luxurious wreckage. Walk just past the glittering peacock statues and extravagant mosaics to find rickety cots, shabby walls, and dirty sheets.
A battalion of American soldiers have taken up residence here too, following their failed evacuation attempt, and their military outposts add an ominous air of conflict to the landscape. The artifacts of the aborted exodus tell a story too; cars are abandoned, belongings have been left behind in a hurry, and desperate pleas for help adorn the walls.
These striking scenes are punctuated by the politically charged graffiti that some stranded artist has created around the city, anonymous accusations that target the suffering of the people (smiling images of hotel guests with their eyes hollowed out) and those who helped exacerbate an already bad situation (a skeletal news anchor holding a smiling yellow puppet). The disparate architectural and artistic threads intertwine to create a fascinating landscape, one that is a pleasure to explore. The sights are even more captivating on the PC, as the higher resolutions make for more detailed textures and richer lighting effects.
Unfortunately, no such creativity is found in the actual combat. Gunplay in Spec Ops: The Line is a simple matter of taking cover, popping out to shoot enemies, and advancing to more cover from where you will shoot more enemies. The guns you fire are a fine military array of assault rifles, shotguns, sidearms, and heavy weaponry. The enemies you fire them at return the favor vigorously but lack the kind of artificial intelligence that can liven up a firefight. There are a few neat opportunities to destroy barriers or ceilings and let the environment kill your foes, but the bulk of the time you're serving up headshots to anything that moves (and getting a nice slow-motion flourish for your troubles).
This humdrum gunplay is paired with slightly clunky movement mechanics, which might see you failing to sprint on cue or melee attacking a low barrier instead of vaulting over it. Spec Ops does not compare favorably to its genre peers when it comes to maneuvering around the battlefield, but these shortcomings are rarely an issue in the single-player campaign. In the competitive multiplayer modes, however, they become a hindrance exacerbated by your relative fragility. Some interesting map layouts, a light class system, and a nice array of objective-based modes can create some fun conflicts, but the creaky locomotion makes it unlikely you'll feel invested enough to make a significant dent in the bevy of unlockable weapons, perks, and gear options.
The campaign itself can be completed in under seven hours, and the journey you undertake is inspired by the novel Heart of Darkness, in which a man journeys upriver into the jungle to seek a powerful and enigmatic character who may or may not have gone off the deep end. In Spec Ops, you play as Walker, one of three Delta Force soldiers who arrive in search of Colonel Konrad, an American commander who took his battalion to Dubai against orders in hopes of saving the people trapped therein. It quickly becomes clear that the situation in the city has deteriorated drastically, and there are numerous factions struggling for survival.
Though your mission is to rescue survivors, the first humans you encounter are hostile. A failed attempt at communication leaves you no choice but to fight back, and this pattern repeats throughout much of the campaign, establishing one of the main narrative contrasts of Spec Ops. You're there on a rescue mission, but you just can't seem to stop killing people.
Sometimes, you are given a choice. Try to rescue the potentially friendly operative, or save two innocent civilians? Who is guilty, the man who stole water for his family, or the soldier who administered harsh justice? There are no right or wrong decisions, just a difference in who dies and how. These moments shine a spotlight on your squad chatter as Lugo and Adams chime in on the situation you are presented with. They generally argue different sides and react strongly to what you do, but your character's response is almost always to bully them with talk of "doing what's right" or "doing what you had to do." Then it's back shooting the guys who are shooting at you and exchanging profanity-laden victory shouts. The moments meant to encourage reflection fade to the background, drowned out by the overriding narrative justification of self-defense.
There are some story moments that make an impression, however. There's a humorous homage to the similarly inspired movie Apocalypse Now, and a number of licensed songs are piped in to the battlefield to set an appealing fatalistic tone. Both of these examples are the work of the mysterious Radio Man, a disembodied and incongruously jocular voice emanating from speakers rigged throughout the city. Other moments force you to look at the horrors you've wrought, but these often feel cheap because you so rarely have a choice in your action. It's not until late in the campaign that Spec Ops gets more daring and disruptive with its storytelling, but by then it feels like too little, too late.
The disconnect between the gameplay and the narrative elements of Spec Ops: The Line is numbing, which makes it more difficult to contemplate the murky morality of war in the way the game wants you to. There are some intriguing things to be teased out of your adventure through the lovely ruins of Dubai, but the contrast between ambition and execution makes the experience as unsteady as the shifting sands.
+ Engrossing amalgam of art and architecture
+ Memorable moments, both humorous and shocking
- Stiff movement mechanics
- Relentless killing overrides moral dilemmas

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

One of the best looking games ever, including GPU heavy games like The Witcher III, but this is a 2D metrovania that can run flawlessly on a midrange laptop. The characters and enemies and their projectiles are so well distinguished that I never got confused about what was what. And that's impressive because there's just so much detail put into things. Like, when you level up, there is a small explosioni of level-up-ness that causes the spikes in the game world, but also the plants in the foreground and background to sway and move around, even moreso than they normally do during regular gameplay.
The movement in Ori is really satisfying (though iceless is a PITA), and the movement abilities actually change up the movement of the game, without making it too complicated, nor by making Ori pathetically weak right off the back. There is no "+5% movement speed" bull$#!7 upgrades. There is double and triple jump (of course), but there is also charge jump, where you explosively launch yourself off of a wall/platform at a high rate of speed, and bash, where if you are close enough to an enemy's projectile, you can bash yourself on it, making you go one way, and the projectile another.
The puzzles are all nicely laid out, with none that I remember that stumped me longer than "oh, I guess I don't have this ability, I'll come back to it later" that is common in this type of game, which I found myself saying quite a bit to a lot of the collectable orbs that dot the world.
However, the "bosses" are timed escape sequences (the bridge is falling down, run and parkour over the cars to the land-type of deal). There's only a handful of them (anywhere from three to six depending on how you count it), but each one is distinct enough to not make it feel re-hashed again and again. I did find the Ice path escape sequence to be the hardest one, which is about 2/3 of the way through the game. It is a bit of a difficulty spike each time you have to go through one, but at the end it feels really rewarding.
Hooolly crap is the music fan flipping tastic. The ambiance that the music and sound effects make is really damn good. When you're in the forest, you hear forest-y sounds that make it sound like a forest, but with a large sense of forboding and danger everywhere, in this alien and strange place. It sounds familiar enough that you can say "yes, this is a forest" but with obviously something very wrong with it. Likewise during the lake water section, it sounds very clean and almost "safe" because of story stuff, that you can tell that you did a good thing. The soundtrack is almost worth the price of admission itself, and is a strong recommendation if you play more than two hours.
The one thing that I can complain about though is the story. It's just been done before. Story about an cute innocent thing being lost in a big scary dangerous world. With heapings of love and forgiveness and family thrown in for good measure. I did find myself being attached to every character, but that's probably just me being a softie, rather than good storytelling. The story is told through cutscenes, which, beautifully rendered, don't really engage me as a player. The few times you get to interact with the world, it's done through single button press "Press R2 to place sphere on pedestal, and wait 15 seconds while stuff happens all around you".
Lastly, something I don't think people fully appreciate is that the game is seamless in the (huge) overworld, with just the few dungeons having a very quick (>5s) loading "fade to black, fade to dungeon" thing. Also, fun fact, the whole game is actually rendered in 3D, which makes for some funny positions in 3D space that only work when projected on the 2D game plane. Look up "GDC The Animation Process Of Ori & The Blind Forest" if you want to watch a 30 min talk about it. It's really facinating.
This game is a great buy at $20, and a steal at $10, the community behind it is amazing and lots of fun. It's also a great game to speedrun if you're into that sort of thing. And don't forget the soundtrack.

Mediocre grinding game which delivers GTA 5's multiplayer experience in singleplayer mode. I gave this game two attempts to show me it is worth playing. After one hour playing the game, I had to remove in-game advertisement for Rockstar energy drink by restarting the story. After that I played another three and a half hours and it kept failing over and over to fascinate me. Here is my impression of Mad Max:
Graphics are actually not that bad although they consist of the recent blurry soft-drawn outlines drowning in motion blur. Maxing all graphics option will even make the world look somewhat lively, as far as this is possible in a wide desert. I did not explore the whole map, but it seems to be designed decently for the most part. Designated roads allow faster driving and there is a fast travel system which additionally allows you to highlight POI.
Sound and music are there, but nothing that sticks out. Engine sounds seem to be a little bit emphasized, which fits as cars are important in this game.
The story is potentially intriguing, however after only a few hours of playing I will not judge it further.
Controls are sluggish par exellence and mark this game actually as a poor console port. This sluggishness heavily influences combat which is about half of the game. Perhaps developers were aware of this as slight auto-aiming which cannot be disabled is present. Controller input is a chore and I did not even bother trying mouse & keyboard. There are two button mapping presets for controller input which are only different by exchanging LB and B on Xbox controller. Apparently the game happily cycles those two layouts without noticing you, making controls even more unbearable. In addition, control layout for driving mode cannot be set up separately from normal controls, you either use default layout or alternative layout for both.
Driving sort of works, simultaneously shooting is made easy by weak spot highlighting and slow motion.
On combat system: There are guns and close combat, the latter one being important at least in the game's beginning. Gun handling actually seems to be okay, although I was not able to use it properly since said cycling of button mapping made me fire my shotgun instead of dodging and vice versa. Scarcity of ammunition and a limited supply to carry around prevent you from becoming a mindless gunslinger which is nice.
Close combat consists primarily of pressing and holding one button to execute attacks. Occasionally parrying and dodging with two other buttons are required. Targets are locked on by moving in the desired direction, collateral damage will hit surrounding opponents. Unfortunately your striking animations cannot be interrupted which leaves you vulnerable to attacks. Especially in the beginning of fights, you are very likely to take several hits due to this.
As usual these days, Mad Max features autosaving and does it a terrible job on this. Not only that you have to replay stretching parts of story missions, you will also restart at the last base you visited if you die outside of a mission. This means
travels unless you have unlocked one of the few fast travel points. This is a major letdown.
Gameplay consists mostly of driving around, collecting scrap to buy upgrades, beat up a base of baddies and repeating this. I cannot tell if this will become repetetive (some other reviews mentioned this), but it probably will. What I can tell is that collecting scrap is the most annoying task since you either have to find a small camp with loot boxes or you have to fight enemies and enemy cars and hope they will drop some. Car fights are no rarity but as soon as your opponent's health has almost emptied, they will flee. Congratulations, you just wasted three minutes driving in circles without getting a reward.
This leads me to mentioning GTA 5's multiplayer mode: While driving around the map you will either have the feeling you are the last one on earth or you will be spammed with attacks. The latter one will have you make a stop to repair your vehicle which will leave you inevitably vulnerable. At some point you will be forced to exit it and desperately fight hordes of enemy cars on foot. Instead of a desirable loop of "win fights, gather loot, upgrade, and repeat" another one is established which consists of "barely survive a fight, evenutally find loot, get run over, and reload last checkpoint".
The only thing positive about gameplay is that there is no automatic health regeneration. Instead you rely on finding food and water which are rather scarce. Perhaps designed to keep suspense, this keeps up frustration as low health is a rather common state.
All in all Mad Max is a disappointing and boring experience. Glad I bought it on a sale and not for full price, still it bothers me that I bought it at all. The only thing positive about it is its native Linux support. As mad as I am about this game, I do not recommend it.
###
Additional notes after finishing the game:
First, "mediocre" in the beginning of this review was not supposed to be any reference to scenes from the Mad Max movies. It is merely the attribute that describes this game, although I was tempted to replace it with "average" and even give it thumbs up. Here is why I did not chose to do so:
More than once I had to deal with lagging controller input during close combat. This intensified in later parts of the game where difficulty is raised by spamming more and more enemies which require you hit the right button even more precisely than in the beginning of the game. Switching to mouse & keyboard did not help either.
Car combat was not affected as heavily but still was a chore due to issues with the camera. Both with manual aiming and Chumbucket's auto aiming the camera turning back follows the most awkward way to return to its usual position after successfully engaging an opponent. For example: After looking 90° to the left instead of rotating these 90° back the camera would often decide to go 270° in the opposite direction, presenting your car from all directions. Meanwhile slow motion ends and the road takes a sharp turn. Imagine the rest.
Boss encounters are following the same schematic over and over. Only three stood out, although two of them needed the same tacticts applied. The only one notably different was Scrotus who had to be made smash some barrels. The final boss fight was actually fun but way too short.
Collision detection and protection during cutscenes are two additional weaknesses of this game: In sniper mode there are many single pixels that will bravely protect your target. Ramming your car into other ones, houses or stones will deliver a small amount of damage an make you drift slightly, but beware of gravel that will wreck your car and throw you half a mile away from where you stood. Seeking shelter from storms is often advised but I was hit by debris several times while standing inside a camp or hideout or while I was in a coversation. In addition to this, I was hit by a randomly spawned shortly after I entered the last of the three encounters prior to the final mission, which instantly killed the mood.
On sounds: I mentioned emphasis on engine sounds. I was wrong. I had hopes that as soon as the V8 was unlocked some sort of this sweet chugging which turns into roaring would be audible. Nope. Just a compressor which becomes louder.
After all this ranting: Why did I play Mad Max anyway? Because of the story! I admit that it is pretty shallow and takes some time to kick off but still it caught me in a strange way.
Nevertheless, it does not compensate for all those terrible mistakes in this game and I stay with my opinion of not recommending this game.

I would have to say that this game is one of my guilty pleasures. Why? i love management sims. Rarely, however, do I find a sim like this. As a guy who bought this in Early Access, about five months before release, there's a lot to say about this game.
BASICS:
Prisoners come in three types: Minimum Security, Medium Security, Maximum Security
There are also designations you can add on such as SuperMax and Protective Custody
Each Prisoner type has a monetary value associated with it upon intake. Min Sec is $500, Med Sec is $1000, and Max sec is $1500
There are certain things you need to make your prison function properly:
Showers (for Hygenine)
Cells or Dormitories (to house prisoners)
Canteens and Kitchens (to feed them)
Yard(s) for excersize
In addition to these rooms you will also want to keep in mind that there are other rooms such as common rooms, infirmaries, and visitation rooms that either need to be unlocked or can just be placed down given certain criteria. Once you get your prison going, figure out a formula for maximizing space, you'll be fine.
There's also something to be said about the recently added Escape Mode. This mode, which allows you to escape prisons made either by yourself or others, is very fun. There are a couple issues, like how workers won't repair power stations or how guards sometimes won't be replenished, but overall it's very enjoyable within the right setting.
There are certain failure conditions, such as having too many prisoners die in one day, that lead to you having to cut down on prisoner deaths (5 and you fail). Unlike most games however which will just say "Game Over" and not let you continue, the beauty of this game is that you then get to escape your prison. There is a slight downside, in that if there's a riot you'll probably have to deal with that when you're transported in. Otherwise? It's very enjoyable.
Pros:
+ Indepth Needs Sysytem
+ Good graphics (for 2D)
+ Events can be fun
+ Planning your ideal prison
+ Numerous ways to play as a Warden
+ Escape Mode
+ Unique Failure System
Cons:
- Replayability, after your 100th prison, gets low
- Music can get repetitive (I like to put on Pandora)
- Without frequent security checks, weapons can be brought in
- Juggling prisoner needs with expenses

Like all simulation games, they do get boring at some point. Even with all of the random events and such enabled, you can still lose interest quickly, but for under $10 on the summer sale? The only significant challenge I've faced is not being able to afford new cells when more prisoners come in, which even then isn't a big deal because you have a holding cell.
I recommend this game to anyone looking for an alternative gaming experience. A break from the shooters and adventure games, and go back to a classical management game. It may not be totally worth the listing price unless you're a die hard fan of these types of games and can play them for weeks, but like I said, it's a steal for 75% off.

Being a huge fan of crafting/survival and in particular Terraria, Minecraft, and Starbound is what brought me to Signs of Life. As a rule, I tend not to buy Early Access games, choosing instead to mark them on my wishlist, however I couldn't help but purchase Signs of Life and over a year later I am still quite glad I did.
What I found was a game that had an amazing groundwork laid, but little to fill the time ones I had gotten myself to the highest tier of gear, but such is the case in Early Access games. As time has passed and the Dev's continue to make updates to the game I am more and more reassured that the amazing groundwork they have put in place is going to eventually become the fantastic 1.0 that I look forward to for SoL. And if any of my friends were looking for a crafting/survival I would most definitely point them in SoL's direction if they're willing to be a bit patient.
But even so, this is perhaps the best place to highlight both the positives and negatives of the game, so here I go:
-I love the graphics, pixel art is rarely given so much high fidelity, and I always felt that it fit the game far better than a more 16-bit esque style, similar to Terraria. Sci-Fi looking Hi-Fi is important to me.
-I am intrigued by the story although I will admit ignorance on any new additions to it. The planet is infested and a lot of people are dead and/or missing. I hope I can make a ship or something to get off this crazy planet before I join them, I'm just saying.
-There's a myriad of items and weapons to craft, letting you have a goodly amount of variety when it comes to your favorite monster killing weaponry.
-I actually really like the MEG AI character, I can't put my finger on why but he just manages to toe the line between funny and annoying for me and do so in a way that just makes him more enjoyable. I'm dying horribly and all he has is a pithy one liner, like please I will drop you down a hole the moment I have all the recipes, just you wait.
Cons (these are longer but more due to wanting to be detailed in my constructive criticism than anything else):
-Lack of Difficulty Settings: Call me a baby, but most of my play sessions of Signs of Life come to an end when I die. The punishment of losing all of my items and having to spend the next 45 minutes chaining deaths as I attempt to run back down to whatever pit I lost them down is really frustrating. While the loss of items in Minecraft was also an issue (that many people modded around to be fair), part of what always softened the blow for me was that any items, or armor I made had durability and thus would eventually have run out anyway. This is not really so in Signs of Life, so the need to dive down 4000 feet in only my undies is tantamount, and I've often resorted to console commands just so I can get to the items without dying.
-Lack of Fair Fighting: So just gonna be honest here, my go to strategy when fighting monsters is to build dirt walls around myself in a fit of panic and then stab or shoot them through a hole while they ineffectually try and destroy my hideaway. If this strategy was the one you wanted to encourage in your players then this is not a con (I actually don't dislike doing this), but I always felt that the monsters were far too effective at wrecking my small, shipwrecked♥♥♥♥♥for any other strategy to be viable. Hopefully in the new version things might be different, and I am not suggesting for this strategy to be removed so much as, well, it to be easier to kite or go toe-to-toe with these underground goons.
No Tier Gating: So currently, while there is a wealth of items and tiers of items to experience, I tend to skip right past one or even several of them at once simply because it is practical to do so. Why should I make leather armor when after 15 minutes underground I've enough for copper? Why bother with iron, gold, or silver when I can just spelunk down and get the materials for steel? No solution to this comes to mind really, besides somehow gating the access to higher tiers behind some sort of technology that must be gathered from bases.
-The UI: I'm sure this is a complaint that you have heard often, since your redesign of the UI have been some of my favorite updates to the game, and I feel like you have made some really good choices with the redesign, so I am only here to ask you one thing, please let me control what is on my hotbar. I understand wanting the first button to be on my tools, but I can't count the times where I've been happily mining away and then I accidentally touch my middle mouse button and now I have an axe. Or when I pull out my shotgun in battle but in my panic I accidentally am unleashing flares at the enemy due to fat fingering the middle mouse button. Or even the number of times I have pulled out both my sword and my gun before actually getting to the mapping tool that I wanted. Just an option to either have the hotbar like it is now, or in a more customizable way since I don't really need to always have food readily available to chow down on, but I could always use more melee weapons at the ready, or the ability to swap between MEG and pick without having to scroll through axe, hoe, and who knows what else first.

This game is more than just another ordinary shooter, this game is more than a video game. I got this game through the Humble Bundle deal a while back and I kind of just shrugged it off, didn't think much of it. I can now say that I was foolish for neglecting this game. I had played through the first 30 minutes and then left it for months on end until about a week ago, when I decided to play it again.
Let me tell you something, this game hits you in the blind spot. You expect another shooter but instead, you get this rich story, well developed characters that actually feel important, and gritty action that I have not seen in a shooter in a while. The decisions and consequences of your actions can very well depict the harsh reality of warfare, and the life in general. This game flows really well, and does not miss a beat. The beginning may come off slow, but stick with it and you will be rewarded.
The combat may take a bit to get used to, but the mechanics are fairly decent for a third person shooter. I sometimes found myself getting "lost" during combat, especially when a grenade is thrown, I found myself sprinting towards the grenade because of mechanical issues. Aside from that, I have almost no negative comments about this game.
But to be fair, the game is still far from a 10, so I would give this game a solid 8.5/10. But don't let that score fool you, I still very much enjoyed this game and I'm sure you will too.

Initially, I thought this game would be the direct adaptation of Fury Road but the title already suggested this was something different. The developers brought in George Miller (director of all movies) to assist but eventually decided to go with an antagonist called Scabrous Scrotus (the son of Immortan Joe). We can conclude that the game takes place in the same universe as Fury Road but tells a different story.
Max is beaten by Scrotus and his so-called War Boys. Everything is taken from him so, as it is typical for sandbox games, we start from scratch. We soon meet Chumbucket, a crazy, hunchback mechanic, who has deep respect for Max (considers him some sort of Messiah based on the news he heard of him) and promises to rebuild his car (to be considered his life's work, the so-called Magnum Opus).
As we complete a couple of story missions we'll soon learn how things work in the world of Mad Max. The map is huge and can be divided up into various parts. These territories have a local tyrant whose base of operations Max eventually needs to visit. Everybody hates Scrotus so making an alliance with these individuals will be easy.
By completing so-called projects we can strengthen these strongholds and make them become shelters where our ammo, fuel and life are restored. We regularly run into Scrotus' patrols while on the road - by clearing up minefields, destroying sniper outposts, bases of so-called "top dogs" (gang leaders) and pulling down scarecrows we can gradually decrease Scrotus' influence on these areas.
We travel by car and on foot. Our main currency will be not the fuel but scrap. Every update to Max's clothing, shotgun and to his car requires this which can be found almost everywhere in the game's world. We have approximately 200 scavenging locations - small, makeshift settlements, empty diners from a long lost civilization, caves or underground areas used as shelters by cannibalistic survivers called the buzzards and many more.
On foot, when exploring bases or scavenging locations, we fight similarly to games such as the Arkham series or the Assassins' Creed. We can keep punching our enemies until we are required to counter their attacks during fisticuffs. As we increase our streak Max becomes furious. During this stage much more damaging punches are delivered and during miniboss encounters utilising this will be a must. Shivs can be used for executions, melee weapons can be taken from our enemies and if all else fails our shotgun is there to perform a couple of gutshots.
Driving around by our car we can ram into enemies. Updating our bumpers makes these head-on collisions deadlier and if we feel we are surrounded by 3 or 4 patrolling cars we can shoot exploding sticks at our enemies (thunderpoon), turn on our flamethrower (side burners), use our harpoon to pull off the doors of cars (and eventually, the drivers themselves), put some spikes on our rims or even shoot out the tires with our shotgun.
Regardless of which way we encounter our post-apocalyptic enemies combat feels extremely satisfying. One of the most iconic moments of the movie was when Furiosa was chased by Nux and his gang. The approaching storm picked up the cars that were destroyed as lightning struck. From time to time Max and Chumbucket face the same danger. Chumbucket will be the one notifying us of an oncoming storm.
Interestingly, while waiting in a shelter the storm lasts longer. The game appreciates if we are willing to go out and drive (and even kill enemies) and to show this appreciation boxes of scrap appear that hold a greater quantity of this currency compared to the usual we can get at scavenging locations.
I'm afraid Immortan Joe is wrong. Max's canteen need to be filled with water regularly. This will be our source of healing when exploring the world of Max Max. Make sure your canteen is full before taking down a Top Dog. Water sources are indicated on the map; in fact, lizards or rats, too, can be a food source (Max is even willing to eat bugs from maggot-infested corpses).
Max Max wouldn't be a modern sandbox game if it didn't have some minimalistic RPG elements. As we drive around and fight every action we perform against our opponents is taken into account. As we complete challenges during the ground and vehicular combat we obtain tokens. These can be sold to Griffa, a mysterious person who, in return, strengthens our abilities (less use of fuel and water, greater efficiency with melee weapons etc.).
The game is huge and is stunningly beautiful. Every tyrant is responsible for supervising a different area that looks visually different. We can race on zigzagging roads in dark valleys, can drive endlessly on sand dunes until we reach the remains of a huge airport. Wherever we are we can see the refineries of Gastown in the distance as they emit smoke and fire. Once we reach mentioned building we'll see it is surrounded by a junkyard. As we drive in the wasteland we see pipes, abandoned oil rigs, collapsed bridges and remains of a ship and even a silo. A simple desert would have been sufficient for me but I have to applaud the creators for making every single location so diverse.
Beside the stunning visuals (and well-optimised gameplay), great combat (both vehicular and on foot) Max Max has its issues. First of all, some of the missions are extremely mediocre and the overall story missions can be completed in 10-12 hours. The game's "Bio" section offers detailed description of the characters we encounter during Max's story, however, these often include entries of people we only meet once.
Make no mistake, some missions are great (and often hilarious, for instance, at one point we have to go underground to steal some Christmas lights) and the game offers a decent amount of side missions (referred to as wasteland missions), still, Gastown we can reach in a matter of hours when we realise some more exploration is needed to begin later missions either with a better-equipped car or better-armored Max. So, my 65 hours basically includes completely exploring the world and finding all the available collectibles and making sures all territories have zero threat from Scrotus and his War Boys.
Mad Max is an exceptionally good sandbox game. Putting aside a relatively mediocre story (that could have been much longer) it offers great ground and vehicular combat and a very detailed, very rich post-apocalyptic environment whose exploration is extremely satisfying. A must-have in our library!

Ori and the Blind Forest is a metriodvania action platform game.  It also very immersive and has an impressive soundtrack.  Metriodvania's are my favorite genre so as a result this review may be very picky in some area's.
The story of Ori begins with a sombre note of loss and sadness.  You are a creature of the spirit tree a white rabbit type thing.  After getting swept up into a storm you are found by somebody who nurtures and takes care of you.  Sometime later the forest dies and it's up to you to save it.  I don't want to completely spoil the beginning but it's one of the most emotional beginning's I’ve experienced.  Metriodvania's are not known for having an interesting story but this game focused a lot more on it I feel.  The story is not told really in words.  The spirit tree says a bunch of things throughout the journey but maybe 20 sentences max.  Most of the story is shown to you and it's easy to understand without words.
I feel like this game is much more story centred, which in my mind takes away from the aspects I enjoy.  I wish the game were longer and had a lot more exploration which really makes the metroidvania genre for me.  I like how in metriod you would get upgrades and then at the end it would force you to use them all to get to certain area's.  I don't feel like this game brought that to the table, it just feels like a more casual metroidvania which is ok just not for me.  As for the movement, it feels really good.  The abilities like jumping climbing launching slamming, all feel perfect.  The slam for instance shakes the ground and has a big boom as if you are hitting the ground with force.  The launching although at first seemed a bit odd it becomes second nature and is really fun to use.  One thing I feel this game excels at is the ramping difficulty.  You get new abilities then the game askes you to do harder and harder things with it.  In the beginning it's just basic things you do but by the end you are doing much harder tasks that make you feel satisfied. The other ability in the game is the fireball.  Which is an attack you get right at the start for fighting enemies.  It's basic because it shoots at all angels and you don't have to aim it but it feels alright.  You also get a few abilities that add to the fireball but that’s not the games main focus.  There aren't any true boss fights just a few mini bosses.  As for the enemies I feel they fit the levels but are somewhat recycled, that being said each enemy that isn't recycled feels different.
This game has a level up feature.  You get experience from killing enemies and finding ability point orbs. You put your ability points into one of three separate categories.  Efficiency, Utility and Combat.  Efficiency helps you with finding all the hidden collectables.  Utility allows you to get more out of your healing abilities and soul power which allows you to save.  Combat which makes you do more damage and attack more enemies.  I feel it's alright but on a second play through you would avoid Efficiency because you would know where everything is.  Some of the abilities later in Utility are really strong giving you triple jump and the ability to breath underwater.  The combat ones don't do anything visual.  That being said the game does make you feel like you are gaining strength.  The collectables in this game are just HP and Soul power, there are not many of them either.  Most of the pickups are ability point orbs which if you want to max level are needed.
This games soundtrack is amazing.  At first it feels kind of slow and boring but as you go it starts to really pick up.  That being said I feel like the soundtrack always fit what was going on, on the screen.  Without the game I feel the soundtrack isn't the greatest, thats not a problem for me but it's just a thing.  During the intense parts the music is intense, during the sad parts sad it's just fits perfectly with the game.  There isn't much to say I feel as during the game it went together but on it's own it's not very memorable.
Overall as a complete package I think the game is perfect.  In it's: Length, sound, movement, action, platforming, fighting.  Everything just goes together completely.  Although as a metroidvania I feel it kind of misses it's mark in terms of exploration and length.  That being said, Ori and the Blind Forest made me feel emotions I didn't expect.  By the end of the journey even though it was short I felt like I had accomplished a big task.  At the end I felt a bit emotional because it felt like the end to a long journey and that makes me recommend it for sure.
